rabat: Rabat stands on Morocco's northwestern Atlantic coast, at the mouth of the river Bou Regreg, opposite Salé, the city's main commuter town. The name comes from the Arabic ar-Ribat, a ribat being an Islamic base or fortification. It is short for Ribat al-Fath, the ribat of conquest or stronghold of victory, a title given by the Almohads when they established the city as a naval base in 1170. The oldest part of the present city is the Kasbah of the Udayas, built by the Almohads in the 12th century.

In the first millennium BCE the Phoenicians founded trading colonies along the Atlantic coast, although archaeologists have debated whether a Phoenician settlement called Sala existed here. By the first century BCE the region had come under the influence of Rome, which annexed the Mauretanian Kingdom and built a city called Sala Colonia at the site now known as Chellah, just south of the walled city. With Lixus it was one of the two main Roman naval outposts on the Atlantic coast of Mauretania Tingitana. In the 10th century the Umayyads of Córdoba, or their Zenata Berber allies, founded a ribat in the area against the Barghawata Berbers.

In 1609 Philip III decreed the expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain. About 2,000 refugees from Hornachos settled around Salé and occupied the kasbah, and Rabat and Salé united in 1627 to form the Republic of Bou Regreg, a base for corsairs known as the Salé Rovers. Al-Rashid, founder of the 'Alawi dynasty, conquered the area in 1666, though the sultans allowed piracy to continue until the early 19th century, and Austria shelled the city in 1829 after losing a ship to a pirate attack.

After the Treaty of Fes established the French protectorate in March 1912, General Hubert Lyautey moved the capital from Fez to Rabat. He argued that its coast was pleasanter and more accessible and that it lay close to Casablanca, which he expected to become the main economic centre. In 1913 he hired Henri Prost to design the Ville Nouvelle as an administrative sector. Rabat became the capital of independent Morocco in 1956.

Rabat is the capital of Morocco and one of the country's four imperial cities, and its medina is a World Heritage Site. The Kasbah of the Udayas is a residential district of white and blue houses and contains the Old Mosque, founded in 1150 and largely restored in the 18th century. The Oudayas Museum, in a pavilion built by Sultan Moulay Isma'il, opened in 1915 and is one of the oldest public museums in Morocco. The city hosts the headquarters of several international and African organisations, and Mohammed V University was founded there in 1957.
rabbi-akiva: Akiva ben Joseph was born about 50 CE to humble parents, and according to some sources he descended from converts to Judaism. The Talmud tells that he was an unlettered shepherd in the service of Ben Kalba Sabuaʿ, a wealthy citizen of Jerusalem, when the man's daughter, named Rachel in a later version, offered to marry him if he would begin to study Torah.

Her father drove her from his house, and the couple lived in great poverty. Another tradition has Akiva, at the age of 40, attend the academy of his native town, Lod, headed by Eliezer ben Hurcanus. He also studied under Joshua ben Hananiah and Nachum Ish Gamzu, and later moved his own school to Beneberak.

Akiva was a member of the Sanhedrin that determined the final canon of the Hebrew Bible, and he played a decisive part in the inclusion of the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes. He is called Rosh la-Hakhamim, Chief of the Sages. He worked on the Halakha, systematising its traditional material and developing a method of exegesis. He held that in the language of the Torah nothing is mere form, so that every peculiarity of diction, every particle and every letter carries meaning. Tradition holds that he arranged the Mishnah, and the Mishnah of Judah ha-Nasi and most of the halakhic Midrashim are regarded as derived from his school.

The leading tannaim of the middle of the second century came from his school, among them Rabbi Meir, Judah bar Ilai and Simeon bar Yochai. The Aggadah gives the number of his disciples variously as 12,000, 24,000 and 48,000. He supported Rabban Gamaliel II's aim of a central authority but held that the patriarch's power was limited by the written and oral law. He was in Rome in 95-96 CE, and before 110 in Nehardea. His disciple Aquila gave Greek-speaking Jews a rabbinical Bible.

Accounts of Akiva's death vary, but all agree that he defied a Roman prohibition on teaching Torah, that the consul Turnus Rufus, as Jewish sources call him, ordered his execution, that he was flayed alive and that his last words were the Shema.

In the Babylonian Talmud he explains to his students that he had long wondered how he could fulfil the command to love God 'with all your soul', and he extended the final word Echad, meaning One, until his life expired. He was executed in the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba revolt, on 28 September 135 CE. Tradition also holds that he alone of four sages who entered the Pardes absorbed its wisdom.
rabindranath-tagore: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi. His mother died in his early childhood, and he was raised mostly by servants. The family was at the forefront of the Bengal Renaissance, hosting literary magazines, theatre and recitals of Bengali and Western classical music. Tagore wrote poetry at eight, and at sixteen published poems under the pseudonym Bhanusimha that literary authorities took for long-lost classics.

Tagore wrote novels, essays, short stories, travelogues, dramas and thousands of songs. He is credited with originating the Bengali short story. Gitanjali, Gora and Ghare-Baire are his best-known works, and his compositions became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. In 1912 he took translations of his works to England, where William Butler Yeats, who wrote the preface to the English Gitanjali, and others noticed them.

He opposed imperialism and supported Indian nationalists, yet he rebuked strongly nationalist forms of the independence movement. In 1925 he attacked the Swadeshi movement in an essay, The Cult of the Charkha. He urged the masses to seek self-help and education rather than blind revolution, and his religious and philosophical ideas appear in the 1922 lectures Creative Unity and the 1931 Hibbert Lectures at Oxford, published as The Religion of Man.

Tagore conceived a new kind of university to make Santiniketan a connecting thread between India and the world. He named it Visva-Bharati; its foundation stone was laid on 24 December 1918, and teaching was often done under trees. He died on 7 August 1941 at Jorasanko Thakur Bari, the house in which he was born.
racial-segregation: Racial segregation is the separation of people into racial or other ethnic groups in daily life. It can mean spatial separation and the compulsory use of different institutions, such as schools and hospitals, and it may apply to restaurants, buses, housing, hotels and places of worship. Segregation often allows close contact between members of different groups in hierarchical situations, for example when a person of one race works as a servant for a member of another. Involuntary segregation was often used to secure the advantages of a dominant group, such as the Mongols, the Bantu and the Aztecs.

Before modern concepts of race developed, some states enforced separation on grounds of ethnicity or religion. In late antiquity Roman law restricted some marriages between provincials and barbarian soldiers. Legal distinctions between Goths and Romans in Visigothic Spain lasted until 654, and in 1366 the Statutes of Kilkenny prohibited marriage and other close relations between the English and the Irish. In Tang China an edict of 779 forced Uyghurs to wear their ethnic dress and banned them from marrying Han Chinese women, and in 836 the governor of Canton, Lu Chun, banned intermarriage and made it illegal for foreigners to own property.

In 1204 the papacy required Jews to separate themselves from Christians and to wear distinctive clothing, and forced segregation spread across Europe in the 14th and 15th centuries. In the Russian Empire Jews were confined to the Pale of Settlement. From the early 15th century Jews in Morocco were confined to walled quarters called mellahs.

Racial segregation has generally been outlawed worldwide, and can amount to the international crime of apartheid and a crime against humanity under the 2002 Rome Declaration of Statute of the International Criminal Court. In French Algeria a colonial law of 1865 allowed Arab and Berber Algerians to apply for French citizenship only if they gave up their Muslim identity. In Canada segregation was embedded in society before the constitution of 1982, and the Supreme Court upheld it in 1939. The last school segregated for Black pupils in Ontario closed in 1965, the last in Nova Scotia in 1983, and the last racially segregated Indigenous school, in Saskatchewan, in 1996.
raciborz: Racibórz lies in the southwest of the Silesian Voivodeship on the upper Oder, near the border with the Czech Republic, in the Racibórz Basin, which forms the southeastern extension of the Silesian Lowlands. It is the administrative seat of Racibórz County. The town grew at a hill fort where the old trade route from the Moravian Gate down to Kraków crossed the Oder. Its name is Slavic and probably derives from that of a Duke Racibor, the city's founder. It is one of the historic capitals of Upper Silesia, with Opole.

The first confirmed mention is of 1108, in the chronicle of Gallus Anonymus, when the Polish duke Bolesław III Wrymouth was fending off attacks from Duke Svatopluk of Bohemia. From 1155 it was the seat of a castellany, and in 1172, at the first partition of Silesia, the Piast duke Mieszko I Tanglefoot established the Duchy of Racibórz there. He had the settlement beneath his residence laid out and colonised by Flemish merchants, and the first coin with the Polish inscription MILOST was issued in Racibórz in 1211.

In 1241 the local duke Mieszko II the Fat won the Battle of Racibórz during the first Mongol invasion of Poland. Brewing was an important source of the town's income, and from 1299 it was ruled by an autonomous council under Magdeburg law.

In 1327 Duke Leszek paid homage to King John of Bohemia, and when Leszek died in 1336 the Silesian Piast line was extinct and the duchy fell to Bohemia. It was then ruled by the Opava branch of the Přemyslid dynasty until the last duke, Valentin, died in 1521. Later it fell to the Habsburg king Ferdinand I, and the Thirty Years' War devastated the town's economy. After the First Silesian War in 1742 it was ceded to Prussia under Frederick the Great, and in 1871 became part of the German Empire.

In the plebiscite of 1921, 90.9 per cent of votes in the town were for Germany and 9.1 per cent for Poland, so it remained in Germany as a border town. Nazi Germany persecuted local Polish activists from 1937, and during World War II operated a prison and forced labour camps in the town. The Red Army occupied and devastated it on 30 March 1945, and it returned to Poland.

Racibórz has about 55,000 inhabitants. A flood devastated the town in 1997, and the Racibórz Dolny flood control reservoir nearby, with a capacity of 185 million cubic metres, was built in response and opened in 2020. Its German name is Ratibor.
radar: The idea that radio waves could locate objects is older than the systems built on it. In 1886 the German physicist Heinrich Hertz showed that radio waves could be reflected from solid objects. In 1897 Alexander Popov, a physics instructor at the Imperial Russian Navy school in Kronstadt, was testing radio equipment for communication between two ships in the Baltic Sea when he noticed an interference beat caused by the passage of a third vessel. He wrote in his report that the effect might be used for detecting objects, but he did nothing more with it.

Before the Second World War radar research was carried on in the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Soviet Union and the Netherlands. In France in 1934 the research branch of the Compagnie générale de la télégraphie sans fil, headed by Maurice Ponte, began developing an obstacle-locating radio apparatus, parts of which were installed on the ocean liner Normandie in 1935.

A radar system has a transmitter that produces radio or microwave waves, a transmitting antenna, a receiving antenna, often the same one, and a receiver and processor. The waves reflect off objects and return, giving their position and speed. Metals, seawater and wet ground reflect them especially well, which suits the detection of aircraft and ships. A moving object changes the frequency of the returning waves through the Doppler effect.

Distance is found from the time a short pulse takes to return: it is half the round-trip time multiplied by the speed of the signal, since the signal travels to the object and back. In the early days a user marked positions with a grease pencil on the radar screen and worked out the speed with a slide rule; modern sets do the same by computer.

The first use of radar was military: to locate targets in the air, on land and at sea. The device was developed in secret by several countries before and during the Second World War. A key development was the cavity magnetron in the United Kingdom, which allowed relatively small systems with sub-metre resolution. Britain shared the technology with the United States during the Tizard Mission of 1940, and Alfred Lee Loomis organised the secret MIT Radiation Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which developed microwave radar in the years 1941–45. Its use later spread to the civilian field, with applications for aircraft, ships and automobiles, including air traffic control, marine radars and the monitoring of rainfall.
radioactivity: Radioactive decay, also called nuclear decay or radioactivity, is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by radiation. The three most common types are alpha, beta and gamma decay. Ernest Rutherford named them in increasing order of their ability to penetrate matter, after early researchers found that an electric or magnetic field could split radioactive emissions into three beams. Beta decay is seen in all elements, while alpha decay is observed only in heavier elements of atomic number 52 and above.

For single atoms the process is random: according to quantum theory it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay. For many identical atoms the overall rate is expressed as a decay constant or a half-life, and half-lives range from nearly instantaneous to far longer than the age of the universe. Except in gamma decay, the process transmutes the nucleus, and when the number of protons changes an atom of a different element is created. Lead, with atomic number 82, is the heaviest element with stable isotopes. Twenty-eight naturally occurring elements are radioactive, among them uranium and thorium.

Radioactivity was discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel, who was working with phosphorescent materials. He wrapped a photographic plate in black paper and put various phosphorescent salts on it. Results were negative until he used uranium salts, which blackened the plate despite the paper. In 1897 Marie Curie began studying the radiation from uranium compounds, named it rayons de Becquerel, and showed that the rays were a property of atoms. The SI unit of activity, the becquerel, equals one decay per second.

The dangers were slow to be recognised. Physicians and companies marketed radioactive substances as patent medicines, including radium enemas and radium waters, and Marie Curie warned that radium is dangerous in untrained hands. She later died of aplastic anaemia, likely caused by radiation. By the 1930s, after cases of bone necrosis and death among enthusiasts, such products had largely left the market. The first International Congress of Radiology met in 1925 to consider protection standards, and in 1927 Hermann Joseph Muller published research showing genetic effects, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1946.

An atomic battery uses the energy of decay to generate electric power without a chain reaction. Such batteries are costly but long-lived, and power equipment that must run unattended for long periods, such as spacecraft and pacemakers.
raetia: Little is known of the origin of the Raetians, who appear in the records as one of the most powerful and warlike of the Alpine tribes. Livy states that they were of Etruscan origin; a tradition reported by Justin and Pliny the Elder held that they were driven into the mountains from the plain of the Po by invading Gauls, and took their name from a leader called Raetus. Celtic tribes already held much of the land when the Romans learned of it, and the later Raetians may generally be regarded as a Celtic people. They kept their independence until they were subjugated in 15 BCE by Tiberius and Drusus.

At first Raetia was a province of its own, but towards the end of the 1st century CE Vindelicia was added to it. It was governed first by a military prefect and then by a procurator, and had no standing army until the 2nd century, relying on native troops and militia. Under Marcus Aurelius it was governed by the commander of the Legio III Italica, based by 179 at Castra Regina (Regensburg).

The province lay between the Helvetii in the west, Noricum in the east, Vindelicia in the north and Venetia et Histria in the south. It covered eastern and central Switzerland, southern Germany, most of Tyrol in Austria and part of northern Lombardy. Its northern border under Augustus and Tiberius was the Danube; later the Limes Germanicus marked it. The capital was Augusta Vindelicorum, present-day Augsburg.

Two great Roman roads crossed it: the Via Claudia Augusta, from Verona and Tridentum over the Reschen Pass to Augsburg, and another from Brigantium (Bregenz) by Chur and Chiavenna to Como and Milan. The country was very mountainous, and its people lived chiefly by breeding cattle and cutting timber. Some valleys produced wine that was rated equal to any in Italy, and Augustus preferred it to any other.

Under Diocletian Raetia was divided into Raetia prima, with its governor at Curia (Chur), and Raetia secunda, with its governor at Augsburg. In its last years under the Western Roman Empire the land was desolate; occupation by the Ostrogoths under Theodoric the Great revived its prosperity to some extent. Much of Raetia prima remained a separate political unit, Raetia Curiensis, for several centuries, until it was attached to the Duchy of Swabia in 917. The Rätikon mountain range takes its name from Raetia.
rafael-trujillo: Rafael Leónidas Trujillo Molina was born on 24 October 1891 in San Cristóbal, into a lower-middle-class family. In 1916 the United States began its occupation of the Dominican Republic, after 28 revolutions in 50 years. Trujillo, then 25, worked as an overseer on a sugar plantation at Boca Chica. In 1918 he joined the National Guard, the constabulary the occupiers had created, was soon promoted to second lieutenant and trained with the US Marines.

Trujillo ruled from August 1930 until his death. He was president from 1930 to 1938 and from 1942 to 1952, and held the post of generalissimo throughout, ruling through figurehead presidents when he did not hold the presidency himself. Two and a half weeks after he took office, Hurricane San Zenón killed 2,000 people in Santo Domingo. He declared martial law, rebuilt the city and renamed it Ciudad Trujillo. In 1931 he made the Dominican Party the sole legal party. Government employees had to give 10 percent of their salaries to the treasury, and statues, slogans and renamed places formed a personality cult.

Opponents were killed from the start, first by a gang known as The 42 and later by the secret police, the SIM. Estimates of deaths in the country under his regime range from 25,000 to over 50,000. In 1937 the Dominican Army killed between 17,000 and 35,000 Haitians in the Parsley Massacre. His agents operated abroad: Jesús Galíndez disappeared in New York in 1956, and in June 1960 an attempt to kill Venezuela's president Rómulo Betancourt with a car bomb failed. The murder of the Mirabal sisters in 1960 added to the international condemnation, and the Organization of American States imposed sanctions.

On 30 May 1961 conspirators led by General Antonio Imbert Barrera ambushed Trujillo's car on a road outside the capital and shot him dead. The plotters failed to take control. His son Ramfis took temporary control and executed most of the conspirators, while Imbert was the only one of the seven assassins to survive. By November 1961 the family was pressured into exile by the titular president Joaquín Balaguer. Civil strife followed, ending in the Dominican Civil War and a US-OAS intervention, and in 1966 the country stabilised under a multi-party system.

Trujillo remains a polarising figure in the Dominican Republic. His supporters credit him with long-term stability and economic growth, while critics denounce the violence of his regime, its xenophobia towards Haitians, and the family's corruption and nepotism.
rafic-hariri: Rafic Bahaa El Deen al-Hariri was born on 1 November 1944 to a modest Sunni Muslim family in the port city of Sidon. He went to school there and graduated in business administration from Beirut Arab University. In 1965 he went to Saudi Arabia, where he taught for a short time before moving into the construction industry, and in 1978 he took Saudi citizenship alongside his Lebanese one.

After a small subcontracting firm failed, he went into business with the French construction firm Oger on a hotel at Ta'if, whose timely completion won praise from King Khaled. Hariri took over Oger, formed Saudi Oger, and it became the main builder for the Saudi royal family's major projects. In 1979 he founded the Islamic Association for Culture and Education, later the Hariri Foundation, which built educational facilities in Lebanon. During the civil war he acted as an envoy of the Saudi royal family and laid the groundwork for the Taif Agreement, which Saudi Arabia organised to bring the warring factions together.

In 1992 Hariri became the first prime minister after the civil war, under President Elias Hrawi, and also served as finance minister. He headed the reconstruction plan Horizon 2000, whose centrepiece was Solidere, a company formed to rebuild central Beirut. Solidere was given powers of compulsory purchase and compensated owners in company shares rather than cash; critics said owners were underpaid. Inflation, running at 131 percent in 1992, fell to 12 percent within two years, but public debt rose sharply. His first term ended in 1998, after a power struggle with President Émile Lahoud.

He was appointed again in October 2000. In his second term the Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon ended an occupation of eighteen years. In September 2004 he defended UN Security Council Resolution 1559, which called for all remaining foreign forces to withdraw from Lebanon, and on 20 October 2004 he resigned.

On 14 February 2005 explosives equivalent to about 1,800 kilograms of TNT, hidden in a parked van, were detonated as Hariri's motorcade passed the St. George Hotel in Beirut. Twenty-three people died, among them Hariri, several bodyguards and the former economy minister Bassel Fleihan. On 14 March between 1.2 and 1.5 million people assembled in Beirut to demand an end to Syria's occupation. These protests, called the Cedar Revolution, were followed by the withdrawal of Syrian troops.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon was created at his instigation. In August 2020 it convicted Salim Ayyash, a Hezbollah member, in absentia and acquitted three others; the judges found no evidence of involvement by Hezbollah's leadership. Beirut International Airport was renamed after Hariri in 2005, and his son Saad Hariri succeeded him as leader of the Future Movement.
rainier-iii-prince-of-monaco: Rainier Louis Henri Maxence Bertrand Grimaldi was born at the Prince's Palace of Monaco on 31 May 1923, the first native-born prince since Honoré IV in 1758. He was the only son of Hereditary Princess Charlotte, whom her father Louis II had legitimised by adoption, and Count Pierre of Polignac, who took the Grimaldi name on marriage. His parents divorced in 1933. He was educated in England at Summerfields and Stowe School, then at the Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland, the University of Montpellier and Sciences Po in Paris. In 1944 his mother renounced her right to the throne and he became Louis II's direct heir. He joined the Free French Army that September and received the Croix de Guerre.

Rainier became Sovereign Prince at 25, when Louis II died on 9 May 1949. He found a treasury that was practically empty, since Monaco's traditional gambling clientele had less money after the Second World War and rival gambling centres had opened. He chose to promote Monaco as a tax haven, a commercial centre and a tourist attraction. The Greek shipping owner Aristotle Onassis took control of the Société des Bains de Mer and wanted a gambling resort alone, but Rainier regained control in 1964.

He suspended the constitution in 1959 and ratified a new one in 1962. It reduced the sovereign's power, ended autocratic rule and placed power with both the prince and a National Council of eighteen elected members. In 1956 he married the American film actress Grace Kelly, with a civil ceremony on 18 April and a religious wedding at Saint Nicholas Cathedral on 19 April, watched by more than 30 million people. Their children were Caroline, Albert and Stéphanie.

Princess Grace died in 1982 after a car crash caused by a cerebral haemorrhage, and Rainier did not remarry. He founded the Princess Grace Foundation-USA that year to support young American artists, and established a postal museum in 1995. He died of complications of a lung infection on 6 April 2005, aged 81, and was buried beside his wife. His son succeeded him as Albert II. His reign lasted 56 years.
raipur: Raipur lies near the centre of a large plain in central India, sometimes called the rice bowl of India, where hundreds of varieties of rice are grown. The Mahanadi River flows to the east of the city and dense forests lie to the south. The Maikal Hills rise to the north-west, the land to the north merges with the Chota Nagpur Plateau, and the Deccan Plateau lies to the south. The climate is tropical wet and dry. Temperatures stay moderate through the year except from March to June, when they sometimes rise above 48 °C, and about 1,300 mm of rain falls, mostly between mid-June and early October.

Raipur district, like the rest of the Chhattisgarh plain, was once known as Dakshina Kosala and is considered to have been under the Maurya Empire. A Gupta inscription of the sixth century at Arang, near Raipur, shows Gupta hegemony over the region. In the seventh century a Buddhist kingdom based at Bhandak, in modern Maharashtra, ruled it and was described by Xuanzang. A branch of that family moved to Sirpur and took control of all Dakshina Kosala, reaching its height under Tivaradeva, whose son inscribed almost all the temples at Sirpur. The Sharabpuriyas later ousted them and ruled for several centuries.

By the early ninth century the Kalachuris held the region. The Kalachuris of Ratnapura ruled at Ratnapur until the thirteenth century, and by the fourteenth century the Raipur branch had gained power. One of its kings is said to have conquered eighteen garh, or forts, of the enemy, which gave Chhattisgarh, the thirty-six forts, its name. The British set up the Raipur Municipal Committee on 17 May 1867, and it became a municipal corporation in 1973. Raipur was part of Madhya Pradesh until the state of Chhattisgarh was formed on 1 November 2000.

Raipur is the capital of Chhattisgarh and the administrative headquarters of Raipur district and Raipur division. It is the state's most populous city, and the 2011 census counted 1,010,433 people in the municipal corporation and 1,122,555 in the urban agglomeration. Raipur forms a tri-city metropolitan area with Bhilai and Durg. Steel, iron and rice milling are major industries, and a newer capital district, Naya Raipur, lies close by. Raipur Junction station stands on the Howrah–Nagpur–Mumbai line, and the Swami Vivekananda International Airport, formerly Mana Airport, lies 15 km south of the city. Swami Vivekananda spent two teenage years in Raipur, from 1877 to 1879, and Rajkumar College there was founded in 1882.
rajahmundry: Rajahmundry stands at an average elevation of 14 metres, with the River Godavari flowing to its west. The Rajahmundry Traps, part of the Deccan Traps, lie on the river and interest geologists. The climate is hot and humid, with heavy monsoon rain at the end of summer. Paddy, sugarcane and many kinds of flowers are grown in the area. The earlier name Rajamahendravaram comes from the Sanskrit Rajamahendrapuram, meaning the city of King Mahendra. Under the Qutb Shahi, Mughal and Nizam rulers government records called it Rajmandri, which the British adapted as Rajahmundry. The state government restored the older name officially on 10 October 2015.

The city was established by Ammaraja Vishnuvardhana I (919–934 CE) and can be traced as a prominent settlement to the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra, who reigned around 1022 CE. Remains of 11th-century palaces and forts still exist. Later rulers included the Cholas, Kakatiyas, the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the Reddy Kingdom, the Gajapati Empire, the Vijayanagar Empire, the Bahmani and Golconda sultanates, and Nizam rule. The Dutch built a fort in 1602, which the British conquered in 1857 and converted into a jail in 1864.

The district of Rajahmundry was created in the Madras Presidency in 1823 and was reorganised in 1859 into the Godavari and Krishna districts. Rajahmundry was the headquarters of Godavari district until it was split into East and West Godavari in 1925. In the 19th century the city became a centre of reform. Kandukuri Veeresalingam, the author of Rajasekhara Charithram, the first Telugu novel, founded a monthly magazine and a girls' school at Dowleswaram in 1874, and the first widow remarriage took place on 11 December 1881. Julia Maitland founded a multilingual school and reading room in the town in 1837.

Rajahmundry is acclaimed as the birthplace of Telugu literature. The poet Nannayya, called Adi Kavi, the first poet, wrote the first third of the Andhra Mahabharatam, a Telugu retelling of the Mahabharata, with Tikkana and Yerrana completing the work. The city is the district headquarters of East Godavari in Andhra Pradesh. Its floriculture is known, and the Havelock Bridge of 1897 and the Godavari Arch Bridge of 1997 cross the river.
rajasthan: Rajasthan covers 342,239 square kilometres, about 10.4 per cent of India's area, and includes most of the wide and inhospitable Thar Desert, also called the Great Indian Desert. The Aravalli Range runs through the state from south-west to north-east for more than 850 kilometres, with Mount Abu, the state's only hill station, at its south-western end. About three fifths of the state lies north-west of the range. It borders the Pakistani provinces of Punjab and Sindh and five Indian states. The name means Land of Kings, from the Sanskrit rājā and sthāna. It first appears in print in the 1829 Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, and Rajputana, the earlier name for the region, appears in George Thomas's memoir of 1800.

Parts of the area belonged to the Vedic and Indus Valley civilisations. Kalibangan, in Hanumangarh district, was a major provincial capital of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and a settlement at Balathal, in Udaipur district, dates from 3000 to 1500 BCE. Stone Age tools between 5,000 and 200,000 years old have been found in Bundi and Bhilwara districts. The Rajputs, according to Topsfield, entered India from the north-west in the first millennium CE and set up kingdoms in what is now Rajasthan. The Pratiharas, with their seat at Kannauj, were acknowledged by almost all of North India up to the 10th century.

In 1178 a confederacy of Rajputs under Mularaja II of the Kingdom of Gujarat defeated the Ghurids at the Battle of Kasahrada. Prithviraj Chauhan led a confederacy of Rajput clans that defeated Muhammad Ghori at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191, but Ghori decisively defeated him at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192, and part of Rajasthan then came under Muslim rulers, with centres at Nagaur and Ajmer. At the beginning of the 13th century Mewar was the most powerful state of the region. The Rajputs resisted the Muslim incursions from the 13th century onwards and preserved Hindu culture at their courts.

The modern state was formed from the states of the Rajputana Agency of British India, which merged into the Indian Union. It includes most of Rajputana: nineteen princely states, three chiefships and the British district of Ajmer-Merwara. Jaisalmer, Marwar (Jodhpur), Bikaner, Mewar (Chittorgarh), Alwar and Dhundhar (Jaipur) were among the main Rajput states, Bharatpur and Dholpur were Jat states, and Tonk was ruled by Pathans.

Rajasthan is a state of India with its capital and largest city at Jaipur. Its main features include the Indus Valley ruins at Kalibangan, the Jain pilgrimage site of the Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu and Keoladeo National Park at Bharatpur, a World Heritage Site known for its birds.
rajendra-prasad: Rajendra Prasad was born on 3 December 1884 into a Kayastha family at Ziradei, in what is now the Siwan district of Bihar. His father, Mahadev Sahai, was a scholar of Sanskrit and Persian, and his mother, Kamleshwari Devi, told him stories from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. He was the youngest child, and an elder sister cared for him after his mother died. He placed first in the entrance examination of the University of Calcutta, joined the Presidency College there in 1902 and took his M.A. in Economics with a first division in December 1907. In 1906 he helped to form the Bihari Students Conference at Patna.

He taught English at the Langat Singh College in Muzaffarpur, where he became principal, and later studied law in Calcutta. He passed the master's examination in law in 1915 with a gold medal, took a doctorate in law at Allahabad University and in 1916 joined the High Court of Bihar and Odisha. He formally joined the Indian National Congress in 1911 and met Mahatma Gandhi at the Lucknow session of 1916. Moved by Gandhi's conviction, he gave up his law practice and university duties when the Non-Cooperation resolution passed in 1920.

He organised relief after the Bihar earthquake of 15 January 1934, and was elected President of the Indian National Congress in October 1934, again in 1939 and a third time in 1947. After the Quit India Resolution of 8 August 1942 he was arrested and held in Bankipur Central Jail until 15 June 1945. In the interim government of 1946 he held the food and agriculture portfolio, and on 11 December 1946 he was elected President of the Constituent Assembly.

After the Constitution was ratified on 24 January 1950 he was elected the first President of India. As a ceremonial head of state he acted independently of any party and left Congress politics. He travelled widely abroad and was re-elected in 1952 and 1957, the only president to serve two terms. He took a more active part in state affairs after the dispute over the Hindu Code Bill. He retired in May 1962 and returned to Patna, was honoured with the Bharat Ratna and died on 28 February 1963, aged 78.
rajgir: Rajgir lies in the Nalanda district of Bihar. Its name, from Rājagṛha, means 'house of the king', and it has also been called Girivraja, which Buddhaghosa explains as 'an enclosure of hills'. The Ramayana attributes its founding to Vasu, fourth son of Brahmā, and the Mahabharata to Bṛhadratha. The date of origin is unknown, though ceramics dating to about 1000 BCE have been found there.

Old Rajgir lies in a valley within low hills and was surrounded by an almost 50 km cyclopean wall that followed the hilltops, with 16 towers. Its walls are dated by excavation to about the 6th century BCE. New Rajgir, next to the modern town, was probably fortified around the 1st century BCE.

The Mahabharata tells of the city's king Jarasandha, whom Bhima killed in a wrestling match by splitting him in two. Rajgir was the first capital of Magadha, under the Haryanka kings Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, who kept his father Bimbisara in captivity there. The sources do not agree which of the two built its fortifications. Udayin, son of Ajatashatru, moved the capital to Pataliputra, modern Patna.

The Buddha spent several months at Rajgir meditating and preaching on Gridhra-kuta, the Hill of the Vultures, and initiated King Bimbisara there. The First Buddhist Council was held in the Saptaparni Cave under Maha Kassapa. Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, spent fourteen years at Rajgir and Nalanda, and Jains hold that Munisuvrata, the 20th Tirthankara, was born there. After the 1st or 2nd century CE the city seems to have declined; Xuanzang, visiting in the 7th century, found two old Buddhist monasteries still active but wrote mainly of its past.

Rajgir is a town in Bihar, known for its natural springs and the hills that dominate it. It remained important to Jains, and the Naulakhā temple of Munisuvrata at the foot of the hills holds an image installed in 1447. The cyclopean wall, about 2,500 years old, survives in places along the hills. Nalanda University, founded in 2010 nearby, is named after the ancient Nalanda university that lay near Rajgir.
rajiv-gandhi: Rajiv Gandhi was born in Bombay on 20 August 1944, the son of Indira and Feroze Gandhi, and belonged to the Nehru-Gandhi family, which was associated with the Indian National Congress; he was not related to Mahatma Gandhi. He attended The Doon School and then the University of Cambridge, returned to India in 1966 and became a pilot for the state-owned Indian Airlines. Although his mother was prime minister for much of the 1960s and 1970s, he remained apolitical.

After his younger brother Sanjay died in a plane crash on 23 June 1980, he entered politics at his mother's urging, addressing a national farmers' rally in Delhi on 16 February 1981. He won Sanjay's seat of Amethi that year.

On 31 October 1984 Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, after Operation Blue Star, the military action against Sikh separatists in the Golden Temple. Pressed by Zail Singh and others, Rajiv Gandhi became prime minister that day, at 40 the youngest in India's history. Mobs rioted against Sikhs in the following days, and sources estimate the Sikh dead at between 8,000 and 17,000. In December Congress won 414 of 541 seats in the Lok Sabha, the largest majority to that date.

His first measure, in January 1985, was an anti-defection law. He signed the Rajiv-Longowal Accord with the Akali leader H. S. Longowal in an effort to settle the Punjab problem. He appointed Sam Pitroda as adviser on public information infrastructure, and the public telecom companies MTNL and VSNL were developed. He also tried to liberalise the economy and trade policy. His government's handling of the Shah Bano case, in which Parliament in 1986 overrode a Supreme Court judgement, drew criticism, and in 1987 he sent peacekeeping troops to Sri Lanka, leading to open conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

The finance minister V. P. Singh, moved to defence, uncovered what became known as the Bofors scandal, concerning alleged payoffs by the Swedish arms company Bofors. Later reporting implicated Gandhi personally, though in 2004 he was posthumously cleared. Congress lost the 1989 election.

Gandhi remained Congress president and was campaigning for the 1991 elections when he was assassinated at Sriperumbudur on 21 May 1991. A woman, identified as Kalaivani Rajaratnam of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, bent to touch his feet and detonated explosives under her dress, killing him and at least 14 others. The Supreme Court judgement held that the LTTE chief Prabhakaran acted from personal animosity arising from the sending of the Indian Peace Keeping Force to Sri Lanka. In 1991 the Indian government posthumously awarded him the Bharat Ratna.
rajputs: Rajput, from the Sanskrit rajaputra, "son of a king", names a large cluster of castes, kin bodies and local groups of the northern Indian subcontinent that share a status and an ideology of descent. The literal sense is misleading, because although many Rajputs belonged to ruling clans, most were farmers. Before the 15th century the word meant a horse soldier, a trooper, a village headman or a subordinate chief. Modern scholars hold that nearly all Rajput clans arose from peasant or pastoral communities, and Satish Chandra describes them as miscellaneous groups that included Shudra and tribal groups and some Brahmans who took to warfare.

Scholars date the rise of Rajput clans to the seventh century, when dynasties such as the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Chahamanas, the Tomaras of Delhi, the Chaulukyas, the Paramaras, the Gahadavalas and the Chandela became lords of various localities. The lineages that faced the Ghaznavid and Ghurid invaders in the 11th and 12th centuries were called Rajput only later. Membership of the class became largely hereditary between the 12th and 16th centuries. A list of 1324 names 72 clans, among them the Chouhana, Pamara, Chandella, Kachchvaha and Guhilot.

From the reign of Akbar, Rajput leaders were drawn into the Mughal ruling elite through court appointments and marriage alliances, and the emperors Jahangir and Shah Jahan were born to Rajput mothers. The Sisodia clan of Mewar refused to send its women to the Mughal harem, which led to a siege and a mass suicide at Chittor. Between 1815 and 1823 the British East India Company took many Rajput states, including Udaipur, Jaipur, Bikaner and Sirohi, under its protection in return for tribute. In 1947 the rulers of the 22 princely states of Rajputana acceded to India, and the states were merged into Rajasthan in 1949 and 1950.

Rajput identity rests on patrilineal descent and marriage within recognised clans. In medieval Rajasthan the word was restricted to certain clans, while communities to the east had a fluid and inclusive usage, and the Rajputs of Rajasthan refused to acknowledge claims such as those of the Bundelas. In 1988 about 79 per cent of roughly 38 million Rajputs were estimated to be Hindu, nearly 20 per cent Muslim and about 0.5 per cent Sikh. Many clans honour Karni Mata as a family goddess, and Shiva and Durga are widely worshipped. The British classed Rajputs as a martial race, and the term Rajput painting is used for the art of Rajput courts in Rajasthan, central India and the Punjab Hills.
rakvere: Rakvere is the administrative centre of Lääne-Viru County, about 100 kilometres south-east of Tallinn and 20 kilometres south of the Gulf of Finland. The earliest signs of settlement, from the 3rd to 5th centuries CE, were found on Theatre Hill, and a wooden stronghold was built on the nearby hill of Vallimägi, the town's highest point.

A settlement called Tarvanpea, meaning head of an aurochs, was first mentioned in 1226 in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry. The Danish stronghold was recorded as Wesenbergh, a Middle Low German adaptation, in 1252, and the town was widely known as Wesenberg until the early 20th century.

After Denmark conquered northern Estonia it began building in stone in 1220. King Erik VI Menved granted Rakvere Lübeck rights on 12 June 1302. Denmark sold its Estonian lands to the Livonian Order in 1346, and a large stone castle was then built on Vallimägi, protected by towers and courtyards.

Russian troops captured Rakvere in 1558, the first year of the Livonian War, and Sweden heavily damaged it in the Siege of Wesenberg in 1574. Sweden took the town in 1581 and passed it to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1602; Polish troops destroyed the castle in 1605, after which it was never rebuilt. The town was burned down in 1703 during the Great Northern War. Estonia and Livonia capitulated in 1710, and under the Treaty of Nystad of 1721 the region became part of the Russian Empire for the next 200 years.

The Red Army held Rakvere from 16 December 1918 to 12 January 1919, during the Estonian War of Independence. Hundreds of Rakvere's residents were deported on 14 June 1941, and Germany occupied the city from 7 August 1941 to 19 September 1944. Rakvere again became a self-governing municipality on 24 January 1991.

The ruins of the castle on Vallimägi are open to visitors, with exhibitions on everyday life in the 16th century. Trinity Church, originally dedicated to St Michael, dates from the 15th century and was rebuilt after damage in the Livonian War and later conflicts. Pikk Street is the oldest street in the town. A bronze aurochs by Tauno Kangro, unveiled in 2002 for the town's 700th anniversary, recalls the old name Tarvanpea. The composer Arvo Pärt lived in Rakvere from 1938 until at least 1965. Rakvere is reportedly Europe's smallest town with its own professional theatre.
ram-mohan-roy: Ram Mohan Roy was born on 22 May 1772 at Radhanagar in Hooghly District, in the Bengal Presidency. His great-grandfather was a Rarhi Kulin Brahmin; in the 19th century Kulinism was a synonym for polygamy and the dowry system, both of which he later campaigned against. He became a scholar of Sanskrit, Persian and English, and also knew Arabic, Latin and Greek. In his childhood he witnessed the death of his sister-in-law by sati; he tried to protest, but she was burned alive.

From 1803 to 1815 he worked in the East India Company's Writing Service, first as private clerk at Murshidabad and then with the collector John Digby. In 1804 he wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin, A Gift to Monotheists, in Persian.

In 1814 he started the Atmiya Sabha, a discussion circle in Calcutta that propagated the monotheism of the Vedanta and campaigned against idolatry, caste rigidity and meaningless ritual. He wrote against Trinitarian Christianity and published The Precepts of Jesus in 1820. He founded the Anglo-Hindu School in 1822 and the Vedanta College in 1826. His Bengali weekly Sambad Kaumudi, begun in 1821, covered freedom of the press and the admission of Indians to high office. His Gaudiya Vyakaran, published in 1826, was the first complete Bengali grammar.

In 1828 he founded the Brahmo Sabha with Debendranath Tagore, a forerunner of the Brahmo Samaj, whose beliefs rested on the worship of one God and the equality of all people. He attacked sati, polygamy, child marriage and caste, and he petitioned against sati in 1829. In 1830 he went to England as an envoy of the Mughal emperor Akbar II, who had given him the title of Raja, to make sure that Lord William Bentinck's Bengal Sati Regulation of 1829 was not overturned and to seek a larger stipend for the emperor.

In early September 1833 Roy came to Bristol to visit his Unitarian friend Lant Carpenter. He fell ill in mid-September and died at Stapleton on 27 September 1833 of meningitis or a chronic respiratory ailment. He was first buried at Stapleton Grove and in 1843 reburied at Arnos Vale Cemetery, where a chhatri designed by William Prinsep stands over the tomb.

Roy tried to join Western culture with the best of India's own traditions. His commitment to English education later prompted a debate between Mahatma Gandhi, who objected to it, and Rabindranath Tagore, who answered that Roy had the full inheritance of Indian wisdom and was never a schoolboy of the West.
rama: The word Rama is Vedic Sanskrit with two contextual meanings. In the Atharva Veda it means dark or black, and in other Vedic texts pleasing, delightful or beautiful. The primary source of his life is the Sanskrit epic Ramayana, composed by the sage Valmiki, which exists in many versions across the regions of India.

Some Hindu texts place Rama in the Treta Yuga, which their authors estimate to have existed before about 5000 BCE. The archaeologist H. D. Sankalia calls this estimate pure speculation and suggests that the incidents of the story could have taken place between 1,500 and 700 BCE. Jain and Buddhist texts also tell the story, calling him Pauma or Padma in Jain accounts, with details that differ from the Hindu versions.

According to Valmiki, Rama was born in Ayodhya, capital of Kosala, to Dasaratha and his first wife Kausalya, and had the half-brothers Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna. He married Sita and spent fourteen years in forest exile, during which Sita was kidnapped by the demon-king Ravana. After the war he returned to Ayodhya and was crowned, and his rule, Rama rajya, is described as just and fair. Many believe that people lit lamps for his return, which links the festival of Diwali with him.

Hindus hold Rama to be a complete avatar of Vishnu, and some regard him as the ultimate Brahman. He is also viewed as the ideal man. By Hindu belief this avatar does not display Vishnu's divine powers and lives as a human. Scholars such as Paula Richman note that there are hundreds of versions of his story, none the single original, each valid in its local tradition.

The Ramayana has been retold in most major Indian languages, among them Kambar's Tamil Ramavataram in the 12th century, Krittibas Ojha's Bengali version in the 15th and Tulsidas's Awadhi Ramacharitamanasa in the 16th. Kalidasa's Raghuvamsa suggests that the legend was well established by the 4th or 5th century CE. The Ramanandi Sampradaya, founded by the 14th-century poet-saint Ramananda, became the largest Hindu monastic community in modern times.

The story arrived in Southeast Asia in the 1st millennium CE, and its influence grew in Java, Bali, Malaya, Burma, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. It inspired Madhubani and Rajput paintings and the Ramlila performances held each autumn.
rama-i: Rama I was born Thongduang in 1737, during the reign of King Boromakot of Ayutthaya. His father, Thongdi, was a nobleman of Mon ancestry at the royal court, a descendant of Kosa Pan, who had led King Narai's embassy to the French court. His mother, Daoreung, was the eldest daughter of a wealthy Hokkien Chinese magnate. As a young man he entered the court as a royal page to King Uthumphon, spent a time as a monk in 1757, married Nak in 1760 and became deputy governor of Ratchaburi, a frontier town on the western approaches of the kingdom.

When Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, he joined Phraya Wachiraprakan, later King Taksin, who founded the Kingdom of Thonburi in 1768. Together with his brother Bunma he became Taksin's most successful general. He rose to Chaophraya Chakri, chief minister for the northern provinces, and commanded armies against the Burmese, Khmer and Lao. In 1774 he went to Lan Na to free it from Burmese rule with the help of Phraya Kawila of Lampang, and in 1778 the three Lao kingdoms of Vientiane, Luang Prabang and Champasak fell to Siam. He became the first Somdet Chao Phraya, a rank equal to that of royalty.

In 1781 he was campaigning in Cambodia when the rebellion of Phraya Sun deposed Taksin. Returning in 1782, he defeated the rebels, took power and crowned himself on 6 April 1782, founding the Chakri dynasty. Later sources widely report that Taksin was executed, contradicting some earlier ones. Rama I moved the capital to the east bank of the Chao Phraya River, for its better position and to start with a clean slate, and named it Rattanakosin, keeping place of the Emerald Buddha, which he installed at Wat Phra Kaew within the new Grand Palace.

The Burmese–Siamese War of 1785 to 1786, called the Nine Armies War, was the last major Burmese assault on Siam; King Bodawpaya's attack was defeated, and a second attempt the next year was quickly beaten at Tha Din Daeng. He convened a council on the Buddhist canon in 1788, and in 1805 the court compiled the Three Seals Law, which served as a reference for Siam's traditional legal system into the modern reform era.

Rama I died in Bangkok on 7 September 1809, aged 72, after a short acute illness, and was succeeded by his son Prince Isarasundhorn as Rama II. His reign marked a revival of Siamese culture and state organisation after the collapse of the kingdom in 1767, and Siam reasserted itself as a mainland Southeast Asian power with suzerainty over Laos, Cambodia and the northern Malay states.
ramadan: Muslims hold that the Quran was revealed during Ramadan, and that Muhammad received his first revelation on Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, generally believed to be an odd-numbered night in the last ten days of the month. They also hold that all earlier scriptures were revealed in this month. They were first commanded to fast in the second year of the Hijra, 624 CE, but believe that fasting has always been necessary for believers to attain fear of God. Philip Jenkins argues that the fast grew out of the strict Lenten discipline of the Syrian Churches, a view other scholars share and some Muslim academics dispute.

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and each month begins when the first crescent of the new moon is sighted. Since the calendar has no intercalation, Ramadan migrates through the seasons. It lasts 29 or 30 days. Many Muslims insist on a local sighting of the moon to mark the start, while others use the calculated time of the new moon or the declaration of Saudi Arabia, so dates differ between countries, usually by a day.

Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory for Muslims who have reached puberty and are not ill, travelling, elderly, breastfeeding, pregnant or menstruating. The predawn meal is the suhur and the meal that breaks the fast at sunset is the iftar, traditionally opened with dates in memory of Muhammad's practice. Muslims also abstain from sinful speech, devote more time to prayer and charity, and are encouraged to read the whole Quran over the month. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, declared after the crescent of the next month is sighted or after 30 days of fasting.

Customs of the month vary widely. In some Islamic countries lanterns are strung up in public squares, a tradition believed to have originated under the Fatimid Caliphate, when the rule of Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah was acclaimed by people holding lanterns. In the Middle East a mesaharati beats a drum through the neighbourhood to wake people for suhur. In Shia Islam the 19th to 21st days of the month are marked in mourning for Ali, the fourth Rashidun caliph, who was struck during morning prayer on the 19th day in 40 AH and died on the 21st. In the USSR the practice of Ramadan was suppressed by officials, and in Albania Ramadan festivities were banned during the communist period, though many Albanians fasted in secret.
ramanuja: Ramanuja was born into a Tamil Brahmin family at Sriperumbudur, in present-day Tamil Nadu, under the Chola Empire. The traditional hagiographies, some written centuries after his death, name his parents as Kanthimathi and Asuri Keshava Somayaji and give his life as 1017 to 1137. Modern scholars, using temple records and regional literature from outside the Sri Vaishnava tradition, suggest 1077 to 1157, but one of them notes that reconstructing his historical life is nearly impossible.

He studied at Kanchipuram under Yadava Prakasa, a scholar traditionally placed in the Advaita Vedanta school but probably a Bhedabheda teacher. The two disagreed over the interpretation of the Upanishads and parted. According to tradition, Ramanuja was the great-grandson of Yamunacharya, the head of the Sri Vaishnava community at Srirangam, but Yamunacharya died before they could meet. One hagiography states that Periya Nambi, also called Mahapurna, initiated him into Sri Vaishnavism.

Ramanuja served at the Varadharaja Perumal temple at Kanchipuram and later led the community at Srirangam. According to hagiographies composed centuries after his death, a Chola king called Krimikanta Chola persecuted Sri Vaishnavas, and Ramanuja's disciple Koorathazhwan persuaded him to leave. He spent 14 years in the Hoysala kingdom, where King Vishnuvardhana helped him build the Thirunarayanaswamy temple at Melukote. Some historians hold that the king's hostility to Ramanuja was personal and not a persecution of Vaishnavas. He is also said to have drawn people regarded as untouchables into the movement, calling them Tirukulattar, of noble descent, and admitted them to the temple at Melukote.

The tradition attributes nine Sanskrit works to him, among them the Vedarthasamgraha, the Sri Bhashya, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, the Bhagavad Gita Bhashya and the Gadya Trayam. Some scholars question the authenticity of all but the three largest works and the Gadya Trayam.

Ramanuja is the chief proponent of Vishishtadvaita, qualified non-dualism, one of the three most influential Vedantic philosophies of the second millennium, with Shankara's Advaita and Madhva's Dvaita. He holds that Brahman is identical with Vishnu-Narayana and has infinite auspicious attributes. Passages describing Brahman as without attributes, he argued, deny only worldly, defiling attributes. He affirms three equally real things: matter, conscious souls and God. The universe, both souls and matter, forms the body of God. Against Shankara he opposed the idea of maya, or illusion.

For Ramanuja liberation is the joy of contemplating Brahman, reached by devotion, bhakti, in which the soul keeps its own existence and does not become identical with Brahman. He also taught sharanagati, complete surrender to Vishnu, as a path open to all regardless of caste, status or gender. After Ramanuja's time the Sri Vaishnava community split into the Vadakalai and Tenkalai groups.
ramayana: The Ramayana is a Hindu smriti epic poem, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, and one of the two Itihasas, narratives of past events interspersed with teachings on the goals of human life; the other is the Mahabharata. Its name means Rama's journey. Scholars place the oral composition of its core before the rise of Buddhism, since the narrative does not mention Buddhism and names Ayodhya as the capital of Kosala rather than by the later name Saketa. Later stages of the text extend over centuries. Two major regional recensions, the northern and the southern, descend from a common oral source; the southern is more archaic and is the backbone of modern critical editions.

In its extant form the poem has over 24,000 couplet verses, called shlokas, in seven kāṇḍas, or books. Rāma, prince of Ayodhya and son of King Daśaratha, is to be crowned, but Kaikeyī, provoked by the maidservant Mantharā, demands that Rāma be exiled for fourteen years while her son Bharata succeeds. Sītā and his brother Lakṣmaṇa follow him into the forest.

Rāvaṇa, the king of Lanka, carries off Sītā. Rāma allies himself with the vānaras, among them Hanumān, who becomes his biggest devotee. Hanumān leaps across the sea to Lanka to find Sītā, and the army crosses over a bridge built by the vānaras Nala and Nīla. In the war that follows Rāma defeats Rāvaṇa, and he returns to Ayodhya with Sītā to be crowned.

The Ramayana strongly influenced later Sanskrit poetry and Hindu life and culture, and its moral influence includes the ideal of Rāmarājya, a state in which Rama is king. Diwali marks Rama's return to Ayodhya. There are many other versions, including Buddhist and Jain adaptations. Kamban wrote the Tamil Ramavataram in the 12th century. In Cambodia the Reamker is a national epic; the earliest mention of its manuscript is a 7th-century inscription, and the surviving text dates from the 16th century.
ramesses-ii: Ramesses II was not born a prince. His grandfather Ramesses I was a vizier and military officer under the pharaoh Horemheb, who named him as his successor when Ramesses II was about eleven. His father Seti I made him prince regent at about the age of fourteen. His date of accession is recorded as the 27th day of the eleventh month, which most Egyptologists take to be 31 May 1279 BCE, when he was about 25. A papyrus calendar and the historian Josephus agree that his reign lasted 66 years and about two months, the longest recorded reign of any pharaoh.

In his second year he defeated the Sherden sea pirates, who raided cargo ships on the Mediterranean routes to Egypt, by ambushing them in a sea battle near the mouth of the Nile. He founded Pi-Ramesses in the Nile Delta as a new capital, close to his territories in Canaan and Syria, with huge temples and a vast palace. His campaign in Syria in his fourth year took the Hittite vassal state of Amurru, and in his fifth year came the Battle of Kadesh against the Hittite forces of Muwatalli II, generally considered a stalemate.

In his twenty-first year, 1259 BCE, he concluded a treaty with the Hittites at Kadesh, after a crisis over the fugitive Hittite king Muršili III brought the two empires close to war. He also campaigned in Nubia and Libya.

Ramesses began in his third year the most ambitious building project since the pyramids, building from the Delta to Nubia. He had his carvings cut deep into the stone so that later rulers could not easily alter them, and he used reliefs as propaganda for his victories. His mortuary temple at Thebes is known as the Ramesseum, and in 1255 BCE he and his queen Nefertari went into Nubia to inaugurate the temple at Abu Simbel. He held thirteen or fourteen Sed festivals, more than any other pharaoh.

Ramesses died in about July 1213 BCE, probably at Pi-Ramesses, at the age of about 90 or 91 by the most likely estimate. He was buried in tomb KV7 in the Valley of the Kings, but because of looting priests moved the body several times, and it was found in 1881 in the tomb TT320. It now lies in the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo. Later pharaohs called him the Great God, and he was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a deity in his lifetime. Greek sources knew him as Ozymandias.
ramesses-iii: Ramesses III was the son of Setnakhte and Tiy-Merenese, and was not closely related to Ramesses I or Ramesses II. Setnakhte's origin is unknown. He seized the throne during a time of crisis and unrest, probably from Twosret, and was presumably a minor descendant of Ramesses II through a different family line from that of Seti II, Siptah and Twosret. Scholars differ on the dates of Ramesses III's reign, and one calculation gives about 31 years.

His reign fell in the Late Bronze Age collapse, and Egypt faced invaders including the Sea Peoples and Libyans, along with economic difficulties. In Year 5 and Year 11 he fought Libyan tribesmen in the Western Delta. In Year 8 the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, Denyen, Shardana and Tjekker, invaded by land and sea. He defeated them at the Battle of Djahy on the eastern frontier and at the Battle of the Delta, where he ambushed their ships at the mouth of the Nile with a fleet and archers on the shore. He settled the defeated Sea Peoples in southern Canaan, and their presence there may have contributed to the rise of states such as Philistia.

The cost of these wars drained the treasury. In Year 29 the first known labour strike in recorded history took place at Deir el-Medina, when rations could not be supplied to the royal tomb-builders. His monuments ignore such troubles. He added to the temples at Luxor and Karnak and built Medinet Habu, one of the largest and best-preserved funerary temples in Egypt, enclosed by massive fortifications.

Trial papyri record a harem conspiracy against his life, made at a celebration at Medinet Habu. It was instigated by his wife Tiye, who hoped her son Pentaweret would inherit; Ramesses III had not clearly settled the succession among his sons. Many officials were implicated, three trials were held, and 38 people were sentenced to death. A CT scan of his mummy showed a deep knife wound across the throat, which would have been rapidly fatal.

The conspirators failed in one respect: the crown passed to his designated successor, Ramesses IV. The succession crisis accelerated Egypt's decline, and Ramesses III is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to have wielded substantial power.
rameswaram: Rameswaram lies in the Ramanathapuram district of Tamil Nadu, on Pamban Island, which is separated from mainland India by the Pamban channel. The island is shaped like a conch, with the Palk Strait to the north-west and the Gulf of Mannar to the south-east, and it lies about 40 kilometres from Mannar Island in Sri Lanka.

Its average elevation is 10 metres, and about 74 per cent of its area has sandy soil. The Pamban Bridge, a cantilever railway bridge of 2,065 metres with a double-leaf bascule section that can be raised for ships, opened to traffic in 1914. Dhanushkodi, at the southern tip of the island, was washed away in the cyclone of 1964, though its temple of Rama alone remained intact.

The history of Rameswaram centres on its role as a transit point to Sri Lanka and on the Ramanathaswamy Temple. Tamil hymns of the 7th and 8th centuries on Shiva by the Nayanars Appar, Sundarar and Sambandar glorify the temple. The Chola king Rajendra Chola I, who reigned from 1012 to 1040 CE, held the town for a short time.

The Jaffna kingdom, which lasted from 1215 to 1624 CE, had close ties with the island, made generous contributions to the temple and took the title Setukavalan, meaning custodians of Rameswaram; Setu appeared on its coins and inscriptions. The temple in its present form was built in the 12th century by the Pandya dynasty.

The name means Lord of Rama in Sanskrit, an epithet of Shiva. According to the Ramayana and the Puranas, Rama prayed to Shiva after his war against the demon-king Ravana. Hanuman was sent to bring a lingam from the Himalayas, and because he took too long, Sita made one of sand from the shore, which is believed to be the one in the sanctum. Tradition also places the bridge Rama built to Lanka near here.

Rameswaram has been run by a municipal body since 1994, and its population was 44,856 at the 2011 census. It is the end of the railway line from Chennai and Madurai. Tourism and fishing are the main sources of employment. The Ramanathaswamy Temple is one of the 12 Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva and is described as having the longest corridors of any Hindu temple in India, columned passages 5.2 to 6.4 metres wide and 7.6 metres high.

Rameswaram is one of the four Char Dham sites, with Badrinath, Puri and Dwarka, and many Hindus hold that a pilgrimage to Varanasi is incomplete without one to Rameswaram. Pilgrims bathe in its holy water bodies, of which there are sixty-four in and around the town.
ramiz-alia: Ramiz Alia was born on 18 October 1925 in Shkodër to Gheg Albanian parents who were Muslim and had fled persecution in Yugoslavia. He grew up in Tirana, joined the underground Albanian Communist Youth Organisation in 1941 and became a member of the Albanian Communist Party in 1943.

He rose rapidly under the patronage of Enver Hoxha. He was elected to the Central Committee in November 1948, became a candidate member of the Politburo in 1956 and a full member by 1961, and was the party's chief ideologist in social and cultural fields. Hoxha named no official successor, but there were clear signs that he favoured Alia.
Alia was the second and last leader of the People's Socialist Republic of Albania, serving as First Secretary of the Party of Labour from 1985 to 1991. He was also head of state from 1982 to 1992.

Alia tried to change the system on a limited, cautious basis, but reform from above threatened to become reform from below, largely because of the demands of Albania's youth. On 9 December 1990 students marched in Tirana demanding reforms, and Alia met them and agreed to further steps towards democratisation. On 12 December 1990 he signed a law allowing political pluralism, which he later called a failure.

In the 1991 elections, the first democratic ones in the country, he ran for parliament in a Tirana constituency and was defeated by the mining engineer Franko Kroqi, a candidate of the new Democratic Party of Albania. After that loss and the Democratic Party's landslide in the spring 1992 general election, he resigned as president on 3 April 1992. On 9 April the People's Assembly elected the party's leader, Sali Berisha, as head of state.

Alia was placed under house arrest in August 1992 and imprisoned in August 1993. In May 1994 he went on trial with other senior officials for abuse of power and misappropriation of state funds and received a nine-year sentence, later cut on appeal. He was freed on 7 July 1995 and charged again in 1996 with crimes against humanity. He died in Tirana on 7 October 2011.

His legacy remains polarising. Some dissidents accuse him of continuing Hoxha's repressive practices, while others praise him for dissolving the Party of Labour's monopoly peacefully and avoiding the bloodshed seen in Romania.
ramla: Ramla lies in the Central District of Israel. Its strategic and economic value came from its position at the crossing of the Via Maris, the road linking Egypt with Syria, and the road from the Mediterranean port of Jaffa to Jerusalem. It takes its name from raml, the Arabic word for sand, from the sandy ground on which it stands. Its limited water was gathered in cisterns.

Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik founded Ramla as the seat of his administration of Jund Filasṭīn, replacing Lydda, the first Muslim provincial capital, before he became caliph in 715. He built it close to Lydda but not inside it, probably for lack of space and because agreements from the Muslim conquest of the 630s limited the seizure of property there. His first buildings were a palace that also housed the administration, the House of the Dyers and a congregational mosque, later called the White Mosque, completed under Umar II. An aqueduct brought water from Gezer. Many of Lydda's Christian, Samaritan and Jewish inhabitants were moved to the new city, which became the commercial centre of Palestine, a market for dyeing, weaving, pottery and olive oil.

The Abbasids confiscated the Umayyad properties in 750. The Fatimids took Ramla in 969, and about ten years later the Jarrahids, a branch of the Tayy tribe, destroyed it. The geographer al-Muqaddasi still called it a fine city. The city lost its role as capital shortly before the First Crusade, and the crusaders took it without a fight in 1099. It became the seat of a lordship in the Kingdom of Jerusalem and a station for pilgrims.

By the 19th century Ramla was a decaying town of about 3,000 people. Napoleon Bonaparte used the Franciscan hospice as his headquarters on 2 March 1799. Ramla had an almost exclusively Arab population until it was captured by Israeli forces on 12 July 1948, shortly after Lydda, and most remaining inhabitants were expelled; some scholars, including Ilan Pappé, call this ethnic cleansing, a claim that is disputed.

Ramla is one of Israel's mixed cities, with both Jewish and Arab citizens. The White Tower, six storeys high, was built in the 13th century as the minaret of the White Mosque, of which only remnants survive. The Pool of Arches, an underground cistern built in 789, and the Great Mosque, a Crusader cathedral converted by the Mamluks, also stand. The city is the centre of Karaite Judaism in Israel.
ramon-llull: Llull was born in Palma in 1232 or 1233 into a wealthy family of Barcelona patricians who had come to the Kingdom of Majorca in 1229 with the armies of James I of Aragon. Muslims still made up a large part of the island's population, and Jews were present in its cultural and economic life. In 1257 he married Blanca Picany, with whom he had two children.

In 1263, by his own account, he saw Christ on the Cross five times while writing a love song. The visions gave him three aims, among them to convert Muslims to Christianity. He sold his possessions, went on pilgrimages, and on returning to Majorca bought a Muslim slave to teach him Arabic. In 1270 he founded the hermitage of Miramar.

In 1274, at Puig de Randa, Llull says the form of his great book was given to him by divine revelation. This was the Art, a system of universal logic made of general principles and combinatorial operations, meant to prove Christian doctrine to people of every faith. It is distinctive for its use of letters and diagrams, which give it an algebraic character.

To make the Art accessible he wrote in Catalan as well as Latin. The Book of the Gentile and the Three Wise Men, written in the 1270s, imagines a Muslim, a Jew and a Christian showing a Gentile their faiths with the help of trees whose leaves carry the principles of the Art. Blanquerna, written about 1276 to 1283, is the best known of his novels. His first work was a compendium of the logic of Al-Ghazali.

Llull urged the teaching of Arabic and other languages in Europe, and a language school for Franciscan missionaries was founded at Miramar in 1276. He travelled to Tunis about 1291 and again about 1304. In 1315 he was stoned by a mob in Bougie or Tunis; tradition held that he died of this and was a martyr, but there is evidence that he was rescued and died early the next year, at sea or shortly after reaching Majorca. His tomb, made in 1448, is in the Franciscan church in Palma.

His Art was never adopted by mainstream academia, and the inquisitor Nicholas Eymerich condemned Lullism in Aragon in the 1360s. Nicholas of Cusa and Gottfried Leibniz drew on his ideas, and in the early modern period alchemical treatises were falsely attributed to him. He was beatified by Pope Pius IX on 11 September 1847, and some regard his ideas as prefiguring computation theory.
ramon-magsaysay: Ramon del Fierro Magsaysay was born at Iba on 31 August 1907, of mixed Tagalog, Visayan, Spanish and Chinese descent. His father was a blacksmith and his mother a schoolteacher. He studied at the University of the Philippines and then took a degree in commerce at José Rizal College, and worked as a bus company mechanic and shop superintendent.

When the Bataan garrison surrendered in 1942 he escaped to the hills and organised the Western Luzon Guerrilla Forces. He was commissioned captain on 5 April 1942, and later commanded a force of 10,000. He helped clear the Zambales coast of the Japanese before the American landing in January 1945. In April 1946 he was elected to the House of Representatives for the Liberal Party, and was re-elected in 1949.

In September 1950 President Elpidio Quirino appointed him Secretary of National Defense after Magsaysay offered a plan to fight the Hukbalahap guerrillas, drawing on his wartime experience. With Colonel Edward Lansdale, a former advertising man and CIA agent, he sent soldiers to distribute relief goods and aid in outlying communities, and the army's image improved among rural people who had regarded it with apathy and distrust.

In 1951 he went to Negros Occidental after the torture and killing of his ally Moises Padilla, and carried the body himself to the morgue. He resigned on 28 February 1953 and ran for president for the Nacionalista Party. He won the election of 10 November 1953 over Quirino and was the youngest president elected to that date.

Magsaysay was sworn in on 30 December 1953 wearing the barong tagalog, a first for a president, and he opened the gates of Malacañang Palace to the public. His Presidential Complaints and Action Committee heard nearly 60,000 complaints in a year. His agrarian laws included the Agricultural Tenancy Act of 1954 and the Land Reform Act of 1955, and he created the National Resettlement and Rehabilitation Administration, which gave land to landless families, and the Agricultural Credit and Cooperative Financing Administration for rural credit.

In 1954 the Hukbalahap leader Luis Taruc surrendered on 17 May, and the number of Huks fell below 2,000. He brought the Philippines into the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization, founded at Manila on 8 September 1954, and worked towards the Reparation Agreement, in which Japan obliged itself to pay 550 million dollars for war damages. Magsaysay died in a plane crash at Cebu on 17 March 1957.
ranjit-singh: Ranjit Singh was born to Maha Singh and Raj Kaur in Gujranwala, in a Sandhawalia Jat Sikh family. He was named Buddh Singh at birth, and his father renamed him Ranjit, 'victor in battle', to commemorate his army's victory over the Chattha chief Pir Muhammad. Smallpox in infancy cost him the sight of his left eye. His father died in 1792, when he was about twelve, and he became the minor head of the Sukerchakia Misl, raised by his mother. He never learned to read or write beyond the Gurmukhi alphabet, but was trained at home in riding, musketry and other martial arts.

Ranjit Singh was prominent among the Sikh leaders who opposed the Durrani ruler Zaman Shah's third invasion of the Punjab. After Zaman Shah's retreat in 1799 he attacked the Bhangi Sikhs who held Lahore with an army of 25,000, joined by another 25,000 led by his mother-in-law Rani Sada Kaur. The Bhangis escaped, and the people of Lahore welcomed his rule. In 1802 he took Amritsar and promised to rebuild the Harmandir Sahib in marble and gold. On 1 January 1806 he signed a treaty with the East India Company by which neither side would cross the Sutlej River in arms.

By 1813 he had annexed the Sikh misls; later decades brought Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. At his death the empire reached from Ladakh to the borders of Sindh, and from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej. Muslims made up about 70 per cent of its population, Hindus about 24 per cent and Sikhs 6 to 7 per cent. His army and government included Sikhs, Muslims, Hindus and Europeans such as the Frenchman Jean-François Allard, though he avoided recruiting Britons. Nineteenth-century Muslim writers such as Shahamat Ali judged his government despotic.

In the 1830s Ranjit Singh suffered several health complications and a stroke, which some records attribute to alcohol. He died in his sleep on 27 June 1839. Among his possessions was the Koh-i-Noor diamond, taken from Shuja Shah Durrani, which he left to the Jagannath Temple in Puri.

After his death the empire failed to create a stable succession or lasting structure of government. Clive Dewey argues that its decline owed much to the jagir tax system inherited from the Mughals, over whose spoils nobles and his family fought. Palace coups and assassinations followed, and the British and the Sikh Empire fought two Anglo-Sikh wars, the second ending the empire. His lasting legacy is the restoration of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, much of whose gilding and marblework dates from his time.
ranoji-scindia: Ranoji Scindia, also known as Ranoji Sendrak, was born about 1700 into a Maratha family. His father, Jankoji Rao I, was hereditary patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed, a village in the present Satara district of Maharashtra. In earlier centuries his forefathers had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, under the Bahmani Sultanate, and had held jagirs. As a young man he entered the service of Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath. Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar, one of the Peshwa's diplomats, recognised his talents and had him made personal bodyguard to the Peshwa's son, Baji Rao I.

When Baji Rao was appointed Peshwa at the age of twenty by Chhatrapati Shahu, the appointment aroused the jealousy of senior officials at the Maratha court.
