He therefore promoted talented young men, barely out of their teens, to command his troops, among them Ranoji Scindia, Malhar Rao Holkar, the Pawar brothers, Pilaji Jadhav and Fateh Singh Bhosle. None of them came from families that had held hereditary deshmukhi rights under earlier rulers such as the Deccan Sultanates.

Ranoji was in charge of the Maratha campaign that Baji Rao began in Malwa in 1726, and after it he established his capital at Ujjain in 1731. He appointed Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar as his dewan, or administrator, and Yashaji Rambhaji as commander of his army, and himself spent most of his life on campaign. Some historians credit him with bringing the Kumbh Mela to Ujjain in 1732.

Ranoji died on 3 July 1745. He had five sons: Jayappa Rao, Jyotiba Rao, Dattaji Rao, Tukoji Rao and Mahadji. The four eldest died in battles in northern India between 1750 and 1761. The dynasty went on to dominate central and northern India in the later 18th century through its presence at Delhi, its collection of chauth from neighbouring rulers and a modernised army, and his descendants ruled the princely state of Gwalior under the British.
raoul-wallenberg: Raoul Wallenberg was born on 4 August 1912 in Lidingö, near Stockholm. His father, a naval officer, died of cancer three months before his birth, and his mother and grandmother raised him together. His paternal grandfather, Gustaf Wallenberg, had been a diplomat and envoy to Tokyo, Istanbul and Sofia. He worked as an architect and businessman. From 1941 he made frequent trips to Budapest as the representative of his business associate Kálmán Lauer, and he learned Hungarian. Within a year he was a joint owner and international director of the company.

The War Refugee Board recruited Wallenberg in 1944. He reached the Swedish legation in Budapest on 9 July 1944. Miklós Horthy had halted the transports from Hungary two days earlier, after warnings from Roosevelt, Churchill, the King of Sweden and the Pope, but between May and early July Eichmann and his associates had deported more than 400,000 Jews, all but 15,000 of them to Auschwitz-Birkenau. About 230,000 Jews remained.

With the Swedish diplomat Per Anger and Miklós Krausz, he issued protective passports identifying the bearers as Swedish subjects awaiting repatriation. The documents were not legal, but they looked official and were generally accepted by German and Hungarian authorities, who were sometimes bribed. He also sheltered Jews in buildings declared Swedish territory. Some have claimed that he rescued 100,000 Jews, but historians regard that figure as an exaggeration; Yad Vashem estimates that about 4,500 people received protective paperwork.

On 17 January 1945, during the Siege of Budapest, Wallenberg went to Marshal Malinovsky's headquarters in Debrecen to answer allegations of espionage and was detained by Soviet agents. On 6 February 1957 the Soviet government released a document dated 17 July 1947 which said that he had died in his cell, probably of heart failure. Vyacheslav Nikonov, investigating in 1991, concluded that he was executed in 1947, but there is no conclusive proof, and some former prisoners claimed to have seen him later. The Swedish Tax Agency declared him dead in absentia in 2016.
Yad Vashem named him one of the Righteous Among the Nations in 1963. In 1981 he became an honorary citizen of the United States, the second person after Winston Churchill.
raphael: Raphael was born in Urbino, a small city of the Papal States whose court had been established by Federico da Montefeltro, created Duke of Urbino by Pope Sixtus IV. His father, Giovanni Santi, was court painter to the Duke and also a poet who wrote a rhymed chronicle of Federico's life. Raphael's mother Màgia died in 1491, and his father on 1 August 1494, so that he was an orphan at eleven. His guardian became his uncle Bartolomeo, a priest, who engaged in litigation with his stepmother. Raphael probably took part in managing his father's workshop from a very early age.

He probably trained in the workshop of Pietro Perugino and was described as a fully trained master by 1500. From about 1504 he spent a good deal of time in Florence, though possibly never as a continuous resident. A letter of recommendation of October 1504 describes him as a young painter who had decided to study there.

In 1508 Raphael moved to Rome, where he lived for the rest of his life. Pope Julius II invited him, perhaps at the suggestion of the architect Donato Bramante, who came from just outside Urbino and was distantly related to him. Julius at once commissioned him to fresco what was meant to become the Pope's private library in the Vatican Palace, a far larger commission than any he had had before. The Raphael Rooms, with The School of Athens in the Stanza della Segnatura, became the largest work of his career.

According to Vasari, Raphael eventually had a workshop of fifty pupils and assistants, arguably the largest team under any single old master painter. The most important were Giulio Romano and Gianfrancesco Penni, who were left many of his drawings and continued the workshop after his death. In 1514 he became engaged to Maria Bibbiena, Cardinal Bibbiena's niece, but the marriage had not taken place when she died in 1520.

Raphael was one of the finest draftsmen in the history of Western art and used drawings extensively to plan his compositions; over four hundred sheets survive. He made no prints himself but collaborated with Marcantonio Raimondi on about fifty engravings, which were the main way his art was experienced outside Italy until the twentieth century. His influence in his own century was less than that of Michelangelo, but those who disliked the excesses of Mannerism soon held him up as the ideal balanced painter. In the 18th and 19th centuries his serene and harmonious qualities were again regarded as the highest models.
raqqa: Raqqa lies on the north bank of the Euphrates in Syria, about 160 kilometres east of Aleppo. The mounds of Tall Zaydan and Tall al-Bi'a, the second identified with the Babylonian city of Tuttul, show that the area was inhabited from remote antiquity. The modern city traces its history to the Hellenistic foundation of Nikephorion, which Pliny attributes to Alexander the Great and Appian to Seleucus I Nicator. Seleucus II Callinicus enlarged it and renamed it Kallinikos after himself. In Roman times it belonged to the province of Osrhoene.

The Byzantine emperor Leo I rebuilt the city in 466, but the name Kallinikos prevailed. By treaty it was one of the few official cross-border trading posts between the Byzantine and Sasanian empires. It fell to the Muslim commander Iyad ibn Ghanm in 639 or 640 and took the Arabic name al-Raqqah, 'the morass', after its marshy surroundings. Its Christians were allowed to keep their existing churches but not to build new ones. In 770-1 the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur began a new garrison city, al-Rafiqah, about 200 metres west of Raqqa, to strengthen the frontier with the Byzantine Empire; about 2,660 metres of its walls survive, with its congregational mosque.

The caliph Harun al-Rashid made the city his capital from 796. Raqqa declined in the late 9th century through warfare between the Abbasids and the Tulunids and the rise of the Qarmatians, and declined rapidly under the Hamdanids in the 940s. From the late 10th century to the early 12th it was controlled by Bedouin dynasties such as the Banu Numayr. Under the Zangid and Ayyubid dynasties it flourished again on agriculture and industry, and the blue-glazed Raqqa ware dates from then. The Mongol invasions of the 1260s destroyed it. The Ottomans established a garrison there in 1864, which began the revival of the modern city.

Raqqa is a city of Syria on the Euphrates. Its growth in the 1950s was stimulated by a worldwide cotton boom, and cotton is still the main agricultural product of the region. The Baghdad Gate, the Qasr al-Banat and the Abbasid walls and mosque are among the surviving monuments. From 2014 to 2017 the city was the capital of the Islamic State. The Raqqa Museum held many cuneiform tablets, some excavated at Tell Sabi Abyad, which survive today as casts and 3D reconstructions.
ras-al-khaimah: The name Ras Al Khaimah means 'Headland of the Tent'. The Arabic word khaimah means tent, but it also refers to the palm frond or areesh houses that were common in the area. A creek divides the city into two parts, the old town in the west and Al Nakheel in the east.

The site has been continuously inhabited for 7,000 years, with finds dating back to the Neolithic. The city succeeded the port and trading hub of Julfar, which was a separate settlement with its own history and was abandoned in the early 17th century as Ras Al Khaimah rose. Julfar itself had a predecessor, Kush, in the suburbs to the north.

The navigator and cartographer Ibn Majid came from the town, and his writing suggests that it was already called Ras Al Khaimah, having eclipsed Julfar as the principal port of the Shimal coast. From 1507 the city came under Portuguese control. In the early 18th century the Qawasim, the Al Qasimi, established themselves at Ras Al Khaimah and Sharjah and became a significant maritime force with holdings on both the Persian and Arabian coasts, often in conflict with British shipping.

After attacks on shipping the British mounted the Persian Gulf campaign of 1809, which largely destroyed the Al Qasimi fleet; the expedition ended on 14 November with British casualties of five killed and 34 wounded. An arrangement of 1815 broke down, and in November 1819 a second expedition under Major-General William Keir Grant bombarded the town and stormed it on 9 December, finding it nearly deserted.

At Dhayah Fort, 398 men and some 400 women and children held out for three days before they surrendered on 22 December. The General Maritime Treaty of 1820, which called for the end of piracy and slavery, laid the foundation of the British protectorate over the Trucial States, which lasted until 1 December 1971.

Ras Al Khaimah became fully independent of Sharjah in 1869. It was part of Sharjah again from September 1900 until 7 July 1921. Under Sheikh Saqr bin Mohammad Al Qasimi it was the last of the Trucial States to join the United Arab Emirates, on 10 February 1972, following the Iranian seizure of Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs.

Ras Al Khaimah is an industrial port city and the capital of the Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates. Arabic is the language of the government-funded schools, and the city also has Indian schools and several colleges, among them the American University of Ras Al Khaimah and the Ras Al Khaimah Medical and Health Sciences University.
rashi: Rashi was an only child, born at Troyes in Champagne, in northern France. His mother's brother, Simeon bar Isaac, was rabbi of Mainz. According to tradition his father, Yitzhak, brought him to learn Torah at the age of five and remained his main teacher until his death. At seventeen Rashi married and went to study in Worms at the yeshiva of Yaakov ben Yakar. When Yaakov died in 1064 he studied for another year under his relative Isaac ben Eliezer Halevi, then moved to Mainz to study under Isaac ben Judah.

His teachers were students of Gershom ben Judah, and he was also influenced by the exegetical principles of Menahem Kara. Jewish oral tradition holds that he was a vintner; there is no evidence for it, though his writings show extensive knowledge of winemaking.

Rashi returned to Troyes at the age of 25 and joined the beth din, the rabbinical court. He began answering halakhic questions, and on the death of its head, Zerach ben Abraham, led the court. Around 1070 he founded a yeshiva that attracted many disciples. In 1096 the People's Crusade swept through Lorraine, murdering 12 Jews and uprooting whole communities, and among those killed at Worms were three sons of his teacher Isaac ben Eliezer Halevi. Rashi wrote penitential poems mourning the slaughter, seven of which survive.

He had no sons. His three daughters married his disciples, and most present-day Ashkenazi rabbinical dynasties trace their descent to Miriam or Yocheved. Yocheved's sons Rashbam, Rivam and Rabbeinu Tam were among the most prolific Tosafists. Rashi died on 13 July 1105 and was buried in Troyes.

Rashi wrote the first comprehensive commentary on the Talmud, covering 30 of the 39 tractates of the Babylonian Talmud. It explains each passage phrase by phrase and translates difficult words into the spoken Old French of his day. It has been included in every edition since the first printing. His commentary on the Tanakh, which covers all books except Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah, concentrates on grammar and word choice and seeks the plain meaning, or peshat, together with such rabbinic interpretations as fit the words. It was accepted as authoritative by Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities alike.

About 300 of his responsa survive. His commentary on the Chumash is the basis of more than 300 supercommentaries. The French monk Nicholas de Lyra, called the ape of Rashi, relied on it in a work that was among the sources for Luther's Bible.
rashid-al-din-hamadani: Rashid al-Din was born in 1247 into a Persian Jewish family from the province of Hamadan. His grandfather had been a courtier to Hulagu Khan, founder of the Ilkhanate, and his father was an apothecary at the court. He converted to Islam around the age of thirty. He trained as a physician and entered service under Hulagu's son Abaqa Khan, rose to be grand vizier, and served as vizier and physician under the Ilkhans Ghazan and Öljaitü. He kept the office of vizier until 1316.

Ghazan commissioned the Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh, the Compendium of Chronicles. It began as a history of the Mongols and their dynasty and grew into a history of the world from Adam to Rashid al-Din's own time. He was helped by Bolad, a Mongol nobleman and the Great Khan's emissary at the Ilkhanid court, and the work was completed between 1307 and 1316. Its first volume covers the Turkish and Mongol tribes and the Mongol conquests from Genghis Khan to the end of Ghazan's reign; the second describes the peoples with whom the Mongols fought or exchanged embassies. A third volume, on historical geography, is lost or was never finished.

The work includes a history of the Franks and, in twenty chapters, the most extensive and well-informed presentation of Buddhism in any Muslim source. Abu al-Qasim Kashani claimed that he was the true author, and the work is generally considered a collective effort, partly carried out by research assistants.

In 1314 Öljaitü died and power passed to his son Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, who sided with Rashid al-Din's rival Taj-al-Din Ali-Shah Jilani. In 1318 Rashid al-Din was charged with having poisoned Öljaitü and was executed on 13 July. His Jewish ancestry was referred to repeatedly at court. His property was confiscated and the Rab'-e Rashidi, his scriptorium with its precious copies, passed to the Mongol soldiery. His son Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad briefly served as vizier after him. A century later, in the reign of Timur's son Miran Shah, his bones were dug up from the Muslim cemetery and reburied in the Jewish one.
rashid-ali-al-gaylani: Rashid Ali was the son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab al-Gailani and belonged to a prominent Baghdad family whose name points to an origin in Gilan in Iran and which traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad; he also descended from Circassian governors of the Ottoman period. He studied at the law school in Baghdad and practised as a lawyer before entering politics.

In 1924 Yasin al-Hashimi made him minister of justice in his first government, and he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies in 1925 and 1926. Both men were nationalists opposed to any British part in Iraq's internal politics. They rejected the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty signed by the government of Nuri as-Said in 1930 and formed the Party of National Brotherhood. Gaylani was prime minister for the first time from March to November 1933.

He returned to the premiership on 31 March 1940, after the early death of King Ghazi, when Emir Abdul-Illah was regent for the four-year-old Faisal II. Gaylani refused Allied troops passage through Iraq, rejected calls to break with Fascist Italy and sent his justice minister, Naji Shawkat, to Ankara, where on 5 July 1940 he met the German ambassador, Franz von Papen. Britain imposed economic sanctions, and under pressure from the regent he resigned on 31 January 1941.

With the Golden Square he then planned to assassinate the regent, who discovered the plot on 31 March and fled. The coup followed on 1 April, and on 3 April a National Defence Government took office under Gaylani. He sent artillery against the RAF base at Habbaniya. On 2 May the base's commander struck first at the Iraqi positions; within a week the Iraqis left the escarpment, and British forces advanced through Fallujah on Baghdad. Gaylani fled to Iran on 30 May. An armistice was signed the next day, and the regent returned on 1 June. Immediately afterwards the Farhud, a violent pogrom against Jews, took place in Baghdad.

After British and Soviet forces invaded Iran on 25 August 1941 he went on to Italy and then Berlin, where Adolf Hitler received him and he was recognised as leader of an Iraqi government in exile. On Germany's defeat he found refuge in Saudi Arabia. He returned to Iraq only after the revolution of 1958 that overthrew the monarchy, plotted a revolt against the government of Abdul Karim Kassem and was sentenced to death. Pardoned in July 1961, he lived in Lebanon, where he died on 28 August 1965 at the age of 72.
rashidun-caliphate: According to the traditional account, Muhammad began receiving what Muslims consider divine revelations in 610 CE and migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. By his death in 632 CE almost all the tribes of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam, but Muslim leaders disagreed over who should lead the community. The Rashidun caliphs were not hereditary rulers: they were chosen by a small group of prominent members of the Quraysh tribe in shūrā, or consultation, or nominated by their predecessor, as Umar was by Abu Bakr.

Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close companion and father-in-law, was chosen first caliph in Medina and reigned from 632 to 634. Umar ruled from 634 to 644, Uthman from 644 to 656, and Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, from 656 to 661. The term Rashidun, meaning rightly guided, comes from Sunni doctrine. Shi'a Muslims accept only Ali as a legitimate caliph.

After suppressing rebellions in Arabia, Abu Bakr sent Khalid ibn al-Walid into Sasanian-controlled Iraq in 633 with an army of 18,000, and Khalid won four battles in succession before the city of Hira fell. Under Umar the caliphate expanded at an unprecedented rate and took more than two-thirds of the Byzantine Empire and nearly the whole of the Sasanian Empire; Uthman's reign completed the conquest of Persia in 651. The conquests are explained partly by the exhaustion of both empires in the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602 to 628.

Umar allowed local administrations of conquered lands to continue much as before, appointing a governor with full powers over each province. Dhimmis, meaning Jews, Zoroastrians and Christians, kept their religion and a measure of autonomy in return for paying the jizya. Uthman was assassinated in June 656 and Ali's accession led to the First Fitna, in which the governor of Syria, Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, refused to recognise him until Uthman's killers were punished.

The Battle of Siffin between Ali's Iraqi army and Mu'awiya's Syrian forces ended in stalemate and an inconclusive arbitration, after which the Kharijites seceded. A Kharijite assassinated Ali in 661. Mu'awiya then invaded Iraq, obliged Ali's son Hasan to abdicate and founded the Umayyad Caliphate. Three of the four caliphs died by assassination.

Later historians wrote of this period as a golden age, and Sunni tradition holds it second in sanctity only to Muhammad's lifetime. Some scholars, among them Donner and Chamieh, write that the community came to regard the four as rightly guided only after memories of the fighting had faded.
rasht: Rasht is the capital of Gilan province, of Rasht County and of its district, and the largest city on Iran's Caspian Sea coast. It lies between the coast and the mountains, and the climate is humid subtropical and among the wettest in Iran, with average humidity above 80 percent. A temperate rainforest lies to its south, in contrast to the mostly arid rest of the country. Its nickname is the City of Silver Rain. The name has several explanations: the word resh, meaning very light rain; the verb reshtan, to spin, from the silk thread trade; or a low, sunken place, from an early market called rasht bazar. The people are mostly Gilaks, who speak the Rashti variety of Western Gilaki.

Rasht was first mentioned in Umayyad historical documents in 682 CE. The Hudud al-'Alam, a tenth-century geography, names it as a district. Its modern history dates to the Safavid era, when it was a major centre of the silk trade with many textile workshops. Cossacks under Stenka Razin plundered it in 1669, an earthquake destroyed it in 1714, and Russia occupied it from 1722 to 1732. In the Qajar period it became the gateway to Europe for Iran, trading with Russia through the port of Bandar-e Anzali; Russian, British, French and Ottoman consulates opened there. A Russian visitor at the end of 1860 counted 5,463 houses, 22 mosques and 27,314 people. The plague devastated the city in 1901.

People of Rasht played a prominent part in the Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1907, and Mīrzā Kūchak Khān, a leader of its Jangali movement, was born there. In 1920, after the defeat of the constitutional forces, he and Iranian communists established a short-lived socialist republic in Gilan, supported at first by the Russian Red Army, with its capital at Rasht. The Soviet government withdrew its support, internal conflicts divided the republic, and the Iranian army under Reza Shah defeated it. Iran's first public library, first girls' school and first fire station are said to have been built in Rasht, and the Nasim-e-Shomal newspaper was first published there. Its first university was established in 1974.

The 2016 census counted 679,995 people in the city, the most populous in northern Iran. Rasht is a major trade centre between Caucasia, Russia and Iran, using the port of Bandar-e Anzali, and the surrounding plain is the most important rice-growing region of Iran. The resort village of Masouleh lies in the nearby mountains. In 2015 UNESCO admitted Rasht to its network of creative cities for gastronomy. Its cuisine includes Mirza Ghassemi, and Rasht embroidery is a local handicraft. The Rosa 'de Rescht', a rose reported in England at the end of the nineteenth century, was rediscovered near the city by Nancy Lindsay in 1945.
rashtriya-swayamsevak-sangh: K. B. Hedgewar, a doctor in Nagpur, founded the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh in 1925, to propagate the ideology of Hindutva and give what it called new physical strength to the majority community. Its initial aim was character training and 'Hindu discipline' in order to unite the Hindu community and establish a Hindu Rashtra, a Hindu nation. After Tilak died in 1920, Hedgewar and other followers of Tilak in Nagpur parted ways with Gandhi, whose stance on the Khilafat Movement concerned them and whose Congress did not take up cow protection. Hedgewar was jailed for a year in 1921 on a charge of sedition.

The 1920s saw Hindu-Muslim relations deteriorate, with the Moplah rebellion of August 1921 and riots in Nagpur in 1923. Christophe Jaffrelot describes a theme of stigmatisation and emulation: Muslims, Christians and the British were treated as foreign bodies, and Hindu nationalists copied what they saw as the source of their strength, such as paramilitary organisation and unity. The Hindu Mahasabha was an important influence.

The organisation kept apart from political organisations then fighting British rule, and it did not take part in the independence movement against British rule. During the Partition it helped Hindu refugees fleeing West Punjab, and its activists also took part in communal violence in North India. It was banned briefly in Punjab Province in January 1947, and after independence three times: in 1948, after Nathuram Godse, a member, assassinated Mahatma Gandhi; during the Emergency of 1975 to 1977; and after the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992.

In a letter of December 1947 Jawaharlal Nehru called it a private army proceeding on the strictest Nazi lines. It at first did not recognise the national flag or the Constitution of India, and its magazine Organiser criticised the Constitution on 30 November 1949 for not mentioning the Manusmriti. In 1954 its volunteers took part in the removal of Portuguese rule from Dadra and Nagar Haveli.

The RSS has no formal membership. Men and boys join by attending the nearest shakha, or branch, which is the basic unit, and women are not allowed to join. It is the progenitor and leader of a large body of Hindutva organisations, the Sangh Parivar, which includes the Bharatiya Janata Party. Its affiliated organisations have set up numerous schools, charities and clubs. Its supporters describe an aim of upholding Indian culture and its civilisational values, while critics accuse it of intolerance of minorities, particularly Muslims.
rastafari: Rastafari developed out of the legacy of the Atlantic slave trade and of British rule in Jamaica, where slavery was abolished in 1834 but racial prejudice remained. It drew on Christian Revivalism, Ethiopianism and the Back-to-Africa movement promoted by black nationalists such as Marcus Garvey. Haile Selassie was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, and several Jamaican clergymen said that his coronation fulfilled prophecies in the Book of Revelation, the Book of Daniel and the Psalms. Street preachers including Leonard Howell, Archibald Dunkley, Robert Hinds and Joseph Hibbert began to teach that he was the returned Jesus, first in Kingston and then across a Jamaica hit hard by the Great Depression. The movement grew among poor and disenfranchised Afro-Jamaicans.

Rastafari is an Abrahamic religion with no central authority and much diversity among its followers. Its beliefs rest on a reading of the Christian Bible. Rastas worship one God, Jah, a shortened form of Jehovah, who is held to dwell within each person, and they speak of knowing Jah rather than believing in him. They give Haile Selassie central importance: many see him as the Second Coming of Jesus and Jah incarnate, while others regard him as a human prophet. Rastas call the Western world Babylon, where the African diaspora lives in exile, and they see Zion, meaning Ethiopia or Africa more broadly, as the ideal to which they aspire.

Their way of life is called livity. It includes ital food, often grown organically and avoiding pork and crustaceans, and dreadlocks, which Rastas link to the Book of Numbers and to the hair of Samson. Communal meetings, called groundings, feature drumming, chanting, hymns and poetry, and the smoking of cannabis, the movement's principal ritual. Rastas also use their own speech, called Iyaric or dread talk, which developed in Jamaica in the 1940s.

For its first thirty years Rastafari had a conflictual relationship with the Jamaican authorities. Police arrested Rastas for cannabis possession, and in 1958 militants tried unsuccessfully to capture Kingston and Spanish Town in the name of Haile Selassie. The Coral Gardens incident of 1963 caused several deaths, and in 1964 the government passed tougher cannabis laws. In the 1960s and 1970s the movement won greater respectability in Jamaica, and the worldwide popularity of reggae, above all Bob Marley, introduced Rastafari themes to audiences abroad. Many Rastas resented the commercialising of their faith by those who listened to reggae without sharing its beliefs.

The movement has no single leader. Its main branches, called mansions, are the House of Nyabinghi, the Bobo Ashanti and the Twelve Tribes of Israel. An estimated 700,000 to 1 million Rastas live worldwide, with the largest population in Jamaica, and communities exist in Britain, North America, Ghana, Ethiopia, Australia and New Zealand.
rastatt: Rastatt is a town in the district of Rastatt in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It lies in the Upper Rhine Plain, on the Murg River, 6 kilometres above the river's junction with the Rhine. Close to the Black Forest and the French border, it has a Baroque core.

Until the end of the 17th century Rastatt held little influence. After the French destroyed it in 1689 it was rebuilt on a larger scale by Louis William, Margrave of Baden, the Imperial general in the Great Turkish War, who was popularly known as Türkenlouis. The town remained the residence of the Margraves of Baden-Baden until 1771. It was the location of the First and Second Congress of Rastatt. The first gave rise to the Treaty of Rastatt, which belongs to the War of the Spanish Succession, while the second ended in failure in 1799.

In the 1840s fortifications were built around the town to form the Fortress of Rastatt, and for about 20 years before 1866 it was occupied by troops of the German Confederation. The Baden Revolution of 1849 began with a mutiny of soldiers at Rastatt in May of that year, under Ludwik Mieroslawski and Gustav Struve, and ended there a few weeks later with the capture of the town by Prussia. For some years Rastatt was one of the strongest fortresses of the German Empire, until its fortifications were dismantled in 1890. In the same year the railway station was moved closer to the centre of the town.

Between 1946 and 1954 about 20 major criminal proceedings, known as the Rastatt Trials, took place before the Tribunal Général of the French Military Administration. They concerned crimes against foreign workers and prisoners in the smaller camps of the National Socialist camp system in south-western Germany, and involved more than 2,000 defendants.

Rastatt has a population of around 51,000. Its historical buildings include the palaces of Schloss Rastatt and Schloss Favorite. A Mercedes-Benz car factory began production in the town in 1992. Rastatt also appears in literature: the historical novel The Lenz Papers by Stefan Heym, published in London in 1964, is set there in 1849, during the failed revolutions in Germany.
ratzeburg: Ratzeburg is surrounded by four lakes, and the isthmuses between them form the access lanes to the town. It is the capital of the district of Herzogtum Lauenburg in Schleswig-Holstein. The town was founded in the 11th century as Racisburg, a name traditionally derived from the local Wendish ruler, Prince Ratibor of the Polabians, who was nicknamed Ratse.

In 1044 Christian missionaries led by the monk Ansverus came to the region and built a monastery, which a pagan rebellion destroyed in 1066; the monks were stoned to death. Ansverus was canonised in the 12th century and his relics were entombed in the cathedral. Henry the Lion became ruler of the town in 1143 and founded a bishopric in 1154. He also had the late Romanesque cathedral built in the north German red-brick style. From 1180 part of the diocese formed a prince-bishopric, the last state in northern Germany to remain Catholic, which turned Lutheran in 1554.

The town itself lay outside the prince-bishopric, in the old Duchy of Saxony, and became part of Saxe-Lauenburg around 1296, staying with that duchy until 1876. In 1619 the capital of Saxe-Lauenburg moved to Ratzeburg from Lauenburg on the Elbe. In 1693 Christian V of Denmark bombarded the town into rubble in an unsuccessful attempt to win the dukedom from the House of Hanover; it was rebuilt in the baroque style, but the castle was never rebuilt. After the Second Schleswig War of 1864 the estates offered the dukedom to the Prussian Hohenzollern dynasty, and on 1 July 1876 the duchy merged into the Kingdom of Prussia's Province of Schleswig-Holstein.

The Romanesque cathedral survives, and monuments in two of the town's churches commemorate the missionaries of 1066. From 1945 to 1989 the Iron Curtain ran just east of the town, which stood on the border with the German Democratic Republic. The sculptor Ernst Barlach made his home in Ratzeburg and is buried in one of its cemeteries.
raul-alfonsin: Raúl Ricardo Alfonsín was born on 12 March 1927 in Chascomús, 123 kilometres south of Buenos Aires. His parents were shopkeepers. He attended the General San Martín Military Lyceum, because his father thought a military school would match a private school in quality at less cost. Alfonsín disliked the military, but the schooling helped him understand its outlook. He did not pursue a military career and studied law at the National University of La Plata and the University of Buenos Aires.

He joined the Radical Civic Union, in the faction of Ricardo Balbín, and was elected to the legislature of Buenos Aires Province in 1958. During the National Reorganization Process he opposed both sides of the Dirty War and filed writs of habeas corpus on behalf of victims of forced disappearance. After Balbín's death he became leader of the party and won the 1983 election.

Alfonsín governed from 10 December 1983 as the first democratically elected president after the military regime. Three days after taking office he sent Congress a bill to revoke the military's self-amnesty law and ordered cases against guerrilla leaders and the heads of the juntas. He set up the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, whose Nunca más report documented the scope of the crimes, and the Trial of the Juntas followed. Discontent in the army led to the Carapintada mutinies, which he answered with the full stop law and the law of Due Obedience.

His government settled the Beagle dispute, increased trade with Brazil and legalised divorce in 1987, over the opposition of the Church. It clashed with the trade unions, which Peronism still controlled. The UCR lost its legislative majority in 1987, and the Austral plan and the Spring plan failed to bring inflation under control. After the Peronist Carlos Menem won the 1989 election, Alfonsín handed over power on 8 July, five months earlier than scheduled.

Alfonsín led the UCR again in later years and negotiated the Pact of Olivos with Menem, which set the terms for the constitutional amendment of 1994. Historians disagree about it: Félix Luna thought it a necessary evil, while Miguel Angel de Marco and Fernando Rocchi saw it as the biggest mistake of his career. He died of lung cancer on 31 March 2009, aged 82, and was buried in La Recoleta Cemetery.
The same historians praise his role in the aftermath of the Dirty War and the restoration of democracy. He received the Princess of Asturias Award for international cooperation in 1985.
ravi-shankar: Ravi Shankar was born Robindro Shaunkor Chowdhury on 7 April 1920 in Benares, now Varanasi, into a Bengali Hindu family, the youngest of seven brothers. His father, Shyam Shankar Chowdhury, a barrister, served as dewan of Jhalawar State and later worked in London. At the age of 10 Shankar went to Paris with the dance group of his brother, the choreographer Uday Shankar, and toured Europe and the United States in the early and mid-1930s. On tour he was sporadically taught by Allauddin Khan, the court musician of Maihar, who offered serious training on condition that he give up touring.

In 1938 Shankar left dancing and went to Maihar, where he lived with Khan's family and learned the sitar and surbahar, studying with Khan's children Ali Akbar Khan and Annapurna Devi. He made his sitar debut in December 1939. After finishing his studies in 1944 he moved to Mumbai, and from 1949 to 1956 was music director of All India Radio in New Delhi, where he founded the Indian National Orchestra. He also composed the music for Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy.

He resigned in 1956 to tour the United Kingdom, Germany and the United States, and recorded the album Three Ragas in London that year. The Beatles' guitarist George Harrison took lessons from him in India in 1966 and 1968, and the friendship helped bring Indian instruments into Western pop music. Shankar played at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 and at the Concert for Bangladesh in August 1971, whose live album won him a Grammy Award. He sat in the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of India's Parliament, from 1986 to 1992.

Shankar gave his last concert with his daughter, the sitarist Anoushka Shankar, on 4 November 2012 in Long Beach, California, and died on 11 December 2012 in San Diego at the age of 92. His other daughter is the singer Norah Jones.

His concerts opened with a slow alap, jor and jhala shaped by the dhrupad tradition, followed by a tabla section in the khyal style. He introduced at least 31 ragas and popularised the jugalbandi duet format. Among his honours were the Bharat Ratna in 1999, the Polar Music Prize in 1998 and four Grammy Awards.
razia-sultan: Razia was the eldest daughter of Shamsuddin Iltutmish, an Ilbari Turkic slave (mamluk) of his predecessor Qutb ud-Din Aibak, and probably his first-born child. Her mother, Turkan Khatun, was a daughter of Aibak. Iltutmish had groomed his eldest son, Nasiruddin Mahmud, as his successor, but the son died unexpectedly in 1229.

Minhaj-i-Siraj is the only near-contemporary source for the story that Iltutmish ordered a decree naming Razia his heir and told doubting nobles that she was more capable than his sons. He did not witness it: he was in Gwalior and did not return to Delhi until 1238. After Iltutmish died the nobles appointed his son Ruknuddin Firuz, and the story may have been circulated by Razia's supporters after her accession.

Ruknuddin left the administration to his mother, Shah Turkan. Their blinding and execution of Iltutmish's popular son Qutubuddin led several nobles to rebel. While Ruknuddin marched against them, Shah Turkan planned to execute Razia. At a congregational prayer Razia roused the people of Delhi, a mob attacked the palace and detained Shah Turkan, and nobles and the army pledged allegiance to Razia. Ruknuddin was imprisoned and probably executed on 19 November 1236.

Turkic nobles opposed her from the start, since she had come to power through the support of Delhi's people rather than that of the provincial governors. The wazir Nizamul Mulk Muhammad Junaidi and four Turkic nobles marched against her. Razia led an army out of Delhi and camped on the Yamuna; two of the rebels joined her, and the others were captured, killed or fled. She appointed Malik Jamaluddin Yaqut as Amir-i Akhur. On 5 March 1237 the Qarmatian leader Nuruddin Turk and his followers entered the Jama masjid in Delhi and began killing Sunnis at the Friday prayers, before being killed themselves.

The nobles who backed Razia had meant her to be a figurehead, but she asserted herself. Her first coins carried her father's name, and by 1237–1238 she issued them in her own. According to Isami she at first observed purdah, but later appeared in public in male dress and rode elephants through Delhi. Her appointment of non-Turkic officers, above all the Abyssinian Yaqut, angered Turkic officers, and several chroniclers blame her closeness to Yaqut for her fall. In April 1240 her army at Tabarhinda rebelled, killed Yaqut and imprisoned her.

Delhi's nobles set Muizuddin Bahram, a son of Iltutmish, on the throne. Razia married the rebel Ikhtiyaruddin Altunia in September 1240 and tried to win the throne back, but they were defeated by Bahram in October and killed soon after. Her grave lies near Turkman Gate in Old Delhi, and Ibn Batuta records that her tomb had become a pilgrimage centre.
recife: Recife stands on the northeastern Atlantic coast of Brazil, at the confluence of the Beberibe and Capibaribe rivers before they drain into the South Atlantic. The city is formed by three islands, Recife, Santo Antônio and Boa Vista, with other rivers including the Jiquiá, Tejipió, Jordão and Pina. More than 50 bridges link them, and the city is often called the Venice of Brazil. Its name alludes to the stone reefs that lie offshore. The climate is tropical monsoon, warm to hot with high humidity throughout the year, relieved by trade winds from the ocean.

Recife began as a collection of fishing shacks, inns and warehouses on the delta between the two rivers, in the captaincy of Pernambuco, sometime between 1535 and 1537, in the earliest days of Portuguese colonisation of the land later called Brazil. It was a settlement of fishermen and a way station for Portuguese sailors and passing ships. It became the main harbour of the Captaincy of Pernambuco, known for its large-scale production of sugar cane.

Portuguese rule lasted from the founding to 1630. The Dutch West India Company then held the city from 1630 to 1654, when it was known as Mauritsstad and served as the capital of the colony of New Holland in Dutch Brazil. Portuguese rule resumed in 1654 and continued through the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves (1815 to 1822), the Empire of Brazil (1822 to 1889) and the Republic of Brazil from 1889. Many places of significance in the city date to both the Portuguese and Dutch periods. Football in Pernambuco began in 1902, when English and Dutch sailors landed at Recife and played a game on the beach.

Recife is the capital of the state of Pernambuco and its largest city, with 1,488,920 residents at the 2022 census and a metropolitan population of 3,726,974. It is a major seaport and the most important commercial hub of the north and northeast of Brazil. The Federal University of Pernambuco is the largest university in the state. The Historic Centre of Olinda, 7 kilometres to the north, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, and the carnivals of Recife and Olinda are nationally known. Frevo and maracatu are characteristic music and dance of the region.
recklinghausen: Recklinghausen is the northernmost city of the Ruhr area and the capital of the Recklinghausen district. It borders the rural Münsterland, and its landscape is characterised by large fields and farms in the north and industry in the south. Its Westphalian name is Riäkelhusen. The city is linked to the larger waterways by the Rhein-Herne-Kanal, and the motorways A2 and A43 cross its area.

The settlement was first mentioned in 1017 as Ricoldinchuson. In 1236 it received town privileges, and Jews are recorded there as early as 1305. As part of the County of Vest, its ownership changed several times in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and in 1576 the whole county was pawned to the Elector of Cologne. In 1582–83, and again in 1586 and 1587, partisan armies plundered the city during the Cologne War, a feud over religious parity in the Electorate of Cologne and electoral influence in the Holy Roman Empire.

More than 100 witchcraft trials were held in Recklinghausen between 1514 and 1710, with peaks in 1580–81 and 1588–89. The last person convicted was Anna Spickermann, who spent 16 months in prison and was sentenced to death by the sword and then burned. Around 1600 the administration of the Vest was divided in two, and Recklinghausen administered the eastern part. From 1803 to 1811 it was the capital of a sovereign principality of the Dukes of Arenberg, and around 1815 the Vest became a Bürgermeisterei with the town as its seat. Herten joined it in 1819 and Erkenschwick in 1821.

During World War II a prisoner-of-war camp, Stalag XX-B, was founded there in December 1939 but moved after a few days, and a forced labour camp operated from 1941 to 1943. The RAF bombed oil production at Recklinghausen on 15 January 1945, and the US 137th Infantry captured the south of the city on 1 April 1945.

Recklinghausen has a museum of icons, founded in 1956, which holds more than 1,000 Orthodox works from Russia, Greece and the Balkan countries as well as early Coptic Christian art from Egypt; it is the largest such museum outside the Orthodox world. The Ruhrfestspiele, a cultural festival with an international reputation, takes place every year from 1 May, with its main stage at the Ruhrfestspielhaus. A sculpture by Henry Moore stands there, and a large brick sculpture by Per Kirkeby stands at the Lohtor before a memorial to the dead of the First World War. The central station is served by Intercity and EuroCity trains.
reconquista: In 711 a predominantly Berber army under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and defeated the Visigothic King Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete, at a time of severe division in the Visigothic kingdom. In the north, a Visigothic nobleman named Pelagius was chosen leader of the Asturians and led an uprising. Traditional historiography dates the start of the Reconquista to his victory at Covadonga, about a decade after the conquest began, where the army of the Kingdom of Asturias won its first victory over the forces of the Umayyad Caliphate. Medieval writers did not use the word Reconquista; it developed in modern historiography.

The northern realms grew from mountain strongholds into the kingdoms of León, Castile, Navarre and Aragon, with Portugal proclaimed in 1139. The Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba fell apart in civil wars by 1031 into up to 34 small taifa kingdoms, which often paid tribute called parias to the Christian kings. Alfonso VI of León and Castile took Toledo in 1085. The Almoravids, called in by the taifa rulers, defeated him at Sagrajas in 1086 and halted the Christian advance, and the Almohads later took over most of al-Andalus.

A Christian coalition defeated the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Córdoba fell in 1236 and Seville in 1248, and by 1252 only the Emirate of Granada remained. Christian rulers often fought each other or allied with Muslim kings. Ferdinand and Isabella waged the Granada War from 1482, and Granada surrendered on 2 January 1492.

After Granada's surrender the whole peninsula was under Christian rulers. On 30 July 1492 some 200,000 Jews of Castile and Aragon were forcibly expelled. Muslims in Castile, Navarre and Aragon were forced to convert by edicts between 1499 and 1526, and from 1609 decrees expelled them from Habsburg Spain; about three million Muslims emigrated or were driven out between 1492 and 1610.

In the nineteenth century Spanish historiography consolidated the idea of a single continuous Reconquista, tied to Spanish nationalism. Recent scholarship describes it as a process of several episodes that varied by region and questions the national myth. The festivals called moros y cristianos, held especially in towns of the Valencian Community, still recreate the fighting as parades.
records-of-the-grand-historian: The work was begun by Sima Tan, Grand Historian (Taishi) of the Han court in the late 2nd century BCE, who drafted plans for it and left fragments and notes that may have been incorporated into the final text. After his death in 110 BCE it was continued and completed by his son and successor Sima Qian, who is generally credited as its author. Its original title was Taishigongshu; the name Shiji, 'Historical Records', was originally used for any historical text and came to mean this work only after the Three Kingdoms period.

Sima Qian had access to the early Han archives and to ancient books on bamboo and wooden slips, many now lost. He also interviewed people and travelled across China to check what he was told, and he often names his sources. He noted that records were fragmentary and contradictory, and in one chapter wrote that he had set down only what was certain and left doubtful cases blank.

The Shiji runs to about 526,500 Chinese characters in 130 chapters, in five sections. The twelve Basic Annals cover periods and dynasties, then rulers from the First Emperor of Qin to the early Han, and include de facto rulers such as Xiang Yu and Empress Dowager Lü. Ten chapters of Tables give reigns and lineages in chronological form, and eight Treatises deal with ritual, music, the calendar, astronomy, sacrifices, rivers and canals, and finance.

The Hereditary Houses hold accounts of the leading states of the Zhou period, such as Qin and Lu, and biographies from the Han. The Ranked Biographies make up 42 per cent of the work and profile about 130 men, from Boyi and Laozi to Sima Qian's near contemporaries, some in groups such as assassins or Confucian scholars. They use anecdotes to show character and have supplied many set phrases (chengyu) still used in Chinese.

The Shiji is the first of the Twenty-Four Histories and set the model for later dynastic histories. Sima Qian has been observed to place favourable material in the annals of rulers and less favourable matter in other chapters, so the work must be read as a whole. Scholars doubt the historicity of its earliest rulers, the Five Emperors. Joseph Needham noted, however, that twenty-three of the thirty Shang rulers' names appear on the Anyang oracle bones.

After about 91 BCE the manuscript was hidden in the house of Sima Qian's daughter, and it was made public under Emperor Xuan by his grandson Yang Yun. Other writers added to it, such as Chu Shaosun, and ten chapters were lost in the Eastern Han and later reconstructed. The earliest printed editions are of the Song dynasty.
red-army: The Workers' and Peasants' Red Army was the army and air force of the Russian Soviet Republic and, from 1922, of the Soviet Union. It was established in January 1918 by a decree of the Council of People's Commissars to oppose the forces of the new state's adversaries in the Russian Civil War, above all the groups known together as the White Army. In September 1917 Vladimir Lenin had written that the standing army should be replaced by the arming of the entire people. The Imperial Russian Army was by then collapsing: the Tsarist general Nikolay Dukhonin estimated 2 million deserters, 1.8 million dead, 5 million wounded and 2 million prisoners.

At first the Red Army was a voluntary formation, without ranks or insignia, and its officers were chosen by democratic election. A decree of 29 May 1918 imposed compulsory military service for men aged 18 to 40.

In 1919 the White armies advanced from the south under General Anton Denikin, from the east under Admiral Aleksandr Kolchak and from the northwest under General Nikolai Yudenich, and at first beat the Red Army back on each front. Leon Trotsky reformed it and counterattacked: Kolchak's army was repelled in June and those of Denikin and Yudenich in October. The Red Army also invaded Poland in the Polish-Soviet War, reaching the centre of the country in 1920 before a decisive defeat at Warsaw ended the war.

In the 1930s the army fought border conflicts with Japan, culminating in the victory at Khalkhin Gol in September 1939. In the Winter War against Finland, which began on 30 November 1939, it had three times as many soldiers as the Finns and a hundred times as many tanks, but its performance was hindered by the Great Purge of 1937, in which more than 30,000 of its officers were executed or imprisoned. Finland held out much longer than the Soviets expected.

In the Second World War, which the Soviets called the Great Patriotic War, the Red Army provided the largest ground force in the Allied victory in Europe and fought the largest and deadliest land war in history. Up to 34 million soldiers served in it. Its performance in the opening stages of Operation Barbarossa was mixed and often poor, but it ultimately broke the Axis front and took Berlin. Its personnel were also involved in Soviet war crimes against civilians and prisoners of war, particularly in Eastern and Central Europe. Officially it lost 8,668,300 killed, missing or dead of disease or in captivity, though other estimates run to almost 11 million.
In February 1946 the Red Army was renamed the Soviet Army. After the dissolution of the Soviet Union it was split between the post-Soviet states, and its bulk became the Russian Ground Forces.
red-fort: Shah Jahan commissioned the fort after deciding to move the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi. Its design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the architect of the Taj Mahal. Supervised by the emperor, it was completed on 6 April 1648. It was originally known as the Blessed Fort, Qila-i-Mubarak, and was adorned in red and white. The later name Lal Qila comes from its red sandstone walls.

The boundary walls are asymmetrical, unlike those of other Mughal forts, so as to contain the older Salimgarh Fort. The fort straddles the Yamuna River, which once fed the moats around most of the walls, and it formed the centrepiece of Shahjahanabad, the city now called Old Delhi. Aurangzeb later added the Moti Masjid, the Pearl Mosque.

The fort is octagonal, with its north to south axis the longer, and is enclosed by 2.41 kilometres of walls that rise from 18 metres on the river side to 33 metres on the city side. The Lahori Gate, named for its orientation towards Lahore, is the main entrance and leads to the Chhatta Chowk, a covered bazaar where silk and jewellery were sold to the imperial household.

The Diwan-i-Aam, the Public Audience Hall, was where the emperor heard matters brought by commoners, such as taxation and inheritance. The Diwan-i-Khas, the Hall of Private Audience, was built of white marble inlaid with precious stones; François Bernier described seeing the Peacock Throne there in the 17th century. The World Heritage Convention calls the fort the zenith of Mughal creativity, combining Persian and Indian traditions.

Nadir Shah of the Afsharid Empire plundered the fort in 1739, seizing its treasures, including the Peacock Throne. After the British defeated the Marathas at the Battle of Delhi, the East India Company installed a resident at the fort. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor to occupy it, became a symbol of the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and was tried in 1858 and exiled to Rangoon.

After the rebellion the British demolished about 80 per cent of the fort's structures, replacing the harem apartments and gardens with stone barracks, though the defensive walls largely survived. Lord Curzon began restoration after 1899. The trials of Indian National Army officers took place there from November 1945, and on 15 August 1947 Jawaharlal Nehru raised the Indian flag above the Lahori Gate. The Red Fort Complex was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
red-river-asia: The Red River, or Hong River, is 1,149 km long. It is also called the Sông Cái, "Main River", in Vietnamese and the Yuan River in Chinese. It begins in the mountains of Yunnan south of Dali and flows south-east through areas of the Yi and Dai peoples, entering Vietnam at Lào Cai province, where it forms part of the border with China. Its main tributaries, the Black River and the Lô River, join it near Việt Trì. Below Việt Trì the river and its distributaries spread out into the Red River Delta, pass Hanoi and empty into the Gulf of Tonkin.

It takes its name from the reddish-brown silt it carries. It is known for violent floods and wide seasonal changes in volume, and the delta, a major agricultural area with much land under rice, is protected by an elaborate network of dikes and levees.

In the 19th century the Red River was thought to be a lucrative trade route to China. Late in the century French explorers travelled up it as far as Manhao in southern Yunnan and then overland towards Kunming. It remained the main commercial route between French Indochina and Yunnan until the Kunming–Haiphong Railway opened in 1910. French steamers could go as far upstream as Lao Cai in the rainy season, but from November to April steamships could not pass Yên Bái, and goods went in small vessels such as junks.

Because of the river, Haiphong was in the early twentieth century the sea port most easily reached from Kunming. Western authorities reckoned the journey at 28 days: 16 by steamer and small boat up the river to Manhao and 12 overland. Yunnan products such as tin came down to Manhao by pack mule. Going upstream from Manhao to Lao Cai was much harder than going down; one report gives 10 hours downstream and 10 days, sometimes a month, in the other direction.
red-sea: The Red Sea is a mediterranean sea lying between the Arabian Peninsula and Africa, an inlet of the Indian Ocean. It connects to the ocean in the south through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden. To the north lie the Sinai Peninsula, the Gulf of Aqaba and the Gulf of Suez, which leads to the Suez Canal. It is about 2,250 km long and 355 km across at its widest point, with an average depth of 490 m and a maximum of 2,730 m in the central Suakin Trough.

The sea lies over the Red Sea Rift, part of the Great Rift Valley. It formed as the Arabian Peninsula split from the Horn of Africa, a movement that began in the Eocene and accelerated in the Oligocene. The sea is still widening and is considered likely to become an ocean in time. With high evaporation, little rain and no significant rivers draining into it, it is one of the saltiest bodies of water in the world.

The earliest known exploration was by the ancient Egyptians, who sought commercial routes to Punt. One such expedition took place around 2500 BCE and another around 1500 BCE, under Hatshepsut. The Book of Exodus tells of the Israelites crossing a sea that the Hebrew text calls Yam Suph, traditionally identified as the Red Sea; Rabbi Saadia Gaon (882 to 942 CE) placed the crossing at the Gulf of Suez.

In the Middle Ages the sea formed an important part of the spice trade route. In 1183 Raynald of Châtillon launched a raid down the sea against Muslim pilgrim convoys, causing fury across the Muslim world, although his target appears to have been the lightly armed convoys rather than the cities of Mecca and Medina. The opening of the Suez Canal in November 1869 let more than a thousand marine species of the Red Sea migrate northward into the Mediterranean.

Six countries border the Red Sea proper: Saudi Arabia and Yemen on the eastern shore, and Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Djibouti on the western. The Gulf of Suez lies wholly within Egypt, while the Gulf of Aqaba borders Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Ships passing between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean shorten the route between Asia and Europe by almost half compared with sailing round Africa. Its shallow shelves hold coral reefs, and more than 1,200 fish species have been recorded, about 10 per cent of them found nowhere else.
red-square: Red Square is one of the oldest and largest squares in Moscow, lying in the historic centre along the eastern wall of the Kremlin and north of the Moskva River. It is almost rectangular, 70 metres wide and 330 metres long, and covers almost 73,000 square metres. It is bounded on the northeast by the GUM department store and the old district of Kitay-gorod, on the northwest by the State Historical Museum and the Resurrection Gate, and on the southeast by Saint Basil's Cathedral. A moat that separated it from the Kremlin was paved over in 1812.

The eastern side of the Kremlin was the most vulnerable to attack, since no river protected it, so the wall was built highest there. Italian architects convinced Ivan the Great to clear the area outside it, and decrees of 1493 and 1495 called for the demolition of all buildings within 110 sazhens of the wall. The square was meant to serve as Moscow's main marketplace and was the site of public ceremonies and proclamations, and occasionally a coronation.

It was once called Pozhar, the burnt-out place, because earlier buildings on the site had burned down. Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich extended the name Red Square, which originally described only the area between Saint Basil's Cathedral, the Spasskaya Tower and the Lobnoye Mesto, to the whole square. In old Russian the word krasnaya meant beautiful.

Under Catherine the Great the upper floor of the market lines was made of stone in 1786. The square was paved in stone in 1804, and after the Napoleonic invasion and the fire of 1812 the moat was filled in 1813 and rows of trees planted. The Monument to Minin and Pozharsky was erected in 1818. The State Historical Museum was built in the years 1875 to 1883.

In the Soviet era Red Square became the official address of the Soviet government and a showcase for military parades from 1919 onward, and Lenin's Mausoleum was part of the square from 1924, serving as a grandstand for dignitaries. In the 1930s the Kazan Cathedral and the Iverskaya Chapel with the Resurrection Gates were demolished to make room for heavy military vehicles; both were rebuilt after the fall of the Soviet Union. A legend holds that Lazar Kaganovich showed Stalin a model of the square without Saint Basil's, and Stalin answered: Lazar, put it back.

Red Square has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990. Apart from the road leading through it to the Savior Gate of the Kremlin, it is a pedestrian zone. It has been the scene of executions, demonstrations, riots, parades and speeches, and its history is reflected in paintings by Vasily Surikov and Konstantin Yuon.
redonda: Redonda is the remnant of an ancient extinct volcano in the Leeward Islands. The island is about 1.6 kilometres long and 0.5 kilometres wide, and 296 metres high at its highest point. It lies 56.2 kilometres south-west of Antigua, 22.5 kilometres north-west of Montserrat and 32 kilometres south-east of Nevis. The land rises mostly as sheer cliffs, especially on the western side, to a tilted area of grassland at the top that slopes to the east. Its land area is hard to estimate because of the steep slopes. There is no fresh water except rain and no safe place to land a boat, which makes the island inhospitable to people.

In 1493, on his second voyage, Christopher Columbus and his crew became the first known Europeans to see the island. He claimed it for the Crown of Castile without landing, and named it Santa María la Redonda, meaning Saint Mary the Round, after its apparent profile seen from the side. Because it offered little to the powers colonising the Americas, it was for centuries a refuge for pirates.

Deposits of phosphate derived from seabird guano were found in the 1860s, and commercial mining began, with labourers from Montserrat. The island was annexed to the British colony of Antigua to regulate extraction, and the Redonda Annexation Act of 1872 formalised the step. The annual yield was up to 7,000 tons, and 120 people lived there in 1901. Aluminium phosphate for gunpowder was mined later, and a cableway carried the material down to the pier.

Mining stopped in 1914 during the First World War. Maintenance workers stayed until 1929, when a hurricane destroyed almost all the remaining facilities, and the island has been uninhabited since. Two stone huts of the mining period still stand. In 1967 Redonda became a dependency of Antigua, now part of Antigua and Barbuda, though Montserrat and Nevis are closer.

Redonda is uninhabited and is a dependency of Saint John, Antigua and Barbuda. It is a breeding colony of seabirds, including red-footed, brown and masked boobies and frigatebirds, and BirdLife International has designated it an Important Bird Area. The Redonda ground dragon and the Redonda anole live only here. Goats and rats introduced to the island harmed its ecology for almost a century, and a restoration programme began in 2016 with the removal of about 60 goats and 6,000 rats. A literary legend, begun by the author M. P. Shiel, claims a Kingdom of Redonda whose title has been passed down since.
reggio-calabria: The history of the area before the Greeks arrived in the eighth century BCE is not reliably known. Mythical accounts name a series of peoples there, among them the Osci, Trojans, Oenotrians, Ligures, Ausones and Sicels, and say the land was first called Saturnia or Neptunia.

The name Italia first referred to the area around Reggio before it spread to southern Calabria and, around the third century BCE, to the whole peninsula. By tradition it comes from Italus, an Oenotrian king. The city has borne many names: Rhegion in Greek times, briefly Phoibeia under Dionysius II of Syracuse, Regium or Rhegium in Latin, Rhegium Julii under the empire, Riyyu under the Emirate of Sicily and Rìsa under the Normans.

In the 5th and 6th centuries the Vandals, Lombards and Goths invaded. Under Byzantine rule Reggio became a metropolis of the Byzantine possessions in Italy and several times the capital of the Duchy of Calabria between 536 and 1060. Spanish Habsburg viceroys governed it from 1504 to 1713.

The 16th and 17th centuries brought decay through taxes, plague, the earthquake of 1562 and Ottoman raids: in 1534 the townspeople fled a fleet under Hayreddin Barbarossa, who captured eight hundred who remained and burned the town, and Barbary pirates took most of the inhabitants as slaves to Tripoli after an attack in 1558. On 21 August 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi took the city from the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

Reggio lies near the fault line where the Eurasian and African plates meet along the Strait of Messina, and earthquakes have destroyed it several times: in 91 BCE, after which Augustus ordered its reconstruction, then in 17 CE, 305, 374, 1562, 1783 and 1908. The quake of 1562 destroyed the medieval port and submerged the promontory of Calamizzi, where the first Greek settlers had landed. The 1783 and 1908 disasters, the second the worst natural calamity in Europe in human memory, produced the present layout of straight, intersecting streets, planned by Giovanbattista Mori in 1784 and Pietro de Nava in 1911.

Reggio Calabria is the largest city of Calabria, on the toe of the Italian peninsula opposite Sicily, with a population of 167,925. Its National Archaeological Museum of Magna Graecia houses the Bronzes of Riace, which have given it the nickname City of Bronzes. It is also called the City of bergamot, which is cultivated only in the region. Travellers who visited it include Pieter Bruegel around 1550, Stendhal in 1817, Edward Lear in 1847 and D. H. Lawrence around 1920.
reggio-emilia: Reggio Emilia lies on a plain crossed by the Crostolo stream, in the region of Emilia-Romagna. Its old town has a hexagonal form that derives from its ancient walls, and its main buildings date from the 16th and 17th centuries. The city began with the construction of the Via Aemilia from Piacenza to Rimini by Marcus Aemilius Lepidus in 187 BCE. It became a judicial centre with a forum first called Regium Lepidi, then simply Regium, which gave the city its name. Its people are called Reggiani, and until 1861 the city was known as Reggio di Lombardia.

In the Roman age Regium was a flourishing municipium with its own statutes, magistrates and art colleges, though by the end of the 4th century Saint Ambrose counted it among the dilapidated cities. It passed through the realm of Odoacer, then came under Ostrogothic control and later to the Lombards, who made it the seat of a duchy, until the Franks took it in 773. In 899 the Magyars heavily damaged it and killed Bishop Azzo II.

Reggio became a free commune about the end of the 11th or the start of the 12th century, belonged to the Lombard League in 1167, and signed the Treaty of Konstanz in 1183. Violent struggles between noble and plebeian parties and between Guelphs and Ghibellines marked the 12th and 13th centuries.

The city then passed between several lords, among them the Gonzaga and the Visconti. In the early 15th century Nicolò III d'Este became its lord, and in 1452 Frederick III made Borso d'Este Duke of Modena and Reggio. The poets Matteo Maria Boiardo and Francesco Guicciardini served as its governors, and Ludovico Ariosto, author of Orlando Furioso, was born there in 1474. Este rule continued until 1796, apart from short interruptions.

French republican troops drove off the ducal garrison on 21 August 1796. Napoleon formed the Cispadane Republic, which was proclaimed in Reggio on 7 January 1797; the Italian tricolour was sewn on that occasion by Reggio women. In the same period the Polish lieutenant Jozef Wybicki composed there the Mazurek Dąbrowskiego, which became the Polish national anthem in 1927. After the Este returned in 1815 and the revolts of 1831 and 1848, Reggio joined united Italy in 1859, confirmed by the plebiscite of 10 March 1860.

Reggio Emilia, with a population of 172,921, is the fourth-largest city in Emilia-Romagna. Jews began to settle there in the early 15th century, and its rabbinic scholars were numerous; an unused synagogue and burial ground remain. The Basilica della Ghiara, begun at the end of the 16th century on a site where a miracle was believed to have occurred, is among its buildings.
rehoboam: According to the Hebrew Bible, Rehoboam was the son and successor of Solomon and a grandson of David, and the last king of the united kingdom of Israel. His mother, Naamah, was an Ammonite, one of the foreign wives whom Solomon married. The biblical account says that Solomon had angered God by marrying foreign women and building shrines to the gods of Moab and Ammon, and that God declared he would tear the kingdom away from Solomon's son. Even before Solomon's death Damascus under Rezon had won independence, and Jeroboam, a superintendent of works, had fled to Egypt.

Rehoboam's reign is told in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, and the Bible gives it as 17 years. The ten northern tribes met at Shechem to proclaim him king and asked for relief from Solomon's burdens. The older men advised him to speak to them civilly, but the young men he had grown up with told him to show no weakness and to tax them more, and he did. Jeroboam and the northern tribes then rebelled and formed a separate kingdom, leaving Rehoboam the Kingdom of Judah with Jerusalem as capital. He raised an army of 180,000 against Israel but was advised not to fight his brethren.

In the fifth year of his reign Shishak, king of Egypt, invaded and took the fortified towns on the approach to Jerusalem. Rehoboam gave him the treasures of the temple, and Judah became a vassal of Egypt. Shishak is generally identified with Shoshenq I, whose record at the Bubastite Portal in Karnak confirms an invasion, though its surviving list does not include Jerusalem.

Rehoboam had 18 wives and 60 concubines, who bore him 28 sons and 60 daughters. His son Abijah succeeded him, and he was buried beside his ancestors in Jerusalem. Outside the Bible there is little evidence of a stable monarchy in Judah in his time, and Christian Frevel suggests that the accounts of Rehoboam and Jeroboam may be a later construction projected back onto the past. In the Gospel of Matthew he appears in the genealogy of Jesus.
reichenau-island: Reichenau lies in Lake Constance almost due west of the city of Konstanz, between the Gnadensee and the Untersee, the two parts of the lake. The island has a land area of 4.3 square kilometres and a circumference of 11 kilometres. It is 4.5 kilometres long and 1.5 kilometres wide at its widest, and its highest point, the Hochwart, stands about 43 metres above the lake. A causeway completed in 1838 connects it to the mainland, crossed by a waterway, the Bruckgraben, which a low road bridge spans.

People lived on Reichenau in the Bronze Age and Iron Age, but archaeological evidence suggests that it was abandoned in the Roman era and stayed empty until 724. In that year the monk Pirmin received the support of the Carolingian ruler Charles Martel to build a monastery. The first monastery, at Mittelzel, was of wood and had been replaced in stone by 746.

In the early 9th century the community flourished under the patronage of the Carolingian and later the Ottonian dynasty. In 816 the monastery church was rebuilt as a cruciform basilica. Two further churches were built, for Saints Peter and Paul, consecrated in 799, and for Saint George, in 896. Relics of Saint Mark arrived at the abbey in the middle of the 9th century.

The abbey produced poets and authors such as Walafrid Strabo, who served as abbot, and scholars such as Hermann of Reichenau and Abbot Reginbert, as well as artists. The Ottonian murals of the miracles of Christ in the church of Saint George are unique survivals from the 10th century, and the Plan of St. Gall, the only surviving architectural drawing from the Middle Ages, may also have been made on the island.

In the 16th century the territory of the Prince-Bishopric of Constance was extended to include Reichenau, and the abbey's influence waned. When the Prince-Bishopric was secularised in 1803, many smaller chapels were demolished, the manuscripts and archives went to Karlsruhe and the University of Heidelberg library, and the surrounding farms were divided up and sold.

The three churches and the abbey were declared a World Heritage Site in 2000. The abbey's bailiff lived in a two-storey stone house to which two more storeys of timber framing were added in the 14th century, one of the oldest timber-frame buildings in southern Germany, now a museum of local history. The island is also known for its vegetable farms, and the Wollmatinger Ried beside it is a large reed wetland and nature reserve where many birds stop on their annual migration.
reichswehr: After Germany's defeat in World War I the Imperial German Army was dissolved to be reshaped into a peacetime army. On 10 November 1918 Chancellor Friedrich Ebert and General Wilhelm Groener concluded the Ebert–Groener Pact. Groener assured Ebert of the armed forces' loyalty; Ebert promised action against leftist uprisings and that the military would keep its command within the professional officer corps and its traditional status as a state within a state, largely independent of civilian government.

A provisional Reichswehr was formed in March 1919. Under Part V of the Treaty of Versailles the army was limited to 100,000 professional soldiers and the navy to 15,000, with no general staff, no air force, no submarines or large warships, and no armoured vehicles or heavy weapons above set calibres. Officers had to serve 25 years and others 12, to prevent a pool of trained reservists. The official formation took place on 1 January 1921, once the limits had been met.

The Republic used the Reichswehr mainly against left-wing insurgents, such as the Spartacist uprising of 1919. In March 1920 its generals, among them Hans von Seeckt, advised against using troops against the Kapp Putsch, Seeckt reportedly saying that Reichswehr would not fire on Reichswehr. Seeckt took over army command and had the Communist and Nazi parties banned in 1923.

The leadership evaded the Versailles limits in secret. It sponsored the Black Reichswehr, civilian work groups of about 20,000 men, and from 1923 cooperated with the Soviet Union, training pilots at Lipetsk and tank specialists at Kazan. Philipp Scheidemann disclosed the cooperation to the Reichstag in December 1926. Seeckt resigned in October 1926 after inviting Crown Prince Wilhelm to manoeuvres in imperial uniform, and Kurt von Schleicher then gained power.

After Adolf Hitler became chancellor in January 1933 he promised the generals that the Reichswehr would remain the sole armed force. The Reichswehr supported him against the SA in 1934; in the Night of the Long Knives the SA's leadership and the generals Schleicher and Ferdinand von Bredow were murdered, and the officer corps acknowledged this without objection. The name ended with Hitler's 1935 proclamation of the restoration of military sovereignty, when it became part of the Wehrmacht.

The Reichswehr consisted of the Reichsheer, with seven infantry and three cavalry divisions in seven military districts, and the Reichsmarine, in two naval stations. The treaty allowed 4,000 army officers; the actual corps numbered 3,718, down from 227,081 in 1918. An average of 23.8 per cent of its officers were of noble origin, and most held a conservative, monarchist outlook. Recruits were preferred from rural areas, and its members could not vote.
reign-of-terror: Historians disagree about when the Terror began. Some give 10 March 1793, when the Revolutionary Tribunal was created, or 5 September 1793; others point to the September Massacres of 1792. France had declared war on 20 April 1792, and after the execution of Louis XVI the First Coalition, made up of Russia, Austria, Prussia, Spain, Holland and Sardinia, attacked from all sides. Albert Soboul wrote that terror, at first an improvised response to defeat, became an instrument of victory once it was organised.

Within France, the Federalist revolts and the rising in the Vendée, which began in March 1793 in response to mass conscription, added to the sense of emergency. The urban workers known as sans-culottes pressed the National Convention for harsh measures against opponents. Robespierre held that a republic needed virtue and that those who resisted it had to be removed.

On 6 April 1793 the Convention established the Committee of Public Safety, which gradually became the wartime government. On 2 June the sans-culottes surrounded the Convention, which arrested 29 Girondist leaders. Robespierre joined the Committee on 27 July. On 5 September Bertrand Barère proposed that terror be made the order of the day. The Law of Suspects of 17 September authorised the imprisonment of vaguely defined suspects and overfilled the prisons. Marie Antoinette was executed on 16 October and the Girondins on 31 October.

In the provinces, representatives on mission put down revolts: Joseph Fouché and Jean-Marie Collot d'Herbois at Lyon, Jean-Baptiste Carrier at Nantes, where he ordered drownings. In March 1794 the Hébertists were executed, and on 5 April the Dantonists, led by Georges Danton, who had called for clemency. The Law of 22 Prairial, passed on 10 June, simplified procedure; the period that followed is called the Great Terror, and 1,366 people were executed between 10 June and 27 July.

The French victory at Fleurus on 26 June 1794 undermined the case for wartime measures. Robespierre was overthrown by men who wanted a more radical policy together with moderates who opposed the revolutionary government; the Law of 22 Prairial was one of the charges against him. He was arrested, wounded in the jaw in circumstances that remain unclear, and guillotined the next day with Saint-Just and Georges Couthon.

At least 300,000 suspects were arrested; some 17,000 were officially executed, and perhaps 10,000 more died in prison or without trial. Jean-Clément Martin argues that the Convention never instituted a system of terror as such, while Albert Mathiez held that terror was a necessary reaction to circumstances.
reims: Before the Roman conquest of northern Gaul, Reims was the capital of the Remi tribe, founded about 80 BCE. In Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul the Remi allied themselves with the Romans and secured the special favour of the imperial power. Christianity was established there by 260, when Saint Sixtus of Reims founded the diocese. The Vandals captured the city in 406 and killed Bishop Nicasius, and in 451 Attila the Hun put it to fire and sword.

Remigius, bishop of Reims, baptised Clovis, King of the Salian Franks, with oil from a sacred phial said to have been brought from heaven by a dove. For centuries the monarchy used the event as a symbol of the divine right to rule. Archbishop Adalberon, with the monk Gerbert, later Pope Silvester II, founded schools in the 10th century that taught the liberal arts.
