The archbishops held the right to consecrate the kings of France, which they exercised, with few exceptions, from Philippe II Augustus, anointed in 1179, to Charles X, anointed in 1825.

In 1429 Joan of Arc had Charles VII consecrated in the cathedral. In the First World War German bombardment and fire in 1914 severely damaged the cathedral. On 7 May 1945 General Eisenhower and the Allies received the unconditional surrender of the German Wehrmacht at Reims, signed by General Alfred Jodl.

Reims is the most populous city of the department of Marne, 129 kilometres north-east of Paris on the Vesle river. Reims Cathedral, the adjacent Palace of Tau and the Abbey of Saint-Remi were listed together as a World Heritage Site in 1991. The Basilica of Saint-Remi is the largest Romanesque church in northern France. The city lies on the northern edge of the Champagne wine region, and many of the major champagne houses have their headquarters there.
reinforced-concrete: The early development of reinforced concrete took place in parallel in England and France in the mid-19th century. The French builder François Coignet was the first to use iron-reinforced concrete as a building technique. From 1853 he built for himself a four-storey house in the suburbs of Paris. His descriptions suggest that he reinforced the concrete not to add strength but to keep walls in monolithic construction from overturning.

In 1854 the English builder William B. Wilkinson reinforced the concrete roof and floors of a two-storey house he was building. The placing of his reinforcement showed that, unlike his predecessors, he understood tensile stresses. Between 1869 and 1870 Henry Eton designed, and Messrs W and T Phillips of London built, the wrought iron reinforced Homersfield Bridge, which has a span of 15.25 metres over the River Waveney between Norfolk and Suffolk.

Reinforced concrete is a composite material in which concrete's low tensile strength and ductility are compensated for by reinforcement of higher tensile strength, usually steel bars known as rebar. Concrete is a mixture of coarse and fine aggregates with a paste of binder, usually Portland cement, and water. Typical mixes resist compression well, at about 28 megapascals, but any appreciable tension, for instance from bending, breaks the rigid lattice and causes cracking.

Steel placed in the concrete takes the tension, so the composite resists compression, bending and other tensile actions and can be made into almost any shape. The two materials work together for three reasons: the steel bonds well to the hardened cement paste, their coefficients of thermal expansion are close, which avoids large internal stresses, and the concrete protects the embedded steel from corrosion and from softening at high temperature.

In prestressed concrete, the steel in the part of a beam that will be in tension in service is stretched before the concrete is poured around it. When the concrete has hardened and the tension is released, a built-in compressive force remains, and since the concrete is then always under compression it is less liable to crack.

Reinforced concrete can fail through inadequate strength or through loss of durability. Rust expands and flakes, cracking the concrete and unbonding the bar, and de-icing salts are probably one of the main causes of early failure of bridge decks and roadways. High alumina cement was banned in the UK in 1976 after three roofs of prestressed beams collapsed, though inquiries found the beams improperly made.
reinhard-heydrich: Reinhard Tristan Eugen Heydrich was born on 7 March 1904 in Halle an der Saale. His father, Richard Bruno Heydrich, was a composer and opera singer who founded the Halle Conservatory of Music, Theatre and Teaching, and his mother taught piano there. Heydrich was trained in music from an early age and kept up the violin into adulthood. In 1922 he joined the German Navy as a cadet at Kiel and became a first lieutenant in July 1928. His discharge from the navy took legal effect on 30 May 1931. He joined the Nazi Party in Hamburg that year, and the SS on 14 July 1931.

In 1931 Heinrich Himmler hired him to set up an intelligence service for the SS, and in mid-1932 Heydrich became chief of the Sicherheitsdienst (SD). On 22 April 1934 Himmler named him head of the Gestapo. With Himmler, Göring and others he drew up the lists of those to be killed in the purge of the SA on 30 June 1934, the Night of the Long Knives. In 1938 he coordinated the pogrom of Kristallnacht on 9–10 November by telegram to SD and Gestapo offices, authorising arson and the arrest of as many Jews as the detention facilities could hold. From September 1939 he led the Reich Security Main Office.

On 27 September 1941 he was appointed Deputy Reich Protector of Bohemia and Moravia, replacing the policies of Konstantin von Neurath. Heydrich proclaimed martial law, and 142 people were executed within five days of his arrival in Prague. In January 1942 he chaired the Wannsee Conference, which formalised plans for the deportation and murder of all Jews in German-occupied Europe.

The Czechoslovak government-in-exile in London resolved to kill him, and Jan Kubiš and Jozef Gabčík, trained by the British Special Operations Executive, parachuted into the Protectorate on 28 December 1941. Heydrich was ambushed in Prague and mortally wounded on 27 May 1942 in Operation Anthropoid, and died of sepsis on 4 June. German intelligence falsely linked the assassins to the villages of Lidice and Ležáky. Both villages were razed, the men and boys aged 14 and over were shot, and most of the women and children were deported and murdered in concentration camps. Hitler called Heydrich the man with the iron heart, and many historians regard him as one of the most sinister figures of the Nazi regime.
rembrandt: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was born on 15 July 1606 in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic, the ninth child of Harmen Gerritszoon van Rijn and Neeltgen Willemsdochter van Zuijtbrouck. The family was quite well-to-do: his father was a miller and his mother a baker's daughter. His mother was Catholic and his father belonged to the Dutch Reformed Church. As a boy he attended a Latin school and in 1620 enrolled at Leiden University, but he leaned towards painting and was soon apprenticed to Jacob van Swanenburg, with whom he spent three years. He then spent six months with the history painter Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam, and a few months with Jacob Pynas in 1625.

In 1625 Rembrandt opened a studio in Leiden, which he shared with his friend and colleague Jan Lievens. He began to accept students in 1627, among them Gerrit Dou and Isaac de Jouderville. In 1629 the statesman Constantijn Huygens discovered him and procured important commissions from the court at The Hague, and Prince Frederik Hendrik went on buying his paintings.

At the end of 1631 he moved to Amsterdam, a city rapidly expanding as a centre of business and trade, and practised as a professional portraitist for the first time, with great success. He first stayed with the art dealer Hendrick van Uylenburgh and in 1634 married Hendrick's cousin Saskia van Uylenburgh. That year he became a citizen of Amsterdam and a member of the local painters' guild. He ran a large workshop, and his pupils included Ferdinand Bol and Govert Flinck. His influence on painters around him was so great that it is hard to tell who worked in his studio and who only copied his style.

Unlike most Dutch painters of the 17th century, Rembrandt worked in a wide range of styles and subjects: portraits and self-portraits, landscapes, genre scenes, allegorical and historical scenes, biblical and mythological subjects and animal studies. He never went abroad, but was influenced by the Italian Old Masters and by Dutch and Flemish artists who had studied in Italy. His roughly 100 self-portraits, over 40 of them paintings, form an intimate autobiography. Among his best-known works are The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp (1632) and The Night Watch (1642). In 1633 he began signing with the spelling Rembrandt, adding a d to the Rembrant he had used before.

The size of his surviving output has been revised. Early in the 20th century connoisseurs credited him with well over 600 paintings, nearly 400 etchings and 2,000 drawings. The Rembrandt Research Project, begun in 1968, reassessed the attributions with technical methods, and recent scholarship puts his paintings nearer 300. His prints number slightly under 300.
renaissance: Many scholars place the origin of the Renaissance in Florence at the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries, with the writings of Dante Alighieri and Petrarch and the paintings of Giotto di Bondone. One proposed starting point is 1401, when Lorenzo Ghiberti and Filippo Brunelleschi competed for the contract for the bronze doors of the Baptistery of Florence Cathedral. Italy was divided into city-states and was one of the most urbanised areas of Europe, with many cities standing among Roman ruins.

Scholars have pointed to the Black Death of 1348 to 1350 and to the patronage of the Medici banking family, but no single factor fully explains why it began in Florence. Historians disagree on whether the Renaissance broke with the Middle Ages or extended them.

Renaissance humanism was less a philosophy than a method of learning. Humanists studied ancient texts in their original languages and appraised them with reasoning and empirical evidence, rather than resolving contradictions between authors as medieval scholastics did. Their education rested on the Studia Humanitatis: poetry, grammar, history, moral philosophy and rhetoric. In the 14th century scholars such as Petrarch and Poggio Bracciolini searched European libraries for Latin works by authors such as Cicero, Lucretius, Livy and Seneca. By the early 15th century a Greek phase was under way, recovering Greek literary, historical and theological texts.

In art, the Renaissance developed linear perspective. Giotto is credited with first treating a painting as a window into space, and Brunelleschi and Leon Battista Alberti formalised the technique. Printing with movable type, from a single shop in Mainz around 1440, had spread to around 270 cities and produced more than 20 million volumes by the end of the 15th century. Navigation also advanced: Columbus sailed in 1492 and the Magellan–Elcano expedition made the first circumnavigation between 1519 and 1522.

From Florence the Renaissance spread across Italy and by the 16th century through Europe, changing as it met local cultures. Albrecht Dürer and the printing press marked its arrival in Germany, Erasmus was the best-known humanist of the Netherlands, and the Elizabethan era is usually seen as the height of the English Renaissance. Many leading theologians, including Erasmus, Huldrych Zwingli, Thomas More, Martin Luther and John Calvin, followed the humanist method.

The artist and writer Giorgio Vasari first used the term rinascita in The Lives of the Artists (1550). The word Renaissance comes from French and was popularised by the historian Jules Michelet in 1855. The term has also been applied to earlier revivals, such as the Carolingian and Ottonian Renaissances and the Renaissance of the 12th century.
renault: The company was founded on 25 February 1899 as Société Renault Frères by Louis Renault and his brothers Marcel and Fernand. Louis, a young engineer, had already designed and built several prototypes. He handled design and production, while Marcel and Fernand, who had gained their business skills in their father's textile firm, managed the business. The first Renault car, the Voiturette 1CV, was sold to a friend of Louis' father after a test ride on 24 December 1898. Louis also invented a direct drive gear with no drive belt, which gave much better performance uphill. Marcel Renault's racing interests took the firm into motor sport early: he won the 1902 Paris-Vienna rally but lost his life in the Paris-Madrid rally of 1903.

After 1918 Louis Renault widened the firm's scope to agricultural and industrial machinery. The war of 1914 to 1918 had led to many new products, and the first Renault tractor, the Type GP, built from 1919 to 1930, was based on the FT tank. The company struggled to compete with increasingly popular small, affordable cars, and in 1920 Louis signed one of its first distribution contracts with Gustave Gueudet of Amiens.

After the French capitulation in 1940 German forces took control of the Renault factories. On 3 March 1942 the Royal Air Force sent 235 low-level bombers against the plant on the Île Seguin at Billancourt, the largest number aimed at a single target during the war; 460 metric tons of bombs fell on the plant and its surroundings, with heavy civilian casualties. American bombing followed on 4 April 1943, and the plant was hit again in September of that year. Under Pierre Lefaucheux after the war the company recovered commercially but met labour unrest that continued into the 1980s.

The Renault 5 of January 1972 anticipated the energy crisis of 1973, and the Espace of 1984 was Europe's first multi-purpose vehicle. In 1984 the company was losing a billion francs a month, and the government installed Georges Besse as chairman; he sold non-core assets and cut staff, but was murdered by the group Action Directe in November 1986. His successor Raymond Lévy sold American Motors to Chrysler in 1987. The state-owned company was privatised in 1996.

Renault has been prominent in motor sport. It won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1978 with the Alpine A442 and introduced the turbo engine to Formula One with the RS01 at Silverstone in 1977. Its early work on mathematical curve modelling for car bodies is significant in the history of computer graphics. It is headquartered at Boulogne-Billancourt, near Paris, and has belonged to an alliance with Nissan since 1999.
rene-descartes: René Descartes was born in La Haye en Touraine, in the Province of Touraine, on 31 March 1596. His mother, Jeanne Brochard, died in May 1597, a few days after giving birth to a stillborn child, and he lived with his grandmother and great-uncle. His father, Joachim, was a member of the Parlement of Rennes. In 1607, late because of his fragile health, he entered the Jesuit College of La Flèche, where he was introduced to mathematics and physics. He then studied at the University of Poitiers and took a degree in canon and civil law in 1616, as his father wished.

His Discourse on the Method of 1637 introduced essays on optics, meteorology and geometry. The Meditations on First Philosophy followed in 1641, and the Principles of Philosophy, a Latin textbook meant to replace the Aristotelian ones used in universities, in 1644. The Discourse appeared in a single edition of 500 copies, and the French edition of the Meditations had not sold out by his death, but a Latin edition of the Meditations was a commercial success. He died on 11 February 1650.

Descartes used hyperbolic doubt: he rejected any idea that could be doubted, then tried to rebuild knowledge on a firm foundation. The first principle he reached was that he thinks, expressed as cogito, ergo sum, or I think, therefore I am. Since doubting needs a doubter, the fact of doubt proved his existence. He concluded that perceiving his body through the senses was unreliable evidence, and that the only indubitable knowledge was that he is a thinking thing.

In mathematics he and Pierre de Fermat developed analytic geometry, which uses algebra to describe geometry; the Cartesian coordinate system is named after him. He is credited with representing unknowns by x, y and z and with using superscripts for powers. In his Principles he stated three laws of motion and claimed that the total quantity of motion in the universe is conserved, and Isaac Newton's laws were later modelled on his exposition. By shifting the question from what is true to what he could be certain of, he is often called the father of modern Western philosophy.
rene-magritte: René François Ghislain Magritte was born on 21 November 1898 in Lessines, in the province of Hainaut, the oldest son of Léopold Magritte, a tailor and textile merchant, and Régina, a milliner before her marriage. Little is known of his early life. He began drawing lessons in 1910. On 24 February 1912 his mother drowned herself in the River Sambre at Châtelet, after an earlier attempt. Some writers have linked the image of her dress covering her face to paintings of 1927–28 showing people with cloth over their faces, such as Les Amants.

His earliest paintings, from about 1915, were Impressionistic. He studied at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels in 1916–18 but found the teaching uninspiring. In 1922 he married Georgette Berger and saw a reproduction of Giorgio de Chirico's The Song of Love, which moved him to tears. He worked as a poster designer until a contract with Galerie Le Centaure in Brussels let him paint full-time in 1926, the year of his first surreal painting, The Lost Jockey.

His first solo exhibition, in Brussels in 1927, was poorly reviewed, and he moved to Paris, where he befriended André Breton and joined the Surrealist group. In 1930 he returned to Brussels and went back to advertising with his brother Paul. He stayed in Brussels during the German occupation, which led to a break with Breton. In 1946 he signed the manifesto Surrealism in Full Sunlight. During the lean postwar years he produced fake works by Picasso, Braque and de Chirico, and at the end of 1948 returned to his prewar style.

Magritte showed ordinary objects in unfamiliar settings, giving new meanings to familiar things. The Treachery of Images shows a pipe above the words Ceci n'est pas une pipe; asked about it, he replied that it was not a pipe, since one could not fill it with tobacco. He often painted rocks floating in the sky. His surrealism was more representational than the automatic style of Joan Miró, and he said that his paintings were visible images that conceal nothing.

Popular interest rose in the 1960s, and he influenced pop, minimalist and conceptual art, although he rejected the connection with pop art. He died of pancreatic cancer on 15 August 1967, aged 68. The Magritte Museum opened in Brussels on 30 May 2009.
rennes: Rennes lies in the east of Brittany, in northwestern France, at the confluence of the rivers Ille and Vilaine. The ancient centre is built on a hill, with the north side higher than the south. The city is about 50 km from the English Channel, near Saint-Malo, Dinard and Mont Saint-Michel, and has an oceanic climate with much less rain than western Brittany. A protected green belt lies between the dense city and the rural parts of its urban area.

Rennes goes back more than 2,000 years, to a small Gallic village named Condate. Together with Vannes and Nantes it was one of the major cities of the old Duchy of Brittany. From the early 16th century until the French Revolution it was the parliamentary, administrative and garrison city of the province of Brittany within the Kingdom of France, as its 17th-century Parlement de Bretagne shows. The city played an important role in the Stamped Paper Revolt of 1675.

Its ramparts were built between the 3rd and the 12th centuries and were largely destroyed between the early 16th century and the 1860s. In 1720 a great fire destroyed most of the timber-framed houses in the northern part of the city. The north was rebuilt in stone on a grid plan, while the poorer southern part was not. Because the Parlement sat there, many hôtels particuliers were built in the richer northern half in the 18th century.

Rennes remained mostly rural until the Second World War. From the 1950s it grew through migration from the countryside and modern industry, partly in the automotive sector, and in the 1980s it became a centre of telecommunications and high-tech industry.

Rennes is the prefecture of the Brittany region and of the Ille-et-Vilaine department, with 230,890 inhabitants in 2023. It is labelled a city of art and history, with over 90 buildings protected as historic monuments. The Parlement de Bretagne, its main 17th-century building, was rebuilt after a fire in 1994 and houses the Rennes Court of Appeal. Colourful half-timbered houses survive along streets such as Saint-Georges and Saint-Michel, and the weekly Marché des Lices is one of the largest markets in France.
republic-of-serbian-krajina: The name Krajina, meaning frontier, came from the Military Frontier that the Habsburg monarchy carved out of Croatia and Slavonia between 1553 and 1578 against the Ottoman Empire. In the 1991 census Serbs made up about 12.2 per cent of the population of Croatia. After Franjo Tuđman was elected president of Croatia in April 1990, the Serb Democratic Party of Jovan Rašković broke with the Croatian parliament. In August 1990 Serbs blocked roads with logs in what became known as the Log Revolution, cutting Dalmatia off from the rest of the country, and a referendum confined to Serbs backed Serb sovereignty and autonomy by 99.7 per cent.

The Croatian constitution of December 1990 reduced the Serbs from a constituent people to a national minority. On 21 December 1990 the administration of Milan Babić announced a Serbian Autonomous Oblast of Krajina, which on 1 April 1991 declared that it would secede from Croatia.

Wider war began in August 1991. Between August and December approximately 80,000 Croats were expelled and some were killed; estimates of all exiled Croats and other non-Serbs range from 170,000, the figure of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, to a quarter of a million, that of Human Rights Watch. On 19 December 1991 the autonomous oblasts of Krajina and Western Slavonia proclaimed the republic, and that of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia was added on 26 February 1992.

The Vance plan and the Sarajevo Agreement of January 1992 established four United Nations Protected Areas and froze the front lines for three years. Refugees were not allowed to return. Babić, who opposed the plan, was replaced as president on 26 February 1992 by Goran Hadžić; Milan Martić won the presidency in January 1994. The economy depended wholly on the rump Yugoslavia: by 1994 only 36,000 of 430,000 citizens were employed. Croatian forces took Western Slavonia in Operation Flash in May 1995.

In Operation Storm between 150,000 and 200,000 Serbs fled, and only 5,000 to 6,000, mostly elderly, remained; some who refused to leave were murdered, tortured or expelled by the Croatian army and police. The remaining territory in eastern Slavonia was placed under a United Nations transitional authority by the Erdut Agreement and returned to Croatia in 1998.

The tribunal sentenced Babić, who pleaded guilty, to 13 years in 2004 and Milan Martić to 35 years in 2007. The Croatian generals Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač were convicted in April 2011 of crimes during Operation Storm and acquitted on appeal in November 2012.
republic-of-the-congo: The Republic of the Congo lies on the western coast of Central Africa, west of the Congo River, along the Equator. It is bounded by Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda, and has 170 kilometres of beaches on the Atlantic. The southwest is a coastal plain drained by the Kouilou-Niari River, and the interior is a central plateau between two basins. The climate is consistent year-round, with a dry season from June to August.

The country is named after the Congo River, whose name derives from Kongo, a Bantu kingdom at its mouth around the time the Portuguese first arrived in 1483 or 1484. It is a distinct country from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its capital, Brazzaville, is named for the colony's founder, Pierre Savorgnan de Brazzà. Under France it was known as the French Congo or Middle Congo.

Bantu-speaking peoples mostly displaced and absorbed the earlier inhabitants, the Pygmy peoples, about 1500 BCE. By the 13th century there were three main federations of states in the western Congo Basin: the Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza in the east, Mpemba to its south, and a confederation of Vungu, Kakongo and Ngoyo to the west across the Congo River. The Tio Kingdom formed in the 14th century. The association of kingship with smithing is believed to have originated among the Tio before spreading to Loango and Kongo.

The Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo in 1484, and trade grew between the inland kingdoms and European merchants, who dealt in commodities, manufactured goods and enslaved people. The area north of the river came under French sovereignty in 1880 through Pierre de Brazza's treaty with the Tio king Iloo I, and Iloo's widow, Queen Ngalifourou, upheld its terms. In 1908 France organised French Equatorial Africa, with Brazzaville as federal capital. The Congo–Ocean Railway, built after the First World War, has been estimated to have cost at least 14,000 lives.

The Republic of the Congo became independent from France in 1960 and was a Marxist–Leninist state under the name People's Republic of the Congo from 1969 into the early 1990s. Its capital is Brazzaville. French is the official language, with Kituba and Lingala as national languages, and the Kongo are the largest ethnic group, roughly half of the population. Most of the population lives in the southwest, in Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire and the towns along the railway that joins them.
republican-party-united-states: The Republican Party began in 1854 as an anti-slavery party, formed to oppose the expansion of slavery into the western territories after the Democrats under Stephan Douglas passed the Kansas-Nebraska Act. It was formed in the Northern and Border states but not in the South, and it rapidly gained support in the North, drawing in former Whigs, Free Soil Democrats and former Know Nothings. It emerged as the main rival of the Democratic Party, and the two have dominated American politics since.

The founders chose the name in homage to the republican values of the Democratic-Republican Party that Thomas Jefferson had called the Republican Party. The idea came from an editorial by the party's leading publicist, Horace Greeley, who asked for a simple name like Republican to designate those who had united to restore the Union to its true mission as champion of liberty.

Abraham Lincoln's election as president in 1860 led to the secession of Southern states and the outbreak of the American Civil War. Under Lincoln and a Republican-controlled Congress the party led the effort to preserve the Union, defeat the Confederacy and abolish slavery. By 1865 it encompassed northern Protestants, factory workers, professionals, businessmen, prosperous farmers and black former slaves. Radical Republicans, hard-line abolitionists, pressed for abolition as a war aim and clashed with Lincoln's moderate Reconstruction plans. During Reconstruction the party sought to extend civil rights protections to freedmen, and by the late 1870s it turned its attention to business interests and industrial expansion.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it dominated national politics, promoting protective tariffs and infrastructure development. In the 20th century it split between an Old Right and a moderate faction in the Northeast, and opposition to Roosevelt's New Deal produced the conservative coalition. After the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Southern states became more reliably Republican in presidential elections. The party won five of the six presidential elections from 1968 to 1988, and Ronald Reagan, in office from 1981 to 1989, was a transformative leader.

The nickname Grand Old Party originated in 1875 in the Congressional Record, which referred to the party of the Union's military defence as this gallant old party. The following year the Cincinnati Commercial used the phrase grand old party, and the abbreviation GOP is first recorded in 1884. Nineteen Republicans have served as president, the most from any single party.
republican-peoples-party: The party has its origins in the Defence of Rights Associations, the resistance organisations created in the Turkish War of Independence after the First World War. At the Sivas Congress, Mustafa Kemal Pasha and his colleagues united them into the Association for the Defence of National Rights of Anatolia and Rumelia. Most of its members had earlier been Young Turks associated with the Committee of Union and Progress. The party counts the Sivas Congress as its first party congress. It was founded as the People's Party in 1923 and took the prefix Republican shortly after the proclamation of the Republic.

In 1924 a right-wing opposition led by Kâzım Karabekir, reacting against the abolition of the Caliphate, formed the Progressive Republican Party. It was accused of involvement in the Sheikh Said rebellion and of conspiring to assassinate Atatürk. Martial law was declared, every party but the CHP was banned and Karabekir's supporters were purged from government. Republican Turkey became the third one-party state of interwar Europe, after the Soviet Union and Fascist Italy. After the Second World War İsmet İnönü allowed multi-party elections. The CHP lost in 1950 and stayed in opposition for ten years, during which it began a long shift towards social democracy.

Under Bülent Ecevit, chairman from 1972, the party took a left-wing course, and in 1977 it won 41 per cent of the vote, its best result in a free multi-party election, but not a majority. Political violence and partisan deadlock ended in the military coup of 1980, which banned every party. The name CHP was banned until 1987. Successor parties formed, among them the Social Democratic Populist Party under Erdal İnönü, and on 9 September 1992 Deniz Baykal re-established the CHP under its original name.

The party's logo is the Six Arrows, which stand for the principles of Kemalism: republicanism, reformism, laicism, populism, nationalism and etatism. It is cited as the founding party of modern Turkey, and under its one-party rule it was the main instrument for carrying out far-reaching political, cultural, social and economic reforms. It is the oldest political party in Turkey. In the 2002 election it won 20 per cent of the vote and 32 per cent of the seats, because only it and the new AK Party passed the 10 per cent threshold.
rethel: Rethel is a commune in the Ardennes department of northern France, a sub-prefecture and the third most important city of the department. It stands on the river Aisne near the northern border of Champagne, 37 km from Reims. Its inhabitants are called Rethelois. The name possibly derives from Registestensis, the Roman name of the settlement, and the coat of arms shows three rakes, which suggests a popular derivation from the Old French rastel, "rake". According to legend Julius Caesar founded the city by making a camp on the site during his campaigns.

The parents of Saint Arnulf of Metz were said to have given all they owned in villa Reistete, in Rethel, to Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, so that their prayers for a child would be answered. The city belonged to the Abbey of Saint-Remi and was administered by its advocates, one of whom, Manasses I, became the first Count of Rethel. In 1481 the county, with Rethel as its seat, was raised to the Peerage of France, in 1581 it became a duchy, and in 1663 it became the Duchy of Mazarin. Baldwin II, later King of Jerusalem, was born there in 1075.

During the Franco-Spanish War, Spanish forces under Louis de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, captured the town on 30 October 1652 after a four-year siege, and the French retook it in July 1653. In 1814 Spanish prisoners of war from the Napoleonic Wars brought typhus to the city, and Jean-Baptiste Reberotte-Labesse cared for the sick soldiers. Cholera epidemics struck in 1832 and 1849, and typhoid fever ravaged the town in 1839, killing an average of thirty people a day. In the Battle of France, from May to June 1940, French troops under Jean de Lattre de Tassigny held off German assaults on Rethel for a month before it fell. In 1974 the town absorbed the former commune of Pargny-Resson.
revolutionary-armed-forces-of-colombia: The group grew out of peasant self-defence groups formed from 1948, during the period of La Violencia, and promoted agrarianism and anti-imperialism. The Colombian Communist Party, accredited by the Comintern in 1930, organised peasant leagues and communist-controlled self-defence communities in the south that could resist state forces. In the 1960s the government's Accelerated Economic Development policy favoured large export farms; thousands of peasants were evicted, and the number of landless families rose from 40,000 in 1961 to 400,000 by 1969.

In the early 1960s the government began attacking the communist-held territories. After a military assault on the community of Marquetalia, in which about 16,000 troops faced 48 armed fighters, Manuel Marulanda Vélez and 47 others escaped into the mountains. These 48 men, two of them women, formed the core of the FARC.

At its Seventh Guerrilla Conference in 1982 the group decided to become an irregular army able to stage large attacks, helped by income from the coca boom, and added the letters EP, for Ejército del Pueblo or People's Army, to its name. In November 1998 President Andrés Pastrana granted it a safe haven of 42,000 square kilometres around San Vicente del Caguán in peace talks. Under President Álvaro Uribe, from 2002, military pressure forced it into a strategic withdrawal, and many fighters and commanders were captured or deserted. By 2014 it was avoiding open combat with the army and concentrating on small ambushes.

Its strength varied: 18,000 members by its own claim in 2007, and fewer than 10,000 according to President Juan Manuel Santos in 2011. It was financed by kidnapping for ransom, extortion, taxation of economic activity including the drug trade, and mining. The state, right-wing paramilitaries and other guerrilla groups also committed atrocities in the conflict.

Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the United Nations accused the group of violations including murders of civilians, hostage-taking, the use of landmines and gas cylinder mortars, and the recruitment of children. Women made up perhaps a third of its members, and the group formally banned rape, though former members have reported forced abortions.

In June 2016 the FARC signed a ceasefire with Santos in Havana. A referendum on the first accord failed on 2 October, with 50.24 percent against, and a revised deal was signed in November and approved by Congress. On 27 June 2017 the FARC handed its weapons to the United Nations, and soon afterwards reformed as a legal political party, later renamed the Commons. Dissident groups of about 2,000 to 2,500 people continued to use its doctrine.
revolutions-of-1848: The revolutions grew out of the changes of industrialisation and the political legacy of the French Revolution: rapid population growth, urbanisation, a repressive political order set up in reaction to that revolution, and the spread of liberalism, radicalism and nationalism. In the countryside peasants lost customary rights to common land and forests through enclosure and privatisation.

The most immediate cause, according to the economic historians Helge Berger and Mark Spoerer, was the crisis of 1845-1847. Potato blight devastated harvests in northern Europe from 1845. The Great Famine killed over an eighth of Ireland's population, and the blight caused 60,000 deaths in the Netherlands. Drought in 1846 damaged the grain harvests and food prices rose sharply, and there were more than 400 food riots in France in 1846-1847.

The first revolution came in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in January 1848, but it was France that mattered most to contemporaries. Protests in Paris began on 22 February, and the army's killing of 65 demonstrators on 23 February made them a revolution. On 24 February King Louis Philippe I abdicated and fled. News spread across the continent within a week; on hearing it Klemens von Metternich is reported to have said, in French, that it was all over.

Demonstrations began in Baden on 27 February, and the revolution succeeded in Vienna on 13-15 March and in Berlin on 18-19 March. In Denmark a march to Christiansborg on 21 March led the new king, Frederick VII, to meet the liberals' demands. In Paris the closing of the national workshops on 21 June led to the June Days, an insurrection that General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac suppressed with great bloodshed. In 1849 the revolutions gained new strength in central Italy and Hungary.

Many revolutions were quickly suppressed, tens of thousands of people were killed and more went into exile, since the temporary coalitions of workers and middle-class reformers did not hold together for long. Some lasting changes followed. The Netherlands introduced representative democracy, and Switzerland, after a short civil conflict in November 1847 in which around 100 people died, adopted a new constitution in 1848 that made it a federal state.
revolutions-of-1989: The earliest protests that led to the revolutions began in Poland on 14 August 1980, with a general strike that produced the August Agreements and the independent trade union Solidarity, led by Lech Wałęsa, whose membership peaked at 10 million. On 13 December 1981 the prime minister, Wojciech Jaruzelski, declared martial law, suspended the union and temporarily imprisoned its leaders. Through the mid-1980s Solidarity survived as an underground organisation supported by the Catholic Church.

The rise of Mikhail Gorbachev in 1985 signalled greater liberalisation. The Soviet Union faced severe economic decline and needed Western technology and credit. Gorbachev's abrogation of the Brezhnev Doctrine was perhaps the key factor: once it was clear that the Soviet Army would not intervene, the regimes were exposed to popular uprisings against one-party rule.

In 1988 strikes in Poland forced the government into talks with Solidarity, and in the elections that began on 4 June 1989 Solidarity won an overwhelming victory, so that communism fell peacefully in Poland. Hungary, influenced by Poland, held round-table talks and began dismantling its section of the Iron Curtain. In August 1989 over a quarter of the population of the Baltic states formed a human chain of 675 kilometres in the Baltic Way, and the opening of a border gate between Austria and Hungary set off a chain reaction in which the Eastern Bloc disintegrated.

Mass demonstrations followed in East Germany, and the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, which opened the way to German reunification in 1990. Revolts spread to Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia, and even to Albania. Civil resistance was the common feature, and Romania was the only country where citizens and opposition forces used violence to overthrow the regime. The Tiananmen Square protests in China ended in a military crackdown on 4 June that kept the Communist Party in power.

Between June 1989 and April 1991 every communist or former communist country in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia held competitive parliamentary elections for the first time in many decades. The Warsaw Pact was dissolved on 1 July 1991. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, and many historians treat 26 December 1991 as the true end of the Cold War. Yugoslavia split into five countries, and Czechoslovakia split peacefully on 1 January 1993.

Communist parties lost their monopoly of power in all but five countries: China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea and Vietnam. The breakdown of economic ties brought severe economic crisis and a fall in living standards in the post-Soviet states during the 1990s. In many countries the communist party simply changed its name.
reynosa: Reynosa lies on the south bank of the Rio Grande, directly across the Mexican border from Hidalgo, Texas, and about 18 kilometres south of McAllen. It is the municipal seat of Reynosa Municipality and the largest city of the state of Tamaulipas. The municipality covers 3,156.34 square kilometres, 3.7 per cent of the state's territory. The climate is semi-arid, with short, mild winters and hot summers in which temperatures can exceed 40 degrees from May to August. Annual rainfall averages 452 millimetres.

On 6 July 1686 Agustín Echeverz y Zuvízar, governor of the Nuevo Reino de León, camped on the site during an exploratory expedition. In December 1748 an expedition led by José de Escandón y Helguera left Querétaro to found 14 villages, with 1,500 colonists and 755 soldiers. On 14 March 1749 Captain Carlos Cantú founded the Villa de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe de Reynosa on Escandón's behalf, with 279 pioneer residents in the care of Friar Agustín Fragoso. It was named after Reinosa, the birthplace of the viceroy Juan Francisco de Güemes y Horcasitas.

The first flood was recorded in August 1750. In 1757 inspectors counted 280 inhabitants and obtained royal permission to move the village to Santa María de las Lajas, but Escandón no longer considered the river a risk and it stayed. A great flood in September 1800 forced the villagers to escape to the hills of El Morrillo by canoe and raft, and in 1802 the village moved to its present site, where a census counted 1,631 inhabitants.

The old church of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe was begun in 1810 and finished in 1815. The American army invaded Reynosa during the Mexican-American War in 1846, and General Lucio Blanco took it for the constitutional army on 10 May 1910, in the Mexican Revolution. Reynosa became a city on 24 November 1926.

Reynosa is the largest and most populous city in Tamaulipas, and part of the international Reynosa-McAllen metropolitan area. Several satellite U.S. companies operate there, drawn by lower labour costs and industry incentives. The General Lucio Blanco International Airport serves the city, and the McAllen Miller International Airport in Texas is close by.
reza-shah: Reza Khan was born on 15 March 1878 at Alasht in Savadkuh County, Mazandaran, the son of Major Abbas-Ali Khan, a Mazanderani who served in the Second Herat War of 1856, and Noush-Afarin, whose family had come to Qajar Iran from the Caucasus. He joined the Persian Cossack Brigade at the age of 14 and rose through the ranks. By 1920 the Qajar government had lost virtually all power outside its capital, and British and Soviet forces controlled most of the country. In February 1921, as leader of the whole Cossack Brigade in Qazvin province, Reza Khan marched on Tehran and seized the capital. He installed Zia ol Din Tabatabaee as prime minister, while he became commander-in-chief and minister of war.

Tabatabaee's government soon met resistance from provincial governors and the aristocracy, and Reza Khan became prime minister in 1923. In 1925 a constituent assembly deposed Ahmad Shah, the last Qajar monarch, and amended the constitution of 1906 so that Reza Pahlavi could be elected shah. During his sixteen years of rule the Trans-Iranian Railway was built, highways grew from 2,000 to 14,000 miles and the University of Tehran was founded. He created a 100,000-man army and a 90,000-man civil service and introduced free, compulsory education for boys and girls. In 1935 he asked foreign delegations to use the name Iran instead of Persia.

He clashed with the Shia clergy over a law of 1928 requiring Western dress, over the discouragement of the veil and over the confiscation of land from shrine endowments. Elections to parliament were managed by the interior ministry. In 1932 he cancelled the oil concession of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, and a new concession was signed on 26 April 1933 after the British took the dispute to the League of Nations.

In August 1941 the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union invaded neutral Iran, and its army collapsed within days. Reza Shah was forced to abdicate in favour of his eldest son, Mohammad Reza Shah. He was taken to the British colony of Mauritius and then to Johannesburg, where he died of a heart ailment on 26 July 1944, aged sixty-six. His defenders say that he reunified and modernised Iran; his critics say that his rule was often despotic and that his policy of cultural unity suppressed several ethnic groups. In 1950 the National Consultative Assembly named him Reza Shah the Great.
rhine: The Rhine is about 1,230 kilometres long and drains an area of 185,000 square kilometres. It begins in the Swiss canton of Graubünden, where the Anterior Rhine, traditionally traced to Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass, joins the Posterior Rhine near Reichenau. As the Alpine Rhine it turns north near Chur and forms the Swiss border with Liechtenstein and Austria before entering Lake Constance.

The High Rhine runs west from Stein am Rhein over the Rhine Falls and is joined by the Aare, which more than doubles its discharge. At Basel the river bends north through the Upper Rhine Plain, takes in the Neckar, the Main and the Moselle, and from Bonn runs through the North German Plain as the Lower Rhine. In the Netherlands it forms, with the Meuse and the Scheldt, the largest river delta in Europe, splitting into the Waal, the Nederrijn and the IJssel.

About 11,000 years ago the Rhine's estuary lay in the Strait of Dover, and dry land called Doggerland still joined Britain to the continent until the sea overtopped it about 9,000 years ago. The river enters recorded history in the 1st century BCE, when Roman geographers made it the boundary between Gaul and Germania. By then La Tène culture covered almost its whole length, and the Upper Rhine formed a contact zone between Celtic and Germanic peoples. The Rhine and the Danube made up much of the Roman Empire's northern inland boundary.

By the 6th century the Rhine lay within Francia. In the 9th century it formed part of the border between Middle and Eastern Francia, and in the 10th century it lay wholly within the Holy Roman Empire. The mouths of the Rhine, in the county of Holland, passed to the Burgundian Netherlands in the 15th century. Archduke Sigismund of Austria sold Alsace to Burgundy in 1469, and it fell to France in the Thirty Years' War. When the Holy Roman Empire collapsed, the length of the river fell to the First French Empire and its client states. The many castles along the river show its importance as a trade route.

Among the largest cities on the Rhine are Cologne, Rotterdam, Düsseldorf, Duisburg, Strasbourg, Mannheim, Ludwigshafen, Arnhem and Basel. It passes through four countries and forms six different country borders. The German states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate and the French departments of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin take their names from it, and its name derives from the Gaulish Rēnos.
rhineland: The Rhineland has no fixed boundary. It reaches west to the borders with Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands, east to the Bergisches Land and south to the North Palatine Uplands. Its southern and eastern parts are hill country, the Westerwald, Hunsrück, Siebengebirge, Taunus and Eifel, cut by river valleys, chiefly the Middle Rhine and its tributaries the Ahr, Moselle and Nahe. It also takes in the western part of the Ruhr industrial region and the Cologne Lowland. The lands on the western shore show strong Roman influence, including viticulture, and in the core territories much of the population is Catholic.

At the earliest historical period the territories between the Ardennes and the Rhine were held by the Treveri, the Eburones and other Celtic tribes. Julius Caesar conquered those on the west bank and Augustus set up fortified posts on the Rhine, but the Romans never gained a firm footing on the east bank. As Roman power declined the Franks pushed forward on both banks. In the Holy Roman Empire the Rhineland broke up into many small principalities, among them the ecclesiastical electorates of Cologne and Trier, the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg and the Free Imperial Cities of Aachen and Cologne. Aachen was the place of coronation of the German emperors.

At the Peace of Basel in 1795 France took the whole left bank, then home to about 1.6 million people. French rule until 1814 swept away feudal privileges and historic taxes and introduced the Napoleonic Code, which stayed in effect for a century. The Congress of Vienna gave the lower Rhenish districts to Prussia, and in 1822 they became the Rhine Province.

Allied forces occupied the Rhineland after the Armistice of 11 November 1918, and the Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from the area west of the Rhine and within 50 kilometres east of it. The last occupation ended on 30 June 1930. On 7 March 1936 German troops marched in, in breach of the treaty, and met no opposition from France or the United Kingdom. In 1946 the region was divided among the new states of Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate. North Rhine-Westphalia is a major industrial area, while in Rhineland-Palatinate agriculture matters more, including the vineyards of the Ahr, Middle Rhine and Moselle.
rhineland-palatinate: Rhineland-Palatinate is a landlocked state in western Germany, bordering France, Luxembourg and Belgium. Its major rivers are the Rhine, including the Middle Rhine, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Moselle. The northern half is formed by the Rhenish Massif, which includes the Eifel, the Moselle Valley, the Hunsrück and the Westerwald, while the Palatinate and Rhenish Hesse form most of the southern half. The mild climate of the deep Rhine and Moselle valleys allows fig, olive and almond trees to grow there. Forests cover 42 percent of the area.

The region has a long history, from the control of the Franks to the Holy Roman Empire, and saw fighting in both world wars. The league of ShUM cities, the Jewish communities of Mainz, Speyer and Worms, became the centre of Jewish life in medieval times. The state itself is young. The French military administration formed it on 30 August 1946, mainly from the southern part of the Prussian Rhine Province, Rhenish Hesse, the western part of Nassau and the Bavarian Rhenish Palatinate, and it was the last state in the Western Zone of Occupation to be established. The name Rhineland-Palatinate was first confirmed in the constitution adopted by referendum on 18 May 1947.

War damage meant that Mainz could not house the new administration, and the government and parliament sat provisionally in Koblenz until the Landtag decided on 16 May 1950 to move to Mainz. A sense of community developed only gradually in a state drawn up largely without regard to its inhabitants' historical affiliations. Referendums held on 19 January 1975 on transferring regions to other states produced no majority anywhere.

The state has about 4.05 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Mainz. It became part of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949. Six of Germany's thirteen quality wine regions lie within it, Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Mosel, Nahe, Mittelrhein and Ahr, and between 65 and 70 percent of the country's wine grapes originate there. The chemical industry, represented by BASF at Ludwigshafen, is the principal employer.
rhodes: Rhodes is the largest of Greece's Dodecanese islands and their historical capital, and the ninth largest island in the Mediterranean. It lies northeast of Crete and southeast of Athens. The island is shaped like a spearhead, 79.7 kilometres long and 38 across at its widest, with an area of about 1,400 square kilometres. The city of Rhodes stands at the northern tip, at the site of the ancient and modern harbours. The interior is mountainous and forested with pine and cypress. Its Greek name, Ródos, resembles the word for rose, and it is called the Island of the Sun after its patron god Helios.

Humans lived on Rhodes from at least the late Neolithic. Urban settlements such as Asomatos arose at the end of the third millennium BCE, the Minoan Civilisation established a settlement at Tiranda in the sixteenth century BCE, and Mycenaean Greeks settled in the fifteenth. The Dorians who came in the eighth century BCE built the three cities of Lindus, Ialysus and Camirus. Athens defeated the Persians, who had overrun the island, in 478 BCE, and the Rhodian cities joined the Athenian League.

In the third century BCE the Rhodo-Egyptian alliance with the Ptolemies of Alexandria controlled trade through the Aegean. The Colossus of Rhodes, completed in 280 BCE, fell in an earthquake in 226 BCE. In 164 BCE Rhodes concluded a formal alliance with Rome, which confirmed Rome's predominance in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Byzantine period began in 395, and Rhodes became capital of the Roman province of the Islands. The Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem ruled the island from 1310 to 1522, and an earthquake on 3 May 1481 destroyed much of the city. Under the Ottomans the Kahal Shalom Synagogue was established in 1557. Italy seized Rhodes in 1912, and Turkey ceded it by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. German forces occupied it after the Italian Armistice of 8 September 1943, and most of the Jewish community was deported and killed. The island was ceded to Greece in 1947.

Rhodes forms a municipality of the South Aegean region, with 125,113 inhabitants in 2022. The medieval Old Town of the City of Rhodes is a World Heritage Site. The predominant religion is Greek Orthodox, with Latin Catholic, Muslim and Jewish communities as well. The Kahal Shalom Synagogue, in the Jewish quarter of the old town, is the oldest synagogue in Greece.
rhodope-mountains: The Rhodopes are the largest mountain range by area in Bulgaria, with over 83 percent of their area in the south of that country and the rest in Greece. They are part of the Rila-Rhodope massif, the oldest landmass on the Balkan Peninsula, about 240 kilometres long and 100 to 120 kilometres wide. The highest peak is Golyam Perelik, at 2,191 metres. The range is a complex system of ridges and deep river valleys, with karst areas, gorges and large caves.

The name is of Thracian origin and is interpreted as a river name meaning rusty or reddish river. In Greek mythology, Queen Rhodope of Thrace, wife of King Haemus, offended the gods and was changed into a mountain by Zeus and Hera as a punishment.

The mountains have been inhabited since prehistoric times. The first known inhabitants were the Thracians, who built temples, cities and fortresses, among them the sacred city of Perperikon, 15 kilometres north-east of Kardzhali. Frequent mention of the Rhodope in Greek and Latin sources suggests that the mountain played an important part in the political and religious life of the Thracian tribes. An oracle on its summits was consulted by Alexander the Great and later by the father of Octavian Augustus. The Rhodope was the Thracians' last refuge of resistance against the Romans.

In the Middle Ages the range belonged to the Bulgarian and Byzantine empires, which often exchanged it, and a dense network of castles guarded the trade routes. It fell under Ottoman rule between 1371 and 1375, and in the 16th and 17th centuries the Ottoman authorities began a process of Islamisation. After the April Uprising of 1876 the Ottomans killed about 5,000 people in Batak alone. The northern Rhodopes passed in 1878 to Eastern Rumelia, and the rest of the range was annexed by Bulgaria after the First Balkan War. After the Second Balkan War and the First World War, Greece occupied the southern slopes and the Bulgarian population there fled to Bulgaria.

The range has long been a place of ethnic and religious diversity. Eastern Orthodox Bulgarians and Greeks live there alongside Muslim communities, including the Pomaks in the west and Bulgarian and Greek Turks, especially in the east, as well as Sarakatsani and Aromanians. The Western Rhodopes hold the Eastern Orthodox Bachkovo Monastery and the winter resort of Pamporovo. The Greek part includes the Rodopi Mountain Range National Park and the Dadia Forest reserve, a habitat for birds of prey.
rhone: The Rhône begins as meltwater of the Rhône Glacier in the Swiss canton of Valais, at an altitude of about 2,208 metres. It flows southwest through Gletsch and the Goms, becomes a great mountain river in a glacial valley, and at Martigny turns sharply north. The narrowing of its valley near Saint-Maurice has long given it strategic importance for the control of the Alpine passes. It enters Lake Geneva near Le Bouveret and leaves it at the city of Geneva, after 290 kilometres in Switzerland.

In France it passes through the southern Jura and receives its largest tributary, the Saône, at Lyon, the most populous city on its course. It then follows a southward course in the valley between the Alps and the Massif Central, joined by the Isère, the Durance, the Ardèche and others. At Arles it divides into the Grand Rhône and the Petit Rhône, which form the delta of the Camargue before reaching the Mediterranean. Its name continues the Latin Rhodanus, and the Gaulish name was probably *Rodonos or *Rotonos.

The Rhône has been an important highway since the times of the Greeks and Romans. It was the main trade route from the Mediterranean to east-central Gaul, and helped convey Greek cultural influences to the western Hallstatt and the later La Tène cultures. Celtic tribes living near it included the Seduni, Sequani, Allobroges, Helvetii, Vocontii and Volcae Arecomici.

Navigation was difficult, because of fierce currents, shallows, spring floods and late-summer droughts. Until the 19th century passengers travelled in water coaches drawn by men or horses, or under sail, often carrying a painted cross as protection. Sailing barges of 75 tonnes were hauled upstream by 50 to 80 horses. The first experimental steamboat was built at Lyon by Jouffroy d'Abbans in 1783, and regular steam services ran from 1829 to 1952.

The Compagnie Nationale du Rhône was founded in 1933 to improve navigation, generate electricity, irrigate land and protect riverside towns from flooding. From 1948 the French government built a series of dams and diversion canals, each with a lock beside a hydroelectric plant, and twelve plants were built between 1964 and 1980.

Before railways and highways the river joined Arles, Avignon, Valence, Vienne and Lyon to the Mediterranean ports of Fos-sur-Mer, Marseille and Sète, and a barge trip down it took three weeks. Today a motorised vessel takes three days. The Saône links the Rhône to a canal network reaching the Seine, Marne, Moselle and Rhine. The river is, with the Po and the Nile, one of the three Mediterranean rivers with the largest discharge, and the Rhône valley's dams produce about 16 per cent of French hydroelectric power.
riau: Riau extends from the eastern slopes of the Barisan Mountains to the Strait of Malacca, and includes several large islands in the strait. It borders North Sumatra, West Sumatra and Jambi on land, and has a maritime border with Malaysia. Its climate is wet and tropical, with a rainy and a dry season. Stone tools found in the Sengingi River area suggest the region was inhabited in prehistory.

The name has three suggested origins. One derives it from the Portuguese rio, river, recalling a Portuguese expedition of 1514 up the Siak River in search of a kingdom and of followers of Sultan Mahmud Shah, who had fled after the fall of the Malacca Sultanate.

Muara Takus is a Buddhist temple complex believed to be a remnant of the Srivijaya empire, and many parts of Riau are thought to have been under Srivijaya between the 7th and 14th centuries. Islam reached the archipelago through the Samudera Pasai Sultanate in Aceh, spreading by trade, marriage and the work of clerics. Later the region came under the Malay sultanates of Siak Sri Indrapura, Indragiri and Johor, which became Dutch protectorates and then puppet states of the Dutch East Indies.

Japan occupied Rengat on 31 March 1942 and soon all of Riau. Prisoners of war and more than 100,000 romusha, mostly Javanese, were made to build a 220-kilometre railway from Pekanbaru to Muaro Sijunjung; almost a third of the European prisoners and more than half of the Indonesian workers died. After independence Riau belonged to the provinces of Sumatra and then Central Sumatra, and on 10 August 1957 Central Sumatra was divided into Riau, Jambi and West Sumatra.

Riau is a province of Indonesia with Pekanbaru as its capital and largest city. It is divided into ten regencies and two cities. Indonesian is the official language, while a local dialect of Malay is the lingua franca; Minangkabau, Hokkien and Batak languages are also spoken. Malays are the largest ethnic group, with Javanese, Minangkabau, Batak and Chinese also represented.

The economy rests on petroleum, natural gas, rubber, palm oil and fibre plantations. Forest cover fell from 78 per cent in 1982 to 33 per cent in 2005, and fires linked to clearing have caused haze across the region. Riau is regarded as the homeland of the Malays, and its customs are largely Malay.
ribe: Ribe was a centre of commercial activity in the early 8th century, and the riches of Denmark may have originated there, with royal influence. Coins may have been struck there in 720, and whichever king dug the Kanhave Canal may have been involved in founding the town. Its trade contacts were mostly with Frisia and England.

Of over 300 sceatas found in Denmark, 216 come from in or around Ribe, most of them of the Frisian Wodan type and probably minted there in the early 8th century. In the early 9th century a ditch two metres wide, a demarcation rather than a fortification, was dug round a 12-hectare area, and later in the century it was replaced by a moat six to seven metres wide.

Archaeology shows an active and impressive market place in the 8th and 9th centuries and again at the end of the 11th, with little evidence between, so the town may have dwindled or even disappeared. About 860 Archbishop Ansgar asked King Horik II for the first Scandinavian church to be built in Ribe, then one of the most important trading cities in Scandinavia. Excavations have found between 2,000 and 3,000 Christian graves of the 9th century, which show a large Christian community living peacefully with the Vikings. A bishop and a cathedral are confirmed only from 948, when Leofdag was consecrated the first bishop.

Construction of Ribe Cathedral began in 1150 on top of an earlier church, most probably Ansgar's. The Treaty of Ribe was proclaimed in 1460. The town lies in a large region of low-lying marshland and has been repeatedly hit by storm floods, the most devastating being the Burchardi flood of 1634, whose marks can still be seen on the cathedral walls.

The Catholic diocese was dissolved in 1536 in the Reformation and succeeded by a Diocese of Ribe within the Protestant Church of Denmark. Hans Tausen, the leader of the Reformation in Denmark, was its bishop from 1542 to 1562. Before 1864 Ribe and its surroundings were an exclave of the Kingdom of Denmark, surrounded on three sides by the Duchy of Schleswig, until the Second Schleswig War and the Treaty of Vienna drew a new boundary south of the town.

Ribe is a town in south-western Jutland and is regarded as the oldest town in Denmark. It is the seat of the Diocese of Ribe and, since 2007, part of Esbjerg Municipality. The cathedral school, Ribe Katedralskole, has its roots in the Latin School of Ribe, which dates back to at least 1145. Among the sights are the cathedral, an art museum, the ruins and moat of Riberhus castle, probably built by Eric V of Denmark in the 1200s, and the Wadden Sea Centre.
richard-francis-burton: Richard Burton was born in Torquay, Devon, on 19 March 1821, although his autobiography incorrectly places his birth at Barham House in Elstree, Hertfordshire. His father was an Anglo-Irish army officer, and his mother, Martha Baker, was the daughter of a wealthy Hertfordshire squire, Richard Baker, after whom he was named. He grew up between Elstree and Tours in France, where his father sought a better climate for his asthma. He abandoned his university studies and in 1842 was commissioned into the Bombay Army, beginning an eighteen-year military career.

In India he served in the 18th Regiment of Native Infantry under General Charles James Napier and earned the nickname Ruffian Dick. He passed six formal language examinations and became proficient in Persian, Arabic, Hindustani, Gujarati, Punjabi, Sindhi, Saraiki and Marathi. In 1853 he made the Hajj to Mecca in disguise, as a Persian mirza and then a Sunni sheikh, doctor and dervish, having prepared by studying Muslim culture.

In 1854-1855 he led a Royal Geographical Society expedition to Somaliland with John Hanning Speke. Disguised as an Arab merchant, he reached Harar on 3 January 1855 and spent ten days there, officially a guest of the Emir but in reality his prisoner. In 1857 he and Speke left Zanzibar for the African Great Lakes with a caravan of 132 people, hindered by malaria and other fevers, and became the first Europeans known to have seen Lake Tanganyika. Burton married Isabel Arundel on 22 January 1861 and then entered the Diplomatic Service as consul at Fernando Po. He later served at Santos in Brazil, at Damascus and at Trieste, and was knighted in 1886.

Burton wrote over forty books, including Abeokuta and the Cameroons Mountains (1863), The Highlands of Brazil (1869) and Letters from the Battlefields of Paraguay (1870). With Forster Fitzgerald Arbuthnot he created the Kama Shastra Society to circulate privately books that would have been illegal to publish after the Obscene Publications Act 1857. It printed his translation of The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night in ten volumes in 1885, in a subscribers-only edition of one thousand. Burton died at Trieste on 20 October 1890 of a heart attack. Isabel afterwards burned many of his papers, including a planned translation of The Perfumed Garden, an act that remains controversial, though much of his writing survives at the Huntington Library.
richard-i-of-england: Richard was born on 8 September 1157, probably at Beaumont Palace in Oxford, the third of five sons of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. As a younger son he was not expected to become king, but his two elder brothers died before their father. By the age of 16 he had taken command of his own army to put down rebellions in Poitou against his father. When Henry the Young King led a revolt against Henry II, Richard joined him at the French court, where Louis VII supported them and knighted Richard.

Richard was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 3 September 1189. A rumour that he had ordered all Jews killed set off an attack on the Jews of London, with homes burnt and some forcibly converted. Richard had taken the cross in 1187, and he and Philip II of France agreed to go on the Third Crusade together, each fearing that the other might usurp his lands in his absence.

In Sicily he captured Messina on 4 October 1190, and a treaty with Tancred was signed on 4 March 1191. He took Lemesos on Cyprus on 1 May 1191 after its ruler Isaac Komnenos refused to release prisoners and treasure, and married Berengaria of Navarre there on 12 May. He landed at Acre on 8 June 1191, supporting Guy of Lusignan against Conrad of Montferrat for the kingship of Jerusalem.

On the way home he was captured shortly before Christmas 1192 near Vienna by Leopold of Austria, who accused him of arranging the murder of Conrad of Montferrat. During his captivity his brother John revolted with Philip's help, and Philip took part of Normandy. Richard forgave John and named him his heir. He was crowned a second time at Winchester on 11 March 1194. He spent perhaps as little as six months of his reign in England.

In March 1199 Richard was in Limousin putting down a revolt and besieging the castle of Châlus-Chabrol. On 26 March he was struck in the shoulder by a crossbow bolt, and the wound turned gangrenous. He died on 6 April 1199. According to some accounts he forgave the crossbowman and had him freed with 100 shillings.

Contemporaries admired him as a king and knight famed for martial prowess, though some also called him cruel. Later historians sometimes judged that he treated England only as a source of revenue, a view that modern scholars regard as anachronistic given his continental responsibilities. His second Great Seal of 1198 is the first to show three lions passant-guardant, a design that later became the Royal Arms of England.
richard-ii-of-england: Richard was born on 6 January 1367 at the Archbishop's Palace of Bordeaux, in the duchy of Aquitaine, the younger son of Edward the Black Prince and Joan of Kent. When the Black Prince died in June 1376, the Commons in the Good Parliament feared that Richard's uncle, John of Gaunt, would usurp the throne, and Richard was quickly invested with his father's titles and publicly recognised as heir. His early years as king were governed by regency councils influenced by Gaunt and by Thomas of Woodstock, another uncle.

The poll tax of 1381 sparked the Peasants' Revolt, whose roots lay in tensions between peasants and landowners after the Black Death. Bands under Wat Tyler, John Ball and Jack Straw gathered at Blackheath on 12 June and killed Archbishop Simon Sudbury and Robert Hales. On 20 January 1382 Richard married Anne of Bohemia, daughter of Emperor Charles IV, a match meant to win allies against France; it was unpopular in England and childless. Anne died of plague in 1394.

In 1387 control of government passed to the Lords Appellant. Richard took full control on 3 May 1389 and then ruled peacefully for eight years. In July 1397 he had Gloucester, Arundel and Warwick arrested. Arundel was executed, Gloucester died in custody at Calais, probably on the king's order, and Warwick was condemned but sentenced to life imprisonment. Historians call the following period his tyranny.

Bolingbroke landed at Ravenspurn in Yorkshire at the end of June 1399, and met little resistance because Richard had taken many loyal nobles to Ireland. On 19 August Richard surrendered at Flint Castle, promising to abdicate if his life was spared, and he was imprisoned in the Tower of London on 1 September. After the Epiphany Rising, a plot to restore him, he is thought to have died of starvation at Pontefract Castle on or around 14 February 1400, though the date and manner of his death are questioned. He was buried at Kings Langley Priory on 6 March.

Shakespeare's play shaped his reputation by presenting his misrule and deposition as the cause of the Wars of the Roses, which modern historians do not accept. Most authorities hold that his policies were not unrealistic but that the way he carried them out was unacceptable to the political establishment.
richard-iii-of-england: Richard was born on 2 October 1452 at Fotheringhay Castle in Northamptonshire, the eleventh of the twelve children of Richard, 3rd Duke of York, and Cecily Neville. His childhood fell in the opening phase of the Wars of the Roses, in which the Yorkists, who supported his father, opposed the Lancastrians loyal to the crown. His brother Edward IV gained the throne in 1461 and made him Duke of Gloucester that year. Richard became the richest and most powerful noble in England and showed loyalty to Edward during Warwick's rebellion of 1470. He married Anne Neville on 12 July 1472 and governed the north for Edward as the dominant magnate.

Edward IV died on 9 April 1483 and Richard was named Lord Protector for the 12-year-old Edward V. Robert Stillington, bishop of Bath and Wells, is said to have told Richard that Edward IV's marriage to Elizabeth Woodville was invalid because of an earlier union with Eleanor Butler, which made Edward V and his siblings illegitimate. Richard accepted the throne on 26 June after a petition from London's nobles and commons, and was crowned on 6 July 1483. Edward V and his brother Richard of Shrewsbury, called the Princes in the Tower, disappeared from the Tower of London around August 1483.

In October 1483 a rebellion nominally led by his former ally Henry Stafford, 2nd Duke of Buckingham, failed. Richard set up the Council of the North, with his nephew John de la Pole as president, to keep the peace and settle land disputes; it lasted until 1641. His only son, Edward of Middleham, died on 9 April 1484.

In August 1485 Henry Tudor and his uncle Jasper Tudor landed in Wales with French troops. At the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August Richard's army, believed to be substantially larger, met Henry's. Richard was killed, the last English king to die in battle, and Henry became Henry VII. His body was buried without ceremony in Greyfriars Church in Leicester.

Sources for his reign are largely partisan and none was written by someone who knew him closely, so the debate over his character continues. William Shakespeare made him the protagonist of Richard III. In 2012 a search for the lost Greyfriars site found a skeleton, which the University of Leicester identified through radiocarbon dating, trauma sustained at Bosworth and mitochondrial DNA. He was reburied in Leicester Cathedral on 26 March 2015.
richard-nixon: Richard Milhous Nixon was born on 9 January 1913 in Yorba Linda, California, in a house his father built on the family's lemon ranch. His mother, Hannah Milhous Nixon, was a Quaker, and his father, Francis A. Nixon, converted from Methodism to the Quaker faith. Offered a tuition grant to attend Harvard University, he stayed at home because his brother Harold's illness needed his mother's care, and enrolled at Whittier College in September 1930.

He graduated from Whittier in 1934 and from Duke University School of Law in 1937, was admitted to the California bar that year and practised law in Whittier. In January 1942 he and his wife Pat moved to Washington, D.C., where he worked at the Office of Price Administration. Although he could have claimed an exemption as a birthright Quaker, he sought a commission and was appointed a lieutenant junior grade in the Naval Reserve on 15 June 1942.

Nixon won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1946, defeating Jerry Voorhis, and entered the Senate in 1950 after a bitter campaign against Helen Gahagan Douglas, in which opponents first called him Tricky Dick. As running mate of Dwight D. Eisenhower he served as vice president from 1953 to 1961. He lost the 1960 presidential election narrowly to John F. Kennedy and the 1962 race for governor of California to Pat Brown, then moved to New York. In 1968 he defeated Hubert Humphrey and was inaugurated on 20 January 1969.

His visit to China in 1972 led to diplomatic relations between the two nations, and his first term also saw the end of American combat involvement in Vietnam in 1973, the Apollo 11 Moon landing, the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency and the end of the dollar's direct convertibility to gold in 1971. He was re-elected in 1972, defeating George McGovern.

From 1973 revelations about the administration's part in Watergate, which began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee office ordered by administration officials, eroded his support in Congress and the country. On 9 August 1974, facing almost certain impeachment and removal, Nixon resigned, the only president to do so. On 8 September 1974 his successor, Gerald Ford, granted him a pardon. In nearly twenty years of retirement he wrote nine books and made many foreign trips, rehabilitating his image into that of an elder statesman. He suffered a stroke on 18 April 1994 and died four days later.
richard-wagner: Wilhelm Richard Wagner was born on 22 May 1813 in Leipzig into a family of musicians, the ninth and youngest child of Carl Friedrich Wagner, a clerk in the Leipzig police service, and Johanna Rosine Wagner, a baker's daughter. His father died of typhoid fever six months after his birth. His mother then lived with Carl's friend, the actor and playwright Ludwig Geyer, whom she probably married in August 1814, and the family moved to Dresden. Until he was fourteen Wagner was known as Wilhelm Richard Geyer, and he almost certainly believed Geyer to be his biological father.

Geyer's love of the theatre was shared by his stepson. At nine Wagner was greatly impressed by Carl Maria von Weber's opera Der Freischütz, which he saw Weber conduct. His first creative effort was a tragedy called Leubald, begun in 1826, and he persuaded his family to let him take music lessons. Back in Leipzig he studied harmony from 1828 to 1831. Hearing Beethoven's 7th and 9th symphonies in 1828 inspired him, and he wrote a piano transcription of the 9th.

Wagner wrote both the libretti, which he called poems, and the music of all his stage works. His earliest attempts at opera were often left unfinished. Rienzi (1842) was his first opera to be staged successfully, and he later said he did not consider his early works part of his oeuvre.

From 1849 he urged a new concept of opera, often called music drama, in which musical, poetic and dramatic elements were fused in a Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. He set out these ideas in essays published between 1849 and 1852 and realised them most fully in the first half of The Ring of the Nibelung. The orchestra became as important as the singers, and leitmotifs, musical phrases tied to characters, places and plot elements, are interwoven through the drama. To stage his works he had the Bayreuth Festspielhaus built, which hosted the premieres of The Ring and Parsifal.

Wagner died on 13 February 1883. After his death his wife Cosima took over the leadership of the Bayreuth Festival, which has since remained under the management of their descendants. From Tristan und Isolde onwards he explored the limits of the traditional tonal system, and some music historians date the beginning of modern classical music to its first notes. Anton Bruckner, Hugo Wolf, Richard Strauss and Gustav Mahler were among the composers indebted to him.

He remained controversial in his lifetime and afterwards. His hostile writings on Jews, including Jewishness in Music, correspond to trends of thought in 19th-century Germany, though he also had Jewish friends and supporters. The extent to which antisemitic stereotypes appear in his operas is debated.
richmond-virginia: Richmond stands at the fall line of the James River, the rocky point that separates Virginia's Piedmont from the Tidewater and the highest point the river can be navigated. The Piedmont is a region of low, rolling hills lying between the flat Tidewater and the Blue Ridge Mountains. The site was an important village in the Powhatan Confederacy; the name of the Powhatan people is traced to Pawat-hanne, meaning falls in a stream, a reference to the falls of the James. After Jamestown was founded in April 1607, Captain Christopher Newport led explorers up the river to this inhabited area.

English colonists from Jamestown briefly settled the place from 1609 to 1611. Richmond was founded in 1737, with a street grid laid out between what are now Broad, 17th and 25th Streets and the river, and was incorporated in 1742.

In 1775 Patrick Henry delivered his speech ending 'Give me liberty or give me death!' at St. John's Church. The state capital moved there from Williamsburg on 18 April 1780, partly to give a more central position for Virginia's growing western population. In 1781 Loyalist troops led by Benedict Arnold raided and burned the city, and Governor Thomas Jefferson fled. Richmond recovered quickly.
