The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson, was enacted in 1786, and the State Capitol, designed by Jefferson and Charles-Louis Clérisseau in the Greek Revival style, was completed in 1788.

The Virginia Convention voted to secede from the United States on 17 April 1861, five days after the attack on Fort Sumter, pending a popular vote. On 20 May the Confederate States Congress voted to move its capital from Montgomery, Alabama, to Richmond, and on 23 May Virginia voters ratified the Ordinance of Secession. After the war the city again became a major centre of production, with iron-front buildings and large brick factories, a railway crossroads with what is described as the world's first triple railway crossing, and a centre of tobacco processing.

Richmond is the capital of Virginia and has been an independent city since 1871; its population was 226,610 at the 2020 census. In the early twentieth century its Jackson Ward, a business district built by freed people and their descendants, was known as the Wall Street of Black America, and in 1903 Maggie L. Walker chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank and became the first Black woman to serve as a bank president in the United States. The city contains many buildings in Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival styles, among others, and has designated 45 historic districts.
rieti: Rieti is a town and comune in Lazio, central Italy, the administrative seat of the province of Rieti and the see of a diocese. Its centre stands on a small hilltop at the southern edge of the wide Rieti valley, at the foot of the Sabine hills and the Monti Reatini, which include Mount Terminillo. The Latin name was Reate. The plain is now the fertile basin of the Velino River, and only the small Ripasottile and Lungo lakes remain of the waters that once covered more of it.

According to legend, Reate was founded by a divinity named Rea, and it was founded at the beginning of the Iron Age. It was a major site of the Sabines well before the foundation of Rome. After the final Roman conquest by Manius Curius Dentatus in 290 BCE, it became a strategic point on the Via Salaria, the salt road linking Rome to the Adriatic. The Sabines gained full citizenship in 268 BCE. Curius Dentatus diverted the Velino into the Nera, which created the Marmore Falls and left the fertile Rieti Valley. The town was laid out on Roman lines and fortified, with a stone bridge over the Velino.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire Rieti suffered destruction but remained an important centre during the Lombard domination, and was a county capital under the Franks. Saracens sacked it in the ninth and tenth centuries and King Roger II of Sicily in 1149. From 1198 it was a free commune. As a favourite papal seat it saw Pope Gregory IX canonize Saint Dominic in 1234 and Pope Nicholas IV crown Charles I of Anjou in 1289. It was a provincial capital of the Papal States from 1816 to 1860, and became capital of its own province on 2 January 1927.

Rieti has about 47,700 inhabitants. Piazza San Rufo is traditionally considered the exact centre of Italy. The cathedral was begun in 1109, consecrated in 1225 and almost entirely rebuilt in 1639, with a Romanesque bell tower of 1252. The most striking Roman remains are the stone bridge across the Velino and the viaduct. The Rieti Meeting, an international athletics event, has been held every year since 1971.
rif: The Rif is bounded by the Mediterranean Sea to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Ouergha River to the south and the Moulouya River to the east. It is the homeland of the Riffians, the Senhaja de Srair, the Jebala and the Ghomara. The mountains belong geologically to the Gibraltar Arc and are an extension of the Baetic System of the southern Iberian Peninsula, so they are not part of the Atlas system. The western Rif, often called the Jebala, is largely Arabized and speaks Moroccan Arabic, though the Ghomara keep their own Berber language. The eastern Rif, the Rif proper, speaks Tarifit.

The region has more rainfall than any other part of Morocco, in places over 2,000 millimetres a year. Its western and central parts are forested with Atlas cedar, cork oak and holm oak, and hold the only remaining forests of Moroccan fir. Its mountains shelter subpopulations of the endangered Barbary macaque.

Berbers have lived in the Rif since prehistoric times. From the 11th century BCE the Phoenicians founded trading posts and cities on its coast, such as Rusadir, now Melilla, and in the 5th century BCE Tingi, now Tangier. After the Third Punic War the coast came under Rome and the Rif became part of the Kingdom of Mauretania; when Mauretania was divided under Claudius, Tangier became the capital of Mauretania Tingitana. Roman rule ended in the 5th century CE, and the Byzantine Empire later held part of the region. In 710 Salih I ibn Mansur founded the Emirate of Nekor in the Rif, and the Berbers began converting to Islam.

In the 15th century many Muslims expelled from Spain settled in the western Rif, bringing Andalusian music and founding Chefchaouen. Portugal invaded Ceuta in 1415 and Spain conquered Melilla in 1490. The Hispano-Moroccan War began in 1859 at Tetouan and ended in Moroccan defeat. The Berber guerrilla leader Abd el-Krim proclaimed the Republic of the Rif in 1921, and the Riffians won several victories over Spain in the Rif War before they were defeated; Spanish forces used chemical weapons extensively. Spain restored its zone to Morocco in April 1956, a month after the French zone became independent. The 1958 Rif riots followed, and the Moroccan government suppressed the uprising.

The Rif is divided into an eastern part around Nador, Driouch and Al Hoceima and a western part around Tangier, Tétouan, Chefchaouen and Taounate. Farmers there grow most of Morocco's cannabis. Since the 1950s overgrazing, forest fires and clearing for agriculture have caused heavy deforestation and soil loss.
rigveda: The Rigveda is the oldest known Vedic Sanskrit text, and its early layers are among the oldest extant texts in any Indo-European language. Philological evidence indicates that the bulk of the Rigveda Samhita was composed in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent, most likely between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE, although a wider estimate of c. 1900 to 1200 BCE has also been given. All proposals are inferred from the style and content of the hymns, and the scholars Jamison and Brereton wrote in 2014 that the dating is likely to remain a matter of contention.

According to Witzel, the hymns were first collected after the Bharata victory under King Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings, and the codification took place about 1200 BCE among the early Kuru tribe.

The Rigveda Samhita is a collection of ten books, called maṇḍalas, with 1,028 hymns in about 10,600 verses. Books 2 to 7, the family books, are the oldest and shortest, each associated with a clan, and they mention prominent Bharata and Pūru kings. The ninth book is entirely dedicated to Soma and the Soma ritual. Books 1 and 10 in part deal with philosophical questions such as the origin of the universe.

The hymns are addressed to many deities. Chief among them are Indra, a heroic god praised for slaying his enemy Vrtra, Agni, the sacrificial fire, and Soma, the sacred potion or the plant it is made from. Mitra and Varuna and Ushas, the dawn, are equally prominent. Tradition associates a rishi, or composer, with each verse, and ten families of rishis account for more than 95 per cent of the verses.

The hymns were composed and preserved orally, and memorised and handed on with what is called unparalleled fidelity through structured methods of enunciation. According to Barbara West the text was probably first written down about the 3rd century BCE. Thirty manuscripts, collected in the 19th century and now in Pune, were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2007.

The Rigveda's archaic syntax and morphology are of vital importance for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European, and some verses are still recited at Hindu weddings and other rites of passage, which makes it probably the world's oldest religious text in continued use.
riigikogu: The opening session of the Estonian Constituent Assembly on 23 April 1919 is regarded as the founding date of the Estonian parliament. Under the constitution of 1920 the Riigikogu had 100 members, elected for three years by proportional representation. The first elections took place in 1920, and four more followed between 1923 and 1932. Elections were held on a regional basis, with no threshold in the first two, and a moderate threshold of 2 per cent from 1926. The sessions meet in Toompea Castle, where a new building in an unusual Expressionist style was put up in the former courtyard of the medieval castle in 1920–1922.

In 1933 amendments to the first constitution were approved by referendum, giving more power to an executive president. The following year the president used these powers to adjourn parliament and declared martial law to avert an alleged coup. A second constitution, approved by referendum in 1937, introduced a legislature of two chambers, the Chamber of Deputies (Riigivolikogu) and the State Council (Riiginõukogu). Elections in 1938 allowed only individual candidates to run.

During the Soviet occupation of 1940–41, the German occupation of 1941–44 and the second Soviet occupation of 1944–1991 the parliament was disbanded, and its premises were used by the Supreme Soviet of the Estonian SSR. In September 1992, a year after Estonia regained its independence from the Soviet Union, elections were held under the third constitution, adopted by referendum that summer. It draws on the constitutions of 1920 and 1938 and asserts continuity with the Estonian state as it existed between 1918 and 1940.

Under the 1992 constitution the Riigikogu is again a single chamber of 101 members and holds legislative power. Besides approving laws it appoints high officials, including the prime minister and the chief justice of the Supreme Court, and elects the president, alone or, if necessary, with representatives of local government in a broader electoral college. It also ratifies significant foreign treaties, approves the state budget as law and monitors the executive. Members are elected for four years, and every citizen over 18 may vote, while candidates must be at least 21. The Chancellery of the Riigikogu, established on 5 October 1992, supports its constitutional work.
rijeka: Rijeka lies on the Kvarner Gulf in the northern Adriatic, in western Croatia, 131 kilometres southwest of Zagreb. Its bay is about fifty metres deep, deep enough for large commercial ships, and its position and deep-water port made it fiercely contested over the centuries, between the Holy Roman Empire, the Republic of Venice, the Kingdom of Italy and Yugoslavia. In Croatian the name means river; it is Fiume in Italian, and Latin sources called it Tarsatica, Flumen and Vitopolis. Pliny the Elder mentions it as Tarsatica in the 1st century CE, and Ptolemy about 150 CE.

The earliest settlements on the site were the Celtic Tharsatica, on the hill of Trsat, and the Liburni, a tribe of mariners, in the harbour below, and the city long kept this dual character. Croats settled it from the 7th century, when it was a walled feudal stronghold. It stayed under Habsburg rule for over 450 years, except for brief French rule from 1809, until 1918. Before the First World War its shipyards produced warships for the Austro-Hungarian navy, and it was the main centre for torpedo production. Italy's declaration of war in May 1915 opened a front only 90 kilometres away, and several hundred Italians considered disloyal were deported to camps in Hungary, where many died.

The disintegration of Austria-Hungary in October 1918 produced rival Croatian-Serbian and Italian administrations, and both Italy and the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes claimed the city. On 12 September 1919 Italian nationalist irregulars led by the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio captured it, and they set up the Italian Regency of Carnaro. A free state of Fiume was approved in an election on 24 April 1921, with Riccardo Zanella as its first president, but strife continued, including a Fascist putsch in March 1922. By the Treaty of Rome of 27 January 1924 Italy and Yugoslavia partitioned the territory, and Italy annexed the city on 16 March 1924, beginning about twenty years of Italian government in which the Croatian minority met discrimination.

After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia in April 1941 an insurgency began in the surroundings and lasted until the war's end. After the war the city was ceded to Yugoslavia, and 58,000 of its 66,000 inhabitants gradually chose to emigrate.

Rijeka is the principal seaport and the third-largest city of Croatia, and the seat of Primorje-Gorski Kotar County. Its economy rests on shipbuilding and maritime transport. The 2021 census counted 107,964 inhabitants. Apart from Croatian and Italian, the city has its own dialect of Venetian, Fiuman, which long served as the common language of its peoples. The Rijeka Carnival, held since 1982, is the largest in Croatia.
riksdag: The Swedish word riksdag derives from the genitive of rike, referring to royal power, and dag, meaning diet or conference; the German Reichstag and the Danish Rigsdag are cognate. The roots of the institution lie in a meeting at Arboga in 1435, traditionally thought to be the first assembly, at which probably only three estates were present: the nobility, the clergy and the burghers. In 1527 the first modern Swedish king, Gustav I Vasa, reshaped this informal body to include representatives of all four social estates: the nobility, the clergy, the burghers and the yeomanry, the freehold farmers.

Representation by estate lasted until 1866. On 22 June of that year the Riksdag decided to reconstitute itself as a bicameral legislature. The First Chamber, with 155 members, was elected indirectly by county and city councillors, and the Second Chamber, with 233 members, was elected directly. The reform came out of discontent with the old Estates, which after the beginnings of the Industrial Revolution could no longer represent large parts of the population. The Riksdag did not become a parliament in the modern sense until parliamentary principles were established in the Swedish political system in 1917.

By an amendment to the Instrument of Government of 1809, the general election of 1970 was the first to a single chamber of 350 seats. The election of 1973 gave the government 175 members and the opposition 175, so that tied votes had to be settled by lot. To avoid a repeat, the number of seats was reduced to 349 from 1976.

Today the Riksdag is a unicameral parliament of 349 members, elected proportionally, and since 1994 for fixed four-year terms. It meets in Parliament House on the island of Helgeandsholmen in central Stockholm. It enacts laws, amends the constitution and appoints a government. Constitutional amendments must be approved twice, in two successive electoral periods with a general election between them. Under the Instrument of Government enacted in 1974, the task of commissioning a politician to form a government was taken from the monarch and given to the speaker of the Riksdag, who nominates a prime minister.

A party needs at least 4 percent of the national vote to enter the Riksdag, or 12 percent in a constituency. Of the 349 seats, 310 are fixed constituency seats and 39 are adjustment seats that correct deviations from proportional representation. No party has won a majority on its own since 1968, so parties form coalitions or other alliances.
rila-monastery: The Monastery of Saint John of Rila stands in the deep valley of the Rilska River in the south-western Rila Mountains, 117 km south of Sofia. It is named after its founder, the hermit Saint Ivan of Rila, who lived from 876 to 946. Tradition holds that it was founded during the rule of Tsar Peter I. The hermit himself lived in a cave not far away, and the complex was built by his students.

Almost every tsar of the Second Bulgarian Empire made large donations before the Ottoman conquest, and the monastery became a centre of Bulgarian national consciousness. In the first half of the 14th century the feudal lord Hrelja re-erected it on its present site, and the Tower of Hrelja of 1334 to 1335 and a small church of 1343 survive from that time.

The monastery was destroyed in the middle of the 15th century after Ottoman raids. With donations from Sultana Mara Branković, the Russian Orthodox Church and the Rossikon monastery of Mount Athos, it was rebuilt at the end of the 15th century, and the relics of Ivan of Rila were moved there from Tarnovo in 1469. A fire in 1833 destroyed much of it, and it was reconstructed between 1834 and 1862 under the architect Alexi Rilets.

The rectangular complex centres on an inner yard, and its high stone walls and small windows resemble a fortress. The residential part has 300 chambers, four chapels and a library of 250 manuscripts. The main church has five domes and a gold-plated iconostasis, with frescoes finished in 1846 by masters including the brothers Zahari Zograf and Dimitar Zograf. The museum holds Rafail's Cross, a wooden cross carved by the monk Rafail with 104 religious scenes and 650 miniature figures, completed in 1802.

The monastery acted as a depository of Bulgarian language and culture during foreign rule, and revolutionaries such as Vassil Levski and Gotse Delchev found shelter there. It was declared a national historical monument in 1976 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. Since 1991 it has been wholly subordinate to the Holy Synod of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church. About sixty monks live there, and it is a pilgrimage site for many Orthodox Christians.
rio-de-janeiro: Rio de Janeiro lies near the west end of a strip of Brazil's Atlantic coast, close to the Tropic of Capricorn, where the shoreline runs east and west, so the city faces largely south. It was founded at the entrance to an inlet, Guanabara Bay, which is marked by a point of land called Sugar Loaf. The city occupies 1,182.3 square kilometres, and its residents are known as cariocas. Its parks include the Tijuca National Park, a national park since 1961, and the Passeio Público, described as the first public park in the Americas.

The region was inhabited by the Tupi, Puri, Botocudo and Maxakalí peoples. Europeans first encountered Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502 during a Portuguese expedition, which gave the bay and then the city its name, meaning January River. In 1555 some 500 French colonists under Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon occupied an island in the bay and built Fort Coligny, attempting to found the colony of France Antarctique. The Portuguese saw it as a threat, and from 1560 a long military campaign led by Governor General Mem de Sá and later his nephew Estácio de Sá ended on 20 January 1567 in the defeat and expulsion of the French.

Estácio de Sá founded the city proper on 1 March 1565 and named it São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro, after the patron saint of the Portuguese king Sebastião. Until early in the 18th century it was threatened or invaded by pirates and buccaneers, mostly French. In 1763 it became the capital of the State of Brazil, and in 1808 the Portuguese royal court moved there. Rio remained the capital of the Portuguese monarchy until 1822, the only instance in modern history in which the capital of a colonising country officially shifted to one of its colonies. It then served as capital of the Empire of Brazil until 1889, and of republican Brazil until 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília.

Rio de Janeiro is the capital of the state of Rio de Janeiro, with about 6 million people in the city proper. It is known for its carnival, samba and bossa nova, and for beaches such as Copacabana and Ipanema. Landmarks include the statue of Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado, Sugarloaf Mountain and the Maracanã Stadium.
rio-de-la-plata: The Río de la Plata, in English the River Plate, is the estuary formed by the confluence of the Uruguay River and the Paraná River at Punta Gorda. It flows east into the Atlantic Ocean in a funnel-shaped indentation on the south-eastern coast of South America. It is about 290 km long and widens from about 2 km at its head to about 220 km at its mouth. Geographers disagree whether to call it a river, an estuary, a gulf or a marginal sea. Its drainage basin covers about a quarter of the continent. Part of the border between Argentina and Uruguay runs along it, and its coasts hold the port cities of Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

Nomadic aboriginal peoples lived in the region for thousands of years before European settlers arrived. The Portuguese first explored the estuary in 1512–13. In 1516 the Spanish navigator Juan Díaz de Solís crossed it in search of a passage between the Atlantic and the Pacific. Sebastian Cabot explored the Paraná and Uruguay rivers between 1526 and 1529 and obtained silver trinkets from the Guaraní, which, with legends of a Sierra de la Plata, led him to rename it Río de la Plata, the river of silver. Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires on 2 February 1536, but the settlement was soon abandoned, and Juan de Garay refounded it on 11 June 1580.

The region became the Governorate of the Río de la Plata. Buenos Aires became a centre of trade outside the Spanish fleet system, exporting silver from Potosí and importing European goods, slaves and sugar. In 1776 the Bourbon Crown raised the governorate to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. A British invasion in 1806 and 1807 was defeated by the local garrison and population.

After independence in the early nineteenth century, interests in the territories and navigation rights on the river played a major part in many conflicts, including the Cisplatine and Platine wars and the Paraguayan War. Brazil blockaded the river from 1826 to 1828, the French from 1838 to 1840 and an Anglo-French alliance from 1845 to 1850.

In December 1939 the German pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee fought British and New Zealand cruisers off the estuary in the first naval battle of the Second World War. She put into Montevideo, where her captain scuttled her a few days later.
rio-grande: The Rio Grande, called the Río Bravo in Mexico, is 1,896 miles (3,051 km) long. It rises in Colorado, in the San Juan Mountains, flows through the San Luis Valley and the Rio Grande Gorge into New Mexico, passes Albuquerque and Las Cruces, and reaches El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua. South of El Paso it forms the border between the United States and Mexico as far as the Gulf of Mexico. Its largest tributary by discharge is the Rio Conchos, and the Pecos River drains the largest area. The name means Big River in Spanish; the Navajo call it Tó Baʼáadi.

The earliest traces of people in the valley include Folsom sites near Albuquerque, possibly from about 10,800 to 9,700 BCE. Drought brought the collapse of the Ancestral Puebloan culture at Chaco Canyon around 1130 CE, and many Ancestral Puebloans migrated to the Rio Grande valley, where most of the Tanoan and Keresan pueblos were founded. In autumn 1540 an expedition under Francisco Vásquez de Coronado reached the Tiwa pueblos along the river, and on 12 July 1598 Juan de Oñate y Salazar founded the Spanish colony of New Mexico beside the Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo.

In the late 1830s and early 1840s the river marked the disputed border between Mexico and the Republic of Texas, which Mexico placed at the Nueces River. The disagreement was part of the reason for the Mexican–American War in 1846, and since 1848 the river has marked the boundary from El Paso and Ciudad Juárez to the Gulf. In the nineteenth century over 200 steamboats worked between its mouth and Rio Grande City, and during the American Civil War the Mexican port of Bagdad at its mouth was the Confederacy's only legitimate port.

The river is a vital source of water for seven American and Mexican states and flows mostly through arid and semi-arid land. Its water is shared under treaties signed in 1906 and 1944 and under the Rio Grande Compact of 1938 between Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. Dams include Elephant Butte, Amistad and Falcon. A stretch of 260 miles in New Mexico and Texas is designated the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River. The main border crossings include Ciudad Juárez and El Paso, Laredo and Nuevo Laredo, and Brownsville and Matamoros.
rio-grande-do-norte: Rio Grande do Norte forms the north-eastern tip of the South American continent. Its name means Great Northern River and refers to the mouth of the Potengi river. The coast, about 410 kilometres of sandy beaches, dominates the state, and two climates meet there: humid tropical on the eastern coast and semi-arid over most of the rest, where much of the interior lies in the Polygon of Droughts. The state also includes Rocas Atoll, 260 kilometres north-east of Natal, the only atoll in the South Atlantic.

The first European to reach the region may have been the Spaniard Alonso de Ojeda in 1499. Cape São Roque, to the north of Natal, was visited in 1501 on the Portuguese expedition led by Amerigo Vespucci, which also named the Potengi river and the Rio Grande after which the captaincy and later the state were named. For decades no permanent European settlement was made among the Potiguara, who lived there, and between 1535 and 1598 French pirates came in search of brazilwood. The Portuguese built the Forte dos Reis Magos in 1598 and founded Natal the next year. Cattle and sugarcane then drove the local economy.

In 1633 the area became a battleground between the Portuguese and the Dutch. When sugar prices fell in Amsterdam, a crisis led settlers and native Brazilians to revolt against the Dutch, in what are known as the massacres of Cunhaú and Uruaçu. Religious conflict between Portuguese-Brazilian Catholicism and Dutch Calvinism, Portugal's restoration of its throne in 1640 and the reconquest of Maranhão in 1643 led to the uprising of 1645 under André Vidal de Negreiros and João Fernandes Vieira, in which most of the rebels were Africans and Amerindians. The Dutch were finally driven out in 1654. In the Second World War the state served as an Allied airbase, and in 1964 Latin America's first space launch site, Barreira do Inferno, was built there.

Natal is the capital and largest city, and the state has 167 municipalities and an estimated 3,568,765 inhabitants in 2021. Portuguese is the language of the state. The economy has relied on sugar and cattle, and now also on tourism, petroleum, fruit, sea salt, cashew and carnauba wax. The sixteenth-century Forte dos Reis Magos still stands, and the folklorist Luís da Câmara Cascudo was born and worked in the state.
rio-grande-do-sul: Rio Grande do Sul, meaning Great River of the South, lies in the southernmost part of Brazil. It is bordered by Santa Catarina to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the east, Uruguay to the south and southwest, and the Argentine provinces of Corrientes and Misiones to the west. Its climate is predominantly humid subtropical, and in winter a cold southwesterly wind called the minuano sometimes lowers the temperature below freezing.

Before the arrival of Portuguese and Spanish settlers the area was inhabited mostly by the Guarani and Kaingang peoples. The first Europeans there were Jesuits, followed by settlers from the Azores. By the Treaty of Tordesillas the region was to be Spanish, but Spain's interest lay on the Pacific coast and the River Plate, and the Spanish introduced livestock that escaped into the plains and attracted gauchos. The colonial province saw small wars and border skirmishes between Portugal and Spain. The Portuguese Crown distributed land in enormous latifundia, where cattle raising predominated, while Azorean settlers on smaller properties introduced wheat, the main export until the early 19th century.

In the 19th century the state was the scene of the Ragamuffin War, wars with Argentina and Uruguay, and the Paraguayan War. In the war against the Argentine dictator Juan Manuel Rosas, 75 percent of the Brazilian troops were gaúchos. In 1865 a Paraguayan division occupied Uruguaiana, and troops of the Triple Alliance besieged it until the Paraguayans surrendered. In 1930 Getúlio Vargas, then state president, led a revolt that overthrew the federal government.

Rio Grande do Sul is a state of Brazil divided into 497 municipalities, with Porto Alegre as its capital and largest city. It shares a gaucho culture with Argentina and Uruguay, and its people are known for drinking chimarrão, a local version of mate, and for eating churrasco. Large waves of German and Italian migration have shaped the state.
riobamba: The country around Riobamba was inhabited by the Puruha before the Inca advanced into it in the late 15th century. The Puruha fiercely resisted the Inca conquest of what is now northern Ecuador, and the Inca Huayna Capac had to make an alliance to pacify the tribes that followed Condorazo, the Puruha general. He allied with the Schyris confederation, also called the Caran-Quitu people, who are believed to have developed the Kingdom of Quito. The 18th-century Jesuit historian Juan de Velasco described the confederation as ruled by the Duchicela dynasty. Huayna Capac married the princess Paccha, and their son Atahualpa became the last king of the Inca.

After the Spanish invasion Diego de Almagro founded Riobamba on 15 August 1534 on the plains of San Miguel. It is considered the first city founded in what is now Ecuador, and in 1563 it became part of the newly formed Royal Audience of Quito. An earthquake destroyed it completely in 1797, and it was rebuilt a few years later 14 km from its original site, near the village of Cajabamba. During the Ecuadorian War of Independence the city first declared independence on 11 November 1820 but was soon retaken by Crown forces. In 1822 it became part of Gran Colombia, and in 1830 the Republic of Ecuador established its own independence.

Riobamba is the capital of Chimborazo Province, in the Chambo River Valley of the Andes, 200 km south of Quito at an elevation of 2,754 m, close to the Chimborazo volcano. The name joins the Spanish rio, "river", with the Quechua rispampa, "plain". The city keeps much architecture from the Spanish colonial period, and its historic centre has a number of well-preserved churches. Its economy rests on the agriculture of the surrounding region and on cattle ranching, and indigenous artisans sell textiles, leather goods and dairy products at its open-air market.
ripon: Ripon lies at the confluence of two tributaries of the River Ure, the Laver and the Skell, in North Yorkshire, and was originally known as Inhrypum. The area was once under the Brigantes, who built a large circular earthwork at Hutton Moor. The Romans did not settle at Ripon but kept a military outpost about 8 km away at North Stainley.

Solid evidence for Ripon begins in the 7th century, under the Anglian kingdom of Northumbria. King Alhfrith of Deira gave land to Eata of Hexham for a monastery, with monks including the young Cuthbert as guest-master. When Alhfrith drove Eata out, the abbey passed to Wilfrid, who replaced the timber church with one of stone, using stonemasons, glaziers and plasterers from Lyon and Rome. In 937 King Athelstan granted the church sanctuary for a mile around, and after the Northumbrians rebelled in 948 King Edred had the buildings burned. Prosperity returned by the end of the 10th century, when the body of Saint Cuthbert was moved to Ripon for a time because of the threat of Danish raids.

After the Harrying of the North that followed the rebellion of 1069, Ripon is thought to have shrunk to a small community around the church, and a Gothic Collegiate Church was built over Wilfrid's building. In the 12th century a wool trade drew Florentine merchants, and after 1326 a cloth industry grew that was the third largest in Yorkshire after York and Halifax. The Reformation badly affected the town, and 300 rebels of the Rising of the North were hanged at Gallows Hill in January 1570. In the 16th and 17th centuries Ripon was known for its spurs, which gave rise to the proverb as true steel as Ripon Rowels. A treaty ending the Bishops' Wars was signed there in 1640.

In 1836 Ripon's church became a cathedral when the diocese was created, the first of the Church of England after the Reformation. The council presumed this made the town a city, and the City of Ripon Act of 1865 recognised the status.

The cathedral, an English Gothic building, has been rebuilt many times, and only the Saxon crypt is original. It holds the grave of Wilfrid. The Ripon Hornblower tradition is said to date from 886, and the Ripon Obelisk in the market square was erected in 1702. Nearby are Studley Royal Park and Fountains Abbey, a World Heritage Site.
river-clyde: The Clyde is formed where the Daer Water and the Potrail Water meet at Watermeetings. It runs north-east, then west, past Lanark, where David Dale and Robert Owen built the mills and model settlement of New Lanark beside the Falls of Clyde. It continues north-west past Hamilton and Bothwell into Glasgow, where it becomes tidal below the Tidal Weir, and then west past Renfrew and Dumbarton to the Tail of the Bank off Greenock, where it merges into the Firth of Clyde. Its drainage basin closely resembles the borders of historic Lanarkshire, once known as Clydesdale.

People have lived along the river since the Paleolithic, and artifacts from about 12,000 BCE have been found near Biggar. The earliest recorded form of the name is Klōta, given by Ptolemy in the 2nd century. Roman forts stood on the river at Castledykes, Bothwellhaugh and Old Kilpatrick, and the Antonine Wall lay a few miles away. Later the kingdom of Alt Clut, which became Strathclyde, was ruled from Dumbarton Rock. Norse-Irish raiders from Dublin sacked it in 870, and in the 11th century the kingdom was annexed by the Kingdom of Alba. In the 7th century Saint Mungo founded a Christian community on the Molendinar Burn, which became Glasgow.

Glasgow built its first bridge over the river in the 13th century. Shoals meant only small vessels could use the river, so in 1688 Glasgow merchants built Port Glasgow downstream for seagoing ships. Tobacco and cotton trade drove the economy in the early 18th century. From 1768 engineers built jetties and training walls and dredged the channel, removing much of the Elderslie Rock; the work was not completed until the 1880s. Shipbuilding then replaced trade as the main activity, and the Clyde became the world's pre-eminent shipbuilding centre, with over 370 ships completed in 1913 alone. After the Second World War the yards declined, and Upper Clyde Shipbuilders collapsed in 1971.

The Clyde is about 170 km long, the second longest river in Scotland. The former docklands in Glasgow have been redeveloped as housing and public attractions, among them the Glasgow Science Centre and the Riverside Museum. New Lanark is a World Heritage Site, and the Clyde Walkway follows the river between Glasgow and New Lanark.
river-liffey: The Liffey rises in the Liffey Head Bog, between the mountains of Kippure and Tonduff in the northern Wicklow Mountains, forming from many streamlets near the Sally Gap. It flows for 132 km through counties Wicklow, Kildare and Dublin, crossing from Wicklow into Kildare at Poulaphouca and from Kildare into Dublin at Leixlip, with most of its length in Kildare. Its mouth lies at the midpoint of Dublin Bay. The catchment covers 1,256 square kilometres.

Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle and the River Camac. Towns along it include Blessington, Ballymore Eustace, Kilcullen, Newbridge, Clane, Celbridge, Leixlip and Lucan, before it passes Chapelizod and runs through the centre of Dublin.

The river was earlier called An Ruirthech, meaning fast or strong runner. The name Life or Liphe first belonged to the plain of Kildare through which it runs, and later came to mean the river itself. A legend derives the plain's name from Life, daughter of Canann Curthach, who eloped with Deltbanna mac Druchta, the cup-bearer of the High King Conaire Mór. Scholars have offered other origins, one linking it to the Welsh llif, meaning flood, another to a language spoken in Ireland before the Celts. The Annals of Inisfallen record under 808 a defeat inflicted by the Laigin on Áed, son of Niall, at the river of Liphe.

The river has carried trade since the Viking beginnings of Dublin. The earliest stone bridge of which there is solid evidence was the Bridge of Dublin, which replaced an 11th-century wooden bridge, Dubhghall's Bridge. The Dominicans built it in 1428, with four arches and buildings including a chapel and bakehouse. Island Bridge followed in 1577, and four more bridges were added between 1670 and 1684 as commercial Dublin grew. Floods repeatedly took bridges: one in 1763 destroyed Arran Bridge, and one in December 1801 destroyed the oldest of all, replaced by Whitworth Bridge in 1816. The oldest bridge still standing is Mellows Bridge, built in 1764, and the first iron bridge was the Ha'penny Bridge of 1816.

The Liffey divides the Northside of Dublin from the Southside and is crossed by many bridges. Around 60 per cent of its flow is taken for drinking water and industry, and hydroelectric stations stand at Poulaphouca, Golden Falls and Leixlip. The Liffey Descent canoe race has run each year since 1960. James Joyce made the river the allegorical heroine of Finnegans Wake as Anna Livia Plurabelle.
river-mersey: The Mersey is 69 miles (111 km) long. It is now regarded as beginning at the confluence of the River Tame and the River Goyt in the centre of Stockport, though older definitions and maps place its start near Marple, where the Etherow meets the Goyt. It flows west through south Manchester and, near Irlam Locks, into the Manchester Ship Canal, which obliterated its old course for part of the way. After leaving the canal it runs to Warrington and through the Runcorn Gap between Runcorn and Widnes.

Below it a large estuary opens, 3 miles (4.8 km) across at its widest near Ellesmere Port, then narrows to 0.7 miles (1.1 km) between Liverpool and Birkenhead before it empties into Liverpool Bay. Its tidal range is the second highest in Britain, after the Severn.

The name comes from the Anglo-Saxon words mǣres, of a boundary, and ēa, a river, and may refer to its having been the border between the kingdoms of Mercia and Northumbria. For centuries it has formed part of the boundary between Lancashire and Cheshire. Before the Anglo-Saxon conquest the river had a Celtic name, recorded by Ptolemy as Seteia, as the southern border of the Setantii tribe.

The lowest bridging point was at Warrington, where there has been a bridge since medieval times. Monks from Birkenhead Priory introduced the first ferry across the estuary in the Middle Ages and sheltered travellers at the priory in bad weather.

Birkenhead grew quickly in the 19th century after the paddle steamer Elizabeth of 1815, with docks, shipbuilding, flour milling and soap manufacture. In 1836 Captain William Gill of the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company charted a safe channel, the Victoria Channel, through the estuary. The Mersey Railway tunnel between Birkenhead and Liverpool opened in 1886, and the Queensway Tunnel in 1934.

Liverpool's docks stretch over 7.5 miles (12.1 km). Industrialisation badly polluted the river, and in 1985 the Mersey Basin Campaign began to improve water quality; in 2002 oxygen levels able to support fish were recorded along its whole length for the first time since industry began.

Most of the conurbation on both sides of the estuary is known as Merseyside. The Mersey Ferry still runs from Liverpool to Birkenhead and Seacombe. The wetlands of the estuary are a Ramsar site. The river gave its name to Merseybeat, developed by Liverpool bands including the Beatles.
river-severn: The Severn rises at an altitude of 610 metres on the Plynlimon massif in the Cambrian Mountains of mid Wales and runs through Shropshire, Worcestershire and Gloucestershire. Its average flow of 107 cubic metres per second at Apperley makes it by far the most voluminous river in England and Wales. Its main tributaries are the Vyrnwy, the Tern, the Teme, the Warwickshire Avon and the Worcestershire Stour. By convention the river ends and the Severn Estuary begins after the Prince of Wales Bridge. The estuary leads into the Bristol Channel, which was known until Tudor times as the Severn Sea.

A tidal bore forms upstream of the port of Sharpness: at the highest tides the rising water is funnelled into a wave that travels upstream against the current. The Romano-British name was Sabrina, the Welsh name Afon Hafren is recorded as Habren about 800, and the English name comes from Old English Sæfern.

In the summer of 893 a coalition of the Danish armies in England made a determined attempt to annex western Mercia to Danish Mercia, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the Battle of Buttington. Welsh tradition made the river a drowned princess, Hafren, who in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae is the daughter of Locrin and the captive Germanic princess Estrildis. Her name was later taken for the nymph Sabrina in Milton's masque Comus of 1634.

The Severn Navigation between Gloucester and Stourport was managed by the Severn Commissioners, created by an Act of 1842 and dissolved in 1948, who took tolls and built locks and weirs. Canals joined the river, among them the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal at Stourport, the Worcester and Birmingham Canal at Worcester and the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, which avoids a dangerous stretch of the tidal river.

A three-mile stretch in Shropshire, the Ironbridge Gorge, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 as the centre of the iron industry in the early Industrial Revolution. It takes its name from the Iron Bridge of 1779, the first cast-iron arch bridge ever built. The Severn Tunnel, completed in 1886 by John Hawkshaw for the Great Western Railway, carries the South Wales Main Line under the channel. The Severn Bridge opened in 1966, replacing the Aust Ferry, and the Prince of Wales Bridge opened in 1996. Shrewsbury, Worcester and Gloucester lie on the river.
river-shannon: The Shannon drains a basin of 16,900 square kilometres, about one fifth of the island of Ireland. By tradition it rises in the Shannon Pot, a small pool on the slopes of Cuilcagh Mountain in County Cavan, flows through or between 11 counties and enters the Atlantic through a tidal estuary 102.1 km long, at the head of which stands Limerick. Its fall is slight: it rises only 76 metres above sea level, and it is shallow in places. It divides the west of Ireland, principally Connacht, from the east and south, and there are fewer than thirty-five crossing points between Dowra in the north and Limerick. Many different lengths have been given for it, since an estuary has no definite end.

Ptolemy's Geography of the 2nd century CE already names the river, which had been an important waterway since antiquity. Vikings settled in the region in the 10th century and used the river to raid monasteries deep inland; in 937 the Limerick Vikings clashed with those of Dublin on Lough Ree and were defeated.

In the 17th century the river formed a strategic boundary. In the Irish Confederate Wars the Irish retreated behind the Shannon in 1650 and held out for two more years against English Parliamentarian forces. Oliver Cromwell reputedly said the remaining Irish landowners would go "to Hell or Connacht", meaning west across the river. In the Williamite War the Jacobites also withdrew behind it after the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, and Athlone and Limerick, which command bridges, saw bloody sieges.

Navigation was improved from 1755, when Thomas Omer began lateral canals and locks between Lough Derg and Lough Ree. The Limerick stretch was opened in 1799, and paddle steamers arrived in the 1820s; by 1831 they carried 14,600 passengers and 36,000 long tons of freight. A railway from Dublin to Limerick opened in 1849 and passenger numbers fell sharply. One of the first projects of the Irish Free State in the 1920s was the Shannon hydroelectric scheme at Ardnacrusha, which replaced the old canal from Killaloe to Limerick.

The Royal Canal and the Grand Canal connect the Shannon to Dublin and the Irish Sea, and the Shannon–Erne Waterway links it to Lough Erne. Commercial traffic fell from the 1950s, but leisure boating has since grown steadily. The Shannon Callows, lowland areas along the river, are a Special Area of Conservation. Irish mythology names the river after Sionann, a granddaughter of Manannán mac Lir, drowned when the waters of Connla's Well burst forth after she sought wisdom there.
river-thames: The Thames rises at Thames Head in Gloucestershire, about 1.5 miles north of the village of Kemble in the Cotswolds, and flows into the North Sea near Tilbury in Essex and Gravesend in Kent via the Thames Estuary. It passes through Oxford, where it is sometimes called the Isis, and Reading, Henley-on-Thames and Windsor, and it drains the whole of Greater London. Its lower reaches, the Tideway, extend up to Teddington Lock. Along its course are 45 navigation locks, and the river contains over 80 islands.

Researchers have identified the Thames as a discrete drainage line as early as 58 million years ago. About 450,000 years ago, in the Anglian ice age, the ice sheet dammed the river in Hertfordshire, and the large ice lakes that formed eventually burst and diverted the river onto its present course through the area of London. The name derives from the Brittonic Tamesas, recorded in Latin as Tamesis.

Some of the earliest written references occur in Julius Caesar's account of his second expedition to Britain in 54 BCE, when the river presented a major obstacle and he met the Belgic tribes of the Catuvellauni and Atrebates along it. Until enough crossings existed the river was a formidable barrier, and Belgic tribes and Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were defined by which side of it they lay on. When English counties were established, their boundaries were partly set by the Thames.

In the early modern period the Stuart monarchs and the City of London organised pageants on the river. During cold winters it froze above London Bridge, and a tent city stood on it at the first Frost Fair in 1607. Four serious cholera outbreaks killed tens of thousands of people between 1832 and 1865, and in the Great Stink of 1858 sittings of the House of Commons had to be abandoned. A flood on 7 January 1928 drowned fourteen people in London, and together with the North Sea flood of 1953 helped lead to the Thames Barrier, built in the 1970s.

At 215 miles (346 km) the Thames is the longest river entirely in England and the second-longest in the United Kingdom, after the Severn. It is maintained for navigation by powered craft from the estuary as far as Lechlade, and it supplies drinking water, including through the Thames Water Ring Main in London. The river is the historic heartland of rowing in the United Kingdom. Handel's Water Music premiered on the river on 17 July 1717 for King George I.
river-trent: The Trent rises in the Staffordshire Moorlands, near Biddulph Moor, and flows south past Stoke-on-Trent, Stone, Rugeley, Burton upon Trent, Nottingham, Newark-on-Trent and Gainsborough. At Trent Falls it joins the Yorkshire Ouse to form the Humber estuary, which has often been characterised as the boundary between the Midlands and the North. Its largest tributary is the Tame, which supplies nearly a quarter of its flow, followed by the Derwent, Soar, Dove and Sow.

The name is possibly Romano-British and meant strongly flooding. Another derivation, from Trisantona, gives great thoroughfare. Izaak Walton's explanation of 1653, that the river was named for thirty kinds of fish, is almost certainly wrong.

The river changed its channel during historic times, and has been compared to the Mississippi in this respect. At Repton an abandoned channel was once the main navigable route until the river moved to a more northerly course in the 18th century, and at Hemington archaeologists found a medieval bridge across another abandoned channel. Before the mid-18th century there were only four bridges downstream of the Tame, at Burton, Swarkestone, Nottingham and Newark, all first built by 1204, and over thirty ferries.

Fishing along the river goes back to the Neolithic period, to which a possible fish weir at Hemington may belong. Domesday records mills and fisheries along it, and in the 12th century landlords at Burton upon Trent were paid in salmon in place of rent. Nottingham seems to have been the ancient head of navigation until the Restoration. The Trent Navigation Act 1773 authorised locks at Newark, and tolls fell from £11,344 in 1839 to £3,111 in 1855 as railways took the traffic. The Ministry of Transport took over the navigation on 24 September 1920, and Neville Chamberlain opened Hazelford lock on 25 June 1926.

The Trent also marked the boundary between northern and southern England. Royal forests had different justice in eyre north and south of it, the medieval Council of the North's jurisdiction began there, and Oxford University divided its students into northern and southern nations by it. Industrial growth polluted the river: a salmon fishery taking some 3,000 fish a year in the late 1880s had fallen to 100 a decade later.

The river is known for flooding, with a well-documented flood history of some 900 years, and its tidal lower reaches have a bore called the Trent Aegir, up to 1.5 metres high, which travels as far as Gainsborough. Twelve large power stations were built along its banks from the 1940s, using its cooling water, and at one time supplied a quarter of the electricity of the United Kingdom, giving the valley the name Megawatt Valley. The Trent Valley Way, a long-distance footpath, was created in 1998.
river-tweed: The River Tweed, or Tweed Water, is 97 miles (156 km) long and flows east across the Border region of Scotland and northern England. It rises in the Lowther Hills at Tweed's Well, close to the sources of the Clyde, which drains northwest, and of the Annan, which drains south. A saying of the Border region records this: Annan, Tweed and Clyde rise out of one hillside. The name may represent an Old Brittonic word meaning border, though a proposal deriving it from an Indo-European root meaning swell or grow powerful is doubtful. Tweed cloth takes its name from its association with the river.

East of the settlements of Birgham and Carham, which stand on opposite banks, the river forms the historic boundary between Scotland and England. East of Kelso it becomes part of the eastern border. For only 7 km of its course is it wholly in England, and for 30 km it forms the border. It enters the North Sea at Berwick-upon-Tweed in Northumberland.

The Tweed flows through the Borders region of Scotland, passing Innerleithen, Peebles, Galashiels, Melrose, Kelso, Coldstream and Berwick-upon-Tweed. Its tributaries include the Teviot Water, the Ettrick Water, the Yarrow Water, the Gala Water, the Whiteadder Water, the River Till and the Eden Water. East of St Boswells it runs through a drumlin field, the relic of a former ice stream that flowed through the area during the last glaciation.

The upper catchment is known as Tweeddale, part of which is protected as the Upper Tweeddale National Scenic Area, one of 40 such areas in Scotland. Although the catchment straddles the border, a single body, the River Tweed Commission, oversees water quality, bio-security and the protection of the river's salmon. The Tweed is among the great salmon rivers of Britain and the only river in England where an Environment Agency rod licence is not needed for angling. Historical flooding in the catchment has been studied from documentary records: a study of 1990 by Lindsey J. McEwen reconstructed chronologies of major floods in four sub-catchments of the middle Tweed basin.
river-tyne: The River Tyne is 73 miles (118 km) long, excluding its tributaries. It is formed by the North Tyne and the South Tyne, which meet at Warden near Hexham in Northumberland. The North Tyne rises at Deadwater a few tens of metres short of the Scottish border and flows through Kielder and past Bellingham, passing Hadrian's Wall near Chollerford. The South Tyne rises at Tyne Head on Alston Moor in Cumbria, close to the sources of the Tees and the Wear, and runs beside Hadrian's Wall through the low east-west corridor across the Pennines known as the Tyne Gap.

Below Warden the river flows east by Hexham, Corbridge and Prudhoe, and for 13 miles forms the boundary between Newcastle upon Tyne on the north bank and Gateshead on the south, passing under ten bridges. It then divides Hebburn and Jarrow from Walker and Wallsend, and reaches the North Sea between South Shields and Tynemouth. Before the last ice age the Wear is thought to have followed the course of the lower Team and joined the Tyne at Dunston; ice diverted it to flow east to Sunderland.

Nothing definite is known of the origin of the name, and the river is not known by it until the Saxon period; Tynemouth is recorded in Anglo-Saxon as Tinanmuðe. Because of its closeness to the coalfields the Tyne was a major route for the export of coal from the thirteenth century until mining declined in the later twentieth century. The largest coal staithes stood at Dunston, Hebburn and Tyne Dock. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the lower reaches were also one of the world's most important centres of shipbuilding.

The River Tyne Improvement Act of 1850 created the Tyne Improvement Commission, which lasted until 1968. Over its first seventy years the river was deepened from 6 to 30 feet and 150 million tonnes were dredged from it; the two Tyne piers and the Northumbrian, Tyne and Albert Docks were built, and by 1910 the port handled millions of tonnes of cargo. Islands were removed and meanders straightened. The period from 1850 to 1950 was the worst for pollution of the river. The Port of Tyne Authority has managed the tidal river since 1968.

The wooden coal staithes at Dunston, built in 1890, have been preserved. A bronze figure, River God Tyne, by David Wynne, was unveiled in 1968 at Newcastle's Civic Centre. The Tyne Rivers Trust, a community organisation founded in 2004, works to improve habitat across the catchment.
river-wye: 2 kilometres from the source of the Severn. Although the source lies about 19 kilometres from the Irish Sea, the river at first runs inland. It passes Rhayader, Builth Wells, Hay-on-Wye, Hereford, the only city on the river, Ross-on-Wye, Symonds Yat, Monmouth and Tintern, and meets the Severn Estuary just below Chepstow. The lower 26 kilometres, from Redbrook to Chepstow, form part of the border between England and Wales.
The Welsh name is Afon Gwy, and a mention of Guoy in the Historia Brittonum of the early 9th century may be the earliest reference to the name, whose meaning is not clear.

The Romans built a bridge of wood and stone just upstream of present-day Chepstow. The river is tidal for about 24 kilometres up to Bigsweir, where hard rock forms a natural weir, and spring tides can raise the water by as much as 15 metres. Since Roman times it has carried coal from the Forest of Dean, cider from Hereford, wine, iron, stone and timber.

Early records are fragmentary, but iron appears to have been shipped down the river for the ships of Edward the Confessor in the 11th century. In 1171 and 1172 iron was supplied to Henry II for his invasion of Ireland. Under Edward I a common right of navigation was recorded, with the channel to be kept free of weirs.

Schemes to improve navigation followed. Sir William Sandys was appointed in 1662 to make the Wye and the Lugg navigable with flash locks, but the Wye ran too fast, the locks proved impracticable and costly, and the scheme was abandoned by 1668. The Rivers Wye and Lugg Navigation Act of 1695 authorised Herefordshire to buy and demolish the weirs and declared the rivers free and common. A towing path for horses from Lydbrook to Hereford was authorised in 1809, and barges reached Hereford in January 1811. Passenger boats ran from 1835. Trade declined after the Herefordshire and Gloucestershire Canal reached Hereford in 1845 and railways opened.

The lower valley is a National Landscape, and the river is protected by two Sites of Special Scientific Interest and designated a Special Area of Conservation. It was once known for its large spring salmon, the largest recorded weighing 59 lb 8 oz, caught in 1923. The river is used for canoeing, rowing and walking, and the Wye Valley Walk follows it from near Plynlimon to Chepstow.
riyadh: Riyadh is the largest city on the Arabian Peninsula. It lies in the eastern part of the Najd plateau, at an average elevation of 600 metres above sea level. The climate is hot desert, with long, extremely hot summers and short, cold winters. The city is known for dust storms so thick that visibility can fall under 10 m. The old town within the walls did not exceed an area of 1 km2, and the city is now divided into fourteen branch municipalities and the Diplomatic Quarter.

In the pre-Islamic era the city on the site was called Hajr and was reportedly founded by the tribe of Banu Hanifa. It was the capital of the province of Al-Yamama, whose governors were responsible for most of central and eastern Arabia under the Umayyad Caliphate and Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Yamama broke away from the Abbasid Caliphate in 866, and the Banu Ukhaidhir, who then ruled the area, moved the capital to nearby Al-Kharj. Hajr went into a long decline. In the 14th century Ibn Battuta visited it, and described it as the main city of Al-Yamama, a city of canals and trees whose inhabitants mostly belonged to the Banu Hanifa.

Hajr later broke up into separate settlements and estates, the most notable being Migrin and Mi'kal. The earliest known reference to the area as Riyadh, meaning gardens, comes from a 17th-century chronicler describing an event of 1590. Dahham ibn Dawwas, a refugee from neighbouring Manfuhah, took control and built a single wall around the various oasis towns, making them in effect one fortress city. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the Emir of Diriyah, Muhammad bin Saud, then took the town from him, but the First Saudi state they formed collapsed in 1818. Turki ibn Abdullah founded the Second Saudi state in the early 19th century and made Riyadh his capital, though a joint Ottoman and Rashidi alliance disrupted his rule.

Ibn Saud retrieved his ancestral rule in 1902 with the Emirate of Riyadh and consolidated it by 1926 with the conquest of the Hejaz. In September 1932 he named his kingdom Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh as the capital. The first major construction beyond the walls was his Murabba Palace, built in 1936-1938, and the government moved there in 1938. In the 1950s the walls were dismantled and the modern city expanded from the old town. The population was 40,000 in 1935 and 83,000 in 1949. Of the old town the Al-Masmak Palace and parts of the wall and its gate survive, restored.
roald-amundsen: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was born on 16 July 1872 in Borge, Østfold, into a family of Norwegian shipowners and captains. His mother wanted him to avoid the maritime trade and become a doctor, a promise he kept until she died when he was 21, after which he quit university for a life at sea. At fifteen he had been enthralled by Sir John Franklin's narratives of his Arctic expeditions. In 1897 he joined the Belgian Antarctic Expedition of Adrien de Gerlache as first mate; its ship Belgica became locked in sea ice and the first expedition to overwinter in Antarctica endured a winter for which it was poorly prepared.

In 1903 Amundsen led the first expedition to traverse the Northwest Passage, in the 45-ton sloop Gjøa with a crew of six. They spent two winters at King William Island, where the Netsilik Inuit taught them Arctic survival skills, such as using sled dogs and wearing animal skins instead of woolen parkas. The ship cleared the Canadian Arctic Archipelago on 17 August 1905, and the crew returned to Oslo in November 1906.

In 1909, hearing of the claims of Frederick Cook and Robert Peary to the North Pole, Amundsen turned to Antarctica without making clear his intentions, and Robert F. Scott felt misled. He left Oslo in the Fram on 3 June 1910 and set up base at Framheim in January 1911. Five men, Amundsen, Olav Bjaaland, Helmer Hanssen, Sverre Hassel and Oscar Wisting, left on 19 October with four sledges and 52 dogs and reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, a month before Scott's group. His success rested on careful preparation, skis, dogs and Inuit-style furred clothing.

From 1918 to 1925 Amundsen led an expedition in the ship Maud through the Northeast Passage, aiming to drift towards the North Pole as Fridtjof Nansen had; the ship froze in the ice and the goal was not achieved. On 12 May 1926 he and 15 other men in the airship Norge became the first explorers verified to have reached the North Pole. In June 1928 he disappeared while flying on a rescue mission for the airship Italia in the Arctic. The search for his remains, which have not been found, was called off that September.
robben-island: Robben Island lies in Table Bay, 6.9 kilometres west of the coast of Bloubergstrand and north of Cape Town. It is roughly oval, 3.3 kilometres long and 1.9 kilometres wide, and so flat that it stands only a few metres above sea level. Its name comes from the archaic Dutch word for seals, robben. Jan van Riebeeck had bonfires lit on its highest point in the 1650s to warn ships, and a lighthouse was completed on Minto Hill in 1865.

The island is said to have been found by Bartolomeu Dias in 1488, and Portuguese, English and Dutch sailors used it as a refuelling station. In 1654 the settlers of the Dutch Cape Colony sheltered livestock there. From the end of the 17th century it was used to imprison mainly political prisoners, with Autshumato probably the first, in the mid-17th century. Political leaders from other Dutch colonies were held there, among them Massavana and Koesaaij, two surviving Malagasy leaders of the mutiny aboard the slave ship Meermin. After the failed uprising at Grahamstown in 1819 the British sentenced the African leader Makanda Nxele to life imprisonment on the island; he drowned in Table Bay after escaping.

From 1845 people with leprosy were moved to the island, at first voluntarily, and after the Leprosy Repression Act of May 1892 admission was compulsory. From 1961 to 1996 the South African government used it to imprison political dissidents, among them the future presidents Nelson Mandela, Kgalema Motlanthe and Jacob Zuma. The maximum security prison closed in 1991 and the medium security prison for criminal prisoners in 1996.

In 1997 the island became a museum and a national monument, and in 1999 it was recognised as a World Heritage Site. The Robben Island Museum runs it as a living museum, and many of the guides are former prisoners. Visitors reach it by ferry from Cape Town's Victoria & Alfred Waterfront and see the maximum security prison, Nelson Mandela's cell, the lime quarry, Robert Sobukwe's house and the Moturu Kramat, a shrine built in 1969 that is a sacred site for Muslim pilgrimage. Administratively it is a suburb of the City of Cape Town.
robert-bosch: Robert Bosch was born on 23 September 1861 at Albeck in the Swabian Highlands near Ulm, one of twelve children of Servatius Bosch, who ran a large progressive farm with a brewery. He attended the Realanstalt in Ulm until 1879, with an apprenticeship as a precision-instrument maker. In 1883 and 1884 he studied at the Stuttgart Technical University. On 24 May 1884 he sailed for the United States and worked as an engineer under Thomas Edison and Sigmund Bergmann in New York; in 1885 he went to London, where he found employment with Siemens Brothers.

On 15 November 1886 Bosch opened his own Workshop for Precision Mechanics and Electrical Engineering in Stuttgart. In 1887 Gottlieb Daimler asked whether he could build a device like the low-voltage magneto with firing points used by the Gasoline Engine Factory Deutz, to produce the spark that ignites the air-fuel mixture at maximum compression, and Bosch made four. In 1893 Frederick Richard Simms proposed adapting the stationary-engine magneto for motor vehicles. Arnold Zähringer and Gottlob Honold modified it to raise the speed of sparks from 250 to 1800 rpm, and orders from Daimler followed after a demonstration in January 1898.

By 1913 the company had branches in America, Asia, Africa and Australia and made 88% of its sales outside Germany. After the First World War Bosch introduced diesel fuel injection in 1927, and in the 1920s he modernised and diversified, turning a small automotive supplier into a multinational electronics group.

Bosch was one of the first German industrialists to introduce the eight-hour day, and he promoted occupational training. He did not wish to profit from armaments contracts of the First World War and gave several million marks to charity, including the Robert Bosch Hospital in Stuttgart. As a liberal he devoted energy and money to reconciliation between Germany and France. His relationship with Nazism is described as complex: as much as 60% of the firm's revenue came from Wehrmacht contracts in the 1940s, yet he worked with Carl Friedrich Goerdeler, central to the plot of 20 July, and his managers joined the Nazi party to keep committed Nazis out of the company.

In 1937 he made the company a private limited company, and his will required that its earnings go to charitable causes. He died on 12 March 1942, survived by four children from two marriages, and was inducted into the Automotive Hall of Fame in 1984.
robert-boyle: Robert Boyle was born at Lismore Castle in County Waterford on 25 January 1627, the seventh son and fourteenth child of Richard Boyle, 1st Earl of Cork, and Catherine Fenton. After his mother's death, when he was eight, he and his brother Francis were sent to Eton College. He then travelled abroad with a French tutor and spent the winter of 1641 in Florence, studying the paradoxes of the elderly Galileo Galilei. He returned to England in 1644, a year after his father's death, and lived at the manor of Stalbridge in Dorset until 1652, working in a laboratory and joining the band of enquirers known as the Invisible College.

Boyle moved to Ireland in 1652 but, frustrated in his chemical work, went to Oxford in 1654. Having read in 1657 of Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump, he set about improving it with Robert Hooke, and his Pneumatical Engine was finished in 1659. In answering the Jesuit Francis Line's objections to his account of the experiments he first mentioned the law that the volume of a gas varies inversely to its pressure. In continental Europe it is sometimes attributed to Edme Mariotte.

In 1663 the Invisible College became the Royal Society of London, and Charles II's charter named Boyle to its council. In 1680 he was elected president but declined from a scruple about oaths. From 1668 he lived in London in the house of his sister Katherine Jones, Lady Ranelagh, with whom he kept a lifelong intellectual partnership. He died on 31 December 1691, a week after her, and was buried at St Martin-in-the-Fields.

Boyle held that knowledge should rest on experiment, writing that he did not love to believe anything upon conjectures when a not over-difficult experiment could test it. He was also an alchemist who thought the transmutation of metals possible. In The Sceptical Chymist he criticised the Spagyrists who held that salt, sulphur and mercury were the true principles of things. He took elements to be the undecomposable constituents of bodies, distinguished mixtures from compounds and gave the name analysis to the detection of their ingredients.

A devout Anglican, he refused holy orders on the ground that his religious writings would carry more weight from a layman, and he argued that the design visible in nature showed God's involvement with the world. From 1680 to 1685 he paid for the printing of the Bible in Irish.
robert-clive: Robert Clive was born at Styche, the family estate near Market Drayton in Shropshire, the eldest of thirteen children of Richard Clive, a lawyer and member of Parliament. His father obtained for him a post as a writer, or clerk, with the East India Company, and in 1743 he sailed for India. After the French took Madras in 1746, during the First Carnatic War, Clive joined the Company's army. He served in a failed expedition to Tanjore and nearly lost his small force at Devikottai.

The death of the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1748 began the Second Carnatic War, in which the French governor Dupleix used small disciplined forces to tip the balance among Indian rulers. He returned in 1755 as deputy governor of Fort St. David. In 1756 the new Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, took Calcutta, and prisoners were put in the cell known as the Black Hole, where 43 of 64 were reported to have died. Clive retook the city and besieged the French colony of Chandannagar. He agreed with Mir Jafar, who led a conspiracy against the nawab, to make him viceroy in return for payments to the Company. Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757 followed.

He went home in 1760 with a fortune, entered Parliament and was made an Irish baron. He returned to Bengal in 1765 and on 12 August of that year obtained from the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, which made the Company the real ruler of some thirty million people. He raised civil servants' pay and forbade gifts from Indians, though corruption continued. He left India for the last time in February 1767.

Back in England he bought Claremont in Surrey, where Capability Brown remodelled the house and garden. Parliamentary debate on the great Bengal famine, which Adam Smith and others blamed on Company officials, reduced his political popularity. On 22 November 1774 Clive died at his house in Berkeley Square after cutting his throat with a paper knife; no inquest was held, and newspapers reported an apoplectic fit.

Clive remains one of Britain's most controversial colonial figures. Lord Macaulay admired him, but modern historians criticise his management of Bengal's revenue, which raised demands on the rural population and increased poverty before the famine of 1770. His statue stands in Shrewsbury and in King Charles Street in London.
robert-curthose: Robert was the eldest son of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders. His birth has been dated to between 1051 and 1053. The epithet Curthose comes from the Norman French courtheuse, 'short stockings'; the chroniclers William of Malmesbury and Orderic Vitalis wrote that his father derisively called him brevis-ocrea, 'short boot'. In 1063 his father made him Count of Maine, in view of his betrothal to Margaret, the heiress of Maine, who died before they could marry. In 1077 a quarrel with his younger brothers William Rufus and Henry led him to attempt to seize Rouen Castle, and he spent the following years in exile, at one point wounding his father in battle in January 1079.

When William died in 1087 he gave Normandy to Robert and England to William Rufus, and Henry received money to buy land. Robert was generous to his barons and the clergy but was almost perpetually short of funds, and the central authority of the duchy weakened. William Rufus bribed many of his vassals away. Robert's support for the Rebellion of 1088 against Rufus failed, and he never joined the English rebels himself.

In 1096 Robert left to join the First Crusade, mortgaging his duchy to Rufus for 10,000 marks. He fought at the Battle of Dorylaeum on 1 July 1097, took part in the siege and battle of Antioch, and was among the crusaders who captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. At Ascalon on 12 August 1099 he commanded part of the crusader centre. On the way home he married Sybil of Conversano, whose dowry helped him buy back his duchy.

Rufus died on 2 August 1100 while Robert was still returning, and Henry seized the English crown. In 1101 Robert landed at Portsmouth with a fleet, but he and Henry agreed the Treaty of Alton, by which Robert recognised Henry's crown in exchange for 3,000 livres. His position in Normandy then deteriorated amid private wars among the barons.

In 1106 Henry decisively defeated Robert's army at the Battle of Tinchebray and claimed Normandy for the English crown, a situation that lasted almost a century. Robert was captured and held at Corfe Castle, then at Devizes Castle and finally at Cardiff Castle, where he died probably on 3 February 1134. He was buried at Gloucester Abbey, where an effigy of bog oak, carved about a century after his death, lies on a mortuary chest. His reputation rests largely on his conduct on the crusade, described as the one period of clear distinction in his career.
robert-e-lee: Robert Edward Lee was born on 19 January 1807 at Stratford Hall Plantation in Westmoreland County, Virginia, the fourth child of the Revolutionary War officer Henry Lee III and Anne Hill Carter Lee. A top graduate of the United States Military Academy, he served 32 years in the United States Army as an officer and military engineer. In 1831 he married Mary Anna Randolph Custis, a great-granddaughter of Martha Washington, and they eventually had seven children.

In the Mexican–American War he was one of Winfield Scott's chief aides, finding routes of attack the Mexicans had left undefended, and he was wounded at Chapultepec. From 1852 he was Superintendent of the Military Academy at West Point. After his father-in-law died in 1857, Lee took leave to run the Arlington estate, which held hundreds of enslaved people. In October 1859 he commanded the force that captured John Brown's raiders at Harpers Ferry.

Lee privately opposed secession, calling it nothing but revolution, but when Virginia seceded in 1861 he followed his state and resigned from the army. He took command of the Army of Northern Virginia in June 1862 and drove George B. McClellan's Army of the Potomac from Richmond in the Seven Days Battles. He defeated John Pope at the Second Battle of Bull Run, and then won at Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville. His invasion of Maryland ended in the inconclusive Battle of Antietam, and his second invasion of the North ended in decisive defeat at Gettysburg in 1863.

In 1864 Ulysses S. Grant fought him at the Wilderness, Spotsylvania Court House and Cold Harbor and pinned him at Richmond, and the Siege of Petersburg followed. Lee became General in Chief of the Confederate armies on 6 February 1865. After the capture of Richmond and the destruction of most of his army, he surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865.

After the war Lee was indicted but not punished, though he lost the right to vote and some property. He became president of Washington College, now Washington and Lee University, in Lexington, Virginia, and supported reconciliation between North and South. He accepted the end of slavery but opposed racial equality for African Americans. He died of pneumonia in Lexington on 12 October 1870, after a stroke.

Among supporters of the Confederacy he was revered more after the surrender than during the war. Historians note contradictions in his views on slavery, which he called a moral and political evil while defending its legality. Promoters of the Lost Cause made him an icon, and after the civil rights movement historians reassessed his failure to support rights for freedmen and his strategic choices.
robert-f-kennedy: Kennedy was born in Brookline, Massachusetts, on 20 November 1925, the seventh of the nine children of Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., a politician and businessman, and Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy. All four of his grandparents were children of Irish immigrants, and both parents came from prominent Irish-American families active in the Massachusetts Democratic Party. He enlisted in the United States Naval Reserve in 1943, entered Harvard University as a junior in 1946, and graduated in 1948 with a degree in political science.

After Harvard, Kennedy toured Europe and the Middle East as a correspondent for The Boston Post. He earned his law degree at the University of Virginia, worked at the Department of Justice, and resigned on 6 June 1952 to manage his brother John F. Kennedy's campaign for the United States Senate. He was chief counsel of the Senate Labor Rackets Committee from 1957 to 1959, where he publicly challenged the Teamsters president Jimmy Hoffa.

President-elect John F. Kennedy appointed him attorney general in 1961, over criticism that he was inexperienced. He built the first coordinated program involving all 26 federal law enforcement agencies against organized crime, and convictions of organized crime figures rose by 800 percent during his term. He authorised the Federal Bureau of Investigation to wiretap Martin Luther King Jr. on a limited basis. He resigned on 3 September 1964 and won a New York Senate seat, defeating the Republican incumbent Kenneth Keating.

In the Senate Kennedy opposed American involvement in the Vietnam War and sponsored legislation to draw private business to poor communities. After the Tet Offensive of early 1968 he entered the race for the Democratic presidential nomination. He won the California and South Dakota primaries on 4 June. Shortly after midnight he left a speech at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles through the kitchen, where Sirhan Sirhan, a 24-year-old Palestinian, shot him three times. He died 25 hours later and was buried near his brother at Arlington National Cemetery.
He married Ethel Skakel in 1950, and they had eleven children. His books include The Enemy Within (1960) and Thirteen Days, an account of the Cuban Missile Crisis published after his death.
robert-guiscard: Robert was the sixth of the twelve sons of Tancred of Hauteville and his second wife Fressenda, and was born in Normandy. From 999 to 1042 Normans had been migrating to Italy, mostly as mercenaries serving Byzantines and Lombard nobles. His elder brothers William Iron Arm and Drogo arrived in 1038 and joined a Lombard revolt against Byzantine rule in Apulia. Robert came in 1047; the Byzantine historian Anna Komnene, who disliked him, says that he left Normandy with five mounted riders and thirty men on foot and became chief of a roving band of robbers.

His sobriquet Guiscard, in contemporary Latin Viscardus, is often rendered as the Resourceful, the Cunning or the Fox. In Calabria he married Alberada of Buonalbergo in 1051. In 1053 he fought in the Battle of Civitate, where the Normans under Humphrey defeated the coalition raised by Pope Leo IX.

When Humphrey died in 1057 Robert succeeded him as count, passing over his elder half-brother Geoffrey. His marriage to Alberada was annulled for consanguinity, probably in 1058, and he married Sikelgaita. By the Treaty of Melfi in 1059 he swore fealty to Pope Nicholas II, who invested him as Duke of Apulia and Calabria and future Lord of Sicily, at a time when the papacy wanted Norman allies against the Holy Roman Emperor.

In Sicily he and his brother Roger took Messina by surprise in 1061. The County of Sicily was created for Roger in 1071, and Palermo fell a year later. Meanwhile Robert besieged Bari by land and water for four years until it surrendered in 1071.
