He took Salerno in December 1076 and the principality of Benevento in 1078, which he returned to the papacy in 1081. In 1081 he crossed to the Balkans and defeated Alexios I Komnenos at the Battle of Dyrrachium in October. In May 1084 he entered Rome to relieve Pope Gregory VII, besieged by Emperor Henry IV.

Robert died of a fever on 17 July 1085 at Atheras on Cephalonia and was buried in the Hauteville family mausoleum, the Abbey of Santissima Trinità at Venosa. His eldest son Bohemond, made illegitimate when the first marriage was annulled, received land around Taranto and later became a leader of the First Crusade and first prince of Antioch. The dukedom passed to Roger Borsa, his eldest son by Sikelgaita.

His conquests of Calabria and Sicily brought Latin Christianity to regions that had followed the Byzantine rite, and the descendants of his brother Roger I later created the Kingdom of Sicily. Dante places his spirit in the Heaven of Mars.
robert-ii-of-france: Robert II was the only son of Hugh Capet and Adelaide of Aquitaine, and was named after his ancestor Robert the Strong, who died fighting the Vikings in 866. His exact birth date and birthplace are unknown, though historians favour the year 972 and the city of Orléans. He was educated at Reims by Gerbert of Aurillac, the future Pope Sylvester II, and as junior king he presided over episcopal synods, including the Council of Saint-Basle de Verzy in 991.

Sole ruler from 996, Robert kept the alliance with Normandy and Anjou and so contained the ambitions of Count Odo II of Blois. His first marriage, to Rozala of Italy, ended in repudiation after three or four years, as she was about 22 years his elder and had borne him no child. A second marriage, to Bertha, daughter of King Conrad I of Burgundy, was also childless. He then married Constance of Arles, who bore seven children.

When Duke Henry I of Burgundy died on 15 October 1002 without a legitimate heir, Robert claimed the duchy as his nearest male kinsman. Henry's stepson Otto-William of Ivrea resisted, but the war ended in Robert's favour in 1005. Around 1007 Robert accused the Jews of complicity with the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, who had persecuted Christians, and chroniclers report spoliations, massacres and forced conversions; Pope John XVIII and his successor Sergius IV demanded an end to them.

Helgaud of Fleury, in his Life of King Robert the Pious, presents Robert as a model of charity and generous giving to religious houses; he was the first sovereign regarded as a miracle worker. After the early death of his eldest son Hugh in 1025, Constance opposed the crowning of Henry and favoured her son Robert, but the king imposed his will and Henry was consecrated junior king at Reims on 14 May 1027. Henry and his brother Robert later revolted against their father. Robert II died on 20 July 1031, after a reign of 35 years, and Henry I succeeded him.
robert-ley: Robert Ley was born in Niederbreidenbach in the Rhine Province, the seventh of eleven children of a farmer. He studied chemistry at Jena, Bonn and Münster. He volunteered for the army in 1914, served in artillery on both the eastern and western fronts, and in July 1917 was taken prisoner when his aircraft was shot down over France. It has been suggested that he suffered a traumatic brain injury in the crash; for the rest of his life he spoke with a stammer and had bouts of erratic behaviour, worsened by heavy drinking.

Released in January 1920, he took a doctorate and worked as a food chemist for a branch of IG Farben. Enraged by the French occupation of the Ruhr, he became an ultra-nationalist and joined the Nazi Party soon after reading Adolf Hitler's speech at his trial after the Beer Hall Putsch. He rejoined the re-founded party in March 1925 and became Gauleiter of the Southern Rhineland that July.

Ley edited a virulently anti-Semitic newspaper, the Westdeutscher Beobachter, from 1928 and sat in the Reichstag from September 1930 until May 1945. Although sympathetic to the working-class wing around Gregor Strasser, he always sided with Hitler in party disputes. When Strasser resigned in December 1932, Hitler took over party organisation and made Ley his chief of staff.

On 10 May 1933, after the suppression of the trade unions, Hitler appointed him head of the new German Labour Front, which became an arm of the state for deploying and disciplining labour, particularly for rearmament. In November 1933 it founded Strength Through Joy, which offered subsidised holidays, cruises, concerts and sport and was among the regime's most popular programmes. The Front also took over the Volkswagen project; the first models appeared in February 1939, but none of the 340,000 workers who paid for a car received one. Ley became notorious for drunkenness and for embezzling the Front's funds.
After the outbreak of war in 1939 his influence declined, as Fritz Todt and later Albert Speer took over direction of the workforce, but he stayed in Hitler's inner circle.

American paratroopers captured Ley on 16 May 1945 in the village of Schleching, where he had given a false name. He was indicted at the Nuremberg trials for conspiracy, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Three days after receiving the indictment, in October 1945, he killed himself in his cell, one of two of the 22 leaders at Nuremberg to do so, the other being Hermann Göring. The psychiatrist Douglas Kelley believed his behaviour came from organic brain damage.
robert-louis-stevenson: Stevenson was born at 8 Howard Place, Edinburgh, on 13 November 1850 and christened Robert Lewis Balfour Stevenson. His father, Thomas Stevenson, was a leading lighthouse engineer, and lighthouse design was the family's profession. About the age of 18 he changed the spelling of Lewis to Louis. Serious bronchial trouble kept him from school for long periods. In November 1867 he entered the University of Edinburgh to study engineering but showed no enthusiasm, and in April 1871 he told his father he would pursue a life of letters. It was agreed that he should read law instead.

In late 1873 he met Sidney Colvin, who became his literary adviser. In 1876 he met Fanny Van de Grift Osbourne, an American and a magazine short-story writer, at Grez-sur-Loing. In 1884 the couple settled in Bournemouth. He is best known for Treasure Island (1883), Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Kidnapped (1886) and A Child's Garden of Verses (1885). W. E. Henley may have provided the model for Long John Silver.

In June 1888 he chartered the yacht Casco and sailed with his family from San Francisco. For nearly three years he wandered the eastern and central Pacific, staying in the Hawaiian Islands, where he befriended King Kalākaua, and visiting the Gilbert Islands, where he spent months on Abemama with the chief Tem Binoka, whom he described in In the South Seas. In December 1889 the family arrived at Apia in Samoa and decided to settle, buying land at Vailima in January 1890. Alarmed at growing European and American influence in the islands, he turned from romance toward realism, notably in The Beach of Falesá.

On 3 December 1894, at Vailima, Stevenson collapsed while talking to his wife and died within a few hours at the age of 44, possibly of a brain haemorrhage. He was a celebrity in his lifetime, admired by writers including Henry James and Rudyard Kipling, and half his original manuscripts, among them that of Treasure Island, are lost.
robert-mugabe: Robert Gabriel Mugabe was born on 21 February 1924 at the Kutama Mission village in Southern Rhodesia. His father was a carpenter and his mother a Christian catechist for the village children, and the family belonged to the Zezuru clan, one of the smallest branches of the Shona people. He worked as a schoolteacher, and in 1949 won a scholarship to the University of Fort Hare in South Africa. There he joined the youth league of the African National Congress and met Jewish South African communists who introduced him to Marxist ideas, though he later said his biggest influence was Mahatma Gandhi. He left in 1952 with a degree in history and English literature.

Mugabe returned to Southern Rhodesia in May 1960. He was arrested in December 1963 and sentenced in March 1964 for subversive statements. He remained in prison for eight years in Salisbury, studying and gaining several degrees from the University of London. In March 1975 he left for Mozambique, where President Samora Machel at first doubted his leadership and kept him under partial house arrest for almost a year before accepting him as head of ZANU. After the Lancaster House Agreement he returned to Salisbury in January 1980 and campaigned without Marxist or revolutionary rhetoric, as Machel had advised. ZANU-PF won the election.

Zimbabwe gained internationally recognised independence on 18 April 1980, and Mugabe took the oath as prime minister. He pledged racial reconciliation and invited members of rival parties into his cabinet. Relations with Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU deteriorated, and in the Gukurahundi of 1982 to 1987 the 5th Brigade crushed ZAPU-linked opposition in Matabeleland in a campaign that killed at least 20,000 people. On 30 December 1987 parliament made him executive president, with power to dissolve parliament and run for an unlimited number of terms.

From 2000 he encouraged black Zimbabweans to seize white-owned farms, and food production fell, followed by famine and hyperinflation. On 6 November 2017 he dismissed Vice-President Emmerson Mnangagwa, and on 15 November the army placed him under house arrest. He resigned, and Mnangagwa succeeded him. Mugabe died in Singapore on 6 September 2019.
robert-owen: Robert Owen was born on 14 May 1771 in Newtown, Montgomeryshire, Wales, the sixth of seven children of a saddler, ironmonger and local postmaster. He received little formal schooling but read avidly. He left school at ten to work four years as an apprentice draper in Stamford, then worked in London drapery shops before moving at about eighteen to Manchester, where he spent twelve years.

In Manchester he borrowed £100 from his brother William to go into spinning mules, then newly invented for cotton thread. In 1792 the mill-owner Peter Drinkwater made him manager of the Piccadilly Mill, and he later helped found and manage the Chorlton Twist Mills. In 1793 he became a member of the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society. He married Ann Caroline Dale, daughter of David Dale, the proprietor of the New Lanark Mills, on 30 September 1799.

At New Lanark Owen tested his ideas on conditions for workers and their children. Visitors including the future Tsar Nicholas I of Russia came to study the mills. He devised a silent monitor, a block hung over each worker's place whose four colours showed the quality of their work, as an alternative to corporal punishment. In 1813 his partners, among them Jeremy Bentham and William Allen, bought out his share, and in the same year he published A New View of Society. He supported the Cotton Mills and Factories Act 1819.

Owen held that character is formed by conditions beyond the individual's control, so that people should be placed under proper influences from the earliest years. In 1824 he sailed to the United States with his son William and in January 1825 bought the town of Harmony on the Wabash River in Indiana from George Rapp's Harmony Society, renaming it New Harmony. At least 16 of about 130 communitarian experiments in the United States before the Civil War were Owenite or Owenite-influenced.

Back in London from 1828, Owen opened the National Equitable Labour Exchange in 1832, a system of labour notes that lasted in London until 1833. He formed the Association of all Classes of all Nations in 1835, in discussions of which socialism first became current in British usage. By 1846 the only lasting result of his agitation remained the Co-operative movement.

In 1817 Owen publicly declared all religions false; in 1854, aged 83, he turned to spiritualism after sittings with the American medium Maria B. Hayden. He died on 17 November 1858. His tomb stands in St Mary's Churchyard in Newtown, with railings added by the co-operative movement in 1902. Critics held his plans unachievable because he set no rules for property and membership, and opponents called him a dictator and a blasphemer.
robert-peel: Robert Peel was born on 5 February 1788 at Chamber Hall in Bury, Lancashire, the son of Sir Robert Peel, 1st Baronet, one of the richest textile manufacturers of the early Industrial Revolution, and of Ellen Yates. He took a double first in classics and mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford, and entered Parliament in 1809, aged 21, for the Irish rotten borough of Cashel, where he was elected unopposed by 24 electors. His sponsor was Sir Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington. His maiden speech in 1810 was described by the Speaker, Charles Abbot, as the best first speech since that of William Pitt the Younger.

Peel became Under-Secretary of State for War and the Colonies in 1810 and Chief Secretary for Ireland in 1812. His Peace Preservation Act 1814 allowed paid special constables to be appointed in disturbed counties, later called peelers, and laid the basis for the Royal Irish Constabulary. He entered the cabinet as Home Secretary in 1822. He cut the number of crimes punishable by death, consolidated criminal statutes into what are called Peel's Acts, and in the Gaols Act 1823 introduced pay for gaolers and education for inmates.

In 1829 he established the Metropolitan Police for London at Scotland Yard, with about 1,000 constables nicknamed bobbies or peelers. Unpopular at first, they cut crime, and by 1857 every British city had to form its own force. The nine Peelian Principles often credited to him were written by Charles Reith in 1948 as a summary of the force's 1829 Instructions. Peel, once a supporter of legal discrimination against Catholics, backed the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829, judging civil strife a greater danger than emancipation.

William IV invited Peel to form a government in December 1834, when he was in Italy, so Wellington acted as caretaker for three weeks. His minority ministry issued the Tamworth Manifesto, pledging modest reform, and was defeated in the Commons on 7 April 1835 by 285 votes to 258 over Church of Ireland revenues. It resigned having established the Ecclesiastical Commission.

He won a majority in the election of July 1841, in a recession with a budget deficit of £7.5 million. His second ministry passed the Mines and Collieries Act 1842, the Income Tax Act 1842, the Factories Act 1844 and the Railway Regulation Act 1844. Historians note that he was an intellectual convert to free trade from the 1820s. The Corn Laws were repealed on 29 June 1846 and he resigned. Leading the Peelites, he stayed influential until his death on 2 July 1850, and was said by some critics to be a traitor to Toryism and by others, like Thomas Carlyle, a reforming Hercules.
robert-schuman: Schuman was born on 29 June 1886 in Clausen, Luxembourg, and inherited his father's German citizenship. His father, a native of Lorraine, had become a German citizen when Germany annexed Lorraine in 1871 and had settled in Luxembourg. Schuman's mother was a Luxembourger, and he grew up in Luxembourg City speaking Luxembourgish. From 1904 to 1910 he studied law, economics, political philosophy, theology and statistics at universities in Berlin, Bonn and Strasbourg, and took a law degree at Strasbourg with the highest distinction. In 1912 he set up as a lawyer in Metz. After Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, he became a French citizen in 1918.

Elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1919, Schuman sat for Thionville until 1958, with an interval during the war. He contributed to the reintroduction of the French Civil and Commercial Codes in Alsace-Lorraine, a harmonisation known as the Lex Schuman, and exposed corruption in the Lorraine steel industries and in the region's railways. In 1940 he joined Paul Reynaud's wartime government in charge of refugees and kept the post under Pétain. On 10 July 1940 he voted to give Pétain full powers, though he refused to stay in the government.

Arrested in Metz on 14 September 1940, he was placed under house arrest and escaped to the unoccupied zone in August 1942. After the liberation he was declared ineligible for public office because of his vote of 1940, and regained his civic rights on 15 September 1945 after Charles de Gaulle answered his appeal favourably.

Schuman was Minister of Finance in 1946 and Prime Minister from 1947 to 1948, then Foreign Minister from 1948 until early 1953. His first government proposed a European Assembly, which became the Council of Europe, whose statutes were signed in London on 5 May 1949. He also signed the North Atlantic Treaty for France. On 9 May 1950 came the Schuman Declaration, prepared by Paul Reuter, Bernard Clappier, Jean Monnet and others, inviting West Germany and other countries to manage their coal and steel industries jointly. Six founder members signed the Treaty of Paris on 18 April 1951, creating the European Coal and Steel Community, and 9 May is observed as Europe Day.

He later served as Minister of Justice and became the first President of the European Parliamentary Assembly, which gave him the title Father of Europe. In 1958 he received the Karlspreis of Aachen. He was a devout Catholic, and in 2021 Pope Francis declared him venerable. He died on 4 September 1963.
robert-schumann: Robert Schumann was born on 8 June 1810 in Zwickau, in the Kingdom of Saxony, the fifth and last child of August Schumann and his wife Johanna Christiane. His father was a bookseller, lexicographer, author and publisher who made considerable sums from German translations of Cervantes, Walter Scott and Lord Byron, and Robert, his favourite child, spent many hours exploring the classics in his father's collection. August died in 1826, and Schumann's mother, less enthusiastic about a musical career, persuaded him to study law. He entered Leipzig University in 1828, but reading and playing the piano occupied much of his time. He discovered the works of Franz Schubert, whose death in November 1828 made him cry all night.

Schumann published his Op. 1, piano variations on a theme spelled from the name of Countess Pauline von Abegg, who was almost certainly his own invention. The use of a musical cryptogram became a recurrent feature of his later music. In 1832 he published Papillons, a programmatic piano piece. He came to regard himself as having two sides to his personality and art, and named his introspective self Eusebius and his impetuous alter ego Florestan. In 1840 he turned to song, producing more than half his total output of Lieder, including Myrthen, a wedding present for Clara, Frauenliebe und Leben and Dichterliebe.

In 1841 he focused on orchestral music. His First Symphony, The Spring, was premiered by Mendelssohn at the Gewandhaus on 31 March, at a concert where Clara also played. In 1842 he wrote three string quartets, a Piano Quintet, written for Clara, and a Piano Quartet. His opera Genoveva, premiered in Leipzig in June 1850, was not the success he hoped for, and Franz Liszt revived it at Weimar in 1855, the only other production in Schumann's lifetime. Schumann wrote more than 300 songs for voice and piano, favouring such later Romantic poets as Heine, Eichendorff and Mörike.

Schumann moved to Düsseldorf in 1850 as the city's director of music but resigned after three years, since his shyness and mental instability made it hard to work with his orchestra. In 1853 he met the twenty-year-old Johannes Brahms and praised him in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. The following year his mental health deteriorated gravely. He threw himself into the Rhine, was rescued and was taken to a private sanatorium near Bonn, where he died on 29 July 1856.

His reputation rests chiefly on the piano works and songs of the 1830s and 1840s. Later composers drew on him, among them Mahler, Richard Strauss, Arnold Schoenberg, Bizet, Fauré, Debussy and Ravel. Elgar called him his ideal, and Tchaikovsky, though critical of his orchestration, described him as a composer of genius.
robert-the-bruce: Robert was born on 11 July 1274, most likely at Turnberry Castle in Ayrshire, the eldest of ten children of Robert de Brus, 6th Lord of Annandale, and Marjorie, Countess of Carrick. From his mother he inherited the Earldom of Carrick and from his father the Lordship of Annandale and a descent from David I that gave a claim to the Scottish throne. In 1298 he became a Guardian of Scotland, and he resigned in 1300 after quarrelling with his rival John Comyn.

Comyn was killed in Dumfries in February 1306, and Bruce was excommunicated by Pope Clement V, though Robert Wishart, Bishop of Glasgow, absolved him. Six weeks later, on Palm Sunday 25 March 1306, Bishop Lamberton inaugurated him as King of Scots at Scone, and the next day Isabella MacDuff, Countess of Buchan, crowned him a second time. After defeat at Methven he went into hiding and returned in 1307 to win at Loudoun Hill. Victories between 1310 and 1314 won him much of Scotland, and he took Berwick, the last English stronghold, in 1318.

After Bannockburn his armies raided Yorkshire and Lancashire. In 1315 he sent his brother Edward to Ireland to open a second front and secure a second crown, and Edward was crowned High King of Ireland in 1316. The Declaration of Arbroath of 1320 strengthened his position with the papacy, and Pope John XXII recognised him in 1324 and eventually lifted his excommunication. The Treaty of Corbeil renewed the Franco-Scottish alliance in 1326, and the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton in 1328 had Edward III renounce all claims to sovereignty over Scotland.

Robert died on 7 June 1329 at the Manor of Cardross, near Dumbarton, leaving his infant son David II in the care of Moray. His body was buried in Dunfermline Abbey beneath a box tomb of white Italian marble bought in Paris, his heart in Melrose Abbey, and his viscera in the chapel of Saint Serf. The tomb was destroyed at the Reformation, and ten alabaster fragments are in the National Museum of Scotland. He is regarded in Scotland as a national hero, and all later Scottish monarchs descend from him. A legend tells that while hiding after Methven he watched a spider fail twice and succeed on a third attempt to span a cave.
robert-walpole: Walpole was born at Houghton, Norfolk, in 1676, one of 19 children and the third son of Robert Walpole, a local gentleman and Whig member of Parliament. He entered Eton College in 1690 as a King's Scholar and matriculated at King's College, Cambridge, in 1696. He left Cambridge in 1698 after the death of his last older brother to help his father run the estate, and abandoned his plan to become a clergyman. His father died in November 1700 and he inherited the estate. In January 1701 he won a seat at Castle Rising, and from 1702 he sat for King's Lynn.

Walpole rose under Queen Anne and was Secretary at War from 1708. After the accession of George I in 1714 the Whigs held power for fifty years, and Walpole became Paymaster of the Forces. When the South Sea Bubble collapsed in 1720, he was recalled to the Cabinet. A committee found corruption among ministers, and Walpole shielded Lords Stanhope and Sunderland, which earned him the nickname the Screen. In 1721 he began his premiership.

When George II succeeded in 1727 it seemed for a few days that Walpole would be dismissed, but Queen Caroline advised the King to keep him. Charles Townshend retired on 15 May 1730, leaving Walpole the dominant partner. Lord Bolingbroke and William Pulteney attacked him in the periodical The Craftsman. Walpole tried to prevent war with Spain but was opposed by the King, the Commons and part of his Cabinet, and in 1739 the War of Jenkins' Ear began.

Walpole resigned in 1742 and became Earl of Orford. A committee inquired into his ministry but found no substantial evidence of wrongdoing. He kept influence with George II as the Minister behind the Curtain. He died on 18 March 1745.

Under Walpole the Tories became a minor faction and the Whigs a dominant party. He is regarded as Britain's first prime minister, though his power rested on the favour of the King and on personal influence rather than on the office, and several decades passed before the premiership became the country's most powerful post. His policy of peace contributed to prosperity and he secured the Hanoverian dynasty.
rochefort-charente-maritime: Rochefort lies on the river Charente, close to its outflow into the Atlantic Ocean, about 30 kilometres southeast of La Rochelle. It is a port on the Charente estuary and a subprefecture of the department of Charente-Maritime. Jean-Baptiste Colbert chose it as a place of refuge, defence and supply for the French Navy.

It is a notable example of a 17th-century ville nouvelle, a new town whose design and building resulted from a political decree. The reason for building it was in large part that royal power could hardly depend on rebellious Protestant La Rochelle, which Cardinal Richelieu had had to besiege a few decades earlier.

The Arsenal de Rochefort served as a naval base and dockyard until it closed in 1926. In September 1757 the town was the target of an ambitious British raid during the Seven Years' War. From 1766 it also had a bagne, a high-security penal colony with hard labour, such as existed at military harbours and naval bases like Toulon and Brest because they provided free labour.

During the Jacobin period of the French Revolution over 800 Roman Catholic priests and other clergy who refused the oath of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy were put aboard prison ships in Rochefort harbour, and most died of the conditions.

On 17 July 1815 Napoleon Bonaparte, who had spent several days on the Île-d'Aix hoping to flee to America, surrendered to Captain F. L. Maitland aboard HMS Bellerophon off Rochefort, ending the Hundred Days. Well into the 20th century Rochefort remained primarily a garrison town.

The buildings of the original naval establishment include a hospital with a School of Naval Medicine, now a museum, and the Arsenal with a monumental gateway and the National Navy Museum. The Rope Factory, the corderie, at over 370 metres long was for centuries the longest manufacturing building in the world. Three dry docks for shipbuilding and repair and a cannon foundry also survive. The Rochefort-Martrou Transporter Bridge, built in 1900, is the only remaining one in France. L'Hermione, a replica of a frigate of 1779, was completed in the town in 2014. The Hôtel de Ville on Place Colbert was completed in around 1770.
rochester-kent: Rochester is a port town at the lowest bridging point of the River Medway, in the unitary authority of Medway in Kent, about 50 km east-southeast of London. It forms a conurbation with Chatham, Rainham, Strood and Gillingham. The Romano-British name Durobrivae is commonly explained as 'stronghold by the bridge' or as a Latinisation of a British word meaning 'swiftstream'. Bede, writing around 730, calls it Hrofes cæster, and from this came the later forms Hrofescester, Rovescester and Rochester. Its street plan was fixed in the Middle Ages by the Medway, Watling Street, Rochester Priory and Rochester Castle.

Remains from the Neolithic have been found near Rochester, which was one of the two administrative centres of the Cantiaci tribe in the Celtic period. During the Roman conquest a decisive battle was fought on the Medway somewhere near it, and the first bridge was built early in the Roman period. In the later Roman period the settlement was walled in stone. King Æthelberht of Kent established a legal system that survives in the 12th-century Textus Roffensis, and in 604 the bishopric and Rochester Cathedral were founded.

The present cathedral was built between 1080 and 1130, with further work in 1227 and 1343. Rochester Castle, built by Bishop Gundulf to guard the river crossing, has one of the best-preserved keeps in England or France. In the First Barons' War baronial forces took it from Archbishop Stephen Langton and held it against King John, who besieged it in 1215. In 1667 a Dutch fleet under de Ruijter broke through the chain at Upnor and sailed to Rochester Bridge, where it captured and burned part of the English fleet.

Rochester was a city from 1211 until 1998, when it lost that status as its local government district was abolished. The Royal Navy dockyard at Chatham closed in 1984 and caused a surge in local unemployment. Rochester has long been tied to Charles Dickens, who owned nearby Gads Hill Place and based many of his novels on the area. The King's School, which grew out of the cathedral's foundation of 604, is recognised as the second-oldest continuously running school in the world.
rodez: Rodez lies about 150 kilometres north-east of Toulouse, in the western foothills of the Massif Central, between the high limestone plateaus of the Grands Causses and the damp hills of the Ségala. The city was built on an isolated conical hill known as Le Piton and gradually spread over the surrounding slopes. The Aveyron crosses the commune. Its altitude is about 550 metres, and it has an oceanic climate that is colder than that of other cities in the south of France.

The name has Gaulish roots. In antiquity the settlement was Segodunum, from sego, strong, and dunum, hill, so that the name means high hill or stronghold. In late Imperial times it was Civitas Rutenorum, the city of the Ruteni, from which the modern name derives. Its inhabitants are called Ruthénois in French.

Rodez has existed from at least the 5th century BCE, when the Ruteni, a Celtic tribe, are said to have founded one of the oppida characteristic of Gallic civilisation here. Elements of its heritage testify to the later Romanisation of Segodunum. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was occupied by the Visigoths and then the Franks. The Moors seized it in 725 and damaged the ancient church. It was later held by the armies of the Dukes of Aquitaine and the Counts of Toulouse, and English troops captured it during the Hundred Years' War.

At the beginning of the 16th century Bishop François d'Estaing finished the Cathedral of Our Lady of Rodez. He added the bell tower, 87 metres high and topped by a Virgin, still the highest bell tower without a spire in France. The work was completed between 1510 and 1526 despite plague in the city. The old rival of Rodez was Villefranche-de-Rouergue, but the French Revolution gave Rodez the role of administrative centre, because of its central position, as prefecture of the new department of Aveyron.

Rodez is the prefecture of the Aveyron department in the Occitania region and the capital of the former province of Rouergue. It is also the seat of the Diocese of Rodez and Vabres. Its population reached a maximum of 25,550 in 1975 and has stayed around 24,000 since. The old town, Vieux-Rodez, keeps the remains of its ramparts, narrow streets and squares such as the Place du Bourg and the Place de la Cité, where markets are held.

The cathedral was made a Historic Monument in 1862. The city has long been a centre of Occitan culture, and troubadours are said to have found refuge there. The Musée Soulages is among its three museums.
roermond: Roermond lies on the lower Roer, on the east bank of the Meuse, in the middle of the province of Limburg. Celtic inhabitants lived on both sides of the Roer. The Romans built a bridge, now called the Steene Brök, and founded the first town there, now the suburb of Voorstad Sint Jacob. Roermond received town rights in 1231.

From about 1180 to 1543 Roermond belonged to the Duchy of Guelders. Otto IV of Brunswick destroyed it in 1213, but by 1232 it had been rebuilt and given its own seal, mint and court. A charterhouse was founded in 1376. Around 1350 it became capital of the Upper Quarter of Guelders. The French besieged it in 1388, it joined the Hanseatic League in 1441, and by 1472 it had the right to coin money.

From 1543 to 1702 the area was part of the Spanish Netherlands. The Battle of Rheindalen, fought near Roermond on 23 April 1568, signalled the start of the Eighty Years' War. William the Silent occupied the town in 1572, and on 23 July of that year Calvinists murdered 13 Catholic clerics there. Under Spanish rule Roermond became a bastion of the Counter-Reformation, and in 1613 64 witches were burnt on the Galgeberg, the largest witch trial in the Netherlands. The Germans occupied it from 1940 to 1945, and by its liberation on 1 March 1945 about 90 per cent of its buildings were damaged or destroyed.

Roermond has been the seat of a Catholic diocese since 1559. Its skyline is dominated by the towers of St. Christopher's Cathedral and the Munsterkerk, and the town centre is a designated conservation area. Other monuments include the Carolus Chapel, the Cuypershuis and the Rattentoren.
roger-ii-of-sicily: Roger was born at Mileto in Calabria in 1095, the youngest son of Roger I of Sicily. By then Norman adventurers, who had reached southern Italy by 999, had become the rulers of the major polities south of Rome. His father died in 1101, and his elder brother Simon died in 1105 at the age of twelve. Roger, aged nine, inherited the County of Sicily under the regency of his mother, Adelaide del Vasto, and his brother-in-law Robert of Burgundy. In 1112, at sixteen, he began his personal rule.

When William II of Apulia died childless in July 1127, Roger claimed the Hauteville possessions on the peninsula. Pope Honorius II opposed the union of Sicily and Apulia, but in August 1128 he invested Roger as Duke of Apulia at Benevento. In 1130 Roger supported Antipope Anacletus II against Innocent II, and Anacletus made him king of Sicily by a bull of 27 September. He was crowned at Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. This brought a ten-year war, in which Bernard of Clairvaux, Louis VI of France, Henry I of England and the emperor Lothair III stood against him, and the southern nobility rebelled.

Roger lost the Battle of Nocera in 1132 and suffered his worst defeat at Rignano in 1137, but he wore down his enemies. In July 1139 his son captured Innocent II at Galluccio, and by the Treaty of Mignano the pope recognised him as king. He then issued the Assizes of Ariano, which gave the king and his officials wide powers over the vassals, and introduced a new coinage, the ducat.

His court at Palermo drew men of several cultures, among them the geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi, and George of Antioch, whom he made ammiratus ammiratorum, the origin of the word admiral, commanded his fleet. George took Tripoli in 1146 and Cape Bona in 1148, and in 1147 raided Corfu, Athens, Thebes and Corinth.

Roger died at Palermo on 26 February 1154 and was buried in the cathedral there. His fourth son, William, succeeded him; the African conquests were lost in William's reign and never became an integral part of the kingdom. The lands Roger gathered formed the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily for the next seven centuries. His royal mantle, dated to 1133-34 by its Arabic inscription, was made in a royal workshop at Palermo and was later used as a coronation cloak by the Holy Roman Emperors. It is now in the Imperial Treasury in Vienna. Karol Szymanowski's opera King Roger of 1926 takes him as its subject.
rogier-van-der-weyden: Few certain facts of Rogier's life survive, because archives were lost in 1695 and again in 1940. He was born Rogelet de le Pasture in Tournai in 1399 or 1400, the son of Henri de le Pasture, a knife maker, and Agnes de Wattrélos. In 1426 he married Elisabeth, daughter of a Brussels shoemaker. On 5 March 1427 the painters' guild records show Rogelet de le Pasture entering the workshop of Robert Campin with Jacques Daret, and on 1 August 1432 he obtained the title of master painter. The close stylistic link between Daret, Campin and Van der Weyden is the main argument for seeing him as Campin's pupil.

By 21 October 1435 the family had settled in Brussels, where he took the Flemish form of his name. From 2 March 1436 he held the post of painter to the town, created for him and linked to a commission for four justice scenes for the Golden Chamber of the city hall.

The Justice of Trajan and Herkinbald panels, each about 4.5 metres across, were finished before 1450 and destroyed in the French bombardment of Brussels in 1695. They are known from descriptions and a tapestry copy at Bern. His Descent from the Cross, painted for Notre-Dame-hors-des-Murs in Leuven, was sent to the King of Spain, and when the ship sank the painting floated. King Juan II of Castile gave the Miraflores Altarpiece to the Charterhouse of Miraflores in 1445.

According to some sources he went to Italy in 1449, and the House of Este and the Medici family commissioned paintings from him. His portraits include those of Philip the Good, Isabella of Portugal and Charles the Bold. He died on 18 June 1464 in Brussels and was buried in St. Catherine's Chapel of the cathedral.

He worked from life models and often idealised their features, enlarging the eyes and strengthening the jaw. He introduced new religious iconography, showing patrons taking part in sacred events and joining half-length portraits of the Madonna with portraits of people at prayer to form diptychs.

No work can be attributed to him with certainty from fifteenth-century documents alone, and later writers confused his identity: Van Mander, misled by Vasari, took Rogier of Bruges and Rogier of Brussels for two painters. Erwin Panofsky established in 1953 that there was only one painter with two names. His influence reached France, Germany, Italy and Spain, and Hans Memling and Martin Schongauer were among those who followed him.
rohingya: The Rohingya are an Indo-Aryan ethnolinguistic group from Rakhine State, historically Arakan, a coastal region on the Bay of Bengal between South and Southeast Asia. By the 4th century Arakan was one of the earliest Indianised kingdoms in Southeast Asia. Arab merchants are recorded on the coast of south-eastern Bengal from the 9th century, and the Rohingya trace their history to this period. Early evidence of Bengali Muslim settlement in Arakan dates from the reign of Min Saw Mon (1430–34) of the Kingdom of Mrauk U, who regained his throne in 1430 with military help from the Bengal Sultanate.

The Rohingya maintain that they are indigenous to western Myanmar, with a heritage of over a millennium; the Myanmar government regards them as migrants from Chittagong in the colonial and postcolonial periods. After the Konbaung Dynasty conquered Arakan in 1785, as many as 35,000 people fled to the Chittagong region in 1799. Under British rule, thousands of Bengalis from Chittagong settled in Arakan in the early 19th century as farm labourers. A separate administrative zone for the Rohingya-majority north, the Mayu Frontier District, existed from 1961 to 1964.

After the coup of 1962 the Rohingya were increasingly deprived of political rights. A military operation in 1978 sent an estimated 200,000 refugees into Bangladesh, most of whom later returned. A citizenship law of 1982 did not list the Rohingya among Burma's 135 national races, which left much of the population stateless. Further crackdowns followed in 1991–1992 and 2012, and from 2016 most Rohingya in Myanmar were driven into Bangladesh. The International Criminal Court began an investigation of crimes against humanity, and the International Court of Justice heard a case alleging genocide.

Before that crackdown about 1.4 million Rohingya lived in Myanmar, chiefly in the northernmost townships of Rakhine, where they formed 80 to 98 per cent of the people. Their language is Indo-Aryan and related to Chittagonian, and both are related to Bengali but are not mutually intelligible with it. It has been written in Arabic, Urdu, Roman and Burmese scripts and in Hanifi, a newer alphabet derived from Arabic. Most Rohingya are Muslim, following a blend of Sunni Islam and Sufism, with Hindu and Christian minorities. Myanmar's governments have rejected the name Rohingya and call the community Bengali.
rohtak: Rohtak is the administrative headquarters of Rohtak district in Haryana. It lies 70 kilometres north-west of New Delhi and 250 kilometres south of the state capital Chandigarh, and forms part of the National Capital Region. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with an average annual rainfall of about 613 millimetres, 80 percent of it falling between July and September, so that farming in the district depends largely on canal irrigation and tubewells. The name is derived from an earlier form, Rohtasgarh, the fort of Rohtas, after a Rajput chieftain associated with the early settlement. The older form Rauhītaka occurs in the 12th-century Rājataraṅgiṇī.

Excavations at Khokhrakot have uncovered clay moulds for casting coins of the Yaudheyas, dated to the 3rd or 4th century CE, with clay seals of that and later periods and Gupta terracotta from the 4th to 6th centuries. The astronomical text Surya Siddhanta, of the 4th century CE, placed a prime meridian between Avanti (Ujjain) and Rohitaka, taken to be Rohtak. A 7th-century statue of Parshvanatha, the 23rd Jain tirthankara, was found at the village of Asthal Bohar, and Jain sources of the 9th century show the prominence of Parshvanatha in the area.

The town flourished until the 10th century, as coins of Samanta Deva of the Hindu Shahi found there show, and the Ghaznavids under Mahmud of Ghazni conquered it between 1020 and 1030. Chahamanas ruled the region in the 12th century.

The Ain-i-Akbari lists Rohtak as a Mughal pargana under the Delhi sarkar, dominated by the Jats, with a brick fort, a revenue of 8,599,270 dams and a force of 2,000 infantry and 100 cavalry. A fort in what is now Qilla Mohallah was besieged by Syed Khizer Khan in 1410 and fell only after six months. In 1762 Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, sent his sons Jawahar Singh and Nahar Singh to capture what is now Haryana, and they took the Rohtak pargana. British officers lived there from 1810, and All Saints Church was completed in 1867.

Rohtak had 373,133 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It is home to Maharshi Dayanand University, founded in 1976, and to the Pandit Bhagwat Dayal Sharma Post Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences, which began as a medical college in 1960. The Baba Mast Nath monastery was founded in 1731, and the town has havelis, mosques and temples in traditional Indian and Mughal styles. It lies on national highways and has a railway junction with connections to Delhi.
rollo: Rollo, in Old Norse Hrólfr, was almost certainly born in Scandinavia, in either Norway or Denmark, but his origin is heavily disputed. Dudo of Saint-Quentin, writing in the late 10th century at the request of Rollo's grandson Richard I of Normandy, called him Danish and said he left after a hostile Danish king killed his brother Gurim. Medieval Norwegian and Icelandic writers identified him with Hrólfr the Walker, son of the jarl Rognvald Eysteinsson of Møre in western Norway.

The debate was begun in the late nineteenth century by the Danish historian Johannes Steenstrup and partly followed national lines. British, French and Norwegian scholars have generally accepted the Norwegian-Icelandic tradition, while Danish, Swedish and German historians have tended to follow Dudo. The question cannot be settled conclusively. Dudo's work was an official biography, and many of his genealogical claims may have been invented to legitimise Rollo's line.

The earliest well-attested event associated with Rollo is the siege of Paris in 885 and 886, in which he was a prominent leader of the Vikings, fended off by Odo of France. In 911 Robert I of France defeated another Viking band at Chartres with his horsemen, which paved the way for Rollo's baptism and settlement. Under the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, Charles III recognised the lands Rollo held in return for baptism and help in defending the realm. Rollo took the baptismal name Robert after his godfather, Robert I, and the agreement was to be sealed by his marriage to Gisela, Charles's daughter.

After his oath Rollo divided the lands between the Epte and the Risle among his chieftains and made Rouen his capital. The earliest record of him is a charter of 918 mentioning Rollo and his associates, and a later agreement under Rudolph of France conceded the Bessin and Maine to a group of Norsemen presumed to be his. He died between a last mention in 928 and 933.

His son and successor William Longsword and his grandson Richard the Fearless forged Normandy into West Francia's most cohesive principality. The descendants of Rollo and his men assimilated with Frankish culture and became known as the Normans. Rollo was the great-great-great-grandfather of William the Conqueror, and his direct male descendants ruled Normandy until Stephen of Blois became King of England and Duke of Normandy in 1135.
roman-empire: By 100 BCE the city of Rome had expanded its rule from the Italian peninsula to most of the Mediterranean, but civil wars severely destabilised the Republic. They culminated in the victory of Octavian over Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE the Roman Senate granted Octavian overarching military power (imperium) and the title of Augustus, marking his accession as the first Roman emperor. The first two centuries of the Empire saw stability and prosperity known as the Pax Romana, and Rome reached its widest extent under Trajan (r. 98 to 117 CE).

Decline began under Commodus (r. 180 to 192). In the 3rd century a 50-year crisis of civil war, plagues and invasions threatened the Empire; the Gallic and Palmyrene empires broke away, and the Empire was reunified under Aurelian (r. 270 to 275). Diocletian (r. 284 to 305) set up two imperial courts, in the Greek East and the Latin West, and Constantine (r. 306 to 337), the first Christian emperor, moved the imperial seat to Byzantium in 330 and renamed it Constantinople. The Western Empire collapsed in 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustus. The Eastern Empire survived until the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Provinces were either senatorial, governed by proconsuls appointed by lot each year, or imperial, belonging to the emperor and governed by legates. The Romans lacked the manpower to rule by force alone, so they cooperated with local elites, and communities that showed loyalty kept their own laws and could collect their own taxes. Latin and Greek were the main languages, and the Empire was deliberately multilingual. By the time of Nero it was not unusual to find a former slave richer than a freeborn citizen. Roman religion rested on correct ritual and sacrifice rather than faith or dogma, and as many as 135 days of the calendar were given to festivals and games.

Several states claimed to be the Empire's successor. The Holy Roman Empire was established in 800 when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Roman emperor, and the Russian Tsardom counted itself the Third Rome, Constantinople having been the second. When the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II made it his capital and claimed to sit on the throne of the Roman Empire. Rome's republican institutions influenced the Italian city-state republics, the early United States and modern democratic republics.
roman-forum: The Forum lies in the small valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills. Its long axis runs northwest to southeast, from the foot of the Capitoline to that of the Velian Hill. The site was originally a marshy lake where water drained from the surrounding hills, and tradition says the Tarquins drained it with the Cloaca Maxima.

Sediment from Tiber floods and from the eroding hills kept raising the ground, and residents paved over debris too great to remove; the final travertine paving, still visible, dates from the reign of Augustus. By the imperial period the large buildings around it had reduced the open space to a rectangle of about 130 by 50 metres, with the Basilica Aemilia on the north and the Basilica Julia on the south.

Pottery shows that people occupied the Forum, Palatine and Capitoline in the Final Bronze Age. In the early Iron Age part of the future Forum was a cemetery, probably until the late 9th century BCE, and in the 8th century BCE it began to change into a public site. Roman tradition links its beginnings to an alliance between Romulus and Titus Tatius, and credits Numa Pompilius with the cult of Vesta and the Regia.

In the Republic the Comitium was the centre of judicial and political life. The earliest Forum temples of known date are those of Saturn (497 BCE) and of Castor and Pollux (484 BCE). Gaius Gracchus is said to have turned from the Senate to speak to the people from the Rostra, as the tribune Caius Licinius had two centuries before.

Julius Caesar built the Basilica Julia and the Curia Julia, and Augustus completed the Forum's final form, adding the Temple of Caesar in 29 BCE. In 69 CE Galba was killed there by Otho's cavalry. Business and legal affairs moved north to Trajan's Forum and the Basilica Ulpia, and the Basilica of Maxentius of 312 CE was the last major expansion.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the population of Rome shrank and the Forum was largely abandoned. The Column of Phocas, erected on 1 August 608, was the last monumental addition. Old buildings were turned into churches, and the Forum became known as the Campo Vaccino, the cattle field.

In the 16th century Pope Paul III used it as a quarry for the new Saint Peter's Basilica. Carlo Fea began clearing the debris in 1803, and the Italian government began official excavations in 1898, led by Giacomo Boni until his death in 1925. Excavations continue. Artists including Claude Lorrain, Turner and Piranesi drew the site, whose ruins today attract more than four million visitors a year.
roman-law: Before the Twelve Tables, Roman private law was the ius civile, which applied only to Roman citizens, was bound to religion and was strictly formal. According to Livy's traditional account, the plebeian tribune C. Terentilius Arsa proposed that the law be written down to stop magistrates applying it arbitrarily. Ten men, the decemviri, were chosen in 451 BCE and produced ten tablets in 450 BCE; a second board is said to have added two more in 449 BCE. Modern scholars doubt that a second decemvirate took place and consider it unlikely that an official delegation went to Greece.

The original text was probably destroyed when the Gauls burned Rome in 387 BCE. The surviving fragments show that the Tables were not a code in the modern sense but specific provisions altering customary law, mostly on private law and civil procedure. The Lex Hortensia of 287 BCE later made the decisions of plebeian assemblies binding on all.

Rome's most important contribution, in this view, was a class of professional jurists and a legal science, rather than well-drafted statutes. Between about 201 and 27 BCE the praetors' edicts created a body of praetoric law that supplemented the formal ius civile and drew on the ius gentium, the law of peoples. Around 130 CE the jurist Salvius Iulianus drafted a standard form of the praetor's edict, which later jurists such as Paulus and Ulpian commented on.

Gaius's Institutes divided private law into persons, things and legal actions, a scheme later reflected in Blackstone's Commentaries, the French Code civil and the German BGB. A person's rights depended on status: citizen or foreigner, free or slave, head of a family or a member under another's authority.

By the middle of the 3rd century jurisprudence had all but ended in the West, and classical law gave way to a vulgar law. In the East, Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis of 529 to 534 remained the basis of legal practice. In the West the Digest was largely ignored until a manuscript was rediscovered in Italy around 1070. Glossators then studied it at Bologna, whose law school gradually became Europe's first university.

By the middle of the 16th century Roman law, mixed with canon law and feudal custom, formed the ius commune of continental Europe. Only England and the Nordic countries did not take part in its wholesale reception. National codes, beginning with the French civil code of 1804 and ending with the German BGB in 1900, brought this practice to an end. The legal systems of South Africa and San Marino are still based on the old ius commune, and the civil law system spread through colonial expansion.
roman-persian-wars: The Romans and the Parthians came into contact through their conquests of parts of the Seleucid Empire. The Parthians, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty, had by the early first century BCE conquered Persia, Mesopotamia and Armenia. In 64 BCE Pompey conquered the remaining Seleucid territories in Syria and advanced the Roman frontier to the Euphrates, where it met Parthian territory.

In 53 BCE the Roman general Marcus Licinius Crassus invaded Mesopotamia and was killed with his son Publius at the Battle of Carrhae by Parthians under Surena, the worst Roman defeat since Arausio. Rivalry over Armenia led to war from 58 CE, ended in 63 CE when Tiridates and his descendants were allowed to rule Armenia on condition that they received the crown from the Roman emperor. In 114 and 115 the Emperor Trajan annexed Armenia and Mesopotamia and captured the Parthian capital Ctesiphon, but revolts forced him to withdraw, and he died in 117.

After Ardashir I founded the Sasanian Empire, he raided Mesopotamia and Syria in 230. The Emperor Gordian III was defeated at Misiche in 244 and Philip paid 500,000 denarii for peace. The Anastasian War began in 502 when Kavadh I seized Theodosiopolis and besieged Amida. Khosrau I broke the Treaty of Eternal Peace in 540, invaded Syria and deported the people of Antioch to Persia; the Lazic War that followed was ended by a truce in 545 secured by Roman payments. A new war from 571 turned on the Caucasus.

In 602 the army mutinied under Phocas, who killed the Emperor Maurice. Khosrau II used the murder as a pretext, and in the following years the Persians took the fortress cities of Mesopotamia one by one, then overran Syria in 611 and entered Anatolia. Heraclius took the throne in 610 but was decisively defeated outside Antioch in 613.

The final war and a century of almost continuous conflict left both empires crippled. Persia fell into dynastic turmoil and civil war after Kavadh II died only months after coming to the throne, and was weakened by economic decline, heavy taxation, religious unrest and the power of provincial landholders. The Byzantine Empire had exhausted its financial reserves, and the Balkans were largely in Slav hands. Both were then attacked by the Rashidun Caliphate, which conquered Persia and took the Levant, Egypt and the rest of North Africa.

Historians note that the frontier in upper Mesopotamia stayed more or less constant for centuries, although Nisibis, Singara and Dara changed hands. Cassius Dio observed a never-ending cycle of armed confrontations.
roman-republic: Rome had been ruled by monarchs elected for life by the Senate. Traditional histories say the last, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled in 509 BCE after his son Sextus Tarquinius raped a noblewoman, Lucretia, and that a revolution led by the semi-mythical Lucius Junius Brutus transferred the king's powers to two consuls elected for one year, each able to veto his colleague. Most modern scholarship describes these accounts as the quasi-mythological detailing of an aristocratic coup within Tarquin's own family, or a consequence of an Etruscan occupation of Rome, rather than a popular revolution.

Republican Rome was in a state of near-perpetual war. After the Gallic sack of Rome it conquered most of the Italian peninsula in a century. It fought three wars against Carthage and defeated it at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, then defeated Philip V and Perseus of Macedon, Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire and Vercingetorix of the Arverni. At home the plebs achieved political equality with the patricians by the 4th century BCE, ending the Conflict of the Orders peacefully.

From 133 BCE the late Republic saw substantial domestic strife. The Social War between Rome and its Italian allies over citizenship expanded civil violence, and mass slavery contributed to three Servile Wars. Powerful semi-autonomous generals led to civil wars, first between Marius and Sulla and in 49 BCE between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Erich S. Gruen holds that civil war caused the fall of the republic, not the reverse. It ended in 27 BCE with the establishment of the Roman Empire.

The constitution was an unwritten, evolving set of principles passed down through precedent. There were annual elections, but the system was an elective oligarchy, with powerful families largely monopolising the senior magistracies. The Senate's decrees were officially advice, yet magistrates usually followed them, and it came to control finances and external affairs. Consuls and praetors held imperium, the authority to command an army. Census figures report 130,000 Romans in 509 BCE and 4,937,000 in 14 CE. From 107 BCE all citizens, whatever their wealth, could enter the army, which became paid and attracted the poorest.
roman-senate: The word senatus comes from senex, 'old man', and means an assembly of elders. In the Roman Kingdom, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, the heads of the leading clans formed a board of elders. The senate is said to have been created by Rome's first king, Romulus. It served as the king's council, and its most important function was to choose new kings: the interrex nominated a candidate, the senate approved him, the people elected him and the senate approved him again. After the last king was overthrown, Lucius Junius Brutus and Publius Valerius Publicola are said to have raised the senate to 300 members in 509 BCE.

In the Republic the senate had 300 to 500 members who served for life, at first only patricians. Its decrees, the senatus consulta, were formally advice to a magistrate and had no legal force, but they were usually obeyed. Only the senate could authorise spending from the treasury, and it decided which magistrate governed which province. After 202 BCE the senatus consultum ultimum replaced the dictatorship in emergencies.

Senators wore a toga with a broad purple stripe and an iron, later gold, ring. They could not engage in banking or public contracts, could not leave Italy without permission and were paid no salary. Meetings opened with a sacrifice and a search for omens and had to end by nightfall, so a determined senator could talk a proposal to death.

The senate reached the apex of its republican power in the middle Republic and declined in the late Republic after the reforms of the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. Under the Principate it kept its legal position but little real authority, though the assemblies' powers passed to it. Around 300 CE Diocletian's reforms ended any illusion that it had independent powers, and Constantine created a second senate in Constantinople.

The Western senate worked under Odoacer and the Ostrogothic kings and was restored after Justinian I's reconquest of Italy, but the long war had mortally weakened it, and it had disappeared by the early 7th century. The Eastern senate lasted into the early 13th century; its last known act was to elect Nicholas Kanabos as emperor in 1204.
roman-von-ungern-sternberg: Ungern-Sternberg was born in Graz to a noble Baltic German family that had settled in present-day Estonia in the Middle Ages. His first language was German, and he became fluent in French, Russian, English and Estonian. His parents divorced in 1891 and he grew up on the estate of his mother's second husband near Reval (Tallinn). He claimed descent from Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and this played a part in his dream of reviving the Mongol Empire.

In the First World War he served with Cossack regiments on the Eastern Front and won several Russian decorations, but he was also known as reckless and unstable and was sentenced to two months in prison after a drunken attack on another officer in October 1916.

An ultraconservative monarchist, Ungern saw the February Revolution as the beginning of the end of Russia. In the Caucasus he met the Cossack captain Grigory Semyonov, and after the October Revolution the two declared allegiance to the Romanov dynasty and joined the White forces in the Transbaikal region. Semyonov refused to recognise Admiral Alexander Kolchak and was supported by the Japanese. Ungern believed monarchs were accountable only to God and wanted the monarchy restored as before 1905. In August 1920 he broke with Semyonov and led his Asiatic Cavalry Division, about 1,500 men, into Outer Mongolia. Assaults on Urga in October and November 1920 failed with heavy losses.

On 21 February 1921, Ungern, with Mongolian lamas and princes, brought the Bogd Khan back to Urga, and on 22 February Mongolia was proclaimed an independent monarchy. The Bogd Khan gave Ungern the title darkhan khoshoi chin wang. During his five-month occupation he kept order in the capital by fear and brutal violence against Bolsheviks and Chinese. Soviet, Far Eastern Republic and Mongolian forces advanced against him in 1921. He was defeated between 11 and 13 June near Troitskosavsk, and the Red and Mongol forces entered Urga on 6 July.

He was taken prisoner by the Red Army and tried for counter-revolution in Novonikolayevsk, now Novosibirsk. After a six-hour show trial he was executed on 15 September 1921. His attraction to Vajrayana Buddhism and his violence towards enemies and his own men earned him the names the Mad Baron and the Bloody Baron. The historian John Jennings argues that his Mongolian campaign removed the one force in the region that might have matched the Red Army and made a Soviet invasion inevitable. Ossendowski's book Beasts, Men and Gods, published in 1922, made his story widely known.
romance-of-the-three-kingdoms: Stories about the heroes of the Three Kingdoms were the basis of entertainment from the Sui and Tang dynasties. By the Song dynasty, professional oral storytellers specialised in them. The earliest written work to combine these stories was a pinghua, the Sanguozhi Pinghua, published between 1321 and 1323. The novel draws on Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, Pei Songzhi's annotations, earlier chronicles and Liu Yiqing's A New Account of the Tales of the World, and it combines historical figures and events with fictional scenes, speeches and supernatural episodes.

Luo Guanzhong, a playwright who lived sometime between 1315 and 1400, is the traditional author. The novel was first printed in 1522 as Sanguozhi Tongsu Yanyi, in an edition with a preface dated 1494, and it may have circulated earlier in manuscript. The standard text most readers know is a recension by Mao Lun and his son Mao Zonggang.

The narrative runs from the decline of the Han dynasty and the Yellow Turban Rebellion to the reunification of China under the Western Jin in 280. It has 120 chapters, about 800,000 words and nearly a thousand characters, most of them historical. Its early episodes include Dong Zhuo's seizure of the capital Luoyang, and the oath of Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei in the Peach Garden. Liu Bei visits Zhuge Liang three times to recruit him; the visits are documented in other sources, but the novel expanded them into a dramatic story.

The Battle of Red Cliffs in 208, won by the allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei over Cao Cao, is followed by Liu Bei's takeover of Yi Province. Sun Quan then takes Jing Province, and Guan Yu is captured and executed. Liu Bei is defeated at the Battle of Yiling by Lu Xun. The narrative gives particular moral and political weight to Liu Bei and Shu Han.

The novel is counted among the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature and is arguably the most widely read historical novel in late imperial and modern China. Its writing belongs to the emergence of written vernacular in the Ming period. Many Chinese proverbs derive from it. Nurhaci is said to have learned Chinese military and political strategy from it, and it was among the first Chinese books translated into Manchu. It has canonical status in Korea, Japan and Vietnam, and has been called the national novel of Korea.

The novel also shaped religious practice. Guan Yu, already honoured in a local cult near a monastery in Hubei, appears in the novel as a spirit asking the monk Pujing for his head; he is still revered as a Bodhisattva in Buddhist tradition. The story has been retold in television series, manga and video games.
romanesque-architecture: Romanesque was the first distinctive style to spread across Europe since the Roman Empire. After the decline of Rome, Roman building methods survived to an extent in western Europe, where Merovingian, Carolingian and Ottonian architects went on building large stone monastery churches and palaces. The round arch stayed in use, but the engineering skills needed to vault large spaces and build large domes were lost. The style emerged nearly simultaneously in several countries, combining features of ancient Roman and Byzantine buildings with local traditions. Rulers founded churches as seats of power and as places of coronation and burial, among them the Abbey of Saint-Denis, Speyer Cathedral and Westminster Abbey.

The general impression is one of massive solidity. Unlike Roman and Gothic building, where the load is carried by columns and arches, Romanesque, like Byzantine architecture, relies on its walls and on sections of wall called piers. The walls are very thick, often double shells filled with rubble, with few and small openings, and are built of local material: brick in Italy, Poland and much of Germany, and limestone, granite and flint elsewhere. Arches are nearly always semicircular, and arcading is the most significant decoration.

Most buildings have wooden roofs. Stone vaults developed from barrel and groin vaults into the ribbed vault, the main structural innovation of the period. A Romanesque doorway has receding planes with a circular shaft in each, sometimes as many as twelve, symbolic of the apostles.

Churches greatly outnumber the castles built in this period, and the late 11th and 12th centuries saw an unprecedented growth in the number of churches, among them Santa Maria in Cosmedin in Rome, San Zeno Maggiore in Verona, Mont Saint-Michel and the abbeys of the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela. The Gothic style then rebuilt most Romanesque churches wholly or partly in prosperous areas such as England and Portugal, so the largest groups survive in regions less prosperous later, such as southern France and rural Spain, Portugal and Italy. The term Romanesque, meaning in the manner of Romans, has been used since early in the 19th century.
romani-people: Linguistic and genetic evidence suggests that the Romani originated in north-western regions of the Indian subcontinent, particularly in present-day Punjab, Rajasthan and Sindh. Because the Romani did not chronicle their history, most hypotheses about early Roma rest on linguistic data. Genetic findings published in 2012 suggest that the ancestors of present-day scheduled caste and scheduled tribe populations of northern India, traditionally called the Doma, are the likely ancestral populations of European Roma.

Historians now believe the westward migration, possibly in waves, occurred around 1000 CE, perhaps in the context of the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni. The Romani moved west into the Ghaznavid Empire and later the Byzantine Empire. Armenian-origin words in Romani indicate that they passed through Armenia.

The Romani arrived in Europe through the Balkans, probably in the twelfth century. A document of 1068 from Constantinople mentions Atsingani, probably meaning Roma. The English word Gypsy comes from Egipcien, the medieval belief that they were itinerant Egyptians. Their reception was mixed. The first recorded transaction for a Romani slave in Wallachia dates to 1385, while Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund issued them safe conduct in 1417.

Expulsions followed: from the Meissen region of Germany in 1416, Lucerne in 1471, Milan in 1493, France in 1504, Catalonia in 1512, Sweden in 1525, England in 1530 and Denmark in 1536. From 1510 any Roma found in Switzerland were to be executed, and Portugal began deporting Roma to its colonies in 1538. Large-scale emigration to the Americas began in the 1860s. In the mid- to late twentieth century forced sterilisation in several European countries reduced Roma populations.

The Romani traditionally led a nomadic, itinerant life. Many subgroups and clans name themselves, among them the Sinti, Kalderash, Lovari and Manouche. The Romani language is Indo-Aryan with strong Persian, Armenian, Greek and South Slavic influence, and its dialects have more than 2 million speakers. Romanipen is the totality of the Romani spirit, culture, law and identity. The first World Romani Congress in 1971 voted to reject all exonyms for the Romani, including Gypsy.
romania: Romania lies on the lower course of the Danube and on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea. It covers 238,397 square kilometres, and its terrain is distributed roughly equally between mountains, hills and plains. The Carpathian Mountains dominate the centre, with 14 ranges reaching above 2,000 metres; the highest is Moldoveanu Peak at 2,544 metres. They are surrounded by the Moldavian and Transylvanian plateaus, the Pannonian Plain and the Wallachian plains.

The Danube flows into the Black Sea and forms the Danube Delta, the second-largest and best-preserved delta in Europe. At 5,800 square kilometres it is the largest continuous marshland in Europe. Romania has one of the largest areas of undisturbed forest in Europe, covering almost 27% of its territory, and about 50% of Europe's brown bears outside Russia.

Human remains from Peștera cu Oase, about 40,000 years old, are the oldest known Homo sapiens in Europe. Salt production at the Poiana Slatinei site began between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE, the earliest evidence for salt exploitation in Europe, and the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture flourished in the 3rd millennium BCE. Greek colonies were established on the Black Sea coast in the 7th century BCE. Burebista, the first Dacian ruler to unite the local tribes, conquered the Greek colonies in Dobruja between around 55 and 44 BCE, and his kingdom collapsed after he was murdered in 44 BCE.

Part of the territory became the Roman province of Dacia after Trajan's Dacian Wars. The modern state was formed in 1859 through the union of Moldavia and Wallachia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza and took the name Romania in 1866. The Great Union of 1918 and the treaties that followed created Greater Romania, which reached its largest territorial extent. King Michael I was forced to abdicate in December 1947, and the communist Romanian People's Republic followed. The revolution of 1989 ended communism.

Romania is a semi-presidential republic with a bicameral Parliament of a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies. It joined the European Union in 2007 and is a member of NATO. The 2021 census counted 19,053,815 people, of whom 89.33% were Romanians, 6.05% Hungarians and 3.44% Roma; the Council of Europe puts the Roma figure higher, at 8.32%.

The name derives from the endonym român, from Latin romanus. The oldest surviving document in Romanian is Neacșu's letter, which mentions Țeara Rumânească, the Romanian Land, meaning Wallachia. About 12 million Romanians and people with Romanian-born ancestors live abroad.
romanians: The lands of present-day Romania and Moldova were inhabited by the ancient Getae and Dacian tribes. King Burebista united the tribes of the Dacian kingdom, and King Decebalus, its last king, saw it conquered by the Roman Empire in 106 CE after two wars with Trajan. Roman administration withdrew between 271 and 275 under Emperor Aurelian. Where the Romanians came from is debated. The Daco-Roman continuity theory holds that they descend from Romans and Romanized Dacians of the province of Dacia. Another holds that their ancestors were Romanized peoples of provinces south of the Danube who later migrated north. Dimitrie Onciul's admigration theory is a compromise between the two.

In the Middle Ages Romanians were mostly known as Vlachs, a term of ancient Germanic origin related to Welsh and Walloon, which Slavs passed on to Hungarians and Greeks. Vlachs lived across the Balkans, in Transylvania, and as far north as Poland and as far west as Moravia. Moldavia and Wallachia stayed autonomous within the Ottoman world, unlike other Ottoman territories in Europe. Transylvania was part of the Kingdom of Hungary until 1541 and later a vassal principality of the Ottomans. The three principalities were united for several months in 1600 under the Wallachian prince Michael the Brave. In 1812 the Treaty of Bucharest gave Russia the eastern half of Moldavia, known as Bessarabia.

During the Second World War the Kingdom of Romania lost Northern Transylvania to Hungary through the Second Vienna Award, while the Soviet Union took Bessarabia and northern Bukovina. After the war the Soviet Union imposed a communist government and King Michael was forced to abdicate. Nicolae Ceaușescu headed the Romanian Communist Party from 1965, and the Romanian Revolution of 1989 ended his rule.

Romanians speak Romanian, a Romance language whose basic vocabulary is Latin, with some words assumed to be Dacian. It borrowed from Slavic languages in the Middle Ages, later from German, Hungarian and Turkish, and in the modern era from French and Italian. The name român comes from Latin romanus; early travellers such as Francesco della Valle in 1532 noted that Romanians called themselves Romans. Closely related peoples are the Aromanians, Megleno-Romanians and Istro-Romanians. The great majority of Romanians belong to the Romanian Orthodox Church. Estimates of their worldwide number range from 24 to 30 million, and large communities live in Italy and Spain.
romanos-i-lekapenos: Romanos took his epithet from his birthplace, Lakape, between Melitene and Samosata. His father was a peasant, Theophylaktos, who had saved the emperor Basil I in battle at Tephrike in 872 and was rewarded with a place in the Imperial Guard and estates. Romanos had no refined education, for which his son-in-law Constantine VII later abused him, but he rose in the army under Leo VI the Wise. He was general of the naval theme of Samos in 911 and later admiral of the fleet. After the Bulgarian victory at the Battle of Acheloos in 917, he sailed to Constantinople and gradually overcame the discredited regency of Empress Zoe Karvounopsina.

On 25 March 919, at the head of his fleet, Romanos seized the Boukoleon Palace and the government. In April his daughter Helena married Constantine VII, and he took the title basileopator. He was named caesar on 24 September 920 and crowned senior emperor on 17 December. He crowned his own sons co-emperors, Christopher in 921 and Stephen and Constantine in 924, but left Constantine VII untouched, and so was called the gentle usurper.

The war with Simeon I of Bulgaria took the first four years of his reign. In 924 he met Simeon at Kosmidion and ended the siege of the capital, in effect by tacitly recognising him as emperor of Bulgaria. After Simeon's death in May 927 his granddaughter Maria, renamed Eirene, married the new Bulgarian emperor Peter I in September.

In the east Romanos' general John Kourkouas campaigned from 926 against the Abbasids and their vassals and won Melitene in 934, often seen as the first major Byzantine territorial recovery from the Muslims. In 944 his withdrawal from Edessa gained the relic called the mandylion. A Kievan raid in 941 was defeated with Greek fire, and in 944 Romanos made a treaty with Prince Igor of Kiev. At home he issued laws protecting small landowners from the dynatoi, increased taxes on the aristocracy and, in 933, made his young son Theophylaktos patriarch.

Romanos grew guilt-ridden over the usurpation of Constantine VII's throne. His eldest son Christopher died in 931. Fearing that Romanos would let Constantine VII succeed, his younger sons Stephen and Constantine arrested him on 20 (or 16) December 944 and forced him to become a monk on the Princes' Islands.

The people of Constantinople rose when the sons threatened Constantine VII, and the sons were also exiled. Romanos died on 15 June 948 and was buried in the church of Myrelaion, the burial church he had built beside his palace. Constantine VII wrote that Romanos was an uneducated man of low descent, and his descendants included every emperor for the next century.
romanos-iii-argyros: Romanos Argyros, born in 968, was the son of Marianos, a member of the Argyros family; his grandfather, another Romanos Argyros, had married Agatha, a daughter of Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos. His siblings included Basil Argyros, a general and governor under Basil II, and Pulcheria Argyropoulina, who reportedly helped him control Zoë's spending. He served as judge in Opsikion, where he persecuted heretics at Akmoneia, then as quaestor and one of the judges of the Hippodrome, appearing in the legal compendium called the Peira. He became patrikios and administrator of the Great Church, and under Constantine VIII was urban prefect of Constantinople, formal head of the Senate.

In late 1028 the dying Constantine VIII, who had no son, summoned Constantine Dalassenos from Antioch to marry his eldest daughter Zoë. The emperor's advisers preferred a less formidable candidate and persuaded him to choose Romanos instead. He was forced to divorce his wife Helena, who was sent to a monastery, and marry Zoë, then 50 to his 60. The marriage took place on 9 November 1028, and Constantine died on 11 November. Romanos idealised Marcus Aurelius and sought to imitate Trajan's military prowess. He spent large sums on buildings and endowed churches and monasteries, and he eased taxation for the aristocracy, abandoning earlier policy against nobles' privileges. Peasants increasingly fell into serfdom, weakening the army's recruiting base.

In 1030 he led an army against the Mirdasids of Aleppo. It camped at a waterless site, its scouts were ambushed and a cavalry attack was defeated; on 10 August it withdrew towards Antioch, discipline broke down and the army fled, with only the imperial bodyguard holding firm. Accounts of the losses differ: John Skylitzes speaks of a terrible rout, Yahya of Antioch of remarkably few casualties. A treaty made Aleppo a tributary. In 1032 George Maniakes captured and defended Edessa. His sister-in-law Theodora was implicated in plots in 1029 and 1031 and was confined at the monastery of Petrion.

Romanos limited Zoë's expenses, which deepened their estrangement; he took a mistress, and Zoë fell in love with Michael, brother of the court eunuch John the Orphanotrophos. Romanos died on 11 April 1034, supposedly poisoned by his wife, and some speculate that he was drowned in a bath on her orders. He was buried in the Church of St Mary Peribleptos, which he had built. Zoë and Michael married the same day, and Patriarch Alexios I crowned Michael IV after receiving 50 pounds of gold. Romanos is recorded as a well-meaning but ineffective emperor who disorganised the tax system and undermined the military.
romanos-iv-diogenes: Romanos was the son of the general Constantine Diogenes and belonged to the Diogenai, a powerful family of the Cappadocian military aristocracy.
