He rose as a commander on the frontiers, serving in Syria and on the Danubian frontier, and in 1067 became duke of a new province centred on Serdica.

He was then convicted of attempting to usurp the throne of the sons of Constantine X Doukas. While he awaited sentence, the regent Eudokia Makrembolitissa pardoned him and chose him as her husband, since the Seljuk Turks had overrun much of Cappadocia and the army needed an energetic general. They married on 1 January 1068, and he was crowned Emperor of the Romans.

Romanos was brave to the point of recklessness, but he inherited an army weakened by years of neglect and made up largely of ill-disciplined mercenaries. His campaigns of 1068 and 1069 against the Turks and the Emirate of Aleppo brought limited success, and Turkish raiders sacked Amorium and Iconium. At home he cut court spending and the salaries of the court nobility, and he antagonised the Doukas family, led by the Caesar John Doukas. In 1071 the last Byzantine outpost in Italy, Bari, fell into Norman hands.

In the spring of 1071 Romanos marched east to recover Manzikert and divided his army. The Seljuk army of Sultan Alp Arslan approached, and the Uzes mercenaries deserted to the Turks. In the battle of 26 August 1071 the Byzantine army was defeated. Romanos fought on after his horse was killed, was wounded in the hand and was taken prisoner. Byzantine sources say Alp Arslan treated him with kindness and released him after about eight days for a treaty and a ransom, first set at 10,000,000 nomismata and reduced to 1,500,000, with 360,000 more a year. Some Muslim sources describe harsher treatment.

While Romanos was a prisoner, the Doukas family declared him deposed and proclaimed Michael VII Doukas emperor, on about 1 October 1071. Romanos gathered troops but was defeated and surrendered at Adana in Cilicia, on assurances that his life would be spared if he retired to a monastery. John Doukas broke the agreement. Romanos was blinded at Kotyaion on 29 June 1072 and exiled to Prote in the Sea of Marmara, where his untreated wound became infected and he died. Historians connect his defeat at Manzikert with the weakening of Byzantine authority in Anatolia and its gradual Turkification.
romanticism: Romanticism originated in Europe towards the end of the 18th century, in response to the Age of Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution. Its first ideas arose from an earlier German Counter-Enlightenment movement, Sturm und Drang (Storm and Stress), which criticised the Enlightenment claim that humans can fully comprehend the world through reason alone. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther, published in 1774, helped to shape its ideals.

The period varies by country and art. Scholars of English literature place it between about 1789 or 1798 and about 1830, and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1798 is often held to mark its start. The consensus is that it peaked between 1800 and 1850.

Romantics rejected the social conventions of their time in favour of individualism, and argued that passion and intuition were crucial to understanding the world. Beauty, they held, was more than form, since it evokes a strong emotional response. Their recurring themes were a reverence for nature and the supernatural, an idealisation of the past as a nobler era, a fascination with the exotic and mysterious, and a celebration of the heroic and the sublime.

They preferred the medieval to the classical, seeing the Middle Ages as an age of chivalry and a more organic relationship between humans and their surroundings, in contrast to an industrial society they thought alienating. The movement shaped literature, painting, music and architecture, and touched politics: Romantic thinking influenced conservatism, liberalism, radicalism and nationalism. In Poland it is often taken to begin with Adam Mickiewicz's first poems in 1822 and to end with the suppression of the January Uprising of 1863 against the Russians, and was strongly marked by interest in Polish history.

By the First World War the cultural climate had changed so far that Romanticism had dispersed into later movements. Late Romantic figures such as Rachmaninoff, who died in the 1940s, were widely respected but seen as anachronisms. Romantic nationalism has been judged to have had a largely negative effect on 19th-century history writing, because each nation tended to produce its own version of the past with clear heroes and villains.

Romantic thought and art went on to influence art and music, speculative fiction, philosophy, politics and environmentalism. The modern sense of romanticising something often has little to do with the historical movement.
rome: Rome lies in the Lazio region of central Italy on the Tiber. The original settlement developed on hills facing a ford beside the Tiber Island, the only natural ford of the river in this area. The Rome of the Kings was built on seven hills: the Aventine, Caelian, Capitoline, Esquiline, Palatine, Quirinal and Viminal. The city centre is about 24 kilometres inland from the Tyrrhenian Sea, though the city territory extends to the shore at Ostia.

The Aniene, which flows into the Tiber north of the historic centre, also crosses modern Rome. Vatican City, the smallest country in the world, is an independent country within Rome's municipal boundaries, the only existing example of a country within a city.

Evidence of human occupation of the Rome area goes back approximately 14,000 years. The view that Rome grew from pastoral settlements on the Palatine Hill, above the future Roman Forum, is supported by several excavations. Today there is wide consensus that the city developed gradually through the aggregation of several villages around the largest, on the Palatine, and archaeological evidence places this in the mid-eighth century BCE. The view that Rome was founded deliberately then, as the legend of Romulus suggests, remains a fringe hypothesis.

By 550 BCE Rome was the second largest city in Italy after Taras, with an estimated population of 35,000, though other sources suggest nearly 100,000. When the Republic was founded in 509 BCE the census recorded 130,000, and the city surpassed 300,000 by 150 BCE. After the fall of the Western Empire the city slowly fell under the political control of the Papacy, and in the 8th century it became capital of the Papal States, which lasted until 1870. Rome became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871.

Rome is the capital of Italy and a special municipality named Roma Capitale, with a population of 2.7 million. It hosts the country's principal political institutions and several United Nations agencies, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Beginning with Nicholas V (1447 to 1455), almost all popes pursued an architectural and urban programme over four hundred years, and Rome became a major centre of the Renaissance and the birthplace of the Baroque and Neoclassicism. Its first university, La Sapienza, was founded in 1303. In 98 CE, according to Sextus Julius Frontinus, Rome had nine aqueducts feeding 39 monumental fountains and 591 public basins.
romulo-gallegos: Rómulo Ángel del Monte Carmelo Gallegos Freire was born in Caracas to Rómulo Gallegos Osío and Rita Freire Guruceaga, into a family of humble origin. From 1903 he worked as a schoolteacher, writer, journalist and enthusiast of classical music. His novel Doña Bárbara, first published in 1929, criticised the regime of the long-time dictator Juan Vicente Gómez, and he was forced to leave the country. He took refuge in Spain, where he wrote the acclaimed novels Cantaclaro (1934) and Canaima (1935). He returned to Venezuela in 1936 and was appointed Minister of Public Education.

In 1937 Gallegos was elected to Congress, and in 1940–41 he served as Mayor of Caracas. He was involved in the coup of 1945 that brought Rómulo Betancourt and the Revolutionary Government Junta to power, in the period known as El Trienio Adeco. In the general election of 1947 he stood for the presidency as the Acción Democrática candidate and won what is generally believed to have been the country's first honest election, with over 74 percent of the vote, which is still a record for a free election in Venezuela.

He took office on 15 February 1948. His government raised the state's share of oil profits through taxation from 43 percent to 50 percent, a scheme known as fifty-fifty that was later copied in other oil-producing countries such as Saudi Arabia. He also began an open-door policy that brought an influx of Italians, who became the largest European population group in Venezuela. In November 1948 the army officers Carlos Delgado Chalbaud, Marcos Pérez Jiménez and Luis Felipe Llovera Páez overthrew him, and he took refuge first in Cuba and then in Mexico.

Gallegos returned to Venezuela after the fall of the dictatorship of Marcos Pérez Jiménez in 1958. He became a senator for life but took no active part in politics. He received the National Literature Prize in 1958 for La doncella and was elected to the Venezuelan Academy of the Language. From 1960 to 1963 he was a commissioner of the newly created Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and its first president.

He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1960 but lost to Saint-John Perse. The Rómulo Gallegos International Novel Prize was established in his honour in 1964. He died in Caracas on 5 April 1969. He is considered the most important Venezuelan novelist of the 20th century.
romulus: In Roman tradition Romulus and Remus were the sons of Rhea Silvia by the god Mars. Their grandfather Numitor, rightful king of Alba Longa, had been deposed by his brother Amulius, who made Rhea Silvia a Vestal Virgin. When the twins were born, Amulius ordered them thrown into the Tiber, but the river was swollen and the servants left them beneath a fig tree at the foot of the Palatine Hill. A she-wolf suckled them until the royal herdsman Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia found them. The brothers grew up among shepherds, and with the help of friends they killed Amulius and restored Numitor.

They then set out to found a city of their own and disagreed over the site. Remus saw six vultures over the Aventine Hill, Romulus twelve over the Palatine, and the quarrel ended with Romulus or one of his followers killing Remus.

Romulus fortified the Palatine, ploughed a furrow for the city's boundary, and accepted the crown with the people's approval. He divided the people into three tribes, the Ramnes, Titienses and Luceres, chose one hundred men to form the Senate, and set up an asylum for fugitives on the Capitoline Hill. Since the city had few women, he invited neighbouring peoples to a festival and the Romans seized the marriageable women among the Sabine guests. War followed. The Sabines under Titus Tatius took the citadel through the treachery of Tarpeia, and fighting ended only when the Sabine women stepped between the armies. The two peoples formed one community, ruled jointly by Romulus and Tatius.

After Tatius was killed in a riot at Lavinium, Romulus is said to have conquered Fidenae and ravaged the countryside of Veii. The founding of Rome was commemorated each year on 21 April at the Parilia.

After a reign of thirty-seven years Romulus is said to have disappeared in a storm while reviewing his troops on the Campus Martius. Livy reports that he was either murdered by the senators or raised to heaven by Mars, and prefers the latter. He gained a cult, later assimilated to that of Quirinus, and was succeeded by Numa Pompilius, a Sabine.

How far a historical figure lies behind the legend is unclear and disputed. Most modern historians think the name Romulus is a back-formation from the name of the city. A rectangular tuff chest of the 6th century BCE, found by Giacomo Boni in 1899 beside the Lapis Niger and rediscovered in 2020, has been called the Tomb of Romulus, but no remains were found and it is more likely a cenotaph.
romulus-augustulus: Romulus was born between about 460 and 465 and was named after his maternal grandfather, a nobleman from Poetovio in Noricum, a comes who was sent on an embassy to Attila in 449. His father Orestes was a Roman citizen from Pannonia who had once served as secretary to Attila. The name of his mother is not known; it might have been Barbaria. On his accession he took Augustus as a proper name, and his coins read Romulus Augustus. The nickname Augustulus, little Augustus, was a derisive reference to his youth, never in official use, and in Greek his first name was twisted into Momylus, little disgrace.

In 475 the emperor Julius Nepos named Orestes magister militum and sent him against rebelling Visigoths and Burgundians. Orestes instead heeded the grievances of his troops, many of them foederati, and marched on Ravenna, which he entered on 28 August 475; Nepos escaped to Salona in Dalmatia.

After an interregnum of two months Orestes proclaimed Romulus emperor on 31 October 475, when he may have been as young as ten. Romulus was little more than a figurehead, and his father ran much of the administration. The eastern emperor Zeno never recognised him, since Nepos, invested by Leo I, still claimed the title in exile. In 476 the foederati in Italy, mainly Herules, Scirians and Turcilingians, demanded land to settle on. Orestes refused, and under their leader Odoacer they defeated and executed him at Ticinum on 28 August 476.

On 4 September Odoacer captured Ravenna and deposed Romulus. He became the first King of Italy, sent the western regalia to Zeno and ruled without a further emperor in the West, nominally under Zeno's authority. Odoacer spared Romulus, on account of his youth and beauty, with a pension of 6,000 solidi and an estate in Campania, the castellum Lucullanum. Little is known of his later life. He may have helped to found a monastery there around the remains of Saint Severinus, and a letter of Theodoric the Great of 507 or 511 to a Romulus may refer to him. Very few records of his reign survive, and no policies, laws or significant inscriptions are known.
ronald-reagan: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on 6 February 1911 in an apartment in Tampico, Illinois, the younger son of Nelle Clyde Wilson and Jack Reagan. His mother was committed to the Disciples of Christ and led prayer meetings; Reagan credited her spiritual influence. His father focused on making money for the family, a task complicated by his alcoholism. The family lived in several Illinois towns before settling in 1920 in Dixon, where Reagan attended Dixon High School and developed interests in drama and football. He graduated from Eureka College in 1932 with a degree in economics and sociology.

Reagan began as a sports broadcaster in Iowa, and a screen test in 1936 led to a seven-year contract with Warner Bros. Pictures. He arrived in Hollywood in 1937 and made thirty films, mostly B films, before beginning military service in April 1942. His part as George Gipp in Knute Rockne, All American (1940) later led reporters to call him the Gipper while he campaigned for president. He served as an officer in the Army Air Forces, producing over 400 training films, and was discharged on 9 December 1945 as a captain. He began his political life as a Democrat, admiring Franklin D. Roosevelt, and registered as a Republican in 1962 after General Electric dropped him as a speaker.

He was elected governor of California in 1966 and served from 1967 to 1975. He accepted tax increases to balance the budget, and by 1973 the state had a surplus. In 1967 he signed the Mulford Act, which prohibited the public carrying of firearms. After losing the 1976 Republican primaries to President Gerald Ford, he won the nomination in 1980 and defeated President Jimmy Carter. He was inaugurated as the 40th president on 20 January 1981. His economic policy, called Reaganomics, combined deregulation with tax cuts, including the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, and he lifted federal oil and gasoline price controls on 28 January 1981.

Reagan left the presidency on 20 January 1989, at the age of 77, and the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library opened in 1991. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 1994, and his capacities gradually deteriorated. He died of pneumonia, complicated by Alzheimer's, at his home in Los Angeles on 5 June 2004. A public funeral was held in the Washington National Cathedral, where Margaret Thatcher, Brian Mulroney, George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush gave eulogies, and he was interred at his presidential library. His tenure is regarded as a realignment toward conservative policies in the United States.
ronda: Ronda sits on the Ronda Depression, a Miocene plateau about 600 to 800 metres above sea level whose fertile land suits wheat, olives and vines. The Guadalevín river divides the city in two and has carved the steep gorge called El Tajo, more than 100 metres deep, above which the town perches. Around it are prehistoric remains from the Neolithic, including the rock art of the Cueva de la Pileta. Ronda is traditionally identified with ancient Arunda, which was populated under Iberians and Romans.

In the fifth century the Suebi, led by Rechila, conquered Ronda. The Eastern Roman Empire retook it in the following century, and the Visigothic king Liuvigild later captured it. In 713 it fell to Umayyad troops, who named it Hisn al-Rundah and made it capital of the province of Takurunna. The polymath Abbas ibn Firnas (810–887) came from the town. After the caliphate of Córdoba broke up, Ronda became the capital of a small kingdom ruled by the Berber Banu Ifran, and most of its Islamic architectural heritage dates from this period. In 1065 the taifa of Seville, led by Abbad II al-Mu'tadid, conquered it.

As part of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, Ronda was seized by the Crown of Castile in 1485 and was granted a fuero copying Seville's. After the conquest Christians were settled in the cities while Muslim majorities stayed in the rural communities. Early in the 16th century edicts required mudéjares of the Crown of Castile to leave or convert. After the Alpujarras revolt, the resettlement of the moriscos de paces in 1570 and thefts and enslavement by Christian militias led by Antonio de Luna, the morisco community of the Serranía de Ronda radicalised and took to guerrilla warfare and banditry.

In the Peninsular War the population fell from 15,600 to 5,000 in three years. The area then became a base for guerrillas and later bandits, whose deeds inspired Washington Irving, Prosper Mérimée and Gustave Doré. In 1918 the Assembly of Ronda designed the Andalusian flag, coat of arms and anthem. The Romero family, from Francisco, born in 1698, to his grandson Pedro, who died in 1839, played a principal role in developing modern Spanish bullfighting.

Three bridges span the Tajo: the Roman or Arabic bridge, the Old Bridge and the Puente Nuevo, whose building began in 1751 and took until 1793; it towers 120 metres above the canyon floor. The Plaza de Toros, built in 1784 by José Martín de Aldehuela, who also designed the Puente Nuevo, is one of the oldest and best-preserved bullrings in Spain. The Arab baths, dating from the 13th and 14th centuries, are among the best preserved in Spain. The railway to Algeciras was built between 1890 and 1892.
rondonia: Rondônia lies in the North Region of Brazil, bordered by Acre to the west, Amazonas to the north, Mato Grosso to the east and Bolivia to the south. Its capital and largest city, Porto Velho, stands on the Madeira River. The state occupies 237,590 square kilometres and has 52 municipalities. It once held over 200,000 square kilometres of rainforest, and by 2003 about 70,000 square kilometres had been cleared. The area around the Guaporé River belongs to the Beni savanna ecoregion, and the Samuel Dam stands on the Jamari River.

Before the arrival of the Portuguese the region was home to Indigenous peoples speaking Arawan, Chapacuran, Macro-Jê, Nambikwaran, Panoan and Tupian languages and several language isolates. Linguists generally accept that the area of Rondônia is the origin of the Tupian languages. The Spaniard Ñuflo de Chávez was the first European explorer to reach the valley of the Guaporé River, between 1541 and 1542, but only passed through. Bandeirantes came around 1650 to seek gold and other minerals, and Jesuit priests founded the first village. After gold was found on the right bank of the Guaporé, the Portuguese Crown founded the Captaincy of Mato Grosso in 1748.

Its governor, Antonio Rolim de Moura Tavares, named Vila Bela da Santíssima Trindade its capital in 1752 and directed the border demarcation that followed the Treaty of Madrid of 1750. Forts were built on the Guaporé to hold the frontier against the Spanish, the last being Forte Príncipe da Beira, built in 1776. The decline of mining left the region of little economic importance until rubber came to a peak late in the 19th century.

The definitive establishment of Acre in 1903 gave impetus to the region, since the Treaty of Petrópolis obliged Brazil to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway. Decree-Law No. 5812 of 13 September 1943 created the Federal Territory of Guaporé from parts of Amazonas and Mato Grosso, and a law of 17 February 1956 renamed it the Federal Territory of Rondônia in honour of Marshal Cândido Rondon.

Brazil nuts and rubber were the main activities until cassiterite was found. In the 1970s and 1980s tax incentives, federal investment, highways, colonization centres and cheap land drew migrants, largely from the Center-South of Brazil, and in 1982 the territory became a state with 13 municipalities including Porto Velho.

Rondônia has about 1.8 million inhabitants, drawn from all regions of Brazil, with settlers from Paraná, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul prominent. It has 21 Indigenous Territories, the largest being the Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau Indigenous Territory of over 1.8 million hectares. Other cities include Ariquemes, Cacoal, Guajará-Mirim, Ji-Paraná and Vilhena.
ronin: The word rōnin is written with characters meaning 'wave' and 'person', and idiomatically means a vagrant or wanderer, someone who belongs to no one place. It arose in the Nara and Heian periods for a serf who had fled his master's land, and later came to be used of a samurai without a master. A samurai became one on the death of his master or after losing his favour or legal privilege. According to the Bushido Shoshinshu, a samurai was supposed to commit seppuku on the loss of his master, and one who did not was meant to suffer great shame.

Until the Sengoku period peasants made up most of the daimyō armies, so they made up most of the rōnin. In that age the bond between lord and vassal was loose, and a rōnin could serve a new lord. Many warriors served a succession of masters, and some became daimyō: Tōdō Takatora served ten lords, and Saitō Dōsan rose from merchant to daimyō.

The Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 led to the confiscation or reduction of the fiefs of many daimyō on the losing side, and many samurai became rōnin. As many as a hundred thousand joined Toyotomi Hideyori at the Siege of Osaka. Afterwards many turned to farming or became townspeople, and a few, such as Yamada Nagamasa, went overseas as mercenaries. Most lived in poverty, and their number approached half a million under the third shōgun, Tokugawa Iemitsu.

Under the Edo shogunate's rigid class system a samurai could no longer take a new master without his previous master's permission. Some rōnin became mercenaries guarding trade caravans or bodyguards of wealthy merchants. Others became bandits or hired muscle for gangs running gambling rings, brothels and protection rackets, which gave rōnin a lasting reputation for disgrace.

The shogunate at first banished them from the cities and forbade them new masters. After rōnin joined the Keian Uprising of 1651 it relaxed its limits on daimyō inheritance, which meant fewer confiscations, and allowed rōnin to join new masters. The status ended when Emperor Meiji abolished the samurai class in the 19th century.
ronnie-brunswijk: Ronnie Brunswijk was born on 7 March 1961; his birth village was Moiwana. He joined the Suriname National Army at the age of 18, was considered a good soldier and was sent to Cuba for commando training, after which he was appointed a personal bodyguard of Desi Bouterse. In 1984 he asked for a raise; instead he was discharged on 16 April and refused his back pay. He then sought recognition and rights for the Maroons of the interior, descendants of Africans who had escaped slavery and founded independent communities in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The Surinamese Interior War began at Stolkertsijver on 22 July 1986, when the Jungle Commando captured twelve soldiers guarding a checkpoint. During the war the group received arms and funding from the Netherlands. On 29 November 1986 the Surinamese army attacked Moiwana, murdered at least 39 villagers, mostly women and children, and burned Brunswijk's house; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights later ordered the government to compensate the survivors. The war caused hundreds of deaths and drove more than 10,000 refugees into French Guiana. A ceasefire was negotiated at Kourou on 21 July 1989, and a final peace treaty was signed on 8 August 1992.

A Dutch court in Haarlem convicted Brunswijk in absentia of cocaine smuggling and sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment, reduced to six years on appeal in 2000; he contested the evidence. He chairs the General Liberation and Development Party and has sat in the National Assembly. He owned a gold-mining company, Robruns NV, whose concessions he transferred to a foundation in July 2020 in order to qualify for the vice-presidency.

In the 2020 elections Brunswijk was elected to the National Assembly, and on 29 June 2020 he became its chairman. On 13 July he was elected vice-president by acclamation, with Chan Santokhi as president, and was inaugurated on 16 July. He also owns the football club Inter Moengotapoe and in 2002 built a stadium in Moengo. On 21 September 2021 he played 54 minutes for the club in the CONCACAF League against C.D. Olimpia of Honduras, aged 60 years and 198 days. After a video showed him paying Olimpia players, CONCACAF disqualified both clubs and banned him from its competitions for three years.
roquebrune-cap-martin: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin lies in the Alpes-Maritimes department of south-eastern France, between Monaco and Menton. It was called simply Roquebrune until 1921, when the name was changed to distinguish it from Roquebrune-sur-Argens in the neighbouring Var. The commune has several parts: the perched village of Roquebrune with its château, the Cap Martin peninsula, the seaside resort of Carnolès bordering Menton, and St. Roman, practically a suburb of Monaco although outside its borders.

Ligurians settled the area before Roman times. The commune, originally Roccabruna, was founded in 971 by Conrad I, Count of Ventimiglia, to protect his western border. In 1355 it came under the control of the Grimaldi family of Monaco, who held it for five centuries and strengthened the castle. It became French in 1793 and returned to Monaco in 1814. In 1804 Napoleon built a road along the coast, which linked the village to the rest of the Côte d'Azur and led to its merger with the smaller town of Cap-Martin.

A revolution related to the Italian Risorgimento in 1848 made Roccabruna and Menton free cities under the protection of the Prince of Savoy. They hoped to join the Italian kingdom of Sardinia, which did not happen; after two years of independence they were administered by the House of Savoy for ten years and were ceded to France by a plebiscite in 1861. Giuseppe Garibaldi complained that the vote was not by universal suffrage. During World War II the coast between Italy and Monte Carlo was occupied by the Kingdom of Italy until September 1943.

The Marseille–Ventimiglia railway made the coast a holiday magnet. Elisabeth of Austria stayed at the Hôtel du Cap Martin from 1894 to 1897, and Eugénie, widow of Napoleon III, owned a villa there. In the 1920s and 1930s buildings such as Coco Chanel's La Pausa and Eileen Gray and Jean Badovici's E-1027 were built. Le Corbusier built a minimalist cabanon and drowned in the sea there on 27 August 1965. The Monte Carlo Country Club, venue of the Monte-Carlo Masters tennis tournament, stands in the commune, not in Monte Carlo.
rosa-luxemburg: Luxemburg arrived in Zurich in early 1889, when Switzerland was the most important centre of Russian and Polish revolutionary Marxism in exile. She enrolled at the University of Zurich in 1890 and from 1892 studied law, public law and political economy under Julius Wolf. When she reached Germany in 1898 the party was divided by the revisionist controversy, begun by Eduard Bernstein, who argued that many of Marx's predictions were outdated and that the party should become a democratic socialist party of reform.

The Russian Revolution of 1905 shaped her theory of the mass strike, set out in a pamphlet published in 1906. On 4 August 1914 the SPD's Reichstag delegation voted unanimously for war credits. With Karl Liebknecht, Clara Zetkin and Franz Mehring she began to organise an opposition, which became the Spartacus League. She was arrested on 18 February 1915 and spent most of the war in prison, where she wrote the Junius Pamphlet.

In Social Reform or Revolution? (1900) she argued that the struggle for reforms was a means to an end, not an end in itself. In The Accumulation of Capital (1913) she held that capitalism could not realise its surplus value within its own closed system and so had to expand into pre-capitalist spheres, above all in colonies abroad. This drive, in her view, was the economic basis of imperialism and militarism. The Junius Pamphlet called the war an imperialist conflict for which all sides were responsible.

She welcomed the Russian Revolution of 1917 but, in a manuscript written in prison in 1918 and published after her death, condemned the Bolsheviks' suppression of the Constituent Assembly and their abolition of democratic freedoms.

Luxemburg was released from prison on 9 November 1918, during the German Revolution of 1918–1919. With Liebknecht she led the Spartacus League and its daily newspaper, Die Rote Fahne. The Spartacist uprising of January 1919 was not a planned putsch by the KPD, and she at first thought it a mistake, but once the masses were on the streets she urged the workers on. After the Freikorps crushed it, she and Liebknecht were captured and killed.

Her death made her a martyr for revolutionary socialists. After Paul Levi published her manuscript on the Russian Revolution in 1922, Lenin answered with a parable that praised her as an eagle while listing her errors. In Germany she and Liebknecht are honoured each January with a demonstration in Berlin.
rosa-parks: Rosa Louise McCauley was born on 4 February 1913 in Tuskegee, Alabama, the daughter of Leona, a teacher, and James McCauley, a carpenter and mason. As a baby she moved with her mother to Pine Level, Alabama, where she attended the African Methodist Episcopal church, to which she belonged all her life. She completed high school in 1933 with the encouragement of her husband, Raymond Parks, at a time when only 7 per cent of Black people in Alabama held a diploma. In 1941 she began work at Maxwell Air Force Base, which was fully integrated, and said it opened her eyes to an alternative to Jim Crow; on her way home she still had to use segregated buses.

Parks joined the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP in 1943 and served as its secretary. After three attempts between 1943 and 1945 she registered to vote despite measures to disenfranchise Black citizens, and she investigated cases of racial and sexual violence, among them those of Recy Taylor and Jeremiah Reeves. Several women had been arrested before her for keeping their seats on Montgomery buses, including Claudette Colvin, aged fifteen, in March 1955, but activists judged Colvin unsuitable as a test case. After Parks's arrest, E. D. Nixon and Clifford Durr favoured her for her standing in the community and her firm quiet spirit.

She agreed after consulting her family, and the lawyer Fred Gray took her case. The Women's Political Council, led by Jo Ann Robinson, had 35,000 leaflets printed announcing a one-day boycott for 5 December 1955, the day of her trial. After she was found guilty the boycott was extended, and the Montgomery Improvement Association ran a network of transport to sustain it.

Parks and her husband lost their jobs and fell into hardship, and in 1957 they moved to Detroit. She took part in the March on Washington in August 1963, and later supported the Free South Africa Movement. She died on 24 October 2005 aged 92. After a service in Montgomery she lay in state in the United States Capitol rotunda, where 40,000 mourners came, and was buried in Detroit. She received the Spingarn Medal in 1979, the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Congressional Gold Medal, and was the first Black American memorialised in the National Statuary Hall.
rose-of-lima: Rose was born Isabel Flores de Oliva in Lima on 20 April 1586, one of eleven children of Gaspar Flores, a harquebusier in the Spanish army, and María de Oliva y Herrera, a criolla native of Lima. Her later name came from an incident in infancy, when a servant claimed to have seen her face change into a rose. In 1597 she was confirmed by Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo, who was also later declared a saint, and formally took the name Rosa.

In emulation of Catherine of Siena she began as a girl to fast three times a week and to perform severe penances in secret. When her beauty was admired she cut off her hair and rubbed peppers on her face. She rejected all suitors, against the wishes of her family, and wanted to take a vow of virginity, which her parents opposed. Her father forbade her to become a nun, so she entered the Third Order of Saint Dominic while living at home, and in her twentieth year took the habit of a tertiary and a vow of perpetual virginity.

She abstained permanently from meat, slept at most two hours a night, and wore a heavy silver crown with small spikes inside, in imitation of the Crown of Thorns. She sold needlework, lace and flowers she grew to help her family and to care for the poor, and she brought sick and hungry people to her room. For eleven years she lived this way, with intervals of ecstasy, praying and doing penance in a small grotto she had built.

Rose died on 24 August 1617, aged 31, after a long illness, and is said to have foretold the date. All the public authorities of Lima attended her funeral in the cathedral. She was beatified by Pope Clement IX on 10 May 1667 and canonised by Pope Clement X on 12 April 1671. The Catholic Church holds that many miracles followed her death, among them that she had cured a leper and that Lima smelled of roses at the hour she died.

Her feast entered the General Roman Calendar in 1729 on 30 August, because 24 August is the feast of Saint Bartholomew; Pope Paul VI's revision of 1969 moved it to 23 August. In Peru and some other Latin American countries 30 August remains a public holiday. Her skull, crowned with roses, is displayed in the basilica in Lima, and many places in the New World are named Santa Rosa.
rose-revolution: The Citizens' Union of Georgia, the party of President Eduard Shevardnadze, began to fall apart in 2000 as deputies defected. Mikheil Saakashvili, the Minister of Justice, left it in September 2001 and founded the National Movement a month later. In the 2002 local elections the party won only 70 of about 4,850 seats. Government revenue fell short of projections year after year, the International Monetary Fund suspended its funding in 2002, and unpaid salaries and pensions reached 120 million dollars by the end of 2003. Corruption among officials and police was widespread.

Non-governmental organizations, partly funded from abroad, and the independent channel Rustavi-2 helped the opposition. After a raid on Rustavi-2 in October 2001, thousands of students protested, Shevardnadze dismissed his cabinet, and Saakashvili and Zurab Zhvania left the ruling party.

Parliamentary elections were held on 2 November 2003. On 3 November international observers concluded that they fell short of OSCE commitments and other standards for democratic elections. Saakashvili claimed victory, which independent exit polls and a parallel vote tabulation by the Georgian monitoring group ISFED supported, and the united opposition urged nonviolent civil disobedience. From mid-November large demonstrations spread from Tbilisi to nearly all major towns, with the youth organization Kmara among those active.

On 22 November Shevardnadze tried to open the new session of parliament. Supporters of two opposition parties, led by Saakashvili, burst in with roses in their hands, which gave the revolution its name, and the president was forced to leave with his bodyguards. He declared a state of emergency, but elite military units refused to support him. On the evening of 23 November, after meeting Saakashvili and Zhvania in talks arranged by the Russian foreign minister Igor Ivanov, he announced his resignation. More than 50,000 people gathered in the streets of Tbilisi to mark the victory.

The parliamentary speaker, Nino Burjanadze, became acting president, and the Supreme Court annulled the results of the parliamentary elections. 2 percent of the vote and was inaugurated on 25 January, aged 36. The National Movement - Democrats won a large majority in the parliamentary elections of 28 March 2004.

In May 2004 protests in Batumi, sometimes called the Second Rose Revolution, ended with the resignation of Aslan Abashidze, the leader of the autonomous region of Adjara. The Rose Revolution is counted among the early colour revolutions, and the Orange Revolution, which followed the disputed Ukrainian presidential election of November 2004, is said to have been partly inspired by it.
rosetta-stone: The Rosetta Stone is a stele of granodiorite, a fragment of a larger stele, carved during the Hellenistic period and believed to have been displayed in a temple, possibly at Sais. The decree it carries was issued by a congress of priests gathered at Memphis after the coronation of Ptolemy V and established the divine cult of the new ruler. Its date corresponds to 27 March 196 BCE, the ninth year of Ptolemy V's reign, and it was designed to re-establish the rule of the Ptolemaic kings over Egypt. The stone's rock resembles granodiorite from a small quarry at Gebel Tingar, west of Elephantine near Aswan.

The decree has only minor differences across its three versions. The top register is in Egyptian hieroglyphs, the middle in Demotic and the bottom in Ancient Greek. The damaged top register has suffered most, and only its last 14 lines remain visible. The Demotic text has survived best, with 32 lines, and the Greek has 54 lines, of which the first 27 survive in full. Three other fragmentary copies were found later, and similar bilingual and trilingual inscriptions are known, including the Decree of Canopus of 238 BCE.

French soldiers strengthening Fort Julien near Rashid (Rosetta) found the slab in mid-July 1799, after Napoleon's invasion of Egypt, when they demolished a wall. Lieutenant Pierre-François Bouchard saw that it might be important. A report by Michel Ange Lancret to the Institut d'Égypte noted that it held three inscriptions and rightly suggested that they were versions of the same text. After the French defeat the stone was taken to London under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801, and since 1802 it has been on display at the British Museum almost continuously.

The first complete translation of the Greek text appeared in 1803. Johan David Åkerblad and Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy identified names in the Demotic text in 1802. In 1814 Thomas Young found the phonetic characters for Ptolemaios in the hieroglyphic text and noted its similarities to the Demotic. Jean-François Champollion announced the transliteration of the Egyptian scripts in Paris in 1822, though it took longer before scholars could read Egyptian inscriptions and literature confidently. Disputes over precedence between supporters of Young and of Champollion continued long afterwards.

Zahi Hawass, then Secretary-General of Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities, asked in 2003 for the stone's return to Egypt. In 2005 the British Museum gave Egypt a full-sized replica. The term Rosetta Stone is now used for the essential clue to a new field of knowledge.
roskilde: Roskilde lies in north-central Zealand at the south end of Roskilde Fjord, the south branch of the Isefjord. The city centre around the cathedral stands about 40 metres above sea level and 1,300 metres south of the fjord, and on the slope down to the harbour there are several springs, the strongest of which is Maglekilde. Saxo Grammaticus and other early sources associate the name, meaning Ro's spring, with King Roar, who possibly lived there in the 6th century.

Roskilde developed as a hub of the Viking land and sea trade routes more than a thousand years ago. From the 11th century until 1443 it was the capital of Denmark, and with the support of kings and bishops it became one of the most important centres in Scandinavia. Adam von Bremen called it Zealand's largest town in 1070. Five Viking ships of the 11th century were scuttled in the fjord to block a channel and protect the city from seaborne attack.

The cathedral was built in the 12th and 13th centuries on the site of a 10th-century wooden church and completed in 1275. It was the first Gothic cathedral in Scandinavia built of brick, a style that spread through northern Europe. At the Reformation in 1536 the town had some 6,000 inhabitants, but war, fire and disease reduced them to only 1,550 by 1753. Fires in the 18th century led to the rebuilding of most of the old town, although the original street plan survives. The first train from Copenhagen arrived on 26 June 1847.

Roskilde is a city 30 kilometres west of Copenhagen. Its cathedral, where 39 Danish monarchs are buried, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. Next to it stands Roskilde Palace, built from 1733 to 1736 on the site of the bishops' residence. The Viking Ship Museum beside the fjord displays the remains of the five ships, excavated in the late 1960s about 20 kilometres north of the city. Roskilde University was founded in 1972, and the Roskilde Festival, a rock music festival, has been held annually since 1971.
rothenburg-ob-der-tauber: The name means Red castle above the Tauber and describes the town's position on a plateau overlooking the Tauber river. Rothenburg Castle, also called the Alte Burg, gave the city its name. The counts of Comburg-Rothenburg built the castle in 1070, and the line died out in 1116 with Count Heinrich. Emperor Heinrich V then appointed his nephew Konrad von Hohenstaufen to succeed to their properties. Konrad, who became King Konrad III, built a Staufer castle on cheaper land nearby in 1142.

The city was founded in 1170, when the Staufer castle was built, around its marketplace and St. James' Church, and walls and towers followed in the 13th century. In 1274 King Rudolf of Habsburg granted it privileges as a free imperial city, three fairs were established, and it grew.

The Heilig Blut pilgrimage attracted many pilgrims, and the city was one of the 20 largest of the Holy Roman Empire, with about 5,500 people within the walls and another 14,000 in the surrounding territory. Rabbi Meir ben Baruch of Rothenburg, who died in 1293, had a great reputation as a jurist in Europe. An earthquake destroyed the Staufer castle in 1356.

In October 1631, during the Thirty Years' War, the Catholic Count of Tilly wanted to quarter his 40,000 troops in Protestant Rothenburg. The town resisted and was quickly defeated. According to the legend of the Meistertrunk, Tilly offered to spare the city if anyone could drink 3 1/4 litres of wine in one draught, and Mayor Georg Nusch did so; the story is almost certainly apocryphal, since it first appears in a chronicle written more than a century later. The troops left the town poor and nearly empty, and a bubonic plague in 1634 killed many more. Without money or power Rothenburg stopped growing and kept its 17th-century state.

Rothenburg lies in Middle Franconia in Bavaria and is on the Romantic Road. It is one of only four towns in Germany with completely intact city walls. Painters of the Romantic period visited it from 1877, followed by the first tourists, and laws were passed to prevent major changes. On 31 March 1945 bombing destroyed around 275 houses and damaged the walls. S. Assistant Secretary of War John J.

McCloy ordered that artillery not be used, and the local commander Major Thömmes gave up the town, American troops occupied it on 17 April 1945. About 32 percent of the town was rebuilt, and rebuilt walls carry bricks naming donors. The Rathaus has a Gothic rear part of 1250 and a Renaissance front begun in 1572, and St. James' Church holds a Holy Blood altarpiece by Tilman Riemenschneider.
rothschild-family: The family's documented history begins in 16th-century Frankfurt. Its name comes from the German zum rothen Schild, "at the red shield", the sign of the house in which it lived for many generations, built by Isaak Elchanan Bacharach in 1567; a red shield still stands at the centre of the family's coat of arms. The family rose to prominence with Mayer Amschel Rothschild (1744-1812), born in the Judengasse, the ghetto of Frankfurt, the son of a money changer, who became a court factor to the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel. Unlike most earlier court factors he managed to pass on his wealth, through five sons whom he installed in Paris, Frankfurt, London, Vienna and Naples.

From London between 1813 and 1815, Nathan Mayer Rothschild was instrumental in financing the British war effort against Napoleon, organising the shipment of bullion to the Duke of Wellington's armies and the payment of British subsidies to the continental allies; in 1815 alone the family provided £9.8 million in subsidy loans. The family dominated international finance in Europe between the 1820s and the 1870s, until joint-stock banks broke its hegemony, and its banks supported railways and complex government financing such as the Suez Canal. In 1816 four of the five brothers were raised to the Austrian nobility by Emperor Francis I, and Nathan in 1818. They were granted the title of Freiherr (baron) on 29 September 1822.

The houses separated over time. The Naples house closed in 1863 after forty-two years, following the unification of Italy and the decline of the aristocrats who had been its main clients. In 1901 the German branch closed after the death of Wilhelm Rothschild without male heirs. By the start of the 20th century national taxation systems had ended the practice of keeping a single set of accounts, and the branches became independent banks. In Austria the family had to surrender its bank to the Nazis and flee during the Second World War; all its members escaped the Holocaust, and in 1999 the Austrian government agreed to return some 250 art treasures looted by the Nazis.

Only the French and British branches still subsist. The family's wealth was divided among many descendants over the 20th century, and its businesses now cover financial services, real estate, mining, energy, agriculture and winemaking; Nathaniel de Rothschild bought Château Mouton Rothschild in 1853 and James Mayer de Rothschild Château Lafite in 1868. The family has often been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories.
rotterdam: Rotterdam lies in the province of South Holland, in the North Sea mouth of the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta, reached by the New Meuse channel, which was dug to connect first to the Meuse and now to the Rhine. The river Nieuwe Maas divides the city into a northern and a southern part, joined by tunnels and bridges. The Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt give waterway access into the heart of Western Europe, including the industrialised Ruhr, and together with rail and road links they earned the city the nicknames Gateway to Europe and Gateway to the World.

The settlement at the lower end of the fen stream Rotte, then called Rotta from words for muddy water, dates from at least the year 950. Around 1150 large floods ended development and led to the building of protective dikes and dams, including Schieland's High Sea Dike along the northern bank of the Nieuwe Maas. A dam on the Rotte was built in the 13th century, at the present-day Hoogstraat, and in 1340 William IV, Count of Holland, granted Rotterdam city rights.

Rotterdam has always been one of the main centres of Dutch shipping. Its Chamber of the VOC, the world's first multinational, was established in 1602. Since 1795 it has hosted the chief congregation of the liberal Protestant Remonstrants, and its Catholic bishopric dates from 1955. The Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus is counted among its former inhabitants. During the First World War, because of Dutch neutrality and the city's position between Britain, Germany and German-occupied Belgium, it was the world's largest spy centre, and MI6 had its main European office on the Boompjes. On average 25,000 Belgian refugees lived there.

In the early stages of the Second World War the German Luftwaffe bombed the city centre and destroyed many of its older buildings. After an initial crisis of reconstruction the centre became a site of ambitious new architecture. Earlier landmarks include the White House of 1898, the tallest office building in Europe in its day, the Van Nelle Factory of 1929, a monument of modern factory design that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and Feyenoord's stadium De Kuip of 1936.

Rotterdam is the second-largest city of the Netherlands by population and the largest by area, and it is Europe's largest seaport. It is the centre of the Rotterdam–The Hague metropolitan area, the most populous in the country. Erasmus University Rotterdam is named after Erasmus. The destruction of the city centre in 1940 gave it a varied architectural landscape, with skyscrapers designed by architects such as Rem Koolhaas, Piet Blom and Ben van Berkel.
rouen: Rouen stands on the River Seine in northwestern France and is the prefecture of the region of Normandy and of the department of Seine-Maritime. The Seine has been central to its prosperity: in the Middle Ages the city had a monopoly on river traffic that reached as far upstream as Paris, and today the Port of Rouen is a major axis for maritime cargo.

Rouen was founded by the Gaulish tribe of the Veliocasses, who called it Ratumacos; the Romans called it Rotomagus. It was considered the second city of Gallia Lugdunensis after Lugdunum (Lyon), and under Diocletian it was chief city of Lugdunensis secunda, with an amphitheatre and baths. In the 5th century it became the seat of a bishopric and later a capital of Merovingian Neustria.

The Normans overran it from 841, and in the early 10th century it became the capital of the Duchy of Normandy until William the Conqueror moved his residence to Caen. It received a charter of self-government in 1150. In the 12th century about 6,000 Jews, a fifth of the population, lived in the town, which had a yeshiva known as La Maison Sublime.

On 24 June 1204 Philip II Augustus of France annexed Normandy, and from the 13th century a textile industry based on English wool made the city prosperous. The mayor was assassinated in 1291, Philip IV expelled the Jewish community in 1306, and the Harelle, a revolt of the underclass, in 1389 was suppressed with the loss of the city's charter. Rouen surrendered to Henry V of England on 19 January 1419 after a long siege.

Joan of Arc was burned at the stake there on 30 May 1431, and Charles VII recaptured the city in 1449. It withstood a five-month siege by Henry IV and an English force in 1591/2, and in the Second World War was heavily damaged and its cathedral almost destroyed by Allied bombs.

Rouen is the seat of an archdiocese, with a university and a court of appeal, and its metropolitan area has 715,239 people. Its monuments include Rouen Cathedral, whose Gothic facade Claude Monet painted in a series, the 14th-century astronomical clock known as the Gros Horloge, and the Church of Saint Ouen and the Gothic Church of St Maclou. The Place du Vieux Marché marks the site of Joan of Arc's pyre.
roxana: Roxana was the daughter of the Bactrian nobleman Oxyartes, satrap of Bactria and Sogdia, who served Bessus and was probably involved in the murder of the last Achaemenid king, Darius III. The date of her birth is unknown, but she was of childbearing age by 326 BCE. After Alexander the Great captured Bessus, Oxyartes and his family fled north and, with the Sogdian warlord Spitamenes, took up position in a fortress known as the Sogdian Rock, where the Macedonians defeated them.

Alexander then reportedly fell in love with Roxana on sight at a celebration. Where it took place is disputed. Arrian states that Oxyartes surrendered when he learned how well Alexander had received his daughter, and A. B. Bosworth raises the possibility that she was captured at the Sogdian Rock and the two married at the fortress of Chorienes.

The marriage took place in 327 BCE and, according to most sources, followed Macedonian rather than Persian custom. Alexander married her despite opposition from his companions, who would have preferred a Macedonian or Greek queen, and the match may also have been political, since the Bactrian and Sogdian armies became more loyal afterwards. According to the Metz Epitome she went with him to India, where their first son died in infancy near the Hydaspes in the autumn of 326 BCE. In 324 BCE Alexander also married Stateira II, a daughter of Darius III.

After Alexander died suddenly at Babylon in 323 BCE, Roxana is believed to have murdered Stateira, and Plutarch says she had Stateira's sister Drypetis killed with the consent of Perdiccas. She was pregnant, and the Macedonians reached a compromise: Philip Arrhidaeus was declared king, and the unborn child was to be king as well if a son. She bore a son, Alexander IV, in 323 BCE.

By 317 BCE the young Alexander had lost his kingship through the intrigues of Philip Arrhidaeus' wife, Eurydice II, and Roxana and her son were protected by Alexander's mother Olympias in Macedonia. After Olympias was assassinated in 316 BCE, Cassander imprisoned them in the citadel of Amphipolis. A peace treaty of 311 BCE confirmed Alexander IV's kingship with Cassander as his guardian, but Cassander ordered Glaucias of Macedon to kill the boy and Roxana, possibly by poison. Scholars disagree on the date of their deaths. Inscriptions at the Acropolis record offerings Roxana dedicated to Athena as Alexander's wife, and the asteroid 317 Roxane is named for her.
royal-air-force: The Royal Air Force was formed towards the end of the First World War, on 1 April 1918, by merging the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service. To emphasise the merger of military and naval aviation, many officers' titles were deliberately chosen to be naval in character, such as flight lieutenant, wing commander, group captain and air commodore. Following the Allied victory over the Central Powers in 1918, the new force emerged as the largest air force in the world.

Titles and insignia of other ranks were based on those of the Army, with some changes in terminology. Early in the war British aircraft had carried the Union Flag, which was easily confused with Germany's Iron Cross, so in October 1914 the French system of three concentric rings was adopted, with the colours reversed to a red disc surrounded by a white ring and an outer blue ring.

The service expanded rapidly before and during the Second World War. Under the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan of December 1939, the air forces of Commonwealth countries trained and formed Article XV squadrons for service with its formations, and exiles from occupied Europe served with its squadrons.

By the end of the war the Royal Canadian Air Force had contributed more than 30 squadrons, and about a quarter of Bomber Command's personnel were Canadian. At its height in 1944 more than 1,100,000 personnel were serving. It defeated the German Luftwaffe's efforts to win air superiority in the Battle of Britain and played a key role in the Combined Bomber Offensive alongside the USAAF.

After the war jet fighters and bombers arrived and the service was reorganised. In the early Cold War one of its first major operations was the Berlin Airlift, between 26 June 1948 and the lifting of the Soviet blockade on 12 May 1949, in which it provided 17 percent of the total supplies delivered. Its first post-war engagements came during the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, when RAF fighters shot down four Egyptian aircraft that had mistakenly attacked an RAF airbase, and in encounters with the Israeli Air Force.

The Royal Air Force has played a significant role in British military history. The Royal Flying Corps had provided the flypast for Trooping the Colour since 1913, and the RAF continues to do so. The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, formed in 1957, flies Spitfire and Hurricane fighters, an Avro Lancaster and a Dakota to commemorate the Second World War. The Red Arrows, its aerobatic team, were formed in late 1964, and the Central Band of the Royal Air Force was established in 1920.
royal-navy: Warships were used by English and Scottish kings from the early medieval period, and the first major maritime engagements were fought in the Hundred Years' War against France. For much of the medieval period fleets, or king's ships, were gathered for specific campaigns and dispersed afterwards, and they were generally merchant ships taken into service. Unlike some European states, England kept no small permanent core of warships in peacetime.

Control of the sea became critical to Anglo-Saxon kings only in the 10th century. The English Royal Navy was formally founded in 1546 by Henry VIII, when a standing Navy Royal with its own secretariat, dockyards and a permanent core of purpose-built warships emerged. The Royal Scots Navy merged with it under the Acts of Union 1707.

Under Elizabeth I, England fought Spain, and privately owned vessels joined the queen's ships in raids on Spanish commerce and colonies. The navy was used in 1588 to repulse the Spanish Armada, but the English Armada was lost the next year.

In the early 17th century England's relative naval power deteriorated until Charles I undertook a major shipbuilding programme, whose financing contributed to the outbreak of the English Civil War. After the Restoration in 1660 the navy took its present title. From the 18th century, voyages commissioned with the Royal Society included three by James Cook, and George Vancouver mapped the western coast of North America.

From the early 18th century until the Second World War it was the world's most powerful navy, and it played a key part in establishing and defending the British Empire, with imperial bases and coaling stations securing its superiority. In the First World War the Grand Fleet confronted the German High Seas Fleet across the North Sea, notably at Jutland in 1916, and the navy ferried the whole British Expeditionary Force to the Western Front without loss of life.

The Washington and London Naval Treaties limited it between the wars. In 1939 it was still the largest in the world, with over 1,400 vessels, and in the Battle of the Atlantic it defended British supply lines against U-boat attack.

After the Second World War the decline of the British Empire and economic hardship forced a reduction in its size and capability, and the United States Navy took on the role of global naval power. During the Cold War it became primarily an anti-submarine force. Royal Navy ships in commission have carried the prefix His Majesty's Ship, abbreviated HMS, since 1789. The navy is known as the Senior Service because it is the oldest of the United Kingdom's armed services, and its uniform is the pattern on which many other navies' uniforms are based.
royal-palace-of-caserta: The palace stands in Caserta, in Campania, 35 kilometres north of Naples. It has a rectangular plan measuring 247 by 190 metres, with two orthogonal arms joining the four sides to form four inner courts. It rises five floors, with a volume of about 2 million cubic metres and a floor area of 130,000 square metres. It has 1,200 rooms, including two dozen state apartments, 1,742 windows, 34 staircases, 1,026 fireplaces, a large library and a theatre modelled on the Teatro San Carlo of Naples. The Palatine Chapel, which Luigi Vanvitelli modelled on the chapel at Versailles, stands inside the palace with direct access from the Upper Vestibule.

Behind the palace stretches a garden of 120 hectares, begun in 1753 and also inspired by Versailles. A long alley with fountains and cascades runs from the back façade, among them the fountains of Diana and Actaeon, Venus and Adonis, the Dolphins, Aeolus and Ceres. In the 1780s Carlo Vanvitelli and the botanist John Graefer designed an English garden in the upper part, an early continental example of the naturalistic taste.

Construction began in 1752 for Charles VII of Naples, later Charles III of Spain, working closely with Vanvitelli. Charles never slept a night there, since he abdicated in 1759 to become King of Spain, and the project was carried only to partial completion for his third son and successor, Ferdinand IV of Naples. Versailles was the model, and the proposal first made by Mario Gioffredo in 1750 envisaged a virtual city housing the court and the elites of the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily.

The king also wanted a court and administrative centre protected from sea attack and distant from the revolt-prone and congested capital. The population of Caserta Vecchia was moved 10 kilometres to provide a workforce, and a silk factory at San Leucio was disguised as a pavilion in the park.

Vanvitelli died in 1773 and his son Carlo and other architects continued the work, but his original project, including a pair of frontal wings, was never finished. From 1923 to 1943 the palace housed the Italian Air Force Academy. In 1943 it became Allied Force Headquarters in the Mediterranean, and on 29 April 1945 the unconditional surrender of German forces in Italy was signed there. An air raid in September 1943 destroyed almost all the paintings of the Palatine Chapel.

The palace was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, together with the park, the Carolino aqueduct and the San Leucio complex. The listing describes it as exceptional for its design, which takes in an imposing palace and park, much of the surrounding landscape and an ambitious new town planned by the precepts of its time.
royal-road: The Royal Road was reorganised and rebuilt for trade in the 5th century BCE by the Achaemenid Empire, to allow fast communication in the western part of the empire between Susa and Sardis. It was probably perfected under Darius I, who improved an existing road network into the road as it is known. Because the route followed neither the shortest nor the easiest line between the empire's main cities and ran through the heart of the old Assyrian empire, archaeologists think its westernmost sections may originally have been built by the Assyrian kings.

Its course has been reconstructed from the writings of Herodotus, archaeological research and other records. Herodotus, an Ionian Greek, saw Persia from the west and did not note the eastern stretches, which can be identified in northern Iran.

The road was above all a post road. It had one hundred and eleven posting stations kept supplied with fresh horses, and relays of swift mounted messengers, called pirradazis, carried messages along it. Mounted couriers of the Angarium were supposed to cover the 2,699 kilometres from Susa to Sardis in nine days, while the journey took ninety days on foot. Stretches across the central plateau of Iran, such as the Great Khorasan Road, coincide with the major trade route known as the Silk Road.
25 metres wide, held within a stone curbing. In 1961 S. F. Starr traced the stretch from Gordium to Sardis, identifying river crossings by the remains of ancient bridge abutments.

Herodotus wrote that nothing in the world travels faster than these Persian couriers. A passage inspired by his praise, that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds, is inscribed on the James Farley Post Office in New York, and is sometimes thought of as the creed of the United States Postal Service, which has no official motto.

The phrase royal road also became a metaphor. Euclid is said to have told King Ptolemy that there is no royal road to geometry, a remark also attributed to Menaechmus in reply to Alexander the Great. Sigmund Freud described dreams as the royal road to the unconscious, and Karl Marx wrote in 1872 that there is no royal road to science.
royal-society: The Invisible College has been described as a precursor group to the Royal Society, consisting of a number of natural philosophers around Robert Boyle. The phrase appears in German Rosicrucian pamphlets of the early 17th century, and Ben Jonson referred to the idea in a masque of 1624/5, related in meaning to Francis Bacon's House of Salomon. In letters dated 1646 and 1647 Boyle writes of "our invisible college" or "our philosophical college". The group's common theme was to acquire knowledge through experimental investigation.

The society's second charter was signed on 22 April 1663. In August 1662 Charles II had told the society that it might use the arms of England as part of its own, and the charter granted the arms, with the motto Nullius in verba, to the president, council and fellows. The motto comes from Horace's Epistles, where the poet compares himself to a retired gladiator, free from control, and signifies the fellows' determination to establish facts by experiment.

In the 18th century the zeal of the early years faded, and few scientific figures of the first rank emerged. In the second half of the century it became customary for the government to refer important scientific questions to the society's council. In 1777 a dispute over lightning conductors spilled into politics: Benjamin Franklin had invented the pointed conductor in 1749 and Benjamin Wilson the blunted one, and opponents of Franklin's design accused its supporters of being American allies. The debate led to the resignation of the president, Sir John Pringle.

The early 19th century has been seen as a time of decline: of 662 fellows in 1830, only 104 had contributed to the Philosophical Transactions. That year Charles Babbage published Reflections on the Decline of Science in England, deeply critical of the society. A Charters Committee set up by James South recommended limiting the number of Fellows elected each year, and the membership became almost entirely scientific. The first women Fellows, Marjory Stephenson and Kathleen Lonsdale, were elected on 22 March 1945, after a postal ballot of Fellows approved the change by 336 votes to 37.

The society is governed by a council chaired by its president, elected from and by the Fellows. Fellows are scientists and engineers from the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth chosen for a substantial contribution to the improvement of natural knowledge, including mathematics, engineering science and medical science. They are elected for life, may use the postnominal FRS, and are chosen by ten sectional committees of existing Fellows. Each Fellow signs the Charter Book, which has been signed continuously since 1663 and which every British monarch has signed except William and Mary, and Queen Anne.
ruben-dario: He was born on 18 January 1867 as Félix Rubén García Sarmiento in Metapa, in Matagalpa (now Ciudad Darío), where his mother Rosa Sarmiento had gone after leaving her husband Manuel García, who was said to drink heavily. His baptism gave the surname García, but his paternal family had long been known as the Daríos, after a great-grandfather nicknamed Don Darío. In El Salvador he met the poet Francisco Gavidia, a connoisseur of French poetry, and with his help first tried to adapt the French Alexandrine to Castilian verse. After a return to Nicaragua and work at the National Library in Managua, he sailed for Chile on 5 June 1886.

In Chile he worked for the newspaper La Época in Santiago and published Abrojos in 1887. His book Azul..., which appeared in Valparaíso in July 1888, was the key work of the modernist revolution that had just begun. Its success brought him a post as correspondent of La Nación of Buenos Aires, then the most widely circulated periodical in Hispanic America. He travelled to Spain in 1892 with a Nicaraguan delegation, lived for a time in Buenos Aires as an honorary Colombian consul, and later sent chronicles from Spain on its mood after defeat by the United States, collected in 1901 as España contemporánea.

He covered the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1900 for La Nación, and those chronicles became Peregrinaciones. He later served as Nicaraguan resident minister in Madrid under José Santos Zelaya, resigning on 25 February 1909 after Zelaya was overthrown. He died in León on 6 February 1916, aged 49.

French poetry shaped him: first the romantics, above all Victor Hugo, then the Parnassians Théophile Gautier, Catulle Mendès and José María de Heredia, José Martí, and the symbolists, especially Paul Verlaine. In the opening poem of Cantos de vida y esperanza (1905) he described himself as strong towards Hugo and ambiguous towards Verlaine. He wrote in thirty-seven different metrical lines and 136 stanza forms. His main works are Azul... (1888), Prosas profanas (1896) and Cantos de vida y esperanza.

The critic Roberto González Echevarría holds that Spanish-language poetry divides into the periods before and after Darío, and Octavio Paz described his as one of the most profound poetic revolutions in Spanish. The National Library of Nicaragua was renamed in his honour, and Madrid has a metro station and a plaza named after him.
rudaki: Little information is available about Rudaki's life, and much of it has been reconstructed from his poems. He lived under the Samanid Empire, in which New Persian literature began to develop and flourish. According to the Tajik writer Sadriddin Ayni, he was born in the village of Panjrud in the former Panjakent District of Tajikistan.

By the age of eight he had reportedly memorised the Qur'an and was skilled in poetry, and a musician named Abu'l-Abak Bakhtiar taught him to play the chang. In his early years he became popular for his fine voice, his poetry and his playing. Early poets such as Daqiqi and Ferdowsi imply that he was blind, and the historian Awfi says he was born blind, which some modern scholars question because of the expressive picture of nature in his writing.

The most important part of Rudaki's career was spent at the Samanid court in Bukhara. He is connected with the amir Nasr II, who reigned from 914 to 943, though the literary scholar Sassan Tabatabai argues from a poem comforting Ahmad Samani after the death of Ismail Samani in 907 that he had already joined the court under Ahmad Samani.

His success was largely due to his main patron, the vizier Abu'l-Fadl al-Bal'ami, who regarded him as the best among Persian and Arab poets. He was a close friend of his student Shahid Balkhi and wrote an elegy for him after his death in 936. After Bal'ami's downfall in 937, his career declined, he fell out of favour with the amir and was dismissed from the court. He lived his last years in poverty and died blind and alone in his hometown.

According to Asadi Tusi, Rudaki's divan consisted of more than 180,000 verses, but most is lost. What remains is mostly single verses preserved in Persian dictionaries, especially Asadi Tusi's Lughat-i Furs. A qasida of almost 100 verses survives in the Tarikh-i Sistan, dedicated to Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad, the Samanid governor of Sistan, who rewarded him with 10,000 dinars.

His best-known work is his versification of the Kalila wa-Dimna, a collection of Indian fables, which Nasr II had Bal'ami translate from Arabic into Persian; interpreters read it aloud so that the blind poet could versify it. Though he showed pro-Isma'ili sympathies, his poetry is secular, and he evoked ancient Iranian and Zoroastrian notions more than Muslim ones. In Iran he is acknowledged as the founder of New Persian poetry and in Tajikistan as the father of Tajik literature.
ruder-boskovic: Ruđer Bošković was born on 18 May 1711 in Dubrovnik, in the Republic of Ragusa, the seventh child of the merchant Nikola Bošković and Paola Bettera, whose family had settled from Bergamo in the early 17th century. His father died when he was 10. At 8 or 9 he was sent to the local Jesuit Collegium Ragusinum, where he gained a reputation for a quick mind and an easy memory.

On 16 September 1725 he left Dubrovnik for Rome in the care of two Jesuit priests. He entered the novitiate in 1731, studied mathematics and physics, and in 1740 was appointed professor of mathematics at the Roman college. He was ordained a priest in 1744 and visited his home town only once more, in 1747.

Bošković published a very large number of dissertations on subjects from the transit of Mercury and the aurora to the figure of the Earth and the theory of comets. In 1742 Pope Benedict XIV consulted him, with other men of science, about a crack in the dome of St Peter's, and his suggestion of five concentric iron bands was adopted. Persuaded by the Pope to stay in Italy rather than join a Portuguese expedition to Brazil, he measured with the English Jesuit Christopher Maire an arc of two degrees of the meridian between Rome and Rimini, begun at the end of 1750 and completed in about two years, with a map of the States of the Church.

He served Lucca as an agent in Vienna in 1757, and in 1760 went to London as ambassador of Ragusa to prove the republic's neutrality, a mission he completed with success; there he was elected a fellow of the Royal Society. From 1764 he held the chair of mathematics at Pavia and directed the Brera observatory in Milan. After the suppression of his order he accepted an invitation from the King of France and became director of optics for the navy in Paris, where he stayed ten years. He returned to Italy in 1783 and died in Milan on 13 February 1787.

In De Viribus Vivis (1745) he sought a middle way between Newton's gravitational theory and Leibniz's monad-points. His best-known work, Philosophiæ naturalis theoria redacta ad unicam legem virium in natura existentium, first published in Vienna in 1758, set out his atomic theory and his theory of forces. In 1753 he discovered the absence of an atmosphere on the Moon, and he devised geometric procedures for finding a planet's equator and orbit from three observations. Nietzsche's ideas of force were influenced by him, and a lunar crater and the Ruđer Bošković Institute in Zagreb bear his name. His nationality is claimed in Croatia, Italy and Serbia alike.
rudesheim-am-rhein: Rüdesheim lies at the foot of the Niederwald on the right bank of the Rhine, in the Rheingau wine region and the Rheingau-Taunus-Kreis district. It belongs to the Frankfurt Rhine Main Region and to the Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site, and its full name distinguishes it from Rüdesheim an der Nahe. The municipality has five quarters: Rüdesheim itself, Eibingen, Assmannshausen, Aulhausen and Presberg. Two ferries, one for pedestrians and one for cars, connect it with the left bank, where the town of Bingen faces it.

The area was settled first by Celts, then by the Ubii and later the Mattiaci. In the first century the Romans pushed forward to the Taunus and kept a bridgehead near what is now Rüdesheim, on the way to the Limes. Alamanni and then Franks followed. Glass finds from the Migration Period suggest that winegrowing was already practised. Rüdesheim was first mentioned in a document in 1074, and its livelihood came mainly from winegrowing and shipping, particularly timber rafting.

The town received town rights on 1 January 1818. After Prussia annexed the Duchy of Nassau in 1867, Rüdesheim became the seat of the new Rheingaukreis and kept that status for 110 years, until a municipal reform in 1977 merged the district into the Rheingau-Taunus-Kreis and moved the seat to Bad Schwalbach. In 1939 the National Socialists forcibly merged the self-governing community of Eibingen with the town, against the wishes of its inhabitants. Assmannshausen, Aulhausen and Presberg were incorporated in 1977.

The Brömserburg, built in the 10th century on the site of a Roman fortification, is the oldest castle in the Rhine Gorge. The Archbishop of Mainz owned it from the 10th to the 13th century, and French troops under Henri II d'Orléans, duc de Longueville, destroyed the top of its tower in 1640. The town bought it in 1941, and it now holds a wine museum. Eibingen Abbey, founded by Hildegard of Bingen, stands above Eibingen. Riesling is the main grape grown, and tourism has increasingly replaced shipping as a source of income.
rudolf-diesel: Rudolf Christian Karl Diesel was born on 18 March 1858 in Paris, the second of three children of Bavarian immigrants. His father Theodor, a bookbinder from Augsburg, became a leather goods manufacturer in Paris, and the family had financial difficulties, so the boy worked in his father's workshop. When the Franco-Prussian War broke out in 1870 the family was deported to England, and his mother sent him to relatives in Augsburg, where he finished his basic education at the top of his class in 1873.

At fourteen he wrote to his parents that he meant to become an engineer. He took a merit scholarship at the Royal Bavarian Polytechnic of Munich against his parents' wishes, studied under Carl von Linde, and graduated in January 1880 with the highest honours.

Diesel returned to Paris and helped Linde build a refrigeration and ice plant, becoming its director a year later. In early 1890 he moved to Berlin to manage Linde's research department. Barred from using his patents there for his own ends, he turned to other fields and built a steam engine using ammonia vapour, which exploded and nearly killed him; he spent many months in hospital with health and eyesight problems.

He worked on an internal combustion engine that could approach the maximum theoretical thermal efficiency of the Carnot cycle, knowing that as much as 90 percent of a steam engine's fuel energy was wasted. In 1892 he received the German patent DRP 67207, and in 1893 he published a treatise on a heat engine to replace the steam engine. By summer 1893 he had realised his first theory was wrong and filed another application. In his engine the heat of compressed air ignited the injected fuel, with no spark plug.

From 1893 to 1897 Heinrich von Buz, director of Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, let Diesel test and develop his ideas, with support from the Krupp firm. The first successful engine, Motor 250/400, a 25-horsepower single-cylinder four-stroke, was officially tested in 1897, and royalties made Diesel wealthy.

On the evening of 29 September 1913 Diesel boarded the steamer SS Dresden at Antwerp, bound for a meeting in London.
