His cabin was empty the next morning, and his hat and folded overcoat were found under the afterdeck railing. Ten days later a Dutch pilot boat's crew found a body in the Eastern Scheldt and took items from its clothing, which his son Eugen identified. Biographers have argued that he died by suicide, others that he was murdered; his death remains unsolved. His engine became an important replacement for the steam piston engine and spread to ships, submarines, locomotives, trucks and automobiles.
rudolf-i-of-germany: Rudolf was born on 1 May 1218 at Limburgh Castle near Sasbach am Kaiserstuhl in the Breisgau, the son of Count Albert IV of Habsburg and Hedwig, daughter of Count Ulrich of Kyburg. He was not educated at the royal court and probably knew neither writing nor Latin. When his father died on the Barons' Crusade, Rudolf assumed sole rule of the main Habsburg line, with estates around Habsburg Castle in Aargau and in Alsace.

He built Neuhabsburg Castle on Lake Lucerne around 1244 and married Gertrude of Hohenberg, which strengthened his position in Swabia. In 1254 he joined the Prussian Crusade. During the Great Interregnum that followed the death of Frederick II in 1250 he took advantage of the disorder, seizing the estates of his maternal uncle Count Hartmann IV of Kyburg in 1264 and fighting successful feuds with the bishops of Strasbourg and Basel.

In August 1273 Pope Gregory X told the electors to choose a king. They elected Rudolf unanimously at Frankfurt on 1 October 1273, and Archbishop Engelbert II of Cologne crowned him at Aachen on 24 October. The pope acknowledged the election on 20 September 1274. The Imperial Diet at Nuremberg ordered the return of crown estates, and when Ottokar II of Bohemia refused to give up Austria, Styria and Carinthia, Rudolf had him placed under the imperial ban. War began in June 1276, and on 26 August 1278 Ottokar was defeated and killed at the Battle on the Marchfeld.

In December 1282, at Augsburg, Rudolf invested his sons Albert and Rudolf II with Austria and Styria, laying the foundation of the House of Habsburg. In 1286 he gave Carinthia to Count Meinhard. He was less successful in restoring internal peace: territorial peaces were ordered and the Synod of Würzburg of March 1287 extended one to the whole Empire, but he lacked the power to enforce them. In 1286 he also declared the Jews servi camerae, serfs of the treasury, which negated their political freedoms.

Rudolf died at Speyer on 15 July 1291 and was buried in Speyer Cathedral. In 1291 he had tried to secure the election of his son Albert as German king, but the electors refused, and after Rudolf's death they chose Count Adolf of Nassau. His reign is most remembered for establishing the Habsburgs as a powerful dynasty in the southeast of the realm, while elsewhere the long decline of imperial authority continued. In the Divine Comedy Dante finds him outside the gates of purgatory and calls him the one who neglected what he ought to have done.
rudolf-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Rudolf was born in Vienna on 18 July 1552, the eldest son of Maximilian II, and his mother was the Spanish princess Maria, a daughter of Charles V. From the age of 11 to 19 he lived in Spain at the court of his uncle Philip II. His father worried about his aloof and stiff manner, while his mother saw courtliness and refinement in him.

He remained reserved, secretive and largely a recluse who disliked travelling or taking part in the daily affairs of state. He was drawn to astrology and alchemy, which were mainstream in the Renaissance, and to horses, clocks and collecting rarities. He suffered periodic bouts of melancholy, which grew worse with age. He never married but had several children with his mistress Catherina Strada.

Rudolf succeeded his father on 12 October 1576, and in 1583 he moved the court to Prague. Although raised at a Catholic court, he was tolerant of Protestantism and of Judaism, and Jewish cultural life flourished under his rule. He backed conciliarists, irenicists and humanists, and when the papacy pressed the Counter-Reformation through agents at his court he supported those he thought most neutral, which led to political chaos. Determined to unify Christendom, he began a long and indecisive war against the Ottoman Empire in 1593, the Long Turkish War, which lasted until 1606.

By 1604 his Hungarian subjects were exhausted by the war and revolted under Stephen Bocskai. In 1605 his family forced him to cede control of Hungarian affairs to his brother Matthias, who made peace with the Hungarians and the Ottomans in 1606. Matthias then forced him to cede the crowns of Hungary, Austria and Moravia. In 1609 Rudolf granted the Bohemian Protestants the Letter of Majesty. When he tried to suppress the Protestant estates with troops of his cousin Leopold V, Bishop of Passau, Matthias's army held him prisoner in Prague Castle until he ceded the crown of Bohemia in 1611.

Rudolf died on 20 January 1612, stripped of all effective power. In May 1618 the Defenestration of Prague, in defence of the Letter of Majesty, began the Thirty Years' War. Historians have traditionally blamed his interest in art and the occult for the disasters of his reign, while more recent ones see his patronage as a key part of the Renaissance.

His Kunstkammer at Prague Castle, with Dürer and Bruegel among its paintings, was the most impressive collection in Europe, and artists such as Giuseppe Arcimboldo worked for him. He patronised the astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler, and Kepler's laws of planetary motion rested on this patronage, as Kepler recognised in the Rudolphine Tables.
rudolph-of-france: Rudolph was born around 890, the son of Richard the Justiciar and Adelaide of Auxerre. In Latin documents his name is usually Rodulfus, and he always used that form himself, as on his seal, although he is often called Raoul in modern French and Ralph in English. He inherited the Duchy of Burgundy from his father in 921 and married Emma, daughter of King Robert I of France.

Robert was killed at the Battle of Soissons fighting the deposed King Charles the Simple, and Rudolph was elected to succeed him. He was crowned by Walter, archbishop of Sens, at Saint-Médard de Soissons on 13 July 923 and passed the duchy to his younger brother, Hugh the Black.

Rudolph first led an army against Henry the Fowler, king of East Francia, who had made a pact with Robert and tried to annex Lotharingia. Peace was made, but in 925 Henry took Lotharingia for good, and Rudolph could not resist. In 924 Vikings raided West Francia from the Loire Valley, attacked Burgundy and moved to Melun. Rudolph raised troops with Hugh the Great, and then with Herbert and Arnulf I of Flanders he fought the Normans near Fauquembergues, where the king was wounded.

Magyars invaded the region around Rheims in 930 and Burgundy in 935, and Rudolph's large army made them retreat without a battle. West Francia was temporarily safe from both Vikings and Magyars at his death.

Herbert II of Vermandois held Charles the Simple prisoner and used him to win the archbishopric of Rheims for his son Hugh and the county of Laon for his son Odo. Charles died at Péronne, and Rudolph was not fully recognised in the south until Charles died in captivity on 7 October 929. He received the homage of William Longsword and in 933 granted him the Channel Islands. In 931 he replaced Hugh at Rheims with Artald, and joined by Hugh the Great he burned Herbert's fortresses and cornered him in Château-Thierry.

In the south he also gave the title of prince of Gothia to Raymond Pons, count of Toulouse, and campaigned against the last Viking strongholds. The two men made peace in 935. Rudolph fell ill and died on 14 or 15 January 936, leaving no sons.
rudolstadt: Rudolstadt lies in the Thuringian Forest in Thuringia, to the south-west of Jena and Weimar. It is built along the river Saale inside a wide valley surrounded by woods. The town was the capital of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, and its landmark is the castle Heidecksburg, which stands on a hill above the old town. The former municipality of Remda-Teichel was merged into Rudolstadt in January 2019.

Archaeological evidence points to a hill fort on the Weinberg in Oberpreilipp from the late Urnfield culture and the early Iron Age. A Celtic settlement followed a Germanic one, and from the 6th century onwards the records suggest Slavic settlement in the area. The place-name is first documented in 776 as Rudolfestat, Rudolf's settlement, in a gift from Charlemagne to Hersfeld Abbey. The town has had municipal law since 1326.

A porcelain manufacture was established at Volkstedt in 1762, and Rudolstadt later became well known for its porcelain factories and for the Anchor Stone Blocks of the toy company Richter. The Thüringer Landestheater traces its origins to a court theatre built in 1792/93. Composers who worked there as composer in residence included Niccolò Paganini, Franz Liszt and Richard Wagner, and the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer wrote his dissertation in the town.

The writer Hans Fallada went to school in Rudolstadt, and Charlotte von Lengefeld (1766-1826) was the wife of Schiller. Princess Anna Sophie of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt was the grandmother of King Leopold I of Belgium. The Rudolstadt Festival, formerly the Tanz&FolkFest, takes place annually on the first full July weekend, and the town is twinned with Letterkenny in County Donegal, Ireland.
ruhollah-khomeini: Ruhollah Mostafavi Khomeini came from a family of small landowners, clerics and merchants and was born in the town of Khomeyn, in what is now Markazi province. His father was murdered when he was a small child, and his mother and aunt raised him. In 1920 he began studies at the seminary in Arak under Ayatollah Abdolkarim Haeri Yazdi and the following year followed his teacher to Qom, where he studied Islamic law and also philosophy and mysticism. His first political book, Kashf al-Asrar, was published in 1942. He became a marja', a source of emulation, in 1963, after the death of Grand Ayatollah Seyyed Husayn Borujerdi.

In January 1963 Mohammad Reza Shah announced the White Revolution, a programme that included land reform and the enfranchisement of women. Khomeini viewed it as an attack on Islam and on 22 January 1963 issued a declaration denouncing the Shah. On 26 October 1964 he denounced the immunity granted to American military personnel. He was exiled on 4 November 1964, first to Bursa in Turkey and from October 1965 to Najaf in Iraq, where his lectures on the Guardianship of the Jurist were compiled as Islamic Government. In 1978 Saddam Hussein expelled him, and he went to Neauphle-le-Château near Paris.

The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, and Khomeini returned on 1 February to a crowd reported to be as many as five million. On 11 February he appointed Mehdi Bazargan as his own prime minister, in competition with the provisional government of Shapour Bakhtiar. He was de facto head of state until his appointment as supreme leader in December 1979. Iraq invaded in September 1980, and the Iran–Iraq War lasted until August 1988. Khomeini also issued a fatwa calling for the killing of Salman Rushdie, author of The Satanic Verses.

Khomeini died on 3 June 1989 after five heart attacks in ten days. His funeral drew up to 10 million people, and at least ten mourners were trampled to death. In March 1989 he had removed Grand Ayatollah Hussein-Ali Montazeri as his chosen successor after Montazeri criticised the execution of political prisoners. His legacy remains disputed: admirers see a champion of Islamic revival and independence, while critics point to the repression and executions of his rule.
ruhr: The Ruhr area, or Ruhrgebiet, is a polycentric urban area bordered by the river Ruhr to the south, the Rhine to the west and the Lippe to the north. Its cities lie, from west to east, along a line running through Duisburg, Essen, Bochum and Dortmund, and the area has no administrative centre: each city has its own administration. Geologically the region is defined by coal-bearing layers of the upper Carboniferous period. The coal seams reach the surface in a strip along the river Ruhr and dip downward towards the north, lying 600 to 800 metres deep beneath the Lippe, which played a decisive role in the development of coal mining.

In the Middle Ages much of the region lay in the County of Mark, the Duchy of Cleves, the State of Berg and the territories of the bishop of Münster and the archbishop of Cologne, within the Holy Roman Empire. It was mainly agrarian. The free imperial city of Dortmund was its trading and cultural centre on the Hellweg, an important east–west trade route that also brought prosperity to Duisburg.

Industrialisation began in the late 18th century in the nearby Wupper Valley in the Bergisches Land. From 1807 to 1813 the area was part of the kingdom of Westphalia, a client state of France ruled by Napoleon's brother Jérôme, and by about 1820 hundreds of water-powered mills produced textiles and iron. As machines moved from water to steam, the Bergische industry ordered more and more coal from the new mining area along the Ruhr, and railways brought coal and later steel from the Ruhr into the hills.

After the Kapp Putsch of March 1920, which a general strike defeated, an armed revolt in the Ruhr aimed to replace the Weimar Republic with a soviet-style council republic. The Ruhr Red Army took control of the industrial area, but the Reichswehr with Freikorps units put the rising down in early April 1920; an estimated 1,000 insurgents and 200 soldiers were killed. In 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the district and seized its main industrial assets in lieu of unpaid reparations. After the Second World War the Ruhr Authority was created to regulate its coal and steel industries.

The Ruhr is the largest urban area in Germany and part of the larger Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region. Since the 1980s it has been the target of financial support from the state, the federal government and the European Union. A supracommunal Ruhr Regional Association has its seat in Essen.
rule-of-law: The phrase dates to 16th-century Britain. In the next century the Scottish theologian Samuel Rutherford used it to argue against the divine right of kings, and John Locke wrote that freedom in society means being subject only to laws written by a legislature that apply to everyone. The jurist A. V. Dicey popularised it in the 19th century. The principle, if not the phrase, was recognised by ancient thinkers: Aristotle wrote that it is more proper that law should govern than any one of the citizens. Its development can be traced to ancient Greece, Mesopotamia, India and Rome.

The Mahabharata, whose earliest versions date to the 8th or 9th century BCE, deals with dharma and the duty of the king, and says that a king who does not protect his people should be executed. In 1481 the General Court of Catalonia approved the Constitució de l'Observança, which subjected royal power to the laws of Catalonia.

In general the rule of law entails that law is clear, consistent and open, that people have access to justice, and that government institutions are subject to the law. It is sometimes put as no one is above the law. Its opposite is the rule of man, where one person or group rules arbitrarily. It is closely related to constitutionalism and to the German Rechtsstaat; in France the equivalent is Etat de droit.

Legal scholars divide into two groups. Formalists, among them Dicey, F. A. Hayek and Joseph Raz, hold that it requires general, public, prospective, consistent, equal and certain laws, but sets no requirement on their content. Substantivists, among them Ronald Dworkin, Lon Fuller and Tom Bingham, hold that it necessarily protects individual rights, and some include democracy.

In 1607 the English Chief Justice Sir Edward Coke told James I that the law was the measure by which the causes of the subjects are tried. The king was greatly offended and said that to place him under the law was treason. Coke answered by quoting Bracton, that the king ought to be under no man but under God and the law.

Hayek argued that under the rule of law individuals can plan and invest with some confidence, since government is prevented from frustrating their efforts by ad hoc action. In 1959 the International Commission of Jurists met in New Delhi, with over 185 judges, lawyers and professors from 53 countries, and issued the Declaration of Delhi, which held that the rule of law implied certain rights and freedoms and an independent judiciary. The Statute of the Council of Europe names it among the principles of genuine democracy, and Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union lists it among the common values of the member states.
rumi: Rumi's father, Baha ud-Din Walad, was a theologian, jurist and mystic from Wakhsh, where he lived until 1212, when the family moved to Samarkand. The advance of the Mongol armies later forced the family west. After time in various cities of Iran, in Baghdad and in Damascus, Rumi settled in Konya at the age of 19. His name means the Roman, because Anatolia had belonged to the Byzantine empire and was still known as Rum. When his father died, Rumi, aged twenty-five, inherited his position at a madrassa, and he was trained in the Shariah and the Tariqa by Burhan ud-Din Muhaqqiq Termazi until 1240 or 1241. He then began a public life as a jurist, issuing fatwas and preaching in the mosques of Konya.

His meeting with the wandering dervish Shams-e Tabrizi on 15 November 1244 changed his life, turning an accomplished teacher into an ascetic. When Shams disappeared, Rumi grieved deeply, and the verses he composed were collected in the Divan. His scribe and favourite student, Hussam-e Chalabi, suggested that he write a book like those of Sanai and Attar, and Rumi then dictated the six volumes of the Masnavi to him over twelve years.

The Masnavi, or Spiritual Couplets, has about 27,000 lines of rhyming couplets and is often called the Quran in Persian. Many commentators have ranked it first among the mystical poems of world literature. The Divan-i Kabir, named in honour of Shams, holds about 35,000 Persian couplets and 2,000 quatrains, with 90 ghazals and 19 quatrains in Arabic and a few Turkish and Greek couplets.

Rumi's poetry speaks of a love that infuses the world, and he held that the oneness of God is lived most fully through love. He was a Muslim who praised the Quran and held Muhammad to be the most perfect of the prophets, yet traces of religious pluralism run through his work: the lamps are different, he wrote, but the Light is the same.

Rumi fell ill in December 1273 and predicted his own death. His followers founded the Mevlevi order, also known as the whirling dervishes, in 1273. Hussam Chalabi led it until his death in 1284, when Rumi's younger surviving son, Sultan Walad, became grand master, and leadership has stayed in Rumi's family at Konya since. His poetry shaped the Ottoman Turkish, Chagatai, Pashto, Kurdish, Urdu and Bengali literary traditions, and it has been translated into many languages. In 2007 UNESCO took part in celebrating the eight hundredth anniversary of his birth.
rurik: The earliest mention of Rurik is in the Primary Chronicle, traditionally ascribed to Nestor and compiled in about 1113. It states that East Slavic and Finnic tribes in 860-862, including the Chuds, Slovenes, Krivichs, Meryans and Ves, drove the Varangians back beyond the sea, refused to pay them tribute and set out to govern themselves.

The tribes then began fighting each other and decided to invite the Varangians, led by Rurik, to restore order. He came with his younger brothers Sineus and Truvor and a large retinue. The chronicle says he was one of the Rus', a Varangian tribe, whom most historians regard as Scandinavian in origin, from the coast of what is now eastern Sweden.

Sineus established himself at Beloozero and Truvor at Izborsk. They died shortly afterwards, and Rurik consolidated these lands into his own territory and extended his rule in northern Russia. The oldest surviving version of the Primary Chronicle, the Laurentian Codex of 1377, states that he first settled in Novgorod, while the Hypatian Codex of the 1420s says he first settled in Ladoga and then moved to the newly founded Novgorod, a fort near the source of the Volkhov River, where he stayed until his death. His followers Askold and Dir, sent to Constantinople, seized Kiev before an attack recorded in Byzantine sources for the year 860.

Rurik is said to have remained in power until some time in the 870s, and the Primary Chronicle places his death in 879. On his deathbed he left his realm to his kinsman Oleg and entrusted to him his infant son Igor. Oleg moved the capital to Kiev by murdering its rulers and founded the state of Kievan Rus', which Rurik's successors ruled until the Mongol invasion in 1240.

The Rurikids were its ruling dynasty and ultimately that of the Tsardom of Russia, until the death of Feodor I in 1598, so Rurik is considered the traditional founder of the Russian monarchy. The historicity of Rurik remains a subject of debate. Some have identified him with Rorik of Dorestad, who appears in Frankish chronicles, an idea revived by Boris Rybakov and Anatoly Kirpichnikov in the mid-20th century and objected to by Alexander Nazarenko and others.
rurik-dynasty: Modern scholars consider Rurik a legendary and perhaps entirely fictional figure. The Primary Chronicle, of the early twelfth century, tells of the Calling of the Varangians: tribes at war with one another invited three brothers from overseas to rule them, of whom Rurik settled in Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor in Izborsk. No earlier Kievan source knew of Rurik, and genealogies of the princes usually stopped with Igor of Kiev. Even if Rurik existed, scholars have long doubted or rejected that he was Igor's father.

Before the mid-15th century no source claims that Rurik founded a dynasty. The tradition was set out by churchmen in the 16th century, in the Book of Royal Degrees of 1560 by Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, which traced the ruling house of Moscow to Rurik and to a supposed kinsman of Augustus Caesar named Prus. For this reason some scholars prefer the name Volodimerovichi, descendants of Volodimer I of Kiev.

The house underwent a major schism after the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, dividing into branches descended from his sons Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. By the middle of the twelfth century Kievan Rus' had dissolved into independent principalities, each under a different branch. Vsevolod's line, the Monomakhovichi, named after Vladimir II Monomakh, became predominant. The Olgovichi, descended from Sviatoslav, ruled in Chernigov until the early 14th century. The Romanovichi, the line of Roman the Great, were crowned kings of Galicia and Volhynia and ruled until 1323.

In the north-east the Yurievichi descended from Yuri Dolgorukiy, the founder of Moscow. His great-grandson was Alexander Nevsky, whose son Daniel of Moscow founded the ruling house of Moscow, the Daniilovichi. In all, the house ruled for 21 generations in the male line, a period of more than 700 years. It was briefly revived in Vasili IV of Russia, of the Shuyskiy line, who died without issue. The Time of Troubles lasted until 1613, when Mikhail I founded the Romanov dynasty; his father was descended from the Rurikids through the female line.

Russian and Ukrainian historians have long debated the inheritance of Kievan Rus'. The Russian view treats the Principality of Moscow as its sole heir, resting largely on religious and historical claims. The Ukrainian view of succession, summarised most clearly by Mykhailo Hrushevsky in his History of Ukraine-Rus', is based on continuity through the Kingdom of Ruthenia, Lithuania-Ruthenia and the Cossack Hetmanate. Several branches of the family survive, among them the houses of Shakhovskoy, Gagarin and Lobanov-Rostovsky.
russelsheim: Rüsselsheim am Main is the largest city in the Groß-Gerau district of the Rhein-Main region. It is one of seven special status cities in Hesse, which carry out several functions that counties normally provide. It lies on the Main between Frankfurt and Mainz, a few kilometres from the river's mouth at Mainz, and Frankfurt Airport is 17 km to the east. The suburbs of Bauschheim and Königstädten belong to it; Haßloch was added in 1951, Königstädten in 1956 and Bauschheim in 1970.

The town's foundation goes back to a Frankish colony in the first half of the 5th century. Its name first appears as Rucilesheim, the house of Rucile, in an inventory of royal hunting rights around 840, and it later grew from a settlement of the Count of Katzenelnbogen. In 1435 Count John IV of Katzenelnbogen was the first to cultivate Riesling there. In the 18th and 19th centuries Rheingau wine estates replanted their vineyards with vines from the Rüsselsheim area, but viticulture disappeared after the First World War.

Adam Opel began as a trainee mechanic and founded a sewing machine factory. The first cars were built in 1899, after his death, when the company was run by his widow and their five sons. The population rose from 1,422 in 1829 to 8,000 in 1914, fell from 16,000 to 9,500 during the Second World War, and reached a record 63,000 in 1978, fed first by refugees from former German territories and then by immigrants drawn to the Opel factories.

The town was bombed several times by the British RAF in the Second World War. On 26 August 1944 residents attacked nine captured American airmen who were walking through the town, after a raid the previous night, and six of them were killed. After the war eleven citizens were tried for war crimes and murder, and six were executed.

Opel remains the best-known name in the town, and the Korean manufacturer Hyundai opened its European centre there in 2003. The Rüsselsheim Museum, which concentrates on labour procedures and conditions from prehistory to the present, received the Council of Europe's museum award in 1980. The town also has a theatre with 865 seats and a branch of the Hochschule RheinMain. It is twinned with Évreux in France, Rugby in England, Varkaus in Finland and Kecskemét in Hungary.
russia: Russia is the largest country in the world, spanning eleven time zones and sharing land borders with fourteen countries. It stretches over the easternmost part of Europe and the northernmost part of Asia, some 9,000 kilometres from east to west, and is one of only three countries bordering three oceans. The Ural Mountains, running north to south through the west, form the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, at 5,642 metres, is the highest peak in Russia and Europe, and Klyuchevskaya Sopka on the Kamchatka Peninsula is the highest active volcano in Eurasia.

Human settlement on Russian territory dates back to the Lower Paleolithic. The East Slavs became prominent in Europe between the 3rd and 8th centuries, and Kievan Rus' was established in the 9th century, adopting Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988. After it disintegrated in the 12th century the Grand Principality of Moscow became the dominant Russian principality and led the unification of Russian lands, culminating in the Tsardom of Russia in 1547. Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721, which became the third-largest empire in history.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 abolished the monarchy and created the Russian SFSR, the first socialist state. After the Russian Civil War it became the principal constituent of the Soviet Union, established in 1922. Amid rapid industrialisation in the 1930s, millions died under Joseph Stalin. The Soviet Union played a decisive role for the Allies on the Eastern Front in World War II, then competed with the United States as a superpower during the Cold War. In 1991 the Russian SFSR emerged from the dissolution of the Soviet Union as the Russian Federation.

Russia had an estimated population of 146 million in 2025, and three-fourths of its people live in urban areas. Moscow is the capital and Saint Petersburg the second-largest city. A constitution adopted after a constitutional crisis in 1993 established a semi-presidential republic. Russian is the official language, and about 81% of the population were ethnic Russians in the 2010 census.
russian-civil-war: The war began with the overthrow of the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution. The monarchy had ended with the abdication of Emperor Nicholas II in the February Revolution of 1917, after which a coalition of centrist parties governed beside soviets of workers, soldiers and peasants. The Bolsheviks directed the Red Guard to seize Petrograd and began taking cities across the former empire. In January 1918 they dissolved the Constituent Assembly, in which the anti-Bolshevik Right Socialist-Revolutionaries had won the most seats. The conflict became a full-scale civil war in May and June 1918.

The two largest combatants were the Red Army, fighting for a Bolshevik-led socialist state under Vladimir Lenin, and the White movement, led mainly by right-leaning officers of the Russian Empire. Ukrainian anarchists and Left Socialist-Revolutionaries also fought the Bolsheviks. Thirteen foreign states intervened against the Red Army, chiefly the Allies, who aimed first to restore the Eastern Front of the First World War. In May 1918 the Czechoslovak Legion revolted in Siberia, and the former tsar and his family were murdered on 17 July. After an uprising of the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries in Moscow that July, executions grew more frequent and the Red Terror began.

In 1919 the Whites attacked from the east in March, the south in July and the west in October, and each advance was checked by a Red counteroffensive. Admiral Alexander Kolchak's army disintegrated in Siberia. The Red Army forced evacuations from Novorossiysk in March and from the Crimea in November 1920, and fighting was then sporadic until Vladivostok was captured in October 1922.

Estimates put the casualties at 7 to 12 million, mostly civilians. A famine caused between 3 and 10 million deaths, and by 1921 heavy industry produced only 20 percent of its 1913 output. One to two million people fled Russia, many with General Wrangel, among them a large share of the educated and skilled population.

Many non-Russian peoples used the disorder to press for independence. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania repelled Soviet invasions, while Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia were occupied by the Red Army. The Basmachi resistance in Central Asia was not dismantled until 1934. With the failure of revolutions elsewhere, the Bolsheviks moved from world revolution to socialism in one country, the Soviet Union.
russian-empire: The foundations of a unified Russian state were laid in the 15th century under Ivan III. Moscow became the leading Russian principality, and by the early 16th century the remaining Russian states were united with it. As the only independent Orthodox power after the fall of the Byzantine Empire in 1453, its rulers took symbolic steps towards empire: they married into the Byzantine imperial dynasty, adopted the double-headed eagle and took the title of tsar. Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547. Peter the Great (r. 1682 to 1725) transformed the tsardom into an empire, fought wars that made Russia a major European power, and moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg.

Catherine the Great came to power in a coup against her husband Peter III and presided over further expansion. Poland was partitioned between 1772 and 1815 and most of its land and population came under Russian rule, and by 1795 Russia was the most populous state in Europe, ahead of France. Alexander I helped defeat Napoleon and established the Holy Alliance. By 1812 Russia had also gained Finland from Sweden, Bessarabia from the Ottoman Empire and some territory in the Caucasus, and it administered Alaska between 1799 and 1867. Most of the empire's growth in the 19th century came from gains in central and eastern Asia.

In 1853 to 1856 Russia fought Britain, France, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire in the Crimean War; the defeat, formalised in the Treaty of Paris of 1856, forced it to demilitarise the Black Sea. After the 1905 Revolution Nicholas II authorised the State Duma, though ultimate authority remained with him. Russia entered the First World War in 1914 on the side of the Allies; high casualties and shortages of food and fuel led to unrest, and the February Revolution of 1917 brought the abdication of Nicholas II and a Provisional Government, which proclaimed a republic in September.

At its height in the late 19th century the empire covered about 22,800,000 square kilometres, roughly one-sixth of the world's landmass and the third-largest empire in history after the British and Mongol empires. By the 1897 census the population was 126 million, with more than 100 ethnic groups, ethnic Russians making up about 45 per cent. The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in the October Revolution, and after winning the Civil War against the Whites established the Soviet Union across most of the former Russian territory.
russian-far-east: The Russian Far East is the easternmost part of Russia and of the Asian continent. It is coextensive with the Far Eastern Federal District, which Russia created in 2000 and which stretches between Lake Baikal and the Pacific Ocean, covering 6.95 million square kilometres, over one third of Russia. Its largest city is Khabarovsk, followed by Vladivostok. It borders Mongolia, China and North Korea, and faces Japan and, across the Bering Strait, the United States. Its geography includes the Amur and Lena rivers, Lake Baikal, the Klyuchevskaya Sopka volcano and the Sikhote-Alin range. Foreign writers often treat it as part of Siberia, but Russian regional schemes have long classed it separately.

Russians reached the Pacific coast in 1647 with the founding of Okhotsk, and the empire consolidated its control in the 19th century after annexing part of Chinese Manchuria in 1858-1860. Primorskaya Oblast was set up in 1856, with its centre first at Nikolayevsk-on-Amur and from 1880 at Khabarovsk. Vladivostok, founded in 1860, was operational only in summer, so Russia leased Port Arthur from China from 1896 as a port open all year. Japan attacked the Russian Pacific Squadron there on 8 February 1904, beginning the Russo-Japanese War, which ended with the Treaty of Portsmouth of 5 September 1905; Japan received the southern half of Sakhalin.

Under Stalin, between 1937 and 1939, the Soviet Union deported over 200,000 Koreans from the region to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, fearing they might spy for Japan; many died on the way. Gulag labour camps developed many remote places, especially in the northern half, until forced labour waned after 1953. Soviet and Japanese forces clashed on the Manchurian border between 1938 and 1945, beginning with the Battle of Lake Khasan in July and August 1938. In August 1945 the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria from Primorsky Krai and Transbaikal, and afterwards annexed the Kuril Islands and southern Sakhalin. In 1952 Vladivostok became a closed city, and it hosted the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks in 1974.

The Far Eastern Federal District has a population of about eight million, most of it in the south and about three quarters urban, which makes it one of the most sparsely populated areas in the world. Ethnic Russians form the vast majority. Its original peoples include the Buryats, Sakha, Chukchi, Koryaks, Evenks, Nanais and Nivkhs. The Trans-Siberian Railway and, since 1984, the Baikal-Amur Mainline link it with the rest of Russia. Its fauna includes the Siberian tiger and the Amur leopard.
russian-orthodox-church: The history of the church begins with the Christianization of Kievan Rus', which commenced in 988 with the baptism of Vladimir the Great and his subjects by clergy of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. Christianity had already begun to take root in the 10th century: Christians are mentioned among the Varangians towards the end of the reign of Igor, and his wife Olga was baptized in the mid-10th century, though scholars dispute the year, between 946 and 960, and the place. Her son Sviatoslav opposed conversion. A later tradition, found in the 12th-century Primary Chronicle, holds that the Apostle Andrew visited the site of Kiev, although there is no historical evidence for it.

After the Mongol invasions Kiev lost its significance, and Metropolitan Maximus moved his seat to Vladimir in 1299. His successor Peter moved to Moscow in 1325, allied himself with the prince of Moscow and was buried in the Dormition Cathedral, so designating Moscow as the future centre of the church. The church declared autocephaly in 1448 by electing its own metropolitan without Constantinople's blessing, and in 1589 the metropolitan see became a patriarchate with Constantinople's consent. After the fall of Constantinople the monk Philotheus of Pskov formulated the idea of Moscow as the third Rome.

In the mid-17th century liturgical reforms led to the Schism of the Russian Church, and its opponents formed the Old Believers. After Patriarch Adrian died in 1700, Peter the Great chose not to have a successor elected. In 1721 he replaced the patriarch with the Most Holy Synod, made up of appointed bishops, monks and priests and overseen by an ober-procurator who reported to the emperor. The Synodal period lasted until 1917.

In 1914 Russia had 55,173 Orthodox churches, 550 monasteries and 475 convents. A Local Council opened in Moscow in August 1917 and restored the patriarchate, and on 5 November Metropolitan Tikhon of Moscow was chosen as the first patriarch in about 200 years. The Soviet Union treated the clergy and active believers as anti-revolutionary elements, who were prosecuted, arrested, exiled and imprisoned, and the church was heavily persecuted. Religious belief nevertheless persisted. Under Patriarch Aleksey II, who took office in 1990, some 15,000 churches were reopened or built.

The church is hierarchical. A parish, usually a single church building and its attendees, is headed by a priest; the parishes of a region belong to an eparchy, equivalent to a Western diocese, governed by a bishop. Its autonomous branches include the Japanese Orthodox Church and the Chinese Orthodox Church. The Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, established by émigrés in the 1920s, reconciled with Moscow in 2007 as a self-governing body.
russian-provisional-government: The authority of the tsar's government began to disintegrate on 1 November 1916, when Pavel Milyukov attacked the government of Boris Stürmer in the Duma. During the February Revolution two rival institutions, the State Duma and the Petrograd Soviet, both met in the Tauride Palace and competed for power. Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March (Old Style) and the regency was offered to his brother, Grand Duke Michael, who deferred accepting imperial power until the Constituent Assembly had decided.

The Provisional Government was formed on 15 March 1917 (New Style) by the Provisional Committee of the State Duma in cooperation with the Petrograd Soviet. Its task was to organise elections to the Constituent Assembly while keeping essential services running. Its first declaration promised a full amnesty, freedom of speech, press, unions, assemblies and strikes, the abolition of hereditary, religious and national restrictions, and the replacement of the police by a public militia.

The government could not take decisive decisions amid factionalism and the breakdown of state structures, and real power lay largely with the Petrograd Soviet, which controlled the army and the railways. On 18 April (Old Style) Milyukov told the Allied governments that Russia would continue the war to its glorious conclusion; demonstrations followed, Milyukov and the war minister Guchkov resigned, and six socialist ministers joined a coalition. The June Offensive, begun on 16 June, fell apart within three days amid desertion and mutiny, with thousands of Russian soldiers dead, and was followed by the armed uprising of the July Days. Kerensky became prime minister on 21 July.

In September General Lavr Kornilov attempted a military coup. Kerensky branded his advancing troops counter-revolutionaries and armed the Red Guard, which left the army distrustful of him and strengthened the Bolsheviks. The Russian Republic was proclaimed on 1 September (Old Style) by a decree signed by Kerensky and the justice minister Zarudny. On 24–26 October (Old Style) Red Guard forces occupied most government offices and captured the Winter Palace, where the ministers had held out. Kerensky escaped to Pskov, where his attempt to retake the capital was beaten at Pulkovo, and later went into exile in France and then the United States.

Despite its brief life the government passed liberal legislation: it abolished capital punishment, separated church from state and affirmed civil rights, while Poland was granted independence and Lithuania and Ukraine gained autonomy. Guchkov said it had only the appearance of authority, the real power lying with the Soviet. Pavel Osinsky described the October Revolution as socialism by default, a result both of the government's failures and of Bolshevik strength, and Nicholas Riasanovsky held that its worst mistake was not holding elections to the Constituent Assembly soon enough.
russian-revolution: The Russian Revolution of 1905 laid the groundwork for 1917. Bloody Sunday triggered nationwide protests and soldier mutinies, and a council of workers, the St. Petersburg Soviet, was created. The revolution was crushed, but it led to the creation of a Duma, which later formed the Provisional Government. Nicholas II was a deeply conservative ruler who believed that his power was granted by Divine Right and, even after 1905 moved him to decree limited civil rights and democratic representation, worked to limit them.

The 1914 Battle of Tannenberg was a disaster for Russia, with over 30,000 troops killed or wounded and 90,000 captured. In autumn 1915 Nicholas took direct command of the army and left his wife Alexandra in charge of the government. Reports of corruption and incompetence spread, and the influence of Grigori Rasputin was widely resented.

On 7 March [O.S. 22 February] 1917 a strike closed the Putilov plant, Petrograd's largest. On International Women's Day women marched to nearby factories and brought out over 50,000 workers, and by 10 March virtually every industrial enterprise in the city was shut. Nicholas abdicated on 15 March [O.S. 2 March], and a provisional government led by the Duma took over. The Petrograd Soviet claimed to represent workers and soldiers, so that Russia had two rival centres of power: the Provisional Government held authority in military and international affairs, the Soviets in domestic matters.

The Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin won support with a programme of peace, land and bread, while the Provisional Government continued the war. The October Revolution began on 7 November [O.S. 25 October], an armed insurrection in Petrograd organised by the Revolutionary Military Committee under Leon Trotsky; its initial assault occurred largely without casualties. The Bolsheviks proclaimed the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in March 1918.

Many groups did not recognise the Bolshevik government, and Russia fell into a civil war between the Reds and an array of enemies including nationalists, other socialists, anarchists, monarchists and liberals. The Bolsheviks murdered Nicholas II and his family at Yekaterinburg on 16 July 1918. Historians consider the revolutionary period to have ended in 1922 with the defeat of the White Army, and the Soviet Union was formed from the Soviet republics. Historians divide into Soviet-Marxist, Western totalitarian and revisionist schools; the totalitarian school describes a coup by a minority, the revisionists stress the revolution's popular character.
russian-revolution-of-1905: Russian peasants had been freed by the emancipation reform of 1861, but their lives remained limited, and by the time of the revolution the nobility had sold off one third of its land and mortgaged another third. A deep industrial crisis followed the contraction of Western money markets in 1899-1900, and workers faced poor conditions and urban unemployment.

The empire was multi-ethnic, and Jews, who were about 4 percent of the population, were forbidden to settle or acquire land outside the cities and towns and were legally limited in schooling. Mounting losses in the Russo-Japanese War added to the discontent. In December 1904 a strike at the Putilov plant in Saint Petersburg grew, with sympathy strikes, to 150,000 workers in 382 factories.

On 22 January 1905, a Sunday, the priest Georgy Gapon led a procession of workers to the Winter Palace to present a petition to the tsar. Troops opened fire, causing between 200 (according to Sergei Witte) and 1,000 deaths. The event became known as Bloody Sunday and is considered by many scholars the start of the active phase of the revolution.

On 2 March 1905 Nicholas II published the Bulygin Rescript, promising a consultative assembly. In June and July peasants seized land and tools in many uprisings, and the Łódź insurrection took place in Congress Poland. Unrest redoubled when the limits of the proposed Duma were revealed, and the Saint Petersburg Soviet called a general strike in October.

The movement was national as well as social. In Estonia the army fired on a meeting in Tallinn on 29 October, killing 94. In Finland the Social Democrats organised a general strike from 30 October to 6 November, and the revolution led to the creation of the modern Parliament of Finland. In Latvia armed conflict between the Baltic German nobility and Latvian peasants began in autumn, and punitive expeditions executed 1,170 people without trial.

Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto on 17 October 1905, promising civil liberties and a Duma without whose approval no law would pass, and extending the suffrage, though the electoral law of 11 December still excluded women. The Fundamental Laws of 1906 confirmed the tsar's control of the executive, foreign policy, the church and the armed forces, and he kept the power of veto.

In July 1906 he dissolved the first Duma and appointed Pyotr Stolypin as prime minister, and in June 1907 the second Duma was dissolved and an electoral reform favouring the propertied class was decreed. Many historians hold that 1905 set the stage for 1917; Lenin called it the dress rehearsal without which the October Revolution's victory would have been impossible.
russification: Russification is a form of cultural assimilation in which non-Russians adopt Russian culture and the Russian language, either voluntarily or as a result of deliberate state policy. The governments of the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union pursued it, either as a goal in itself or as a consequence of centralization and modernization. In politics it can mean assigning Russians to lead administrative posts in national institutions; in culture it consists chiefly of the dominance of Russian in official business. Some researchers distinguish Russification, a change of one's ethnic identity to Russian, from Russianization, the spread of Russian language, culture and people, and from Sovietization.

The assimilation of Volga-Finnic peoples such as the Merya and Muroma began early in the 2nd millennium CE, with the eastward expansion of the East Slavs. After the defeat in the Crimean War in 1856 and the January Uprising of 1863, Tsar Alexander II increased Russification to reduce the threat of rebellion. In Congress Poland the Polish and Belarusian languages were banned in public places in 1864 and Polish in schools in the 1880s, and a secret Polish education network, including the Flying University, arose in response. The Ems Ukaz of 1876 banned printing in Ukrainian.

Under Alexander III an ukaz of 14 September 1885 made Russian mandatory for officials in the Baltic governorates, and by the early 1890s it was the language of instruction in their schools. In Estonia, Tartu University shifted from German to Russian in 1893. In Finland, Russification between 1899 and 1905 and from 1908 to 1917 aimed at ending the country's autonomy, and Finnish opposition was one of the main factors behind its declaration of independence in 1917.

After the 1917 revolution the Soviet authorities abolished the Arabic alphabet for native languages in Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Volga region, replacing it with one based on the Latin alphabet until the late 1930s. In 1939 and 1940 a number of these languages, including Tatar, Kazakh, Uzbek and Azerbaijani, were moved to the Cyrillic script, with spelling that had to follow Russian. After the Second World War the northern part of East Prussia became the Kaliningrad Oblast, whose German population was expelled and replaced by Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians. Some historians who regard the Soviet Union as a colonial empire have applied to it the phrase prison of nations.
russo-japanese-war: The Treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895 ceded the Liaodong Peninsula and Port Arthur to Japan, but Russia, Germany and France forced Japan to give them up in the Triple Intervention. In 1898 Russia obtained a lease of Port Arthur and the surrounding territory from China and began building the South Manchurian Railroad. Russian troops stayed in Manchuria after the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, and by 1903 Russia had set no timetable for withdrawal.

Japan signed the Anglo-Japanese Alliance in 1902 and offered to recognise Russian dominance in Manchuria in exchange for recognition of Korea as part of its own sphere. Russia rejected this. Within the Japanese leadership, Itō Hirobumi and Inoue Kaoru opposed war on financial grounds, while Katsura Tarō, Komura Jutarō and Yamagata Aritomo favoured it.

On the night of 8 February 1904 a Japanese fleet under Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō attacked the Russian ships at Port Arthur with torpedo boat destroyers, three hours before Japan's declaration of war reached the Russian government. Japanese troops landed in Korea and won the Battle of the Yalu River on 1 May. The siege of Port Arthur began in April; after costly frontal assaults, Japanese howitzers on a captured hilltop shelled the fleet in the harbour, and the fortress fell in January 1905.

In the Battle of Mukden, which began on 20 February 1905 and involved about half a million men, Japanese forces pressed both flanks of the Russian line and took the city. The Russian Baltic Fleet under Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky had left in October 1904 on a seven-month voyage round the Cape of Good Hope. It reached the Sea of Japan in May 1905 and was destroyed at the Battle of Tsushima.

The Treaty of Portsmouth, signed on 5 September 1905 and mediated by United States president Theodore Roosevelt, recognised Japanese interests in Korea. It gave Japan Russia's lease on the Liaodong Peninsula, the South Manchuria Railway and the southern half of Sakhalin. Estimates of the dead on both sides run from about 130,000 to 170,000, and Chinese civilians in Manchuria suffered looting and killing by Russian troops.

Observers noted that entrenched infantry with machine guns and artillery had become decisive, a lesson largely disregarded before the First World War. Russia lost two of its three fleets, and its defeat contributed to the 1905 Russian Revolution. Japan's victory was read abroad as a challenge to European dominance in Asia, and in the West it fed fears of a Yellow Peril.
russo-turkish-war-1877-1878: Russia sought to recover the territory lost in the Crimean War of 1853–1856, to re-establish itself in the Black Sea and to support the movements freeing Balkan nations from Ottoman rule. The Ottoman Empire, though on the winning side in the Crimean War, kept declining. Foreign loans at steep interest left it with unpayable debts, and it had to settle more than 600,000 Muslim Circassians expelled by Russia from the Caucasus. In 1875 events in the Balkans brought Europe to the brink of war.

On 30 June 1876 Serbia, followed by Montenegro, declared war on the Ottomans. At Reichstadt Alexander II of Russia and Franz Joseph I of Austria-Hungary agreed without a written text that Russia would support Austrian occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Austria-Hungary would support the return of Southern Bessarabia and Russian annexation of Batum.

On 12 April 1877 Romania allowed Russian troops to cross its territory. Russia declared war on the Ottomans on 24 April, and on 10 May the Principality of Romania, under nominal Turkish suzerainty, declared its independence. Romanians call the conflict the Romanian War of Independence.

In the Caucasus the Russian 1st Caucasus Army Corps, about 50,000 men under Grand Duke Michael Nikolaevich, faced an Ottoman army of 100,000 under Ahmed Muhtar Pasha. The Russians were outgunned by the Krupp artillery Germany had supplied to the Ottomans. Greece, held back by British neutrality, did not declare war, though its army under Skarlatos Soutsos entered Thessaly in January 1878 and won the Battle of Mouzaki. A Kurdish uprising broke out in the Bohtan region as the war ended.

Under British pressure Russia accepted an Ottoman truce on 31 January 1878 but kept advancing towards Constantinople. The British sent a fleet, and the Russians stopped at San Stefano. By the Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March, the Ottomans were to recognise the independence of Romania, Serbia and Montenegro and the autonomy of Bulgaria. Russia gained Kars and Batum and annexed the Budjak. A provisional Russian administration governed liberated Bulgarian territory from April 1877, and the Treaty of Berlin ended it in May 1879, when the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia were established.

Russia, Bulgaria, Serbia, the Ottoman Empire and Albanians all carried out massacres and ethnic cleansing during the war. The conflict also split the emblems of the Red Cross movement: the cross reminded the Ottomans of the Crusades, so they adopted the Red Crescent.
russo-turkish-wars: The first war, in 1568–1570, followed the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan by Tsar Ivan the Terrible. Sultan Selim II sent an expedition to Astrakhan in 1569, which failed, and the Ottoman fleet was wrecked by a storm in the Sea of Azov. The peace confirmed Russian rule on the Volga. The Crimean Khanate, an Ottoman vassal, burned Moscow in 1571 but was defeated at the Battle of Molodi in 1572. A century later the two powers clashed over Ukraine, and the Treaty of Bakhchisarai of 1681 set the border on the Dnieper.

Under Peter the Great, Russia annexed Azov by the Treaty of Constantinople of 1700, but the Prut campaign, after the sultan declared war in November 1710, ended with the Russian army surrounded and Azov returned to the Ottomans. The war of 1736–1739 ended with the Treaty of Niš, after Austria made a separate peace.

Under Catherine II the balance turned. The war that began in 1768 saw Russian victories at Larga and Kagul and the destruction of the Ottoman navy at the Battle of Chesma. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 21 July 1774 gave the Crimean Khanate formal independence, though it became dependent on Russia, and gave Russia two Black Sea ports and a protector's role over Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire. Russia annexed Crimea in 1783. The war of 1787 ended with the Treaty of Jassy on 9 January 1792, which left Crimea and Ochakov to Russia and made the Dniester the frontier in Europe.

In the 19th century Russia gained Bessarabia after the decisive campaign of 1811, and the war of 1828–1829 led to Greek independence and Russian control of the Black Sea coast of the Caucasus. The Crimean War of 1853–1856 went against Russia. The war of 1877–1878 followed uprisings in Herzegovina, Bosnia and Bulgaria; the Treaty of San Stefano gave Romania and Montenegro independence, and the Congress of Berlin in 1878 then reduced Bulgarian territory.

In the First World War the Ottomans were defeated at Sarikamish in January 1915 and at Erzurum in 1916. Both empires dissolved soon afterwards, the Russian in 1917 and the Ottoman between 1918 and 1922.
rusyns: The name Rusyn comes from the archaic ethnonym Rus', and the people have also been called Carpatho-Rusyns, Ruthenians and Rusnaks. They speak Rusyn, an East Slavic language variety treated either as a distinct language or as a dialect of Ukrainian. Their homeland, Carpathian Ruthenia, is a cross-border region that takes in Subcarpathian Rus', the Prešov Region in eastern Slovakia, the Lemko Region in south-eastern Poland and Maramureş in Romania.

There are different theories of their origin. Paul Robert Magocsi holds that it is complex and not exclusively related to Kievan Rus'. Their ancestors included early Slavs whose movement to the Danubian Basin was influenced by the Huns and Pannonian Avars between the 5th and 6th centuries, the White Croats who lived on both slopes of the Carpathians, the Rusyns of Galicia and Podolia, and Vlach shepherds of Transylvania. Ukrainian encyclopedias generally consider them descendants of the White Croats.

The Austro-Hungarian monarchy controlled the Carpathians from 1772 to 1918. In the 19th century increasing Magyarization led some educated Rusyns to move to Budapest, while other intellectuals favoured the Russian Empire. A Rusyn national movement formed that stressed a distinct ethnic identity and literary language. On 2 May 1848, during the Spring of Nations, the Main Ruthenian Council was established in Lemberg as the first political representation of the Galician Rusyns, and Greek-Catholic clergy were the most active stratum among them.

In the Kingdom of Hungary the term Ruthene was the official name for the Rusyns of Transcarpathia until 1945. According to Magocsi, after 1945 Communist authorities treated Carpatho-Rusyns as a branch of the Ukrainian nationality and Rusyn as a dialect of Ukrainian, and banned Rusyn nationality and language. Since the revolutions of 1989 there has been a revival of Rusyn culture and identity.

Many Rusyns are Eastern Catholics of the Byzantine Rite who have been in communion with Rome since the Union of Uzhhorod in 1646. Their church, the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church, keeps the Byzantine liturgy, sometimes in Church Slavonic, and married priests. Orthodoxy also has a place: in the 1890s a movement began to return to it, and Alexis Toth, a former Greek Catholic priest, led as many as 20,000 Rusyn Americans to Orthodoxy.

Rusyn communities also settled outside the Carpathians. The oldest diaspora community lies in the Pannonian Plain, in parts of present-day Serbia and Croatia. At the end of the 19th and the start of the 20th century about 225,000 Rusyns emigrated to the United States, mostly to the industrial centres of the Northeast and Midwest.
rutgers-university: Rutgers was founded two decades after the College of New Jersey, now Princeton University, was established in 1746 by New Light Presbyterians. Ministers of the Dutch Reformed Church, who sought autonomy in ecclesiastical affairs in the Thirteen Colonies, wanted a college of their own to train men for the ministry in the colony. Their religious body later developed into the Reformed Church in America. Jacob Rutsen Hardenbergh, a Dutch Reformed minister who had worked to establish the college, became its first president in 1785.

In its early years, for lack of funds, Queen's College was closed for two extended periods. Early trustees considered merging it with the College of New Jersey at Princeton, but the measure failed by one vote; they later considered moving it to New York City. In 1808, after raising $12,000, the college reopened and broke ground on a building of its own, Old Queens, designed by the architect John McComb Jr. Its third president, Ira Condict, laid the cornerstone on 27 April 1809. The New Brunswick Theological Seminary, founded in 1784, moved to New Brunswick and shared the building, together with the Queen's College Grammar School.

In 1825 the college was renamed Rutgers College in honour of Colonel Henry Rutgers, whose substantial gift had stabilised its finances. The collection of schools became Rutgers University in 1924, as graduate education developed, with Rutgers College continuing as its liberal arts college. University College followed in 1945 and Livingston College in 1969. The state legislature designated Rutgers the state university of New Jersey by acts of 1945 and 1956; as successor to the private college chartered in 1766, it keeps some private rights and protections regarding its character and mission. Before 1930 most of its presidents were clergy of the Reformed tradition.

The university has three campuses, at New Brunswick with the adjacent Piscataway, at Newark and at Camden. The historic core lies along College Avenue in New Brunswick and includes Old Queens, the seat of the university. The Newark campus, originally the University of Newark, took its present name in 1945; the Camden campus began in the 1920s as the College of South Jersey and South Jersey Law School and joined Rutgers in 1950. In 2013 Rutgers merged with the University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey.

Its motto, Sol iustitiae et occidentem illustra, modifies that of Utrecht University and recalls the historic connection of the two. Rutgers is a land-grant, sea-grant and space-grant university. At Rutgers the microbiologist Selman Waksman discovered several antibiotics and, with the graduate student Albert Schatz, streptomycin, the first applied to cure tuberculosis; Waksman received the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1952.
ruud-lubbers: Rudolphus Franciscus Marie Lubbers was born on 7 May 1939 in Rotterdam. He studied economics at Erasmus University Rotterdam, where he was a student of Jan Tinbergen, the first laureate of the Nobel Prize in Economics. His 1962 thesis dealt with the influence of differing productivity trends in various countries on the current account of the balance of payments, and his main interest was monetary affairs. He had planned an academic career but family circumstances obliged him to join the management of Hollandia, the construction and machinery firm that bore his family's name. From 1965 he also worked for the Christian Employers' Association.

Lubbers was Minister of Economic Affairs in the Den Uyl cabinet from 11 May 1973 to 19 December 1977, as a member of the Catholic People's Party. He then returned to the House of Representatives and, after the Christian Democratic Appeal was formed as an alliance of the Christian parties, rose unexpectedly in 1978 when its parliamentary leader Willem Aantjes resigned over accusations that he had served in the Germanic-SS. Lubbers succeeded him. In 1982 Prime Minister Dries van Agt announced that he would not serve a third term and Lubbers took over on 4 November 1982, at the age of 43.

He led three cabinets and left office on 22 August 1994, after announcing in October 1993 that he would not stand again. His years in office were marked by extensive cuts in public spending and far-reaching deregulation and privatisation. One of his campaign slogans was Meer markt, minder overheid, 'more market, less government', and many observers saw him as an ideological heir to Margaret Thatcher. In 1983 a very large demonstration in The Hague opposed the planned installation of nuclear-armed American cruise missiles in the Netherlands; the plan was cancelled after arms reduction talks between the United States and the Soviet Union.

From 1995 to 2000 Lubbers taught globalisation studies at Tilburg University and at Harvard's John F. Kennedy School of Government, and he worked with the Earth Charter Initiative, launched in The Hague in June 2000. Kofi Annan appointed him United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in succession to Sadako Ogata, and he held the post from 1 January 2001. He resigned on 20 February 2005 after a complaint of sexual harassment made in 2004, which he denied and which the Secretary-General had concluded could not be substantiated.

Lubbers was granted the title Minister of State on 31 January 1995 and continued to comment on politics as a statesman. He was married to Ria Hoogeweegen and had two sons and a daughter. He died in Rotterdam on 14 February 2018, aged 78.
ruvo-di-puglia: Ruvo di Puglia has an area of 222.04 km2 and borders Bisceglie, Terlizzi, Bitonto, Altamura, Gravina in Puglia, Spinazzola, Andria and Corato. Its countryside of vineyards, olive groves and arable land has the typical features of an Apulian karst landscape, with sinkholes, karst valleys and caves, among them the Grave della Ferratella, the deepest in the region. Part of the territory lies within the Alta Murgia national park. Two large tectonic valleys hold surface water that has been tapped by wells since ancient times, which favoured the ancient settlements nearby.

The name is first attested on coins of the 3rd century BCE bearing the Greek legends Rhyps, Rhyba and Rhybasteinon. Horace called the inhabitants the Rubi, and Pliny the Elder lists them as the Rubustini. The Iapygians settled the land of Bari and gave rise to the Peucetians, and Ruvo began as a hilltop village. Between the 8th and 5th centuries BCE the Greeks colonised it peacefully. About the 4th century BCE it was at its height, trading with most of the Italic peoples including the Etruscans, minting its own coins and living on olive oil, wine and pottery. After the defeat of Taranto by Rome it became Rubi, a municipium and a station on the Via Traiana.

The Goths reduced the city to rubble in the fifth century, and it was later conquered by Lombards and raided by Saracens. Under Frederick II of Swabia it grew again, and the Romanesque-Gothic cathedral belongs to this age. It became a fief of the Angevins from 1266, and in 1350 Ruggiero Sanseverino razed and sacked it. The Battle of Ruvo, won by Consalvo of Cordova over the French under Jacques de La Palice, destroyed it a third time. Oliviero Carafa bought the fief in 1510, and the Carafa ruled until feudalism was abolished under Napoleonic rule in 1806.

Ruvo di Puglia is a town in the Metropolitan City of Bari. The Jatta National Archaeological Museum, founded on the finds made by the nineteenth-century lawyer Giovanni Jatta, is known for its Hellenistic pieces, among them the Vase of Talos. The cathedral is one of the best-known examples of Apulian Romanesque and was built in the first half of the 12th century. Its coat of arms, recognised by decree in 1950, shows a terracotta amphora on a blue ground. The town produces olive oil and wine.
rwenzori-mountains: The Rwenzori, also written Ruwenzori and known as the Rwenzururu or Rwenjura, are a range in eastern equatorial Africa, about 120 kilometres long and 65 kilometres wide. They consist of six massifs separated by deep gorges: Mount Stanley, Mount Speke, Mount Baker, Mount Emin, Mount Gessi and Mount Luigi di Savoia. The upper regions are permanently snow-capped and glaciated, and rivers fed by mountain streams form one of the sources of the Nile.

The mountains formed about three million years ago, in the late Pliocene, as an uplifted block of crystalline rocks including gneiss, amphibolite, granite and quartzite, and are the highest non-volcanic, non-orogenic mountains in the world. The uplift divided the paleolake Obweruka and created three of the present African Great Lakes: Lake Albert, Lake Edward and Lake George.

The range is occasionally identified with the Mountains of the Moon, described in antiquity as the source of the Nile, and European explorers linked the two for that reason. Samuel Baker reported what he called the Blue Mountains in the distance in 1864, and Henry M. Stanley visited the range in 1875 and 1888, when he recorded the name as Ruwenzori.

In 1906 the Duke of Abruzzi led an expedition whose account was published by Filippo De Filippi. It climbed the highest peaks, several of which the duke named, and Mount Luigi di Savoia was named in his honour. The photographer Vittorio Sella, who accompanied it, recorded glaciers and moraines that already showed the ice in retreat. The first traverse of all six massifs was made between 27 January and 13 February 1975 by the Polish climbers Janusz Chalecki, Stanisław Cholewa and Leszek S. Czarnecki, with Mirosław Kuraś joining the last half. After Uganda's independence the secessionist Rwenzururu movement fought an insurgency in the mountains in the 1960s.

The vegetation runs through five overlapping zones, from evergreen forest up to 2,800 metres through bamboo, heather and alpine zones to the nival zone at 4,400 to 5,000 metres. Giant groundsels and giant lobelias and a heather 6 metres tall grow there, and the vegetation is unique to equatorial alpine Africa. Most of the range is a World Heritage Site, covered by Rwenzori Mountains National Park in southwestern Uganda and Virunga National Park in eastern Congo. In 1906 forty-three named glaciers covered 7.5 square kilometres on six mountains, about half the glacier area of Africa; by 2005 less than half remained, on three mountains, covering about 1.5 square kilometres.
ryazan: Ryazan stands on the Oka River in Central Russia, 196 km south-east of Moscow, and is the administrative centre of Ryazan Oblast. An older city, now called Old Ryazan, lay about 50 km east of the modern one and was the capital of the Principality of Ryazan until the Mongol invasion of 1237. The modern city was known as Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky until 1778, when it was renamed Ryazan by order of Catherine the Great.

The first written mention of the city, under the name Pereslavl, dates to 1095. It became part of the Principality of Ryazan, which had existed since 1129 and was centred on the old city. Lying between woodland and steppe, the principality suffered invasions from the Cumans in the south, and Vladimir-Suzdal had burnt its capital several times by the end of the twelfth century.

Ryazan was the first Russian city to face the Mongol army of Batu Khan. On 21 December 1237, after a short siege, it was completely destroyed and never recovered, and the seat of the principality moved to Pereslavl-Ryazansky, which took its name. In 1380 Grand Prince Oleg of Ryazan and his men were caught between Mamai's coalition and Dmitry Donskoy's army at the Battle of Kulikovo.

The principality was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1521. Its last ruler, Ivan V of Ryazan, was suspected of seeking a treaty with the Crimean Khanate and fled to Lithuania, where he died no later than 1534. As the southernmost border of the Rus' lands, Ryazan kept suffering raids by the Crimean Tatars. A railway connected it to Moscow from 1864, and after World War II it grew rapidly into an industrial, scientific and military centre.

Ryazan is the seat of the Diocese of Ryazan and Kasimov of the Russian Orthodox Church, with the Assumption Cathedral in the Ryazan Kremlin, which is a historic museum. The Pozhalostin Museum, one of the oldest art museums in Russia, and the memorial museum-estate of the physiologist Ivan Pavlov are also in the city.
rye: Rye (Secale cereale) belongs to the wheat tribe, Triticeae, which also includes wheat and barley, and is one of several cereals that grow wild in the Levant and central and eastern Turkey. Evidence from the Epipalaeolithic site of Tell Abu Hureyra in northern Syria suggests that rye was among the first cereal crops to be systematically cultivated, around 13,000 years ago, but critics point to inconsistencies in the radiocarbon dates. Domesticated rye occurs in small quantities at a number of Neolithic sites in Anatolia but is otherwise absent from the archaeological record until the Bronze Age of central Europe, around 1800-1500 BCE.

It probably reached Europe as a minor admixture in wheat and was only later cultivated in its own right. Remains have been found in Roman contexts along the Rhine and the Danube and in Britain and Ireland. Pliny the Elder, writing of a grain that may have been rye, called it a very poor food that only served to avert starvation.

Rye is a tall grass, annual or biennial, reaching 1 to 3 metres, with seeds carried in a curved spike. It is much more tolerant of cold and poor soil than other cereals, grows better than any other in heavy clay and light sandy soil, and survives snow cover that would kill winter wheat. It has therefore been especially valuable where the soil is sandy or peaty. Winter rye, sown in autumn, grows again in spring early enough to provide grazing.

Rye is highly susceptible to the ergot fungus. Eating infected rye causes ergotism, with convulsions, miscarriage, necrosis of the digits, hallucinations and death, and damp northern countries that depended on rye were historically subject to periodic epidemics. Modern grain cleaning has practically eliminated it.

Since the Middle Ages rye has been widely cultivated in Central and Eastern Europe, where it is the main bread cereal in most areas east of the France-Germany border and north of Hungary; in Southern Europe it was grown on marginal lands. In Scandinavia it was a staple food in the Middle Ages, and rye crispbread remains popular there. Rye bread, including pumpernickel, is widely eaten in Northern and Eastern Europe. The grain also makes rye beer and rye whiskey, and the drink kvass is fermented from rye bread or flour and malt.

Rye straw is used as livestock bedding, and in Sweden rye flour is boiled with red iron oxide to make the traditional Falun red house paint. In European folklore the Roggenwolf, or rye wolf, is a wolf-shaped field spirit that steals children, and the last heads of grain were often left as a sacrifice to such spirits. The classical scholar Carl A. P. Ruck links these figures with ergot, whose reddish infected grains were known as wolf teeth.
ryukyu-islands: The chain is also called the Nansei Islands, literally the southwest islands, and Japan has used that name on nautical charts since 1907. Administratively it divides between Kagoshima Prefecture, whose Satsunan Islands include the Ōsumi, Tokara and Amami groups, and Okinawa Prefecture, which holds the Okinawa, Miyako, Yaeyama and Daitō Islands. The larger islands are mostly volcanic and the smaller mostly coral. The climate runs from humid subtropical in the north to tropical rainforest in the south. The Watase Line marks a major biogeographic boundary, with the Ōsumi Islands in the Palearctic realm and the Amami Islands at the northern limit of the Indomalayan realm.

Chinese sources mention eastern islands of immortals, and in 601 and 607 Chinese expeditions visited the Country of Liuqiu. Japanese records list the Southern Islands from 616, and in 997 pirates identified as Amami islanders raided Kyushu. Tanegashima passed into the Shimazu Estate in the 12th century, and around 1543 a Chinese junk carrying Portuguese merchants was driven there; Tanegashima Tokitaka reproduced their matchlock rifles, which spread across Sengoku Japan as tanegashima.

Polities of the Okinawa Islands were unified as the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1429, a tributary state of Ming China, which conquered the Miyako and Yaeyama Islands and at its peak ruled Amami. The Amami Islands were disputed between the kingdom and the southward-expanding Satsuma Domain until Satsuma conquered them in the 1609 invasion of the kingdom, with a fleet of 13 junks and 2,500 samurai. King Shō Nei ordered surrender to spare lives. The kingdom then paid tribute to both the shogun and the Chinese emperor, and the Tokugawa shogunate granted Satsuma the Amami islands in 1624. The Meiji government annexed the kingdom in 1879 and suppressed Ryukyuan identity, tradition and language.

The Amami, Okinawa, Miyako and Yaeyama Islands have a native population called the Ryukyuan people, who traditionally speak several Ryukyuan languages, though Japanese is now the primary language. Their religion centres on ancestor respect and the relations among the living, the dead and the spirits of nature. The islands were held by the United States after the Treaty of San Francisco of 1951 and returned to Japan under the 1971 Okinawa reversion agreement. Yakushima, with its ancient cedars, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
